note: Latin–Greek textual classification of the 5,600 Genesis–Deuteronomy Vulgate comparison cards that were labelled "Assessment open", 2 November 2026. Each entry: card id, category (site definitions), and the note written into layer 1 of the card.

cards.note: Both say God saw the light was good and separated light from darkness; the repeated subject is only English wording.
Both say God named the light Day and the darkness Night, and mark the first day; phrasing only.
Both record the command for a firmament dividing waters; this Greek reading adds "And it was so", which the Latin leaves for the next verse.
Both describe God making the firmament and dividing the waters; the Latin adds "And so it was" (Latin "Et factum est ita"), absent from this Greek reading.
Both name the firmament Heaven and the second day; this Greek reading adds "God saw that it was good", which the Latin lacks.
Both command the waters to gather and dry land to appear; this Greek reading adds that the water was gathered and the dry land appeared, which the Latin lacks.
Both have God naming the dry land Earth and the gathered waters Seas, and seeing that it was good.
Both command the earth to bring forth plants and fruit trees; Greek adds "and likeness" to "according to kind", and Latin has "He said" rather than "God said".
Both report the earth bringing forth plants and fruit trees and God seeing it was good; the Greek adds "and likeness" and "upon the earth" in its wording.
Both mark evening and morning of the third day; "the third" / "a third" is only wording.
Both have lights in the firmament for signs, seasons, days and years; the Greek adds the purpose "to illuminate the earth" here, which the Latin gives in the next verse.
Both say the lights shine in the firmament and give light to the earth, and it was so; verse division differs slightly.
Both say God made two great lights, the greater to rule the day, the lesser the night, and the stars.
Both say God set the lights in the firmament of heaven to shine on the earth; "He" / "God" is only wording.
Both say the lights rule day and night and separate light from darkness, and God saw it was good.
Both mark evening and morning of the fourth day.
Both command the waters to bring forth living creatures and flying creatures; Latin has them "beneath" the firmament, Greek "along" it, and the Greek adds "And it was so".
Both have God producing sea creatures and birds and seeing it was good; created / made differs, and Greek says "they were good" (plural) where Latin has singular.
Both give God's blessing to increase and fill the waters, with birds multiplying on the earth.
Both mark evening and morning of the fifth day.
Both command the earth to bring forth living creatures: livestock, creeping things and wild animals, each according to kind.
Both have God making wild animals, livestock and creeping things; the order of items differs, and Greek has "they were good" where Latin has "it was good".
Both give God's decision to make humankind in His image and likeness, ruling fish, birds, animals, earth and creeping things.
Both say male and female He made them; the Latin has an extra clause that God created man "in His own image" before "in the image of God", which the Greek lacks.
Both give the blessing to increase, fill and subdue the earth; the rule list differs, Latin "every living creature that moves" where Greek has livestock, all the earth and every creeping thing.
Both give every seed-bearing plant and tree as food; the Latin sentence runs on into the next verse, while the Greek closes it with "they shall be food for you".
Both extend the food to animals, birds and creeping things; the Greek adds that "every green plant" is given as food, which the Latin does not state.
Both say God saw all that He had made and it was very good, closing the sixth day.
Both say heaven and earth were completed with all their adornment / ordered array; English wording only.
Both say God blessed the seventh day and made it holy because He ceased from His work; Latin "created to be made" differs from Greek "had begun to make", and work is singular vs plural.
Both speak of the origins of heaven and earth on the day God made them; Greek calls it "the book of the origin" and says "God", Latin has "the Lord God" and "when they were created".

Both describe plants not yet grown, no rain and no human to work the ground; Latin has "the Lord God" and "shrub" / "plant of the countryside", Greek has "God" and "green thing" / "plant of the field".
Both say a spring rose from the earth and watered the whole face of the ground.
Both have the Lord God planting a garden and placing the formed human there; Latin says "of delight from the beginning", Greek names Eden "toward the east".
Both name the pleasant fruit trees, the tree of life in the middle, and the tree of knowledge of good and evil; Lord God / God differs and the wording of the knowledge tree is expanded in Greek.
Both have a river watering the garden and dividing into four; Latin says it flowed from "the place of delight", Greek from Eden, and "branches" / "beginnings" differs.
Both name the first river Pishon, circling the land of Havilah where there is gold; winds / circles is only wording.
Both say the gold of that land is good; the stones differ, Latin bdellium and onyx, Greek carbuncle and green stone.
Both name the second river Gihon, circling the whole land of Ethiopia.
Both name the third river Tigris, flowing toward the Assyrians, and the fourth the Euphrates; toward / opposite is only wording.
Both have the Lord God placing the human in the garden to work and keep it; Greek adds "whom He had formed" and says "paradise" where Latin says "garden of delight".
Both give the command to eat from every tree; Greek names Adam and the Lord God and adds "freely", where Latin says only "He commanded him".
Both forbid the tree of the knowledge of good and evil on pain of surely dying that day; wording only.
Both have the Lord God saying it is not good for the human to be alone and resolving to make a helper; "like himself" / "corresponding" is English wording.
Both have God bringing the formed animals and birds to Adam to be named; Latin says "Lord God" and "animals of the earth", Greek "God" and "wild animals of the field".
Both have Adam naming the creatures with no fitting helper found; Latin lists "all the animals", Greek "all the livestock", and "earth" / "field" differs.
Both have a sleep falling on Adam and a rib taken, with flesh filling its place; Latin "Lord God" and "deep sleep" against Greek "God" and "trance".
Both say the Lord God built the rib into a woman and brought her to Adam; fashioned / built is only wording.
Both give Adam's cry of bone and flesh and the name Woman; Latin says taken "from man" (Latin "de viro"), Greek "from her husband".
Both say a man leaves father and mother, joins his wife, and the two become one flesh.
Both say the two were naked, Adam and his wife, and not ashamed.
Both have the serpent questioning the woman; Latin asks why God forbade eating "from every tree", Greek has God saying not to eat "from any tree", a stronger prohibition.
Both have the woman saying they eat the fruit of the trees of the garden; Greek names the serpent as addressee and says "may eat".
Both give the woman's report that God forbade eating or touching the fruit of the middle tree lest they die; direct / reported speech is only form.
Both have the serpent telling the woman she will certainly not die.
Both give the serpent's claim that eyes will be opened and they will be like gods; Latin "God knows", Greek "God knew".
Both have the woman seeing the tree is good, taking and eating, and giving to her husband; Greek adds "with her" and says "they ate" where Latin says "who ate".
Both say their eyes were opened, they knew they were naked, and they sewed fig leaves into coverings.
Both have them hearing the Lord God walking in the garden and hiding among the trees; Latin has "afternoon breeze", Greek "toward evening".
Both have the Lord God calling Adam and asking where he is; Greek repeats the name "Adam" in the question.
Both give Adam's fear because he was naked and his hiding; Greek adds that God was walking in paradise, where Latin has only "Your voice".
Both ask who told him he was naked and whether he ate the forbidden tree; Greek adds that it is "the only one" forbidden.
Both have Adam blaming the woman God gave him, who gave him fruit; Latin "companion", Greek "to be with me".
Both have the Lord God questioning the woman, who answers that the serpent deceived her and she ate.
Both have the curse on the serpent and eating earth all its life; Greek adds "and belly" to going on the chest, and "livestock" appears where Latin has "animals".
Both curse the ground for Adam's listening to his wife and eating; Greek adds that this was "the only" tree forbidden, and has "works" / "pains" where Latin has "work" / "toil".
Both say thorns and thistles will grow and Adam will eat the plants; Latin "of the earth", Greek "of the field".
Both give sweat of the face, bread, and return to the ground; Latin "you are dust", Greek "you are earth", and "depart" for "return".
Both say Adam named his wife because she was mother of all the living; Latin gives the name Eve (Latin "Heva"), Greek gives the meaning "Life".
Both say the Lord God made tunics of skin for Adam and his wife and clothed them.
Both give God's statement that Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil, lest he take of the tree of life and live forever.
Both say the Lord God sent him out of the garden of delight to work the ground from which he was taken.
Both have cherubim and a flaming turning sword guarding the way to the tree of life; Greek has Adam settled opposite the paradise, which the Latin does not say.
Both say Adam knew Eve, who conceived and bore Cain and spoke of acquiring a man through God.
Both say she bore his brother Abel, a shepherd, while Cain worked the ground.
Both have Cain offering from the fruits of the ground to the Lord after some time; "many days" / "some days" and "gifts" / "sacrifice" differ.
Both have Abel offering firstlings of the flock and their fat and the Lord regarding him; Latin "the Lord", Greek "God".
Both say the offering of Cain was not regarded and his face fell; Latin has Cain "very angry", Greek "deeply grieved".
Both have the Lord questioning Cain about his fallen face; Latin asks why he is "angry", Greek why he is "deeply grieved", and Greek names "Lord God" and Cain.
Both have the Lord asking Cain where Abel is, and Cain answering he does not know and asking if he is his brother's keeper.
Both give God's question and the voice of Abel's blood crying from the ground; ground / earth and "He" / "God" are only wording.
Both curse Cain by the earth that received his brother's blood; Latin "cursed upon the earth", Greek "cursed from the earth".
Both say the ground will no longer yield to Cain; Latin gives "fruits" and "wanderer and fugitive", Greek gives "strength" and "groaning and trembling".
Both have Cain confessing his sin is too great to be forgiven; wrongdoing / guilt is a close synonym.
Latin states as fact that God drives Cain out ("See, You drive me"); the Greek makes it conditional ("If You drive me"), and wanderer / fugitive differs from groaning / trembling.
Both promise sevenfold vengeance on Cain's killer and a sign set on Cain; Latin "the Lord", Greek "the Lord God".
Both have Cain leaving God's presence and living near Eden; the Greek names the land of Nod, the Latin has no name and says Cain was a fugitive east of Eden.
Both have Cain's wife bearing Enoch and Cain naming a city after his son; Greek says he "was building" the city.
Both give the line from Enoch to Lamech; the second and following names are spelled differently (Latin Irad, Mehujael, Methushael; Greek Gaidad, Maiel, Mathousala).
Both say Lamech took two wives, Adah and Zillah.
Both say Adah bore Jabal, father of tent-dwellers; Latin adds "and of shepherds" as a separate group, Greek has "livestock breeders who dwell in tents".
Both name Jubal, brother of Jabal, as the origin of musicians; Latin "father of those who play lyre and pipe", Greek "introduced the harp and lyre".
Both have Zillah bearing a bronze-and-iron smith and his sister Naamah; Latin names him Tubal-cain and adds "craftsman in every kind of work", Greek has Tubal.
Both give Lamech's address to his wives and his boast of killing a man for a wound and a young man for a bruise.
Both contrast Cain's sevenfold vengeance with Lamech's seventy-sevenfold; Latin says vengeance "shall be given", Greek "has been exacted".
Both have Adam and his wife bearing Seth in place of Abel; Greek names Eve, and "appointed" / "raised up" differs.
Both have Seth's son Enosh and the name of the Lord; Latin says he "began" to call on the name, Greek says he "hoped" to call on it.
Latin is the book of Adam's generations, God creating the human in His likeness; Greek is the book of the origin of human beings, God making Adam in His image.
Both say God made them male and female, blessed them, and called their name Adam on the day they were made.
Number differs: Latin gives eight hundred years for Adam after Seth, Greek seven hundred; the rest is parallel.
Both give Adam's total life as nine hundred thirty years, and he died.
Number differs: Latin gives eight hundred seven years for Seth after Enosh, Greek seven hundred seven.
Both give Seth's total life as nine hundred twelve years, and he died.
Number differs: Latin gives eight hundred fifteen years after the birth (of Kenan), Greek seven hundred fifteen.
Both give Enosh's total life as nine hundred five years, and he died.
Number differs: Latin gives eight hundred forty years for Kenan after Mahalalel, Greek seven hundred forty.
Both give Kenan's total life as nine hundred ten years, and he died.
Number differs: Latin gives eight hundred thirty years for Mahalalel after Jared, Greek seven hundred thirty.
Both give Mahalalel's total life as eight hundred ninety-five years, and he died.
Both give Jared eight hundred years after Enoch's birth, with sons and daughters.
Both give Jared's total life as nine hundred sixty-two years, and he died.
Latin says Enoch walked with God three hundred years after Methuselah's birth; Greek says he pleased God two hundred years.
Both give Enoch's total days as three hundred sixty-five years.
Both say Enoch was not found because God took him; Latin "walked with God", Greek "pleased God", and took / transferred differs.
Number differs: Latin gives Methuselah one hundred eighty-seven years at Lamech's birth, Greek one hundred sixty-seven.
Number differs: Latin gives seven hundred eighty-two years for Methuselah after Lamech, Greek eight hundred two.
Both give Methuselah's total life as nine hundred sixty-nine years, and he died.
Number differs: Latin gives Lamech one hundred eighty-two years at his son's birth, Greek one hundred eighty-eight.
Both have Lamech naming Noah as one who brings relief from labor under the cursed earth; Latin says "comfort us in our work", Greek "give us rest from our works".
Number differs: Latin gives Lamech five hundred ninety-five years after Noah, Greek five hundred sixty-five.
Number differs: Latin gives Lamech seven hundred seventy-seven years, Greek seven hundred fifty-three; Greek also says Noah begat "three sons".
Both say that as human beings multiplied upon the earth, daughters were born; wording only.
Both say the sons of God saw the daughters of men were beautiful and took wives from all they chose.
Both have God's spirit not remaining forever and days of one hundred twenty years; Latin speaks of "the human being ... he", Greek "these human beings ... they", and Greek has "Lord God".
Both place giants on the earth when the sons of God went in to the daughters of men; Latin calls the offspring "mighty men of old", Greek "giants of old".
Both say God saw great human wickedness and hearts intent on evil all the time; Greek has "Lord God" and "multiplied" where Latin has "great".
Both have God resolving to wipe out humankind and animals; Latin gives "I regret having made them", Greek "I have become angry that I made them".
Both say Noah found favor before the Lord (God); only the divine title is longer in Greek.
Both call Noah righteous and say he walked with / pleased God; Latin has "blameless" and "walked with God", Greek "complete" and "pleased God".
Both say Noah had three sons: Shem, Ham and Japheth.
Both say the earth was corrupt before God and filled with wickedness / injustice.
Both say God saw the earth corrupted because all flesh corrupted its way; Greek has "Lord God" and ends the sentence, while the Latin sentence runs on.
Both have God telling Noah an end is coming and the earth is filled with wickedness; Latin "end of all flesh", Greek "time of every human", and "destroy them with the earth" differs slightly.
Both command an ark of timber with rooms, coated inside and out; smooth / squared timber, compartments / nests and bitumen / pitch are close synonyms.
Both give the ark as three hundred cubits long, fifty wide and thirty high.
Both give the door in the side and three levels; the Latin includes a command to make a window and finish its top within a cubit, whereas the Greek has no window.
Both have God bringing the flood on the earth to destroy all flesh with the breath of life; everything on earth shall perish.
Both have God establishing His covenant with Noah and Noah entering the ark with his sons, wife and sons' wives.
Both command two of every kind of flesh into the ark; Latin says "to live" and lists "every living creature", Greek says "nourish" and lists livestock, creeping things and wild animals.
Both bring two of each of birds, livestock and creeping things to Noah; Latin says "so that they may live", Greek "to be nourished" and adds "male and female".
Both command Noah to gather every food that can be eaten as food for him and the animals.
Both say Noah did all God commanded him; Greek has "Lord God" and adds "so he did".
Both have the Lord telling Noah to enter the ark with his household because he is righteous before Him; Greek names Noah and "Lord God".
Both command seven pairs of clean animals and two pairs of unclean, male and female.
Both take seven pairs of birds to preserve offspring; the Greek specifies clean birds and adds two by two of unclean birds, which the Latin does not state.
Both announce rain for forty days and nights after seven days and wiping out what God made; Latin "every being", Greek "everything that rises up".
Both say Noah did all that the Lord commanded him.
Both say Noah was six hundred years old when the flood came on the earth.
Both say Noah, his sons, wife and sons' wives entered the ark because of the flood.
Both list clean and unclean animals, birds and creeping things coming to the ark; ordering differs.
Both say they entered two by two, male and female, as commanded; the Lord / God is only wording.
Both say the floodwaters came on the earth after seven days.
Date differs: Latin gives the seventeenth day of the second month, Greek the twenty-seventh; Greek adds "on that day".
Both say Noah entered the ark that day with Shem, Ham, Japheth, his wife and his sons' three wives.
Both list wild animals, livestock, moving things and birds by kind; the Latin adds "all birds and all flying creatures" and starts with "They", which the Greek lacks.
Both say pairs of all flesh with the breath of life entered the ark to Noah.
Both say male and female entered as God commanded and the Lord shut it from outside; Latin "shut him in", Greek "closed the ark from outside him".
Both say the flood lasted forty days and the waters lifted the ark; Greek adds "and forty nights", and Latin says "high above" where Greek says it rose.
Both say the waters prevailed greatly and the ark floated on them.
Both say the waters prevailed greatly and covered all the high mountains under heaven.
Both say the water rose fifteen cubits above the mountains; the Greek words it as covering all the high mountains, the Latin as above those it had covered.
Both say all flesh moving on the earth died: birds, livestock, wild animals, creeping things and all human beings.
Both say everything with the breath of life on the dry land died; word order only.
Both say God wiped out every being on the earth from humans to animals, and only Noah and those with him in the ark remained.
Both say the waters prevailed upon the earth one hundred fifty days; held / remained high is only wording.
Both have God remembering Noah and the animals in the ark and sending a wind so the waters subsided; Greek also lists birds and creeping things.
Both say the springs of the deep and floodgates of heaven were stopped and rain restrained; closed / covered over differs.
Both say the waters receded and began to diminish after one hundred fifty days; Latin "flowing back and forth", Greek "as it went from the earth".
Both date the ark's rest to the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month; the Latin names the mountains of Armenia, the Greek the mountains of Ararat.
Both have the waters decreasing until the tenth month and the peaks appearing on the first day; Latin says that day was in the tenth month, Greek the eleventh.
Both have Noah opening the ark's window after forty days; the Latin includes the release of the raven here, while the Greek puts it in the next verse.
Both say the raven went out and did not return until the waters dried; the Greek adds that it was sent to see whether the water had subsided.
Both say Noah sent out the dove after the raven to see whether the waters had subsided.
Both say the dove found no rest, returned to the ark, and Noah took it in; wording only.
Both say Noah waited another seven days and sent the dove out again.
Both have the dove returning in the evening so Noah knew the waters had subsided; Latin has an olive branch with green leaves, Greek an olive leaf, a dry piece.
Both say Noah waited another seven days and sent out the dove, which did not return.
Both date the waters' going in year six hundred one, first month, first day, and Noah opening the roof; Latin has the ground dry, Greek that the water had left the earth.
Both say God spoke to Noah, saying; the divine title is longer in Greek.
Both command Noah, his wife, sons and sons' wives to come out of the ark.
Both command bringing out the animals and increasing on the earth; Latin adds "go forth upon the earth", and the lists of creatures are worded differently.
Both say Noah went out with his sons, wife and sons' wives.
Both say all the animals went out of the ark by kind; Greek also names birds in the list, Latin names wild animals, livestock and creeping things.
Both say Noah built an altar and offered whole burnt offerings of clean animals and birds.

Both promise not to curse the earth or strike all living things again; Latin gives "because of human beings" and thoughts "prone to evil", Greek "because of human works" and the mind "intently set" on evil.
Both promise seedtime, harvest, cold, heat and day and night will not cease; Latin lists summer and winter, Greek summer and spring.
Both give the blessing to increase and fill the earth; the Greek adds "exercise dominion over it", which the Latin lacks.
Both say fear and dread of humans will be on all animals, birds and creatures, and the fish are given into their hands.
Both give every living moving creature as food as with the green plants; Latin "everything that moves and lives", Greek "every creeping thing that lives".
Both forbid eating flesh with blood; the Greek says "blood of life".
Both have God requiring the blood of lives from beasts and from man; Latin repeats "from the hand of man ... of a man and his brother", Greek has "from a human brother".
Both repeat the command to increase, multiply and fill the earth; Latin adds "go forth upon the earth", Greek ends "multiply upon it".
Both say God spoke to Noah and his sons with him.
Both have God establishing His covenant with Noah's household and offspring after them.
Both extend the covenant to every living creature that came out of the ark; Latin lists birds, livestock and animals separately, Greek gives a shorter list.
Both promise never again to destroy all flesh or the earth by a flood.
Both give the rainbow as the sign of the covenant for all generations; Greek names Noah and "Lord God".
Both say God sets His bow in the cloud as a sign of the covenant with the earth.
Both say the bow will appear in the clouds; Latin says God covers heaven with clouds, Greek that He brings clouds over the earth.
Both have God remembering the covenant and never again flooding to destroy all flesh; Latin "every living soul that gives life to flesh", Greek "every living creature among all flesh".
Both say the bow in the clouds will be seen and God will remember the everlasting covenant with every living creature on the earth.
Both have God telling Noah the bow is the sign of the covenant between Him and all flesh on the earth.
Both say these three were Noah's sons and from them people spread over the earth.
Both say Noah began to work the ground and planted a vineyard.
Both say Noah drank wine, became drunk and was uncovered; Latin says in his "tent", Greek in his "house".
Both say Ham, Canaan's father, saw his father's nakedness and told his two brothers outside.
Both say Shem and Japheth covered their father with a garment, walking backward, faces turned away.
Both say Noah learned what his younger son had done; Latin "awoke from his wine", Greek "sobered up".
Both have Noah cursing Canaan as a slave to his brothers; Latin says "slave of slaves", Greek "household slave".
Both bless the Lord, the God of Shem, and make Canaan his slave.
Both have God enlarging Japheth to dwell with Shem; Latin has Canaan as Japheth's slave ("ejus", his), Greek as the slave of both ("their"), and tents / houses differs.
Both say Noah lived three hundred fifty years after the flood.
Both give Noah's total days as nine hundred fifty years, and he died.
Both introduce the generations of Noah's sons Shem, Ham and Japheth, with sons born after the flood.
Both list the sons of Japheth; the Greek includes Elishah in the list, which the Latin does not.
Both list Gomer's sons: Ashkenaz, Riphath and Togarmah.
Both list Javan's sons Elishah, Tarshish and Kittim; the last is Latin Dodanim, Greek "Rhodians".
Both say the islands of the nations were divided in their lands by language, families and nations.
Both list Ham's sons: Cush, Mizraim, Put and Canaan.
Both list the sons of Cush and the sons of Raamah, Sheba and Dedan.
Both say Cush fathered Nimrod, who began to be powerful on the earth; Latin "mighty", Greek "giant".
Both call Nimrod a mighty / giant hunter before the Lord and give the saying; Greek has "Lord God" and "they will say" where Latin says the saying "went out".
Both give the beginning of his kingdom as Babylon, Erech, Accad and Calneh in the land of Shinar.
Both have Asshur building Nineveh and Calah; Latin says "the city's streets", Greek names the city of Rehoboth.
Both place a city between Nineveh and Calah, the great city; the Latin names it Resen, the Greek Dasem.
Both list Mizraim's descendants; some names are spelled differently (Latin Anamim and Naphtuhim; Greek Enemetiim and Nephthaliim).
Both list the Pathrusim and Casluhim, from whom came the Philistines and Caphtorim.
Both say Canaan fathered Sidon his firstborn and the Hittite.
Both list the Jebusite, Amorite and Girgashite.
Both list the Hivite and Arkite and one more tribe; the last is Latin Sinite, Greek Asennite.
Both list the Arvadite, Zemarite (Samarean) and Hamathite, and say the Canaanite tribes then spread.
Both give Canaan's boundaries from Sidon through Gerar and Gaza to Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Lasha.
Both close the list of Ham's sons by families, languages, lands and nations; the Latin also includes "generations".
Both say children were born to Shem, father of all Eber's sons and elder brother of Japheth.
Both list Shem's sons Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud and Aram; the Greek adds Cainan, which the Latin lacks.
Both list Aram's sons Uz, Hul and Gether; the fourth is Latin Mash, Greek Meshech.
Latin has Arphaxad fathering Shelah, from whom Eber came; the Greek adds a generation, Arphaxad begat Cainan and Cainan begat Shelah.
Both say Eber had two sons, Peleg, in whose days the earth was divided, and Joktan.
Both list Joktan's sons Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth and Jerah.
Both list Hadoram and Diklah among Joktan's sons; the middle name is Latin Uzal, Greek Aizel.
Both list Joktan's sons Abimael and Sheba; the Latin begins with Ebal, which this Greek reading does not include.
Both list Ophir, Havilah and Jobab as Joktan's sons.
Both say their dwelling extended from Mesha to Sephar, the eastern mountain; toward / as far as is only wording.
Both close Shem's sons by families, languages, lands and nations; regions / lands is only wording.
Both close the table of Noah's families and the nations' dispersal after the flood; Greek says "islands of the nations" and adds "by their generations".
Both say the whole earth had one language and the same speech.
Both have them proposing to make bricks and bake them, using brick for stone and bitumen for mortar.
Both have them planning a city and a tower reaching heaven to make a name before being scattered.
Both say the Lord came down to see the city and tower; Latin says "Adam's children" were building, Greek "the human beings".
Both note one people with one language who began this work; Latin says they will not abandon their plans until completed, Greek says nothing they undertake will fail them.
Both have the Lord resolving to go down and confuse their language so they cannot understand each other.
Both say the Lord scattered them over all the earth and they stopped building; Greek adds "and the tower".
Both explain the name by the confusion of language and scattering; Latin gives the name Babel, Greek gives its meaning "Confusion".
Both say Shem was one hundred when he fathered Arphaxad, two years after the flood.
Both give Shem five hundred years after Arphaxad, with sons and daughters; Greek adds "and he died".
Number and son differ: Latin has Arphaxad living thirty-five years and fathering Shelah, Greek one hundred thirty-five years and fathering Cainan.
Latin gives Arphaxad three hundred three years after Shelah; Greek gives four hundred thirty after Cainan and adds Cainan's own years, sons and death.
Number differs: Latin gives Shelah thirty years at Eber's birth, Greek one hundred thirty.
Number differs: Latin gives Shelah four hundred three years after Eber, Greek three hundred thirty; Greek adds "and he died".
Number differs: Latin gives Eber thirty-four years at Peleg's birth, Greek one hundred thirty-four.
Number differs: Latin gives Eber four hundred thirty years after Peleg, Greek three hundred seventy; Greek adds "and he died".
Number differs: Latin gives Peleg thirty years at Reu's birth, Greek one hundred thirty.
Both give Peleg two hundred nine years after Reu, with sons and daughters; Greek adds "and he died".
Number differs: Latin gives Reu thirty-two years at Serug's birth, Greek one hundred thirty-two.
Both give Reu two hundred seven years after Serug, with sons and daughters; Greek adds "and he died".
Number differs: Latin gives Serug thirty years at Nahor's birth, Greek one hundred thirty.
Both give Serug two hundred years after Nahor, with sons and daughters; Greek adds "and he died".
Number differs: Latin gives Nahor twenty-nine years at Terah's birth, Greek seventy-nine.
Number differs: Latin gives Nahor one hundred nineteen years after Terah, Greek one hundred twenty-nine; Greek adds "and he died".
Both say Terah lived seventy years and fathered Abram, Nahor and Haran.
Both give Terah's generations: Abram, Nahor and Haran, and Haran fathered Lot.
Both say Haran died before his father Terah in his native land; Latin names Ur of the Chaldeans, Greek the country of the Chaldeans.
Both say Abram and Nahor took wives, Sarai and Milcah, Milcah daughter of Haran, father also of Iscah.
Both say Sarai was barren with no children.
Both have Terah taking Abram, Lot and Sarai toward Canaan and settling in Haran; Latin says out of "Ur of the Chaldeans", Greek out of the country of the Chaldeans.
Latin gives Terah's total days as two hundred five years, then he died in Haran; Greek ties the two hundred five years to his days in Haran.
Both have the Lord telling Abram to go from his land, kindred and father's house to the land God will show him.
Both promise a great nation, blessing, a great name, and that Abram shall be blessed.
Both say Abram went as the Lord had commanded / spoken, with Lot, at seventy-five years old.
Both say Abram took Sarai, Lot, their possessions and the people gained in Haran, and came to Canaan.
Both have Abram passing through the land to Shechem; Latin ends at "the renowned valley", Greek at "the high oak", and Greek says the Canaanites "inhabited" the land.
Both say the Lord appeared to Abram, promised the land to his offspring, and Abram built an altar.
Both say Abram moved east of Bethel, pitched his tent with Bethel to the west and Ai to the east, built an altar and called on the Lord's name.
Latin has Abram journeying on toward the south; Greek has him departing and encamping in the wilderness.
Both say a famine arose and Abram went down to Egypt to live as a stranger because it was severe.
Both have Abram telling Sarai she is a beautiful woman as they near Egypt; Greek names Abram and says "beautiful in face".
Both give Abram's fear that the Egyptians will say she is his wife and kill him but keep her alive.
Both have Abram asking Sarai to say she is his sister so that he will fare well and live because of her.
Both have Pharaoh's officials praising her and her being taken into his house; Latin has them "report" and a passive "was taken", Greek says they "saw" and "brought" her.
Both say Abram was treated well because of her and gained livestock and servants; the animals differ, Latin oxen and female donkeys, Greek calves and mules.
Both have God afflicting Pharaoh and his house because of Sarai; Latin "the Lord ... very great plagues", Greek "God ... great and grievous afflictions".
Both have Pharaoh summoning Abram and asking what he has done and why he did not say she was his wife.
Both have Pharaoh asking why Abram said she was his sister and telling him to take his wife and go.
Both have Pharaoh ordering men to escort Abram with his wife and possessions; the Greek adds "and Lot with him", which the Latin lacks here.
Both say Abram went up from Egypt with his wife, all he had and Lot; Latin says to "the southern region", Greek to "the wilderness".
Both say Abram was very rich in gold and silver; Greek names livestock as well.
Both have Abram returning to Bethel, to where his tent was before, between Bethel and Ai; Latin says "from the south", Greek "into the wilderness".
Both have Abram calling on the Lord's name at the earlier altar; Latin says it was "made before", Greek "where he had made a beginning".
Both say Lot, who was with Abram, also had sheep, cattle and tents.
Both say the land could not hold them together because their possessions were great.
Both say a quarrel arose between Abram's and Lot's herdsmen, and the Canaanite and Perizzite then lived in the land.
Both have Abram asking Lot for no strife between them or their herdsmen, since they are brothers.
Both have Abram offering Lot the whole land: if he goes left, Abram takes the right, and the reverse.
Both say Lot saw the well-watered Jordan region, like the garden of God and Egypt toward Zoar, before Sodom's destruction; Latin has "the Lord", Greek "God".
Both say Lot chose the Jordan region, departed from the east, and the two separated.
Both say Abram lived in Canaan and Lot lived in Sodom; Latin has Lot in "the towns" (plural) around the Jordan, Greek in "a city".
Both say the people of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinful before the Lord (God).
Both have the Lord telling Abram, after Lot left, to look in the four directions; Latin says west where Greek says "the sea", and Latin has "the Lord", Greek "God".
Both promise all the land Abram sees to him and his offspring forever.
Both promise offspring like the earth's dust / sand, beyond counting; Latin "can be counted", Greek "will be counted".
Both command Abram to walk the land in its length and breadth, since it will be given to him.
Both have Abram moving his tent to Hebron and building an altar; Latin places him by "the valley of Mamre", Greek by "the oak of Mamre".
Both name the four kings; Latin has Arioch king of Pontus and Chedorlaomer king of the Elamites, Greek has Arioch king of Ellasar and Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal / Thargal differs.
Both list the five kings of the Dead Sea cities (Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, Bela / Zoar); several names are spelled differently, such as Bera / Balla.
Both have the kings meeting at what became the Salt Sea; Latin names the Wooded Valley, Greek a salt ravine.
Both say they served Chedorlaomer twelve years and rebelled in the thirteenth.
Both have Chedorlaomer striking peoples in the fourteenth year; the peoples named differ, Latin Rephaim, Zuzim and Emim, Greek giants, strong nations and Ommaeans.
Both say the Horites in Seir were struck as far as Paran in the wilderness; Latin has the "Plains" of Paran, Greek the "terebinth" of Paran.
Both have them coming to Kadesh and striking the Amorites at Hazazon-tamar; Latin strikes the whole region of the Amalekites, Greek all the rulers of Amalek.
Both have the five kings going out and drawing up battle lines; Latin places this in the Wooded Valley, Greek in the salt valley.
Both close with the four kings against five; Latin has Pontus and the Elamites, Greek Ellasar and Elam, and Tidal / Thargal differs.
Both have the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah falling among bitumen pits and survivors fleeing to the hills; Latin calls the place the Wooded Valley, Greek the salt valley.
Both have the victors taking the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah and food and leaving; Latin says "all the possessions", Greek "all the horses".
Both say they took Lot, Abram's nephew, and his goods from Sodom; Latin has "possessions", Greek "baggage" and adds "and went away".
Both have a survivor reporting to Abram, who lived by Mamre the Amorite with allies; Latin has the "valley" of Mamre and Aner, Greek the "oak" and Aunan, and calls Abram "the one from beyond".
Both have Abram hearing of Lot's capture, mustering three hundred eighteen household-born men, and pursuing to Dan.
Both have Abram attacking by night and pursuing to Hobah, left of Damascus; Latin says he "divided his companions", Greek says he and his household attendants fell on them.
Both say Abram brought back Lot, his goods, the women and the people; Latin says "all the possessions", Greek "all the horses of Sodom".
Both have the king of Sodom meeting him after the victory over Chedorlaomer in the valley of Shaveh, the King's Valley / Plain.
Both give the blessing of Abram by God Most High who created heaven and earth.
Both bless God Most High for the enemies given to Abram, and a tenth is given; Latin says "by whose protection", Greek "who delivered", and Latin names Abram as giver.
Both have the king of Sodom asking for the people back; Latin says "take the rest", Greek says "take the horses".
Both have Abram swearing by God Most High and lifting his hand; Latin says "possessor of heaven and earth", Greek "who created" them, and Greek names the king of Sodom.
Both have Abram refusing even a thread or sandal strap so that the king cannot say he made Abram rich.
Both except what the young men ate and the shares of the men with him; one companion is Latin Aner, Greek Aunan.
Both have the Lord's word in a vision telling Abram not to fear and promising reward; Latin "protector and exceedingly great reward", Greek "I shield you; your reward will be very great".
Both have Abram lamenting childlessness; the Latin identifies the heir as the steward's son Eliezer of Damascus, the Greek as the son of Masek, a household-born woman, Damascus Eliezer.
Both have Abram saying he has no offspring and a household-born man will be his heir.
Both have the Lord's word that the household man will not inherit but one from Abram will; Latin "word" and "from your own body", Greek "voice" and "from you".
Both have God bringing Abram outside to count the stars: so shall his offspring be.
Both have God recalling bringing Abram out to give him the land; Latin "I am the Lord" and "Ur of the Chaldeans", Greek "I am God" and "the country of the Chaldeans".
Both have Abram asking how he can know he will possess / inherit the land.
Both command a three-year-old cow / heifer, goat and ram, plus a turtledove and a pigeon.
Both have Abram dividing the animals down the middle, laying the halves opposite each other, and not dividing the birds.
Both have birds coming down on the carcasses; Latin has Abram driving them away, Greek has Abram sitting down with them.
Both have a trance or deep sleep falling on Abram at sunset with a great dark fear.
Both foretell four hundred years as strangers in a land not theirs, enslaved and afflicted; Greek names three verbs (enslave, mistreat, humble).
Both have God judging the nation they serve, and Abram's offspring afterward coming out with great possessions.
Both promise Abram will go to his fathers in peace, buried at a good old age.
Both say they will return in the fourth generation because the Amorites' sins are not yet full.
Latin has deep darkness after sunset; this Greek has a flame appearing. Both then show a smoking furnace and fiery torch(es) passing between the pieces.
Both give the same covenant promise of the land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates; only the phrasing of the river clause differs.
Both list the Hittites, the Perizzites and the Rephaim; Latin "quoque" (also) is only a small English difference.
Greek lists the Hivites among the peoples; the Latin list has no corresponding name. The other four peoples agree.
Both say Sarai bore no children and had an Egyptian maid named Hagar; maidservant / slave woman is only English wording.
Latin has Sarai hoping to receive children herself through the maid; Greek says Abram may have children through her. Latin says he agreed; Greek says Abram obeyed Sarai's voice.
Both give Hagar to Abram as a wife after ten years in Canaan; the Greek names Abram and Sarai more explicitly.
Latin has Hagar despise her mistress after conceiving; Greek has the mistress dishonored before her. Hagar is the actor in the Latin, not in the Greek.

Latin has Sarai say Hagar held her in contempt; Greek has Sarai say she herself was dishonored. Latin "Lord" judges; Greek has God. Latin has Hagar seeing she had conceived, Greek has Sarai seeing it.
Both give Abram handing Hagar over to Sarai to treat as she pleases, and Hagar fleeing; afflicted / mistreated is only wording.
Both have the angel find her by the spring on the way to Shur; Latin adds that this is in the desert.
Both give the angel's question and Hagar's answer that she is fleeing from her mistress Sarai; fleeing / running away is only wording.
Both give the same command to return to her mistress and submit; humble yourself / be humbled is only wording.
Both give the promise to multiply her offspring beyond counting; Latin "Again he said" versus Greek naming the angel is only wording.
Both announce a son named Ishmael because the Lord heard; conceived / pregnant and affliction / humiliation are slightly different nuances.
Both describe the wild man at odds with all; Latin has him pitch tents opposite his brothers, Greek says he shall dwell opposite them.
Latin has her seeing the back of the One who sees her; Greek has her seeing before her the One who appeared to her. Different image of the vision.
Latin names the well for the Living One who sees me; Greek names it as the well where she saw before her. The location between Kadesh and Bered agrees.
Both say Hagar bore Abram a son named Ishmael; Greek states explicitly that Abram named him, where the Latin leaves the subject implied.
Both say Abram was eighty-six when Hagar bore Ishmael; only the word order differs.
Both give the same promise to set the covenant and multiply Abram greatly; exceedingly / greatly is only wording.
Both have Abram falling on his face; the Greek adds that God spoke to him, which the Latin carries into the next verse.
Both promise the covenant and that he will be father of many nations; the Latin carries the introduction that God spoke, and has "Ego sum" (It is I) where Greek has "As for Me, behold".
Both give the name change from Abram to Abraham because he is made father of many nations; only phrasing differs.
Both promise exceeding increase, nations and kings from him; exceedingly / very, very greatly is only wording.
Both establish an everlasting covenant with Abraham and his offspring, to be their God; wording of the final clause differs only slightly.
Both give the land of Canaan as an everlasting possession, with God as their God; land of sojourning / where you sojourn is wording.
Both tell Abraham to keep the covenant, with his offspring through their generations; Latin "again" is only a small difference.
Greek adds "throughout their generations" to the covenant command; the Latin sentence lacks it. Both require every male to be circumcised.
Both command circumcision of the foreskin as a sign of the covenant; you shall circumcise / be circumcised is only voice.
Both require circumcision at eight days, including household-born and purchased foreigners; the Latin adds "in vobis" and the Greek phrases the foreigner clause differently.
Greek repeats that the household-born and the purchased must surely be circumcised before the everlasting-covenant clause; the Latin verse has only the covenant clause.
Greek adds "on the eighth day" and says he scattered the covenant; Latin says he made it void. Both cut the uncircumcised male off from his people.
Both give the change of Sarai's name to Sarah; the phrasing of the command differs only in English.
Both promise a blessed son and kings arising from him; Latin has a son, Greek a child, and "kings of peoples" versus "kings of nations".
Both give Abraham falling down, laughing, and asking whether a hundred-year-old man and ninety-year-old Sarah can bear; heart / mind is only wording.
Both give Abraham's wish that Ishmael live before God; Latin "Utinam" and Greek "Let this" are only phrasing.
Both announce that Sarah will bear Isaac, with an everlasting covenant; Greek opens with an emphatic "Yes, behold".
Latin says Ishmael will father twelve princes (duces); Greek says twelve nations. Latin has "I will bless him"; Greek has "I have blessed him".
Both establish the covenant with Isaac, born to Sarah at this time next year; appointed time / this time is only wording.
Both say that when the speaking ended God went up from Abraham; only the sentence structure differs.
Both have Abraham circumcise Ishmael and every male of his household that very day as God commanded; commanded / spoken is only wording.
Both say Abraham was ninety-nine when he circumcised his foreskin flesh.
Both say Ishmael was thirteen at his circumcision.
Both say Abraham and Ishmael were circumcised on that same day; same day / time of that day is only wording.
Both include all the men of the household, born there and purchased; Latin names foreigners (alienigenae) as circumcised together, Greek says those bought from foreign nations.
Latin places the appearance in the valley of Mamre in the heat of the day, naming the Lord; Greek says by the oak of Mamre at noon, naming God.
Both give Abraham's plea that the Lord not pass his servant by; only phrasing differs.
Both offer water to wash the feet and rest under the tree; Latin has Abraham bringing it, Greek has it brought, which is only voice.
Both offer bread before the guests move on; Latin says strengthen your hearts, Greek says you shall eat, and Latin "idcirco" stresses the purpose of their turning aside.
Both give Abraham telling Sarah to quickly prepare three measures of fine flour as hearth cakes; wording only.
Both have Abraham take a tender, good calf from the herd and give it to the servant to prepare; Latin adds only "tenerrimum" emphasis.
Both have butter, milk and calf set before the guests with Abraham standing under the tree; Greek adds that they ate, which the Latin states in the next verse.
Both ask where Sarah is and Abraham answers in the tent; Latin says they spoke after they had eaten and Greek says only that he spoke.
Latin has Sarah laughing behind the entrance when she heard; Greek has her only hearing, behind him. Latin "vita comite" (life continuing) differs from Greek "when the time comes round".
Both say Abraham and Sarah were old and Sarah's womanly course had ceased; Greek names both explicitly.
Latin has Sarah ask whether she will give herself to pleasure now that she is old; Greek has her say it has not happened to her until now. Different content of her words.
Both have the Lord ask why Sarah laughed at the thought of bearing a child in old age; Latin says as an old woman, Greek splits it into two clauses and adds "within herself".
Both promise return and a son for Sarah; difficult / impossible word differs slightly, and Latin adds "juxta condictum" (at the appointed time).
Both give Sarah's denial out of fear and the rebuke that she did laugh; Latin names the Lord, Greek says "He".
Greek adds Gomorrah to Sodom as the place the men look toward, and says they looked down on it; the Latin names Sodom only.
Greek adds "My servant" after Abraham; Latin has no such phrase. Latin "about to do" is only tense.
Latin says Abraham will become a great and very mighty nation; Greek says a great and numerous nation. Blessing of all nations agrees.
Both have God knowing Abraham will command his household to keep the way of the Lord; tense of knowing and order of justice / righteousness differ slightly.
Both say the outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin very grievous; wording only.
Latin asks whether they have fulfilled the outcry by their deeds; Greek asks whether they are being brought to an end according to the outcry.
Both say the men turned to Sodom while Abraham stood before the Lord; Latin "adhuc" (still) is a small word.
Both have Abraham asking whether God will destroy the righteous with the wicked; the Greek adds that the righteous would then be like the ungodly, which Latin gives in the next verse.
Both ask about sparing the place for fifty righteous; Latin asks whether they shall perish together, Greek asks whether He will destroy them, and Greek adds "whole" place.
Latin includes "non est hoc tuum" (this is not Your way) and a statement that He will not render such judgment; Greek ends with a question, will You not do justice?
Both give the Lord's answer that fifty righteous would spare the whole place; spare / forgive is only wording.
Both give Abraham speaking to the Lord though dust and ashes; dust / earth is only wording.
Latin asks about destroying the city for forty-five; Greek asks about destroying it because of the five lacking. The Lord's answer, forty-five, agrees.
Both have Abraham asking about forty and the Lord refusing to destroy; Latin has "Sin autem" and "percutiam" (strike), Greek has a shorter question and "destroy".
Latin has Abraham say "do not be angry" before speaking; Greek has no such phrase. The question about thirty and the answer agree.
Both have the question about twenty and the answer not to destroy; Latin "interficiam" (kill) and "semel coepi" differ slightly from Greek wording.
Latin has Abraham say "do not be angry" before speaking once more; Greek has no such phrase. The question about ten and the answer agree.
Both say the Lord departed when He finished speaking and Abraham returned to his place.
Both have the two angels reaching Sodom in the evening, Lot at the gate rising to meet them and bowing to the ground; wording only.
Both give Lot's invitation to wash feet and go on in the morning, and the angels' refusal to stay in the square; wording only.
Both have Lot pressing the guests, a feast, unleavened bread and eating; Greek specifies a drinking feast and says they turned aside before entering.
Both have the men of the city surrounding the house, young and old; Greek adds that these were the Sodomites.
Both have the crowd demanding the visitors; Latin "cognoscamus" (know) is the idiom the Greek states plainly as having intercourse.
Both have Lot going out and closing the door behind him; Greek adds that he stood at the vestibule, and the Latin carries his "he said" here.
Both have Lot pleading with the men not to do this evil; Greek carries the "he said" here.
Both have Lot offering his two virgin daughters and asking that the men not be harmed because they are under his roof; wording only.
Both give the crowd's threat to treat Lot worse and press on the door; Greek says he came alone to sojourn and asks will he also judge, where Latin says as a stranger.
Both have the men pulling Lot inside and shutting the door.
Both have the men struck with blindness, small and great; Latin says they could not find the door, Greek says they became helpless seeking it.
Both have the men asking Lot about relatives to bring out of the city; Latin tells him to bring out all his own, Greek makes it conditional on anyone else in the city.
Both give the reason for destroying the place: the outcry before the Lord, who sent them; Latin says destroy them, Greek says wipe out the place.
Latin says the sons-in-law were about to marry Lot's daughters; Greek says they had taken them. Both say they thought he was joking.
Both have the angels urging Lot at dawn to take his wife and two daughters lest he perish with the city's wickedness.
Latin says he delayed (dissimulante); Greek says they were troubled. Both have the angels grasping their hands because the Lord spared him.
Both have the command to save his life, not look back and escape to the mountain; Latin sets only Lot outside, Greek speaks of them, and the final warning differs in wording.
Both give Lot's address to the angel, "my lord" / "Lord"; only the wording differs.
Latin has Lot say the Lord magnified His mercy; Greek says righteousness. Latin has "found favor", Greek "found mercy"; the fear of calamity on the mountain agrees.
Both have Lot pointing to the small nearby city as a place of refuge for his life.
Both promise not to overthrow the city; Latin says He accepted Lot's prayers, Greek says He has regarded his person.
Both tell Lot to hurry there since nothing can be done until he enters; the city is named Zoar (Latin Segor).
Both say the sun rose over the earth and Lot entered Zoar.
Both say the Lord rained sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord out of heaven.
Both say He overthrew the cities, the whole region, the inhabitants and all that grew; wording only.
Both say Lot's wife looked back and became a pillar of salt.
Both say Abraham rose early and went to the place where he had stood before the Lord; with / before is only wording.
Latin has Abraham see rising ashes (favilla) like furnace smoke; Greek has a flame rising like furnace vapor.
Both say God remembered Abraham and delivered Lot from the overthrow; Greek has the Lord wiping out the cities and God remembering, where Latin names God only.
Both say Lot went up from Zoar, afraid to stay there, and lived in a cave with his two daughters.
Both give the elder daughter's plea that their father is old and no man remains to come in to them as is customary.
Both propose getting their father drunk and lying with him for offspring; Latin says preserve offspring, Greek says raise up offspring.
Both say they gave their father wine that night and the elder lay with him without his knowing.
Both give the elder telling the younger to do the same the next night to raise up offspring.
Both say they gave him wine again and the younger lay with him without his knowing.
Both say both daughters of Lot conceived by their father.
Greek adds the explanation of the name, saying "From my father"; the Latin gives the name Moab without it. Both call him father of the Moabites.
Both have the younger bear a son named Ammon (Greek Amman), father of the Ammonites; Latin glosses the name as Son of my people, Greek as Son of my kin.
Both say Abraham went to the southern land and lived between Kadesh and Shur, sojourning in Gerar.
Greek adds that Abraham feared to say she was his wife lest the men kill him; the Latin has no such clause. The sister claim and Abimelech's taking her agree.
Both have God warning Abimelech in a night dream that he will die over the woman; Latin says she has a husband, Greek says she has lived with a husband.
Both say Abimelech had not touched her and ask whether the Lord will destroy an ignorant and righteous nation.
Both give Abimelech's plea that Abraham and Sarah each called the other brother / sister and that he acted with a pure heart and clean hands; wording only.
Both have God affirming Abimelech's pure heart and that He kept him from touching her; Greek adds "in sleep" and orders the cause and result slightly differently.
Both tell him to return the wife to her husband the prophet, who will pray for him, or he and all his shall die.
Latin has Abimelech rise immediately in the night; Greek has him rise early in the morning. He then calls his servants, who are afraid.
Both have Abimelech rebuking Abraham for bringing great sin on him and his kingdom; Latin says things he ought not to have done, Greek a deed no one would do.
Both give Abimelech asking Abraham what he saw that made him do this.
Both give Abraham saying he thought there was no fear of God in the place and they would kill him over his wife; reverence / fear is only wording.
Both say she truly is his sister by his father and not his mother and became his wife.
Both give Abraham's instruction to Sarah to say he is her brother wherever they go; Latin calls it a kindness (misericordiam), Greek a righteousness.
Greek adds one thousand didrachms to the gift and has calves where Latin has oxen. Both return Sarah to Abraham.
Both have Abimelech offering the land for Abraham to live wherever he pleases.
Latin has a thousand silver pieces as a covering for her eyes and tells her to remember she was found out; Greek has didrachms for the honor of her face and tells her to speak the truth.
Both have Abraham praying and God healing Abimelech, his wife and maidservants so that they bore children.
Both say the Lord had closed every womb in Abimelech's house because of Sarah; Greek adds "completely" and "from outside".
Both say the Lord visited Sarah and did as He had promised; wording only.
Both say Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in old age at the time God had foretold.
Both say Abraham named his son, whom Sarah bore him, Isaac.
Both say Abraham circumcised Isaac on the eighth day as God commanded.
Both say Abraham was one hundred years old when Isaac was born.
Both have Sarah saying God made laughter for her and that all who hear will join her; corridebit (laugh with) differs slightly from rejoice with.
Latin asks who would have believed Sarah would nurse a son; Greek asks who will announce to Abraham that she nurses a child, giving the old-age birth as the reason.
Both say the child grew, was weaned, and Abraham made a great feast on the day.
Both have Sarah seeing Hagar's son playing with Isaac; Greek adds that he was born to Abraham and leaves her words to the next verse.
Both give Sarah's demand to cast out the maidservant and her son because he shall not inherit with Isaac.
Both say the matter seemed hard to Abraham on account of his son.
Both give God telling Abraham not to take it harshly and to listen to Sarah, because offspring will be named through Isaac.
Both promise to make the maidservant's son a great nation because he is Abraham's offspring.
Both have Abraham giving bread and a skin of water to Hagar with the boy and sending her away to wander near Beersheba (Well of the Oath).
Both have Hagar laying the boy under a tree when the water ran out; Latin says one of the trees there, Greek says a fir tree.
Latin has Hagar raise her voice and weep; Greek has the child cry out and weep. Latin says she will not watch the boy die, Greek that she will not see his death.
Both have God hearing the boy's voice and the angel calling Hagar from heaven not to fear.
Both tell Hagar to take the boy and hold him by the hand because he will become a great nation.
Both have God opening her eyes to a well, and she filled the skin and gave the boy drink; Greek calls it a well of living water.
Both say God was with the boy, who grew, lived in the wilderness and became an archer.
Both say he lived in the wilderness of Paran and his mother took him a wife from Egypt.
Greek names a third party, Ahuzzath his groomsman, who speaks with Abimelech and Phicol; the Latin names only Abimelech and Phicol.
Latin asks an oath not to harm him, his posterity or his stock, and to repay kindness (misericordiam); Greek has not wronging him, his offspring or his name, and acting according to righteousness.
Both have Abraham reproving Abimelech over his servants' seizure of water; Latin has one well taken by force, Greek has wells taken away.
Both give Abimelech saying he did not know who did this and heard of it only today.
Both have Abraham giving Abimelech animals and the two making a covenant; Latin has oxen, Greek has calves.
Both say Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock apart.
Both have Abimelech asking what the seven ewe lambs set apart mean.
Both have Abraham giving the seven ewe lambs as testimony that he dug the well.
Both explain the place name because both swore there; Latin gives Beersheba passively, Greek has Abraham naming it Well of Swearing.
Both say they made a covenant at the Well of the Oath; Greek adds the return of Abimelech and Phicol (and Ahuzzath), which the Latin gives in the next verse.
Latin says Abraham planted a grove at Beersheba; Greek says a field at the Well of the Oath. Latin also includes the return of Abimelech and Phicol to the Philistines.
Both say Abraham stayed in the land of the Philistines many days; settler / sojourned is only wording.
Both say God tested Abraham, called his name twice and he answered "Here I am."
Latin has Abraham rise in the night; Greek has him rise in the morning. Latin has a donkey, Greek a female donkey.
Both say that on the third day Abraham saw the place from afar.
Both have Abraham telling the servants to wait with the donkey while he and the boy go to worship and return.
Both have Abraham laying the wood on Isaac and carrying the fire and knife as the two went together.
Both have Isaac asking where the offering is; Latin says victim, Greek says sheep for the whole burnt offering.
Both have Abraham answering that God will provide the offering; Latin says victim, Greek says sheep.
Both have the altar built, the wood laid and Isaac bound and laid upon it; Greek specifies that his feet were bound and says the place God told him, where Latin says showed.
Both have Abraham stretching out his hand for the knife to slay his son.
Both have the angel of the Lord calling from heaven and Abraham answering "Here I am."
Both have the angel stopping Abraham because he feared God and did not spare his son; Latin says only-begotten (unigenito), Greek says beloved.
Both have Abraham seeing a ram caught by its horns and offering it instead of his son; Latin has it among thorns behind him, Greek has it in a sabek plant.
Both say the angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven.
Both give the oath by Himself because Abraham did not spare his son; Latin says only-begotten, Greek says beloved.
Latin says his offspring shall possess the gates of their enemies; Greek says they shall inherit the cities of their adversaries. The star and sand promise agrees.
Both promise blessing to all nations of the earth in his offspring because he obeyed God's voice.
Both have Abraham returning to his servants and going together to Beersheba (Well of the Oath) to dwell.
Both say Abraham was told that Milcah had also borne sons to his brother Nahor.
Both list Uz the firstborn, Buz his brother, and Kemuel father of the Syrians.
Both list Chesed, Hazo / Azau, Pildash and Jidlaph; Greek adds Bethuel here, where the Latin gives him in the next verse.
Both name Bethuel and Rebekah and the eight sons of Milcah; Latin says Rebekah was born of Bethuel, Greek says Bethuel begat her.
Both say Nahor's concubine Reumah also bore four sons; the son names differ only in spelling.
Both give Sarah's life as one hundred twenty-seven years.
Greek adds "which is in the hollow" to the city name and names Sarah again; Latin has Arba, which is Hebron. Both say Abraham came to mourn her.
Both have Abraham rising from his dead (from the mourning duties) and speaking to the sons of Heth.
Both have Abraham as a sojourner asking for burial property; Latin asks for the right to a tomb among them, Greek adds that he will bury his dead away from himself.
Both say the sons of Heth answered; Greek names Abraham as the one answered.
Latin calls Abraham a prince of God among them; Greek calls him a king from God. Greek opens with "No, lord".
Both have Abraham asking them to speak for him to Ephron son of Zohar so he may bury his dead.
Both ask for the double cave in Ephron's field for burial at a proper price; Latin says at the edge of the field and fair price, Greek says in a part of it and value in silver.
Both say Ephron answered Abraham in public hearing; Greek names Ephron the Hittite and the sons of Heth and all who entered the city.
Both have Ephron giving the field and cave and telling Abraham to bury his dead; Latin begins "Not so, my lord", Greek "Come to my side".
Both have Abraham offering the price of the field before the people; Latin says the people stood around, Greek says in the hearing of the people of the land and adds "since you are on my side".
Both say Ephron answered; Greek names Abraham as the one answered.
Both have Ephron saying the land is worth four hundred pieces of silver, a trifle between them, and telling Abraham to bury his dead; shekels / didrachms and the opening phrase differ.
Both have Abraham weighing out four hundred pieces of silver in the hearing of the sons of Heth; Latin says public standard, Greek says approved by merchants.
Both describe Ephron's field with the double cave facing Mamre and all its trees as established to Abraham.
Both say the field was made Abraham's possession before the sons of Heth and all who entered the gate / city.
Both say Abraham buried Sarah in the double cave facing Mamre, which is Hebron in Canaan.
Both say the field and its cave were confirmed to Abraham as a burial possession from the sons of Heth.
Both say Abraham was old and advanced in days and the Lord had blessed him in everything.
Both have Abraham telling the elder servant in charge of his household to put his hand under his thigh.
Both have the oath by the God of heaven and earth not to take a wife from the Canaanites for his son; Greek names the son Isaac here, where Latin does in the next verse.
Both send the servant to Abraham's land and kindred for a wife for Isaac; Greek adds "where I was born" and says tribe where Latin says kindred.
Both give the servant asking whether he must take Isaac back if the woman will not come.
Both have Abraham warning the servant not to take his son back there.
Both give the God who took Abraham from his father's house, swore the land, and will send His angel; Greek says to you and your seed, calls Him God of earth too, and names Isaac.
Both release the servant from the oath if the woman is unwilling, but forbid taking the son back.
Both say the servant put his hand under Abraham's thigh and swore to him about this matter.
Both say the servant took ten camels and goods from his master and went to the city of Nahor in Mesopotamia.
Both have the camels made to kneel outside the town by a well at evening when women draw water; Latin carries "he said" to the prayer.
Both give the servant's prayer to the God of Abraham for help and kindness to his master; occurre / grant success is only wording.
Both have the servant standing by the spring as the daughters of the city come out to draw water.
Both give the sign of the girl who offers a drink and water for the camels; Greek says until they stop drinking and names Abraham in the closing line.
Both have Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel son of Milcah wife of Nahor, coming out with her jar before he finished speaking.
Both describe Rebekah as very beautiful, a virgin unknown to man, who went down to the spring, filled her jar and returned.
Both have the servant running to meet her and asking for a little water from her jar.
Both have Rebekah saying "Drink, my lord" and quickly lowering her jar to give him a drink.
Both have Rebekah offering to draw water for the camels until they have all drunk.
Both have her emptying the jar into the trough and running back to the well to draw for all the camels.
Both have the man gazing at her in silence to know whether the Lord had prospered his journey.
Latin gives earrings weighing two shekels and two bracelets of ten shekels; Greek gives earrings of a drachma each and two bracelets of ten gold pieces.
Both have him asking whose daughter she is and whether her father's house has room to lodge.
Both have her answering that she is the daughter of Bethuel, son of Milcah and Nahor.
Both have her adding that they have plenty of straw and feed and room to lodge.
Latin has the man bowing down and worshiping the Lord; Greek says he was pleased and worshiped. Greek carries "saying" into this verse.
Both have blessing of the God of Abraham for guiding him to his master's brother's house; Latin says mercy and faithfulness, Greek says righteousness and truth, and Latin adds "straight way".
Both have the girl running to tell her mother's household what happened.
Both say Rebekah had a brother named Laban who hurried out to the man at the spring.
Both have Laban seeing the earrings and bracelets and hearing Rebekah's report, then going to the man by the camels at the spring.
Latin addresses the man as "blessed of the Lord"; Greek says "blessed be the Lord", a blessing of God rather than a title for the man.
Both have the camels unloaded and given straw and feed, and water brought for the feet of the man and his men.
Both have bread set out and the servant refusing to eat before speaking his message; Latin sets it before him, Greek before them, and "they" answer.
Both give the servant introducing himself as Abraham's servant.
Both say the Lord greatly blessed his master with flocks, silver, gold, servants, camels and donkeys; Latin has oxen (boves), Greek has calves.
Both say Sarah bore Abraham a son in old age and he gave him everything; Greek stresses "one son".
Both repeat Abraham's oath not to take a wife from the Canaanites among whom he lives.
Both repeat the instruction to go to Abraham's father's house and kindred for a wife.
Both give the servant's objection that the woman might not come with him.
Both have the Lord sending His angel with the servant; Latin says the Lord in whose sight Abraham walks and who directs the way, Greek says the Lord whom he has pleased and who prospers the journey.
Both free the servant if the relatives refuse to give her; Greek adds that he will be free from the oath, besides the curse.
Both give the servant's prayer at the spring that the Lord prosper his way.
Both give the sign of the virgin who will give water from her jar; Greek adds that the daughters of the city come out to draw.
Greek calls the woman prepared for the Lord's servant Isaac and adds "By this I will know that You have shown mercy"; Latin ends with her being prepared for his master's son.
Both have Rebekah coming out with her jar before he finished speaking within himself, drawing water, and being asked for a drink.
Both have her quickly lowering the jar, offering water to him and the camels, and watering them.
Both have him asking whose daughter she is, her answer, and his putting the earrings and bracelets on her.
Latin has the servant bowing down and worshiping, led by a straight way; Greek has him pleased and worshiping, guided on the way of truth.
Both ask the family to say whether they will deal kindly with his master and to say so otherwise; Latin says kindness and faithfulness, Greek mercy and righteousness.
Latin says they cannot speak anything else beyond the Lord's pleasure; Greek says they cannot oppose him by setting evil against good.
Both have Laban and Bethuel giving Rebekah to be the wife of his master's son as the Lord has spoken.
Both say that on hearing this the servant bowed to the earth and worshiped the Lord.
Both have silver and gold articles and clothing given to Rebekah and gifts for her family; Latin has her brothers, Greek her brother.
Both have the servant staying overnight and asking to be sent to his master in the morning; Latin describes a feast, Greek says he and his men ate, drank and slept.
Both have the family asking that the young woman stay about ten days before going; Latin says at least ten days, Greek about ten days.
Both have the servant asking not to be delayed because the Lord has prospered his way.
Both have them proposing to call the young woman and ask her.
Both have them asking if she will go with the man and her answering "I will go."
Latin sends Rebekah away with her nurse; Greek sends her with her belongings. Abraham's servant and his men go with her in both.
Latin has her offspring possessing the gates of their enemies; Greek says inherit the cities of their adversaries. Latin says thousands of thousands, Greek thousands of ten thousands.
Both have Rebekah and her maidens mounting camels and following the servant; Greek adds that the servant took Rebekah, and Latin adds that he hurried back.
Latin has Isaac walking along the road to the well called The Living One Who Sees; Greek has him traveling through the wilderness near the Well of the Vision.
Both have Isaac going out to the field toward evening to meditate and seeing camels approaching.
Both have Rebekah seeing Isaac and getting down from the camel; Greek says she leaped down.
Both have Rebekah asking who the man in the field is, the servant saying it is his master, and her covering herself with her veil.
Both say the servant told Isaac everything he had done.
Both have Isaac taking Rebekah as wife and being comforted after his mother's death; Latin says her mother's tent, Greek says his mother's house.
Both say Abraham took another wife named Keturah.
Both list Keturah's sons as Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah.
Greek adds Teman among Jokshan's sons and Raguel and Nabdeel among Dedan's; the Latin lists fewer names. The rest agree.
Both list Midian's sons and say all are Keturah's; the last name differs (Latin Eldaah, Greek Elraga) and Enoch / Hanoch is spelling.
Both say Abraham gave all he had to Isaac.
Both say Abraham gave gifts to his concubines' sons and sent them eastward away from Isaac while still alive.
Both give Abraham's life as one hundred seventy-five years.
Both say Abraham died at a good old age, full of days, and was gathered to his people.
Both say Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the double cave in the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite, opposite Mamre.
Both say the field was bought from the sons of Heth and Abraham and Sarah were buried there.
Both say God blessed Isaac after Abraham's death; Latin names the well The Living One Who Sees, Greek names it the Well of the Vision.
Both open the generations of Ishmael, whom Hagar, Sarah's maid, bore to Abraham; Latin ends with "and", which continues in the next verse.
Both list Ishmael's sons beginning with Nebaioth, Kedar, a third and Mibsam; the third name differs (Latin Adbeel, Greek Nabdeel).
Both list the same sons of Ishmael (Hadar / Choddad, Tema / Teman, Jetur, Naphish, Kedemah); only name spellings differ.
Both close the list as twelve rulers; Latin says by settlements and towns and princes of their tribes, Greek says tents and dwellings and rulers according to their nations.
Both give Ishmael's age as one hundred thirty-seven, and say he died and was gathered to his people.
Latin says he died in the presence of all his brothers; Greek says he lived (settled) opposite all his brothers. The settlement from Havilah to Shur agrees.
Both open the generations of Isaac, Abraham's son, with Abraham begetting Isaac.
Both say Isaac married Rebekah at forty, daughter of Bethuel the Syrian and sister of Laban; Greek also calls Laban the Syrian.
Both say Isaac prayed to the Lord for his barren wife and she conceived.
Latin has the children struggling together in her womb; Greek has them leaping within her. Latin adds "why was there any need to conceive", Greek asks why this is happening.
Both give the oracle of two nations in her womb, one people overcoming the other, and the elder serving the younger.
Both say that when the time to give birth came, twins were in her womb.
Both describe Esau coming out red and hairy; Latin includes Jacob's birth holding the heel and the reason for his name here, Greek in the next verse.
Both give Isaac as sixty when the sons were born; Greek includes Jacob's birth holding Esau's heel here, Latin in the previous verse.
Latin has Jacob a simple man living in tents; Greek has him an unfeigned man dwelling in a house. Esau as a skilled hunter and man of the field agrees.
Both say Isaac loved Esau because of his hunting food while Rebekah loved Jacob.
Both say Jacob cooked a stew and Esau came in weary from the field.
Both have Esau asking for the red stew because he is weary, hence the name Edom.
Both have Jacob asking Esau to sell his birthright; Greek adds "today".
Both have Esau saying he is dying and asking what use the birthright is.
Both have Jacob demanding an oath and Esau swearing and selling his birthright; Greek adds "today".
Both say Esau ate and drank bread and lentil stew, went away, and despised the birthright.
Both say a famine arose in addition to the earlier one in Abraham's days and Isaac went to Abimelech in Gerar; Latin calls the earlier one barrenness, Greek calls it a famine.
Both have the Lord appearing to Isaac and telling him not to go to Egypt but to stay in the land He will show him.
Both promise presence, blessing and the land, fulfilling the oath to Abraham; Latin says all these regions, Greek says all this land, and fulfilling / establishing differ slightly.
Both promise offspring like the stars, the land to them, and blessing to all nations in his offspring.
Both give the reason that Abraham obeyed God's voice and kept His commandments, precepts, rites and laws; the terms for the law differ only in wording.
Both say Isaac stayed in Gerar.
Both have Isaac telling the men of the place that his wife is his sister, out of fear; Greek names Rebekah.
Both have Abimelech seeing Isaac playing with Rebekah through a window after many days; Greek calls him king of Gerar and names Isaac, Latin says king of the Philistines.
Both have Abimelech summoning Isaac, noting she is his wife, and Isaac answering that he feared dying because of her.
Both have Abimelech saying someone might have lain with Rebekah and brought guilt on them; Latin says great sin and ends with the command, Greek says unwitting offense.
Latin forbids touching the man's wife on pain of death; Greek forbids touching the man or his wife.
