Both say Isaac sowed and reaped a hundredfold that year and the Lord blessed him; Greek specifies a hundredfold of barley.
Both say the man prospered and grew until he became very great.
Latin says he had a very large household; Greek says he had many tilled lands. Flocks and herds, and the Philistines' envy, agree.
Both say the Philistines stopped up all the wells Abraham's servants dug and filled them with earth.
Both have Abimelech telling Isaac to leave because he has become much mightier.
Both say Isaac departed to the valley of Gerar and lived there.
Both say Isaac dug again the wells Abraham's servants dug, which the Philistines stopped after his death, and gave them the same names.
Both say they dug in the valley and found living water.
Latin names the well Dispute (Calumniam) after the herdsmen's quarrel; Greek names it Injustice because they wronged him. The herdsmen's claim to the water agrees.
Both say he dug another well, they quarreled over it, and he named it Hostility / Enmity; Greek adds that he moved on first.
Both say he dug another well that they did not contest and named it for the Lord making room for them.
Both say Isaac went up from there to Beersheba (Well of the Oath).

Both give the Lord's night appearance, promise of presence and multiplied offspring for Abraham's sake; Greek has "I have blessed you" and "Abraham your father", Latin has "I will bless you" and "My servant Abraham".
Both have Isaac building an altar, calling on the Lord, pitching his tent and having a well dug; Latin says he commanded his servants, Greek states they dug.
Both have Abimelech coming from Gerar with Ahuzzath and Phicol, commander of the army; friend / groomsman is only wording.
Both have Isaac asking why they come to him whom they hate and have sent away.
Both have them saying they saw the Lord is with Isaac and proposing an oath and covenant.
Latin says they touched nothing of his and harmed him not; Greek says they did not loathe him and treated him well. Both end with sending him away in peace and the Lord's blessing.
Both say Isaac made them a feast and they ate and drank.
Both say they rose early, swore to one another, and Isaac sent them away in peace.
Latin says the servants reported they found water; Greek says they reported they did not find water. The report is the opposite.
Latin names the well Abundance (Abundantiam); Greek names it Oath. Both say the city is called Beersheba / Well of the Oath to this day.
Both have Esau marrying Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Basemath daughter of Elon; Latin calls Elon of the same place, Greek calls him the Hivite.
Latin says both wives grieved the hearts of Isaac and Rebekah; Greek says they were continually quarreling with them.
Both say Isaac grew old and blind, called his elder son Esau, and Esau answered "Here I am."
Both have Isaac saying he is old and does not know the day of his death.
Both tell Esau to take quiver and bow and hunt; Greek states to go out into the plain and hunt game for him, which Latin leaves to the next clause.
Both have Isaac asking for a savory dish as he likes it so that his soul may bless Esau before he dies.
Both have Rebekah hearing Isaac, and Esau going into the field; Latin says to fulfill his father's command, Greek says to procure game, and Greek names Isaac speaking to Esau.
Both have Rebekah telling Jacob she heard his father speaking to Esau; Greek calls Jacob her younger son.
Both give Isaac's words: bring game, prepare food, so that I may bless you before the Lord before I die.
Both have Rebekah telling Jacob to obey her; Latin says follow my counsel, Greek says obey my voice in what I command.
Latin "optimos" (choice) against Greek "tender and good" for the goats; both have Rebekah send Jacob to fetch two young goats for Isaac's favourite food.
Both say he brings the food, Isaac eats, and Isaac blesses him before he dies; only English phrasing differs.
Latin has "He answered her"; Greek names Jacob and his mother Rebekah. Both give the same objection that Esau is hairy and Jacob smooth.
Latin has Jacob fear Isaac will think he meant to mock him; Greek has him appear as one treating his father with contempt. Both end in a curse instead of a blessing.
Latin tells him to bring "what I have said"; Greek tells him to bring "them to me". Both have Rebekah take the curse on herself.
Both have Jacob fetch the goats, give them to his mother, and Rebekah prepare the food as his father liked it.
Greek names Rebekah and calls Esau the older and Jacob the younger son; Latin uses pronouns. Both have Esau's fine garments put on Jacob.
Latin has the goatskins wrapped on his hands; Greek puts them on his arms. Both cover the bare part of the neck.
Both have Rebekah give the dish and the bread she baked; Greek adds that it was placed into the hands of Jacob her son.
Isaac's reply differs: Latin "Audio" (I hear) against Greek "Behold, I am here". Both have him ask who the speaker is.
Both have Jacob claim to be Esau the firstborn and ask Isaac to eat of the game so that his soul may bless him.
Latin: it was God's will that what he wanted met him quickly. Greek: the Lord your God placed it before him. The attribution to God is worded differently.
Both have Isaac ask him to come near so he may feel whether he is truly Esau; wording differs only in English.
Both give the voice of Jacob and the hands of Esau after Isaac feels him.
Both say Isaac did not recognize him because the hairy hands were like Esau's, and so blessed him.
Both have Isaac ask whether he is Esau and Jacob answer "I am."
Latin has Isaac ask for the game and then the wine offered; Greek adds that he ate and drank, and names Isaac. The sequence is the same.
Greek names Isaac his father as speaker; Latin has "give me a kiss" against Greek "kiss me". Same request.
Both have Jacob kiss him, Isaac smell his garments, and bless him with the fragrance of a field the Lord has blessed.
Both give the blessing of the dew of heaven, the richness of the earth, and abundant grain and wine.
Latin: peoples serve and tribes bow, brothers, mother's sons. Greek: nations serve and rulers bow, brother, father's sons. Several terms differ; the blessing and curse formula agrees.
Both have Esau arrive as Jacob left; Greek adds that Isaac had finished blessing Jacob and that Esau came from his hunt.
Both have Esau bring his father the prepared food and ask him to rise and eat so that his soul may bless him.
Both have Isaac ask who he is and Esau answer that he is the firstborn son.
Latin stresses trembling and amazement beyond belief and "blessed he shall be"; Greek has utter astonishment and "Let him be blessed". Same sense.
Latin has Esau cry out with a great cry in dismay; Greek says a great and exceedingly bitter cry and "even me also". Same request for a blessing.
Both have Isaac say his brother came with deceit and took the blessing.
Both give the Jacob (supplanter) wordplay, the birthright and blessing taken, and Esau's plea for a reserved blessing.
Latin states Isaac's act as fact ("I have appointed him lord"); Greek frames it as "If I have made him your lord", with "household slaves" for service.
Both have Esau ask whether he has only one blessing and weep; the Latin carries Isaac's being moved into the next verse.
Latin gives Esau the richness of the earth and dew of heaven; Greek says his dwelling shall be away from them. The blessing is reversed.
Both say he will live by the sword, serve his brother, and one day throw off the yoke from his neck.
Latin has Esau hate Jacob continually; Greek says he was angry. Both have him plan to kill Jacob after the days of mourning.
Greek says Rebekah was told what Esau had said and names the sons as older and younger; Latin says only these things were reported.
Greek adds that Jacob should flee into Mesopotamia, to Laban in Haran; Latin names only Laban in Haran. Same instruction to flee.
Both tell Jacob to stay with Laban a few days until his brother's fury subsides; the clause continues into the next verse in Greek.
Both have Esau's anger turn away and him forget, then Rebekah send for Jacob, lest she be bereaved of both in one day.
Latin: daughters of Heth, "I do not wish to live"; Greek: daughters of the Hittites, "why should I live?". Same complaint, slightly different expression.
Latin forbids a wife from the people of Canaan; Greek from the daughters of the Canaanites. Same command.
Latin says go and journey to Mesopotamia; Greek says arise, flee. Both send him to Bethuel's house and Laban's daughters.
Latin "God Almighty" against Greek "my God"; "multitude of peoples" against "assemblies of nations". Both have God bless, increase and multiply him.
Latin: the land God promised to Abraham, your grandfather. Greek: the land God gave to Abraham, and the blessing of "Abraham my father". Promised / gave differs.
Both have Isaac send Jacob to Laban son of Bethuel the Syrian; Greek adds that Rebekah is the mother of Jacob and Esau.
Both have Esau see the blessing, the sending to Mesopotamia and the command about Canaanite wives; Latin says Isaac sent him, Greek says Jacob went.
Latin says Jacob obeyed his parents and went to Syria; Greek says he obeyed his father and mother and went to Mesopotamia of Syria.
Both say Esau saw that the daughters of Canaan did not please his father; only wording differs.
Both have Esau go to Ishmael and take Mahalath, sister of Nebaioth, besides his existing wives; only clause order differs.
Both have Jacob leave Beersheba and head toward Haran; the Greek renders the place name as Well of the Oath.
Latin says he wished to rest after sunset; Greek says he stayed the night because the sun had set. Both have the stone under his head and sleep.
Both describe the ladder or stairway on earth reaching heaven, with angels of God ascending and descending.
Greek adds "fear not", absent in Latin; Latin has the Lord leaning on the ladder, Greek has him standing firm. The land promise is the same.
Latin: dust of the earth, spreading west, east, north, south. Greek: sand of the earth, spreading toward the sea, south, north, east. The blessing of all tribes agrees.
Greek adds "I am with you" and frames guarding as on every road; Latin has only "I will be your guardian wherever you go". Return and fulfilment agree.
Both have Jacob awake and say the Lord is truly in this place and he did not know it.
Both have Jacob afraid, calling the place awesome, the house of God and the gate of heaven.
Both have Jacob rise early, set up the stone as a pillar and pour oil on it.
Latin names the city Bethel, formerly Luz; Greek says Jacob named the place House of God, formerly Oulamlous. The old name differs.
Latin "If God is with me" against Greek "If the Lord God will be with me"; the rest of the vow conditions agree.
Latin has Jacob return safely; Greek has God bring him back safely. Both make the Lord his God on that condition.
Latin: the stone will be called House of God; Greek: it will be to me the house of God. Both promise a tenth of all given.
Greek continues with "to Laban the son of Bethuel the Syrian, the brother of Rebekah"; Latin ends at coming to the eastern land.
Both describe a well in the field, three flocks resting by it, and a large stone over its mouth.
Both describe the custom of gathering the flocks, rolling the stone away to water them, and replacing it.
Both have Jacob ask the shepherds where they are from and hear that they are from Haran.
Both have Jacob ask whether they know Laban son of Nahor and hear that they do.
Latin has the shepherds say "here comes his daughter Rachel"; Greek makes it narration that Rachel was coming. Same event.
Latin adds that it is not time to bring the flocks to the folds and says to water first; Greek says it is not time to gather the livestock.
Latin: until all the animals gather and "we" remove the stone; Greek: until all the shepherds gather and "they" roll it. Same refusal.
Both have Rachel arrive with her father's sheep while Jacob is still speaking, because she tended them.
Latin has Jacob know her as his cousin and move the stone; Greek names Rachel as Laban's daughter and adds that he watered the sheep.
Both have Jacob kiss Rachel and weep aloud; Latin places the watering of the flock here, Greek in the previous verse.
Both have Jacob tell Rachel he is her father's kinsman and Rebekah's son, and she run to tell her father.
Both have Laban run to meet, embrace and kiss Jacob; Greek adds that Jacob related all these words, where Latin has Laban hearing the reasons.
Both have Laban say Jacob is his bone and flesh, and a month pass.
Latin asks "should you serve me for nothing?"; Greek states "you shall not serve me for nothing". Both ask him to name his wages.
Both say Laban had two daughters, the elder Leah and the younger Rachel.
Both say Leah's eyes were weak and Rachel beautiful; Latin "face" and "lovely appearance" against Greek "form and appearance".
Both have Jacob love Rachel and offer seven years of service for her.
Both have Laban say it is better to give her to Jacob than to another man, and ask him to stay.
Both say Jacob served seven years for Rachel and they seemed a few days because he loved her.
Both have Jacob ask Laban for his wife because the time or days are fulfilled, so he may go in to her.
Latin has Laban call a crowd of friends to a feast; Greek has him gather all the men of the place. Both make a wedding feast.
Both have Laban bring his daughter Leah to Jacob in the evening; Greek adds Jacob going in, which Latin gives in the next verse.
Both have Laban give Zilpah to his daughter; Latin also includes Jacob going in and seeing Leah in the morning, which Greek places in neighbouring verses.
Both have Jacob protest that he served for Rachel; Greek begins with "behold, it was Leah" and says "defrauded" where Latin says "deceived".
Both give Laban's reply that it is not their custom to give the younger before the elder.
Both tell Jacob to complete the week and receive the other for another seven years of service.
Both have Jacob agree, complete the week, and marry Rachel.
Both say Laban gave his maidservant Bilhah to Rachel.
Both say Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah and served another seven years.
Latin: the Lord saw that he slighted Leah; Greek: that she was unloved. Greek names Rachel as barren. Both have him open her womb.
Both have Leah bear Reuben and say the Lord saw her humiliation and her husband will now love her.
Latin "held in contempt" against Greek "unloved"; Greek also says "second son to Jacob". Simeon is named in both.
Latin "joined to me" against Greek "on my side"; Latin has Leah name him Levi, Greek says he was named. Three sons are the reason in both.
Both have Leah bear Judah, give praise or thanks to the Lord, and cease bearing; praise / give thanks is only English wording.
Both have Rachel, seeing she bore no children, envy her sister and ask her husband for children or she will die.
Both have Jacob angrily ask whether he is in the place of God, who has withheld the fruit of the womb.
Both have Rachel offer her maidservant Bilhah so she may bear on her knees and Rachel have children through her.
Both have Rachel give Bilhah to Jacob as wife; Greek adds Jacob going in, which Latin gives in the next verse.
Both have Bilhah conceive and bear a son to Jacob.
Latin: the Lord has judged in my favour; Greek: God has vindicated me. Both say he heard her voice, gave her a son, and she named him Dan.
Both say Bilhah conceived again and bore a second son.
Latin: God has matched me with my sister and I prevailed; Greek: God has helped me, I contended with my sister and prevailed. Naphtali in both.
Both have Leah, seeing she had stopped bearing, give her maidservant Zilpah to Jacob.
Both say Zilpah conceived and bore a son.
Both have Leah cry "Good fortune!" and name him Gad.
Both say Zilpah bore another or second son.
Latin "This is for my happiness" against Greek "Blessed am I!"; both have women calling her blessed or happy, and the name Asher.
Both have Reuben find mandrakes at wheat harvest, bring them to Leah, and Rachel ask for some.
Greek adds Rachel's "Not so"; otherwise both give Leah's complaint and Rachel's offer of a night with Jacob for the mandrakes.
Both have Leah meet Jacob in the evening, say she has hired him for the mandrakes, and he lie with her.
Latin "God heard her prayers" against Greek "God heard Leah"; both have her bear a fifth son.
Greek adds that Issachar "means Reward"; Latin has no such explanation. Leah's saying about wages is the same.
Both say Leah conceived again and bore a sixth son.
Latin: "my husband will be with me"; Greek: "will choose me". Both have a good dowry or gift from God and the name Zebulun.
Both say she afterward bore a daughter named Dinah.
Both say God remembered Rachel, heard her and opened her womb; Lord / God is only English wording.
Both have Rachel bear a son and say God has taken away her reproach.
Both have her name him Joseph and ask that the Lord or God add another son.
Both have Jacob ask his father-in-law Laban, after Joseph's birth, to send him to his own country.
Both have Jacob ask for his wives and children for whom he served, and to be allowed to go, since Laban knows his service.
Latin: Laban has learned by experience that God blessed him because of Jacob. Greek: he would divine by signs, and God blessed him at Jacob's arrival.
Both have Laban tell Jacob to name his wages and he will pay.
Latin: how great your possessions have become in my hands; Greek: how your livestock have fared with me. Both have Jacob appeal to his service.
Latin ends with a statement that it is right to provide for his own household; Greek ends with a question, "when shall I also provide for my own house?".
Both have Laban ask what to give and Jacob answer nothing, offering to tend and guard the flock again if Laban does what he asks.
Latin: separate variegated, dark and spotted sheep and goats as wages. Greek: gray lambs and white-marked, spotted goats. The marked animals are described differently.
Latin: his righteousness will answer when the agreed time comes; Greek: because his wages are before Laban. Both treat unmarked animals as theft.
Latin: "I accept what you ask"; Greek: "Let it be according to your word". Laban agrees in both.
Latin: he separated the variegated and spotted, and gave the single-coloured flock to his sons. Greek: he separated the spotted and white-marked and handed those over to his sons.
Both say a three-day journey was put between them and Jacob tended Laban's remaining flocks.
Different trees: Latin poplar, almond and plane; Greek styrax, walnut and plane. Both have Jacob peel the rods so white shows and the rods look variegated.
Both have Jacob set the rods in the watering troughs so the flocks see them as they come to drink; Greek runs the sentence into the next verse.
Both say the sheep conceived facing the rods and bore marked young; the colour descriptions differ slightly, Latin adding the heat of mating.
Latin: Jacob placed branches before the rams, with white and black animals Laban's. Greek: he set a white-marked ram before the sheep and kept his flocks apart from Laban's.
Latin specifies the early season and rams and ewes; Greek says whenever the sheep were mating. Both have the rods set before them in the troughs.
Latin: the late-born were Laban's, the early-season Jacob's. Greek: the unmarked were Laban's and the marked Jacob's. The basis of the division differs.
Both say the man became very rich with flocks, servants, camels and donkeys; Greek adds oxen, Latin has maidservants and male servants.
Both have Jacob hear Laban's sons say he took all their father's goods and gained wealth and glory from them.
Both say Jacob saw that Laban's attitude toward him was no longer as before.
Both have the Lord tell Jacob to return and promise to be with him; Latin has "fathers" and "kindred", Greek "father" and "relatives".
Both have Jacob call Rachel and Leah to the field where his flock was.
Both have Jacob say their father's attitude has changed but the God of his father has been with him.
Both have Jacob remind them that he served their father with all his strength.
Latin: their father changed his wages ten times. Greek: changed his wages of ten lambs. The number refers to different things.
Both give the two wage terms, variegated and white, and that the sheep bore accordingly.
Latin: God took the father's substance and gave it to Jacob; Greek: God took away all the livestock of the father.
Both give the dream of marked males mounting the females; Greek specifies male goats and rams and slightly different colour terms.
Both have the angel of God call Jacob in the dream; Latin has Jacob reply "Here I am", Greek "What is it?".
Both have the angel tell him to look up at the marked males mounting the females because God has seen Laban's doings; colour terms differ slightly.
Greek adds "and I will be with you" and has God "appear" in the place of God; Latin has the God of Bethel. The vow and the return are the same.
Both have Rachel and Leah ask whether any portion or inheritance remains for them in their father's house.
Both say their father regards them as strangers, has sold them and consumed their price.
Both say God took their father's wealth for them and their children, and tell Jacob to do what God said; Greek adds "glory".
Both have Jacob put wives and children on camels; Latin adds that he departed.
Both have Jacob take his goods from Mesopotamia and go to Isaac in Canaan; Latin names his flocks, Greek his household goods.
Both say Laban had gone to shear his sheep and Rachel stole her father's idols.
Both say Jacob did not tell Laban he was fleeing; Greek calls Laban "the Syrian" and says he concealed his departure.
Both have Jacob go with all he had, cross the river, and head toward the mountain of Gilead.
Both say Laban was told on the third day that Jacob had fled; Greek adds "the Syrian".
Both say Laban took his kinsmen, pursued Jacob seven days and overtook him in the mountain of Gilead.
Latin: Laban saw God in a dream and was told not to speak harshly; Greek adds that it was at night and names Laban the Syrian, with "speak evil".
Latin: Laban pitched his own tent on the same mountain. Greek: Laban stationed his kinsmen in the hill country of Gilead. Both have Jacob already camped there.
Both have Laban accuse Jacob of secretly leading his daughters off like captives; Greek adds "What have you done?" and "defraud".
Latin asks why Jacob fled without telling him, with songs and instruments; Greek states that had he told him he would have sent him off with music.
Both have Laban complain he could not kiss his children and say Jacob acted foolishly; Latin "you did not allow", Greek "I was not thought worthy".
Both say Laban has power to harm Jacob but God spoke to him; Latin "God of your fathers" yesterday, Greek "God of your father" last night.
Both grant Jacob longed for his father's house and ask why he stole Laban's gods; Latin has "Granted", Greek "you have departed".
Latin: Jacob feared Laban would take his daughters by force. Greek: Jacob thought Laban might take the daughters and everything he had.
Greek adds "He identified nothing with him" and has death for the thief as "shall not live"; Latin has the offer to search and the death penalty in one speech.
Both describe Laban searching the tents of Jacob, Leah and the maidservants, then Rachel's; Greek orders them differently and finishes the sentence in the verse.
Both have Rachel hide the idols in the camel's saddle gear and sit on them; Latin adds that Laban's search of the tent found nothing.
Both give Rachel's excuse of the customary condition of women; Greek adds she spoke to her father and that Laban found no idols.
Both have Jacob angrily rebuke Laban and ask what his offense or sin is, that Laban pursued him.
Both ask what Laban found among his goods and tell him to set it before the kinsmen to judge between them.
Latin asks whether this is why he was with Laban twenty years; Greek states the twenty years. Latin "not barren" against Greek "not miscarried".
Both say Jacob made good all losses from beasts and theft; Greek adds "by day or by night", Latin says Laban demanded it.
Both say heat by day and frost by night consumed him and sleep fled his eyes.
Latin: Laban changed his wages ten times. Greek: he cheated him of wages amounting to ten ewe lambs. Fourteen and six years agree.
Both say that without the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac Jacob would have been sent away empty; Latin adds "perhaps" and "affliction" for "humiliation".
Both have Laban claim daughters, sons and flocks as his; Greek adds "and my daughters'" and speaks of the women and their children.
Greek adds that Laban says no one is with them and God is witness between them; Latin has only the proposal of a covenant as testimony.
Both have Jacob take a stone and set it up as a pillar.
Both have Jacob tell his kinsmen to gather stones, make a heap and eat; Greek adds drinking and Laban's saying the heap is a witness.
Latin adds that each named it according to his own language; Greek gives the two names without that clause, and the names are worded differently.
Latin names the mound Gilead, Mound of Witness; Greek adds a pillar and calls it The Heap Witnesses. Laban's "witness today" saying is in both.
Greek adds the name "The Watch" and its reason; Latin has only the prayer that the Lord watch and judge between them.
Latin: no witness of their words except God, who is present. Greek: "there is no one with us". The daughters and other wives condition agrees.
The Greek has no separate text; Latin's statement about the mound and stone set between them appears in Greek in verse 48.
Latin: the mound and stone are a witness if either crosses to harm the other. Greek: neither shall cross the heap and pillar for harm, with no witness clause.
Latin adds "the God of their father" after Abraham and Nahor; Greek omits it. Both have Jacob swear by the Fear of Isaac.
Both have Jacob offer sacrifice on the mountain and call his kinsmen to eat; Greek adds drinking and sleeping there, Latin says they stayed.
Both have Laban rise, kiss and bless his children, and return home; Latin "in the night" against Greek "early in the morning".
Greek adds that Jacob looked up and saw the host of God encamped; Latin has only the angels of God meeting him.
Both have Jacob say it is God's camp and name the place Mahanaim, meaning camps.
Both have Jacob send messengers ahead to Esau in Seir, the country of Edom.
Latin: "Your brother Jacob"; Greek: "Your servant Jacob". Both say he stayed with Laban until now.
Both list Jacob's oxen, donkeys, sheep and servants, and his seeking favour; Latin has him send a delegation, Greek says he has sent to tell Esau.
Both have the messengers report Esau coming to meet Jacob with four hundred men.
Latin: Jacob terrified, dividing people, flocks, sheep, oxen and camels; Greek: afraid and perplexed, dividing people, oxen and sheep, with no camels.
Both give Jacob's reasoning that if Esau strikes one company the other will escape.
Both invoke the God of Abraham and Isaac and recall the Lord's promise to do him good; Latin "Return to your land and birthplace", Greek "Hurry to the land of your birth".
Latin: Jacob is unworthy of God's mercies and faithfulness. Greek: God's righteousness and truth suffice for him. The staff and two companies agree.
Both ask deliverance from Esau for fear he will strike down mothers with children; Greek adds that Esau may strike Jacob himself.
Both recall God's promise to do him good and make his seed like the uncountable sand of the sea.
Both have Jacob sleep there that night and set aside gifts from his possessions for Esau.
Both list two hundred female goats, twenty male goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams.
Number differs: Latin has twenty bulls, Greek ten bulls. The camels, cows, donkeys and young otherwise agree.
Both have Jacob send the herds separately by his servants and tell them to go ahead and leave a space between herds.
Both have Jacob instruct the first servant what to say if Esau asks whose he is, where he goes and whose animals these are.
Both give the answer that the animals are servant Jacob's gifts to Esau and that he is behind them.
Both have Jacob give the same instruction to the first, second, third and all following the herds.
Both add that Jacob follows, and that he means to appease Esau with the gifts and perhaps be accepted.
Both say the gifts went ahead while Jacob spent that night in the camp.
Both have Jacob take his wives, maidservants and eleven sons or children and cross the Jabbok; Latin "rose early", Greek "rose in the night".
Both say Jacob brought across all that he had.
Both say Jacob was left alone and a man wrestled with him until morning.
Both have the man touch Jacob's thigh when he could not prevail; Latin says the sinew withered, Greek says the broad part of the thigh became numb.
Both have the man ask to be let go at dawn and Jacob refuse unless he blesses him.
Both have him ask Jacob's name and Jacob answer "Jacob".
Latin: strong "against" God, so he will prevail more against men. Greek: strong "with" God, and powerful with men. The name Israel is given in both.
Both have Jacob ask his name, hear "Why do you ask my name?", and be blessed there.
Both have Jacob name the place Peniel (Greek renders it Form of God) after seeing God face to face and his life being saved.
Both say the sun rose as he passed Peniel and he limped; Latin says on his foot, Greek because of his thigh.
Both give the reason Israel's sons do not eat the thigh sinew that was touched and became numb.
Both have Jacob see Esau coming with four hundred men and divide the children among Leah, Rachel and the two maidservants.
Both place the maidservants and children first, Leah and hers next, and Rachel and Joseph last.
Both have Jacob go ahead and bow to the ground seven times until he came near his brother.
Both have Esau run, embrace and kiss Jacob and weep; Latin has only Esau weeping, Greek says both wept.
Both have Esau ask about the women and children and Jacob answer that God gave them; Latin adds "Do they belong to you?", Greek says God had mercy.
Both have the maidservants and their children approach and bow.
Both have Leah and her children bow, then Joseph and Rachel last.
Both have Esau ask about the companies he met and Jacob answer that it was to find favour.
Both have Esau say he has plenty and Jacob should keep what is his.
Latin adds Jacob's "Please, not so" and "little gift" and asks Esau to be favourable; Greek has the plain offer of gifts and "you will accept me".
Both have Jacob offer the blessing or gifts because God has been generous to him, and Esau accept under pressure.
Esau proposes travelling together; Latin adds "I will accompany you on your journey", Greek says "set out and go straight ahead".
Both have Jacob say the children are tender and the flocks nursing, and driving them hard for a day would kill them all.
Both have Jacob ask Esau to go ahead while he follows slowly at the pace of the children until he reaches Seir.
Esau offers to leave some of his people with Jacob and Jacob declines, wanting only favour; Latin "There is no need", Greek "Why do that?".
Both say Esau returned that day to Seir.
Both have Jacob go to Succoth (Greek: Booths), build and pitch tents there, and name the place; Greek specifies houses and tents for his livestock.
Both have Jacob reach Salem, city of the Shechemites, in Canaan on returning from Mesopotamia; Latin says he lived beside the town, Greek that he pitched his tent before it.
Both have Jacob buy the field where he pitched his tent for a hundred lambs; Latin from the sons of Hamor, Greek from Hamor.
Both have Jacob erect an altar and call on God; Latin says "the most mighty God of Israel", Greek "the God of Israel".
Both say Dinah, Leah's daughter, went out to see the women of the land.
Latin calls Hamor a Hivite and says Shechem fell in love with her; Greek calls him a Horite and omits the love, saying only that he violated her.
Both say Shechem's soul was attached to Dinah and he spoke tenderly; Latin says he soothed her sadness, Greek that he loved her and spoke to her heart.
Both have Shechem ask his father Hamor to get the young woman for him as a wife.
Both have Jacob keep silent until his sons returned from the field; Greek says he had heard Dinah was defiled.
Both have Hamor, Shechem's father, go out to speak to Jacob.
Greek adds "Such a thing must not happen" and speaks of distress and grief; Latin has the sons very angry over a disgraceful, unlawful act in Israel.
Both have Hamor say Shechem's soul is set on their daughter and ask that she be given to him as wife.
Both propose intermarriage, giving and taking daughters; Greek adds that they take daughters "for your sons".
Both offer them the land to live in, trade and hold; Latin says it is at their disposal and to cultivate it, Greek that it is broad before them.
Both have Shechem ask for favour and offer whatever they ask; Latin has him promise it himself, Greek has "we will give".
Both have Shechem offer a large marriage payment and whatever they ask in return for the young woman as wife.
Both say Jacob's sons answered deceitfully because their sister was violated; Greek names Hamor and Dinah.
Greek names Simeon and Levi as the speakers; Latin has Jacob's sons in general, adding that it is unlawful and shameful. Both refuse an uncircumcised husband.
Both set circumcision of every male as the condition for agreement; Latin frames it as a covenant, Greek as becoming like them.
Both promise to intermarry and live among them; Latin "become one people", Greek "become one family".
Both threaten to leave if not circumcised; Latin "take our daughter", Greek "our daughters", with "if you will not listen".
Both say the proposal pleased Hamor and his son Shechem.
Both say the young man did not delay, loved the girl and was the most honoured in his father's house.
Both have them come to the city gate and speak to the men of the city.
Both say the men are peaceful, may dwell and trade in the broad land, and that they should exchange daughters in marriage.
Both give circumcision of the males as the one condition; Latin calls it the one thing delaying so great a benefit, Greek links it to becoming one people.
Latin states their goods will be ours and they will become one people; Greek asks "shall not their livestock be ours?" and says only that they will dwell with us.
Both say all agreed and every male was circumcised.
Both have Simeon and Levi attack on the third day, in pain, and kill every male; Latin has them take swords "boldly", Greek "unopposed".
Both have them kill Hamor and Shechem and take Dinah from Shechem's house; Greek adds "with the edge of the sword" and "went away".
Latin: the other sons fell upon the slain; Greek: upon the wounded. Both have them plunder the city for the violation of their sister.
Both list sheep, herds or oxen, and donkeys, and all in the houses or city and the fields taken.
Both have wives and children or people led captive; Greek adds household goods and plundering, Latin has little ones and wives.
Both have Jacob rebuke Simeon and Levi for making him hated among the Canaanites and Perizzites and fear destruction.
Both give the brothers' reply asking whether their sister should be treated like a prostitute.
Both have God tell Jacob to go up to Bethel, live there and make an altar to the God who appeared when he fled Esau.
Both have Jacob tell his household to put away foreign gods, purify themselves and change clothes; Greek adds "all who were with him".
Both have Jacob call them to Bethel to make an altar to the God who heard him in distress; Latin says he accompanied him, Greek adds that he preserved him.
Greek adds that Jacob destroyed the buried items "to this day"; Latin only says he buried the gods and earrings under the terebinth behind Shechem.
Both say the terror of God fell on the surrounding cities so they did not pursue; Greek names Israel setting out from Shechem.
Both have Jacob and all his people come to Luz, which is Bethel, in the land of Canaan.
Both have Jacob build an altar because God appeared there when he fled his brother; Latin names the place House of God, Greek Bethel, and names Esau.
Both have Rebekah's nurse Deborah die and be buried under the oak below Bethel; Latin "Oak of Weeping", Greek "Oak of Mourning", named by Jacob.
Both say God appeared to Jacob again after Mesopotamia and blessed him; Greek adds the place, Luz.
Greek adds "Your name is Jacob"; Latin adds that God called him Israel. The change of name is in both.
Latin "I am God Almighty" against Greek "I am your God"; both promise increase, nations, assemblies or peoples, and kings from his loins.
Both promise the land given to Abraham and Isaac to Jacob and his seed; Greek adds "I have given it to you; it shall be yours".
Both say God left him; Greek adds that he went up from the place where he had spoken with him.
Both have Jacob set up a stone pillar where God spoke to him and pour a drink offering and oil on it.
Both have Jacob name the place Bethel.
Latin dates the journey to springtime; Greek has Jacob draw near Chabratha and adds that her labor was hard. Rachel goes into labor on the way to Ephrath.
Both have the midwife comfort Rachel that she has another son; Latin "Do not fear", Greek "Take courage".
Greek gives only "Son of My Sorrow" and the name Benjamin; Latin gives Benoni and its meaning and the meaning of Benjamin, "Son of the Right Hand".
Both say Rachel died and was buried on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem.
Both say Jacob set up a pillar over her grave, which stands to this day.
Latin: beyond the Tower of the Flock; Greek: beyond the Tower of Gader, after leaving Bethel.
Both report Reuben lying with Bilhah and twelve sons; Latin says it did not escape his father, Greek says Israel heard and it seemed evil to him.
Both list Leah's sons: Reuben the firstborn, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun.
Both list Rachel's sons as Joseph and Benjamin.
Both list Bilhah's sons as Dan and Naphtali.
Both list Zilpah's sons Gad and Asher as born in Mesopotamia of Syria.
Latin: Mamre, the city of Arba, which is Hebron. Greek: Mamre, the city of the plain, which is Hebron in Canaan. The city's description differs.
Both give Isaac's days as one hundred eighty years.
Both say Isaac died old and full of days and Esau and Jacob buried him.
Both introduce the generations of Esau, who is Edom.
Latin: Anah is the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite. Greek: Anah is the son of Zibeon. Esau's Canaanite wives Adah and Oholibamah are otherwise the same.
Both name Basemath, daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth.
Both say Adah bore Eliphaz and Basemath bore Reuel.
Both say Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam and Korah, born in Canaan.
Both have Esau take his household and goods and leave Jacob; Latin says to another region, Greek out of the land of Canaan.
Both say their riches were too great for them to dwell together and the land could not support them.
Both say Esau lived in the hill country of Seir; Esau is Edom.
Both introduce the generations of Esau, father of Edom, in the hill country of Seir.
Both name Eliphaz, son of Adah, and Reuel, son of Basemath, as Esau's sons.
Both list Eliphaz's sons as Teman, Omar, Zepho (Sophar), Gatam and Kenaz.
Both say Timna was Eliphaz's concubine and bore Amalek, and these are descendants of Adah.
Both list Reuel's sons Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah, descendants of Basemath.
Latin: Oholibamah is daughter of Anah, daughter of Zibeon. Greek: Anah is son of Zibeon. Her sons Jeush, Jalam and Korah agree.
Both list the chiefs among Eliphaz's sons: Teman, Omar, Zepho (Sophar), Kenaz.
Both list chiefs Korah, Gatam and Amalek in the land of Edom; Latin calls them Eliphaz's sons and Adah's sons, Greek chiefs of Eliphaz and descendants of Adah.
Both list Reuel's sons and chiefs Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah, descendants of Basemath.
Both list Oholibamah's sons as chiefs Jeush, Jalam and Korah; Latin adds that she is the daughter of Anah.
Both close with Esau's sons and their chiefs; Latin adds "he is Edom", Greek "These are the sons of Edom".
Both list the sons of Seir the Horite, Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon and Anah.
Name differs: Latin Disan, Greek Rison (and Eser against Asar). Dishon, the Horite chiefs and Seir's sons in Edom agree.
Both name Lotan's sons Hori and Heman (Aiman), and his sister Timna.
Names of Shobal's sons differ: Latin Alvan, Ebal, Shepho, Onam; Greek Golon, Gaibel, Soph, Oman. Manahath agrees.
Latin: Anah found hot springs in the wilderness; Greek: Onas found Iamin. Zibeon's sons are Aiah and Anah in Latin, Aiah and Onan in Greek.
Both name Dishon and Oholibamah as Anah's children; Latin puts it as Anah having a son and daughter, Greek as his children.
Both list Dishon's sons as Hemdan (Amada), Eshban, Ithran and Cheran.
Greek lists four sons of Ezer (Asar) and Latin three; the names differ (Zaavan against Zoukam, Ioukam).
Father's name differs: Latin Dishan, Greek Rison. Sons Uz and Aran or Aram agree.
Both list the Horite chiefs Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon and Anah.
Latin: Disan, and chiefs ruled in the land of Seir. Greek: Rison, and chiefs by chiefdoms in the land of Edom. The place and names differ.
Both introduce the kings who reigned in Edom before a king reigned over Israel.
Both name Bela (Balak), son of Beor, and his city Dinhabah; Greek adds that he reigned in Edom.
Both say Bela (Balak) died and Jobab son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place.
Both say Jobab died and Husham (Asom) of the Temanites reigned.
City differs: Latin Avith, Greek Geththaim. Hadad's father's name and Moab's region or plain also differ in wording.
Both say Hadad died and Samlah of Masrekah reigned.
Both say the previous king died and Saul or Shaul of Rehoboth by the river reigned.
Both say Saul died and Baal-hanan son of Achbor reigned.
Latin: Hadar, city Pau, wife Mehetabel; Greek: Arad son of Barad, city Phogor. Names differ, and Mezahab is a daughter in Latin, a son in Greek.
Both begin the list of Esau's chiefs, Timna first; Latin lists families, places and names, Greek tribes, places, regions and nations, with differing names (Alvah / Gola, Jetheth / Jether).
Latin gives chiefs Magdiel and Iram; Greek gives Megediel and Zaphoim. Latin ends "father of the Edomites", Greek "father of Edom".
Both say Jacob lived in the land of Canaan where his father had sojourned.
Latin gives Joseph's age as sixteen; Greek gives seventeen. Latin says he accused his brothers of a very grave offense; Greek that he brought a bad report.
Both say Israel (Jacob) loved Joseph most as the son of his old age and made him a many-coloured tunic.
Both say his brothers saw their father loved him more and hated him, unable to speak peaceably to him.
Latin adds that the dream sowed the seeds of greater hatred; this Greek reading omits that clause and instead names Joseph as the dreamer.
Both have him call the brothers to hear his dream; seen / dreamed is only English wording.
Both describe binding sheaves and the brothers' sheaves bowing to his; Latin "quasi" (as if, seemed) softens it, and Greek says the sheaves turned around.
Both give the brothers' two questions about reigning and ruling; Latin frames the closing remark as dreams and words feeding envy and hatred, Greek as hating him even more.
Latin has him tell this dream to his brothers; this Greek reading has him tell it to his father and his brothers.
Both have the father rebuke him over the dream; Latin repeats that he told father and brothers, Greek adds that they would indeed come and bow.
Both have the brothers envious while the father keeps the matter in mind; Latin says he considered it silently, Greek that he kept the saying.
Both place the brothers pasturing their father's flocks at Shechem; Latin says they were staying there, Greek that they went to pasture.
Both have Israel send Joseph to his brothers at Shechem; Greek phrases it as a question and includes Joseph's reply "Here I am", which Latin places in the next verse.
Both send him to check on his brothers and the flock and report back; Latin opens with "I am ready", which Greek has in the previous verse.
Both have a man find him wandering and ask what he seeks; field / plain differs slightly.
Both have him say he seeks his brothers and ask where they pasture; only English wording differs.
Both report the man's word that they went to Dothan and Joseph finding them there.
Both have them see him afar and plot to kill him; Greek adds that they plotted wickedly.
Both have the brothers say the dreamer is coming; only English wording differs.
Both plan to kill him, cast him in a pit and claim a beast devoured him; Latin says an old cistern and what his dreams will avail, Greek one of the pits and what becomes of the dreams.
Latin has Reuben strive to deliver him; Greek says he rescued him. Greek also includes "Let us not take his life", which Latin gives in the next verse.
Both have Reuben say to shed no blood and throw him in the pit while keeping hands off, intending to return him to his father; Latin also repeats not taking his life.
Both have them strip his many-colored tunic; Latin also calls it long ("talari"), Greek adds that he was wearing it.
Both have him thrown into a pit with no water; Latin calls it old, Greek stresses it was empty.
Both have them sit to eat and see Ishmaelites from Gilead with spices, resin and stacte; Greek adds that they were taking them down to Egypt.
Both have Judah ask what is gained by killing their brother and hiding his blood; conceal / hide is only wording.
Both propose selling him to the Ishmaelites rather than lay hands on him, as he is their brother and flesh; Latin "it is better" versus Greek "come, let us sell".
Latin says they sold him for twenty silver pieces; this Greek reading says twenty pieces of gold.
Both have Reuben return to the pit and not find the boy; Greek here adds that he tore his garments, which Latin places in the next verse.
Both have Reuben tell his brothers the boy is gone and ask where he will go; Latin includes the garment tearing here, Greek has it in the previous verse.
Both have them take the tunic and stain it with the blood of a young goat they killed.
Both have them send the tunic to the father asking if it is his son's; Latin "vide" (see) versus Greek "recognize", and Greek calls it multicolored.
Both have the father recognize the tunic and say a wild animal devoured Joseph; Latin says savage beast / wild animal, Greek second verb is snatched away.
Both have him tear his clothes, wear sackcloth and mourn his son; Greek names Jacob and says many days, Latin a long time.
Both have the family try to comfort him and he refuses, saying he will go down mourning to his son; infernum / Hades, and Greek specifies sons and daughters and ends with his weeping.
Latin calls Potiphar commander of the soldiers; this Greek reading calls him the chief cook.
Both have Judah leave his brothers for an Adullamite named Hirah; turned aside / arrived as far as differs slightly.
Both have Judah see a Canaanite's daughter Shua, take her as wife and go in to her; Greek names Judah where Latin uses the verb alone.
Both have her conceive and bear a son named Er; Her / Er is a spelling difference.
Both have her conceive again and name the son Onan.
Latin adds that she stopped bearing after Shelah; Greek instead adds that she was at Chasbi when she bore them.
Both have Judah obtain a wife named Tamar for firstborn Er; gave / took differs in expression.
Both say Er was wicked before the Lord and was put to death; Latin says the Lord killed him, Greek says God did.
Both have Judah tell Onan to go in to his brother's wife and raise up seed; Latin "be joined to her", Greek "perform a brother-in-law's duty".
Both have Onan spill his seed on the ground because the offspring would not be his; Latin states children would not be born in his brother's name, Greek that he avoided giving seed to his brother.
Both say the Lord / God put him to death for what he did; Latin calls it a detestable thing, Greek says it appeared evil before God, and adds "also".
Both have Judah tell Tamar to remain a widow until Shelah grows up, fearing he too would die; Latin opens "for this reason" and says he feared, Greek that he said to himself.
Both have Judah's wife die and him go up to Timnah to the shearers with Hirah; Latin calls her the daughter of Shua, Greek names her Shua.
Both have Tamar told that her father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear sheep.
Latin has her sit at a fork in the road to Timnah; Greek has her adorn herself and sit at the gates of Ainan on that road. Also who withheld Shelah is worded differently.
Both have Judah think her a prostitute because her face was covered so he did not recognize her.
Both have Judah ask to lie with her, not knowing she was his daughter-in-law, and her ask what he will give; Greek says he turned aside to her by the way.
Both have Judah promise a young goat and her ask for a pledge until it is sent; Latin adds that she will allow what he wishes.
Both name ring, staff and a third item (bracelet / necklace) as the pledge, and she conceives; Greek says he gave them and went in to her, Latin says conception came from one act.
Both have her depart and put her widow's garments on again; Latin says she took off the dress she had assumed, Greek her veil.
Both have Judah send the goat by his Adullamite shepherd to recover the pledge, but the shepherd does not find her.
Both have him ask the local men and hear that no prostitute was there; Latin asks for the woman who sat at the fork in the road, Greek for the prostitute at Ainan.
Both have him report that he did not find her and that the local men said there was no prostitute there; Latin says none had ever sat there.
Latin has Judah say she cannot accuse them of lying; Greek has him say lest they become a laughingstock. Both agree he sent the goat and the shepherd did not find her.
Both report Tamar's fornication and Judah ordering her burned; Latin says her womb appears to swell, Greek that she is with child.
Both have her send word that she conceived by the owner of the items and ask him to recognize them; bracelet / necklace differs.
Both have Judah recognize the items, say she is more righteous because he did not give her to Shelah, and not know her again; Greek names Tamar and Judah.
Both report twins in the womb; Latin continues into the hand and scarlet thread, which Greek gives in the next verse.
Both have the midwife say "This one will come out first"; Greek here includes the hand and scarlet thread that Latin places in the previous verse.
Both have the first draw back his hand, the brother come out, and a remark about a barrier broken through, with the name Perez; Latin says she named him, Greek that he was named.
Both have the brother with the scarlet thread on his hand come out afterward and be named Zerah.
Latin calls Potiphar commander of the army; this Greek reading calls him the chief cook.
Both say the Lord was with Joseph, he prospered, and lived in his master's house; Greek names Joseph and specifies the Egyptian master.
Both say his master knew the Lord was with him and prospered all he did; directed / made prosper is only wording.
Both have Joseph find favor and be set over the household; Latin says he ministered to him, Greek that he pleased him.
Both say the Lord blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake in house and field; Greek adds that this followed his appointment and speaks of the blessing being upon all he had.
Both say the master concerned himself with nothing but his bread and that Joseph was handsome; Greek restates that he entrusted everything to Joseph.
Both have his master's wife cast her eyes on Joseph and say "Sleep with me"; Latin says after many days, Greek after these things.
Both have Joseph refuse and speak of everything entrusted to him; Latin calls it a wicked deed and completes the sentence, Greek runs on into the next verse.
Both say nothing is withheld from him except the wife, so how could he sin against God; Latin "in my power" versus Greek "above me".
Both have her press him day after day and him refuse; Latin calls it troubling and the wrongdoing, Greek says he would not obey her.
Both have Joseph enter the house to work with no one else there; Latin "without witnesses", Greek none of the household inside.
Both have her seize his garment, say "Sleep with me", and him flee leaving it; Latin specifies the edge of the garment and a cloak.
Both have her see he left his garment in her hands; Latin adds she felt rejected, Greek adds that he had fled outside.
Both have her call the household and accuse the Hebrew of coming to mock them; Latin man / Greek servant, and Greek has him say "Sleep with me".
Both have him hear her cry out, leave his garment and flee outside; only slightly fuller wording in Greek.
Latin has her keep the cloak as proof and show it to her husband; Greek has her simply leave the garments beside her until the master came home.
Both have her tell the master the Hebrew servant came in to mock her; Greek adds that he said he would sleep with her.
Both have her say he heard her cry out, left his garment beside her and fled outside.
Both have the master hear his wife and become angry; Latin says he was too ready to believe her, Greek quotes her saying this is how the servant treated her.
Both have the master put Joseph in the prison where the king's prisoners were held; prison / fortress is only wording.
Both say the Lord was with Joseph, showed him mercy and gave him favor with the chief jailer.
Both put the prisoners and all that was done in Joseph's charge; Greek names the chief jailer as subject.
Both say the jailer concerned himself with nothing because the Lord was with Joseph; Greek adds the jailer as subject and ends with the Lord prospering all Joseph did.
Both say the cupbearer and baker offended their lord; Greek names them chief cupbearer and chief baker and identifies the lord as the king of Egypt.
Both have Pharaoh angry with the chief cupbearer and chief baker; Latin explains their offices in a parenthesis, Greek calls them his two eunuchs.
Latin sends them to the prison of the commander of the soldiers; Greek puts them in custody under the jailer in the prison where Joseph had been taken.
Both have the jailer entrust them to Joseph and them remain in custody some time; ministered / attended is only wording.
Both have the two see a dream on the same night; Latin says each with a fitting interpretation, Greek says each his own dream and names them as the king's prisoners.
Both have Joseph come in the morning and see them sad / troubled.
Both have Joseph ask why their faces are sad today; Greek adds that they were Pharaoh's eunuchs in custody in his master's house.
Both have them say no one can interpret their dream and Joseph reply that interpretation is God's and ask them to tell it; wording differs slightly.
Both have the chief cupbearer tell his dream first, beginning with a vine before him; Greek adds that he told it to Joseph.
Both describe a vine with three branches budding and the grapes ripening; wording of the growth differs.
Both have him squeeze the grapes into Pharaoh's cup and give the cup to Pharaoh.
Both give Joseph's interpretation that the three branches are three days.
Both say Pharaoh will remember him within three days and restore him to his office of giving the cup.
Both have Joseph ask the cupbearer to remember him, show kindness and mention him to Pharaoh to bring him out of prison.
Both say he was stolen from the land of the Hebrews and is innocent yet put in the pit / dungeon.
Both have the chief baker see the good interpretation and tell of three baskets on his head; flour / coarse bread differs, and Greek names Joseph as addressee.
Both have all kinds of food in the top basket and birds eating it; Greek specifies food Pharaoh eats.
Both give Joseph's interpretation that the three baskets are three days.
Both foretell Pharaoh taking off his head, hanging him and birds eating his flesh; Latin says cross, Greek says tree.
Both place Pharaoh's birthday feast on the third day, where he remembers the cupbearer and baker; Greek says he remembered their offices.
Both have Pharaoh restore the cupbearer to put the cup in his hand; Latin says "the one", Greek names the chief cupbearer.
Both have the other (the baker) hanged, fulfilling the interpretation; Latin says the interpreter's truth was proved, Greek that it was as Joseph had interpreted.
Both say the cupbearer forgot Joseph; Latin adds "as prosperity followed", Greek names Joseph.
Both have Pharaoh see a dream after two years, standing by the river.
Both have seven fine, fat cows coming up out of the river; marshy places / reed grass differs in the grazing place.
Both have seven ugly, lean cows coming up; Latin says they grazed in green places on the bank, Greek that they grazed beside the other cows.
Both have the lean cows devour the fat ones and Pharaoh awake.
Both have Pharaoh sleep and dream again of seven good ears on one stalk.
Both have seven thin, blighted ears come up after them.
Both have the thin ears devour the good ones and Pharaoh awake; Greek adds that it was a dream.
Both have Pharaoh troubled, send for Egypt's interpreters and wise men, and no one interpret; terrified / troubled and the closing clause differ in wording.
Both have the chief cupbearer speak of remembering and his fault; Latin has him confess his fault, Greek says he remembers his offense today and addresses Pharaoh.
Latin has them confined in the prison of the commander of the soldiers; Greek has them put in custody in the chief cook's house.
Both say each saw a dream on the same night; Latin adds that it foretold the future.
Latin calls him servant of the commander of the soldiers; Greek calls him servant of the chief cook, and adds that he interpreted for them.
Both say events proved the interpretation: he was restored to office and the other hanged; Latin says upon a cross, Greek simply hanged.
Both have Joseph brought from prison, shaved, his clothing changed, and presented to Pharaoh; Greek adds that Pharaoh sent for him.
Both have Pharaoh say no one can interpret his dream and that he has heard Joseph can; Latin has plural dreams and says "most wisely".
Latin has Joseph say it is beyond him and God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer; Greek says without God no answer of deliverance will be given.
Both have Pharaoh begin to tell Joseph that he stood on the river bank; Greek adds that it was in his dream.
Both have seven fat, beautiful cows come up from the river and feed; Latin says cropping greenery in the marsh, Greek feeding on sedge.
Both have seven wretched, thin cows following, the like of which Pharaoh had never seen in Egypt; Greek adds that they came up from the river.
Both have the lean cows devour the earlier fat ones.
Both say the lean cows looked as ugly as before after devouring; Latin says they showed no sign of being satisfied, Greek that no one could tell they had entered the belly.
Both have him sleep again and see seven full, good ears on one stalk.
Both have seven other thin, blighted ears come up beside them.
Both have the thin ears devour the good ones and no interpreter able to explain.
Both have Joseph say Pharaoh's dream is one and God has shown Pharaoh what He is about to do.
Both say the seven good cows and ears are seven years; Latin adds that they are years of plenty and share one meaning, Greek repeats that the dream is one.
Both say the seven thin cows and blighted ears are seven years of famine.
Latin introduces how these will be fulfilled in order; Greek instead has Joseph restate that God has shown Pharaoh what He is about to perform.
Both announce seven years of great plenty throughout Egypt.
Both say seven years of famine will follow, the plenty will be forgotten, and famine will consume the land.
Both say the plenty will be lost to the famine; Latin says scarcity will destroy it, Greek that it will not be known because the famine will be very severe.
Both explain the doubled dream as certainty that God's word will come to pass and that He will act quickly; wording differs.
Both advise setting a wise man over Egypt; Latin has the king provide one, Greek commands Pharaoh to look for one.
Both advise appointing overseers to collect a fifth of the produce in the seven years of plenty; Greek adds "Let Pharaoh act".
Both have the grain gathered under Pharaoh's authority and kept in the cities; Latin adds storehouses.
Both say the food is to be reserved against the seven years of famine so the land is not destroyed.
Both say the counsel pleased Pharaoh and his servants.
Both have Pharaoh ask whether such a man with the Spirit of God can be found; Greek specifies he spoke to all his servants.
Both have Pharaoh say God has shown Joseph these things, so none is wiser; Latin puts it as a question, Greek as a statement.
Both have Pharaoh set Joseph over his house, all obeying his word, with only the throne greater.
Both have Pharaoh appoint Joseph over all Egypt; Latin "again" and a completed appointment, Greek "today".
Both have Pharaoh give Joseph his ring, a fine-linen robe and a gold chain / collar.
Latin gives the herald's proclamation that all bend the knee and know he is over Egypt; Greek mentions only that a herald proclaimed.
Both have Pharaoh say that without Joseph no one will act in all Egypt; Latin says move hand or foot at his command, Greek lift up his hand.
Latin gives the new name as Savior of the World; Greek gives Psonthomphanech. Both give the marriage to Asenath, daughter of the priest of Heliopolis.
Both say Joseph was thirty when he stood before Pharaoh and traveled through Egypt; Greek adds that he went out from Pharaoh's presence.
Both speak of the seven years of plenty and sheaves; Latin adds that the crops were gathered into Egypt's storehouses.
Greek adds that he gathered the food of the seven years and stored in each city the food of the surrounding plain; Latin says only the produce was stored in each city.
Both compare the grain to the sand of the sea beyond measure; Latin speaks of abundance equaling it, Greek of Joseph gathering it.
Both say two sons were born to Joseph before the famine, borne by Asenath, daughter of Potiphera.
Both give Manasseh's name explained by God making him forget his labors; Latin adds his father's house, Greek all his father's affairs.
Both give Ephraim's name as God making him increase in the land; Latin says of his poverty, Greek of his humiliation.
Both say the seven years of abundance in Egypt passed.
Both say the seven years of famine began as Joseph foretold, with bread in Egypt; Latin says famine prevailed over the whole world, Greek in all the land.
Both have the hungry people cry to Pharaoh for bread, and Pharaoh send them to Joseph to do whatever he says.
Both have Joseph open the storehouses and sell to the Egyptians; Latin says the famine grew daily and oppressed them, Greek that it was over all the earth.
Both have all the countries come to Egypt to buy food in the famine; Greek says they bought from Joseph and that famine prevailed in all the earth.
Both have Jacob learn that grain is sold in Egypt and ask his sons why they are idle.
Both have Jacob tell them to go down and buy food so they may live; Greek says "a little food" and "not die", Latin necessaries and "not be consumed by scarcity".
Both say Joseph's ten brothers went down to Egypt to buy grain.
Both have Jacob keep Benjamin back, fearing harm on the journey; harm / sickness differs, and Greek calls Benjamin Joseph's brother.
Both say they came among others to buy because of the famine in Canaan; Greek calls them the sons of Israel.
Both say Joseph ruled and sold grain and his brothers bowed to him; Greek adds faces to the ground, while Latin's sentence continues into the next verse.
Both have Joseph recognize them, speak harshly as to strangers, and ask where they come from; they answer Canaan, to buy food.
Both say Joseph recognized his brothers but they did not recognize him.
Both have Joseph remember the dreams and call them spies; Latin says they came to see the weak places, Greek the tracks of the country.
Both have them deny it and say they came to buy food.
Both say they are sons of one man and peaceful; Latin adds they plot no evil, Greek says they are not spies.
Both have Joseph insist they came to see the land's weakness; Latin says unprotected parts, Greek tracks of the land.
Both have them say they are twelve brothers, the youngest with their father and one gone; Latin adds sons of one man, Greek adds "today".
Both have Joseph repeat that they are spies, as he had said.
Both have Joseph swear by Pharaoh that they will not leave unless the youngest brother comes; Latin says he will test them, Greek that they will be exposed.
Both have one sent to bring the brother while the rest are held until their words are proved, or else they are spies; Latin says bound, Greek taken away.
Both have him put them in custody for three days.
Both have him say on the third day that if they do this they will live, for he fears God.
Both have him say that if they are peaceful one brother stays in prison while the rest take the grain home.
Both have him demand the youngest brother and say their words will be proved; Latin says so they do not die, Greek says otherwise they will die.
Both have them admit sin against their brother, whose anguish and pleading they ignored, and say this distress has come on them; Latin adds "deservedly".
Both have Reuben remind them he warned them not to wrong the boy and that his blood is now required.
Both say they did not know Joseph understood, since an interpreter was between them.
Both have Joseph turn away, weep, return and speak to them; Greek adds that he bound Simeon before their eyes, which Latin places in the next verse.
Both have orders to fill their sacks, restore their silver and give provisions; Latin includes Simeon being bound, which Greek has in the previous verse.
Both have them load the grain on their donkeys and depart.
Both have one open his sack at the lodging place to feed his animal and see his silver at its mouth.
Both have him tell his brothers his silver was returned, and them, astonished, ask what God has done to them.
Both have them come to Jacob in Canaan and report all that happened.
Latin says the lord of the land spoke harshly and thought them spies; Greek adds that he placed them in custody as spies.
Both have them tell him they are peaceful men; Latin adds they plot no schemes, Greek says they are not spies.
Both say they are twelve brothers of one father, one gone, the youngest with their father in Canaan.
Both report him saying he will know they are peaceful if one brother stays and the rest take food home; Greek names him the man who rules the land.
Both report that bringing the youngest will show they are not spies and secure the other brother's return and trade; Greek adds that they are men of peace.
Both have each find his bound silver in his sack and be terrified; Greek adds that their father also saw the bundles.
Latin has Jacob say Simeon is held in bonds; Greek has him say Simeon is no more. Both say Joseph is gone and Benjamin will be taken.
Both have Reuben offer his two sons' lives if he does not bring Benjamin back, asking Jacob to entrust him to his hand.
Both have Jacob refuse, saying Benjamin's brother is dead and bringing his old age down in sorrow to the grave; Latin says any misfortune, Greek says sickness.
Both say the famine was heavy on the land.
Both have them finish the Egyptian food and Jacob tell them to go and buy a little more.
Both have Judah repeat the man's warning that they will not see his face without the youngest brother; Latin adds it was under oath.
Both have Judah say that if Jacob sends the brother they will go and buy food.
Both say that otherwise they will not go, since the man said they would not see his face without the youngest brother.
Both have Israel complain that they told the man of another brother; Latin states it as a misery done to him, Greek asks why they treated him so badly.
Both have them explain the man questioned them about their father and brother, and they could not know he would say to bring their brother.
Both have Judah ask that the boy be sent so they may live and not die; Latin says we and our little ones, Greek we, you and our households.
Both have Judah pledge himself for the boy and accept lasting blame if he does not bring him back.
Both say that without the delay they could have returned a second time / twice by now.
Both have Israel tell them to take produce and gifts of resin, honey, stacte, terebinth nuts and nuts; Latin adds finest produce, a little, and storax, Greek has aromatics.
Both tell them to take double silver and return the silver found in their sacks, in case it was a mistake.
Both tell them to take their brother and go to the man.
Both have Jacob pray that God grant favor so the man releases the other brother and Benjamin; Latin ends "I shall be bereaved", Greek "as I have been bereaved, so I am bereaved".
Both have them take the gifts, double silver and Benjamin, go to Egypt and stand before Joseph.
Both have Joseph see Benjamin with them and order his steward to bring them in and prepare a noon meal.
Both have the steward do as told and bring the men into the house.
Both have them fear the returned silver is a pretext for accusing them and enslaving them and their donkeys; Latin says they were terrified there, Greek that they spoke on being brought in.
Both have them approach the steward of Joseph's house at the doorway.
Both have them address him politely and say they came down the first time to buy food.
Both say that at the lodging place they found their silver in their sacks and brought it back in full; Latin adds that they had bought the food first.
Both say they brought other silver to buy food and do not know who put the first in their sacks.
Both have the steward tell them not to fear, that their God gave them treasure, and he has their silver; Latin opens "Peace to you", Greek "May you find favor".
Both have water brought for their feet and fodder for the donkeys; Latin also mentions bringing them into the house.
Both have them prepare the gifts for Joseph's noon arrival, having heard they would eat there.
Both have Joseph enter and them present the gifts and bow to the ground.
Both have Joseph ask after their aged father and if he still lives; Latin has him greet them kindly, Greek has him ask how they are.
Greek adds Joseph's blessing "May that man be blessed by God" in response; Latin has only their answer and bowing.
Both have Joseph see Benjamin, his mother's son, ask if he is the youngest brother they spoke of, and bless him; Greek recalls their promise to bring him.
Both have Joseph moved for his brother and go to his chamber to weep; Latin says he hurried away, Greek that he was troubled and sought a place to weep.
Both have Joseph wash his face, come out, restrain himself and call for bread to be set out.
Both say they were served separately and that Egyptians could not eat with Hebrews; profane / abomination is only wording.
Both have them seated in order of age and astonished; Latin says marveled greatly, Greek that they looked at one another.
Both have portions served from Joseph's table, Benjamin's five times larger, and them drinking to drunkenness with him.
Both have Joseph order the steward to fill their sacks with as much food as they can carry and put each man's money in his sack; Latin says the top of the sack, Greek its mouth.
Both have the silver cup and the grain price put in the youngest's sack, and it was done.
Both say at dawn they were sent away with their donkeys.
Both have Joseph send the steward after them when they had gone a little way out, to ask why they repaid good with evil.
Both have the steward accuse them of stealing the cup used for drinking and divination and of doing evil; Greek puts it as questions.
Both say the steward overtook them and spoke these words.
Both have them protest at the accusation; Latin asks why their lord speaks as if they committed such a crime, Greek adds "Far be it from your servants".
Both have them say they brought back the silver found in their sacks, so would not steal silver or gold.
Both have them say that whoever's sack holds the cup shall die and the rest become slaves.
Both have Joseph's steward agree: whoever is found with it becomes his slave and the others are blameless.
Both have them hurry to lower their sacks to the ground and open them.
Both have the steward search from eldest to youngest and find the cup in Benjamin's sack.
Both have them tear their clothes, load their donkeys and return to the city; Greek says each man loaded his own.
Both have Judah and his brothers come to Joseph and fall to the ground; Latin says Judah went first and Joseph had not yet left.
Both have Joseph ask what they have done and mention divination; Latin says no one equals him in that knowledge, Greek that a man such as he practices it.
Both have Judah say they cannot answer or justify themselves, God has found their iniquity, and all are slaves, including the one with the cup.
Both have Joseph refuse to punish all, keeping only the culprit as slave and letting the rest go to their father.
Both have Judah approach and ask to speak a word, not to anger Joseph, who is next to Pharaoh.
Both have Judah recall Joseph asking whether they had a father or brother.
Both have them say they have an old father and a young son born in his old age, whose brother is dead and whom the father loves.
Both have Joseph tell them to bring the brother to him; Latin says he will set his eyes upon him, Greek that he will take care of him.
Both have them say the boy cannot leave his father, or he will die.
Both have Joseph say they will not see his face again unless the youngest brother comes.
Both say when they went up to their father they told him what Joseph said.
Both have their father tell them to go back and buy a little food.
Both have them say they cannot go unless the youngest goes down with them, or they cannot see the man's face.
Both have the father remind them that his wife bore him two sons.
Both have the father say one went away, they said a wild beast devoured him, and he has not been seen since.
Both have the father warn that if they take this one too and harm comes, they will bring his old age down in sorrow to the grave; Latin says anything, Greek sickness.
Both have Judah say that if he returns to their father without the boy, whose life is bound up with his, the father will be affected; the clause continues into the next verse.
Both say the father will die on seeing the boy absent, and they will bring his old age down in sorrow to the grave.
Both have Judah recall pledging himself for the boy and bearing guilt forever; Latin adds "let me especially be your slave", which Greek has in the next verse.
Both have Judah offer to stay as Joseph's slave in the boy's place and let the boy go up with his brothers.
Both have Judah say he cannot return to his father without the boy and witness the calamity; Greek puts it as a question and "could not bear to see".
Both have Joseph unable to restrain himself and everyone sent out; Latin says no stranger was present at the recognition, Greek that Joseph made himself known.
Both have Joseph weep aloud so the Egyptians and Pharaoh's household heard; Latin says they heard his voice, Greek that the sound reached the household.
Both have Joseph say "I am Joseph" and ask if his father lives, and the brothers cannot answer; Latin says terror, Greek says troubled.
Both have Joseph call them near and say he is Joseph, whom they sold into Egypt; Latin adds that he spoke gently.
Both tell them not to be distressed at his sale, for God sent him ahead; Latin says do not be afraid and for their preservation, Greek do not grieve and for life.
Both say it is the second year of famine with five years remaining without plowing or harvest.
Both say God sent him ahead for their survival; Latin says so they may be preserved and have food, Greek to leave and nourish a great remnant.
Both say God, not they, sent him, and made him like a father to Pharaoh, lord of his house and ruler of Egypt.
Both give the message to Jacob that God made Joseph lord of Egypt and that he should come down without delay.
Both place Jacob in Goshen near Joseph with his family and flocks; Greek names it Gesem of Arabia.
Both have Joseph promise to provide for them there through the five remaining famine years so they are not lost.
Both have Joseph say their eyes and Benjamin's see that it is his own mouth speaking.
Both have Joseph tell them to report his glory to his father and bring him down quickly.
Both have Joseph fall on Benjamin's neck and weep, and Benjamin weep likewise.
Both have Joseph kiss and weep over his brothers, after which they speak with him; Latin says they dared to speak.
Both say the news that Joseph's brothers had come reached Pharaoh's house and Pharaoh rejoiced.
Both have Pharaoh tell Joseph to have his brothers load up and go to Canaan.
Latin has them bring their father and kindred; Greek has them bring their father and their possessions. Both promise Egypt's best.
Both order wagons from Egypt for their children and wives and for bringing the father; Latin adds hurrying to come as soon as possible.
Both promise all Egypt's wealth is theirs; Latin says leave no household goods behind, Greek says do not be concerned about them.
Both say the sons of Israel did so and Joseph gave wagons and provisions for the journey.
Latin has Joseph give Benjamin three hundred silver pieces; Greek has three hundred pieces of gold. Both give five robes to Benjamin and two to the others.
Both have him send his father the same gifts with ten donkeys of Egypt's goods and as many female donkeys / mules; Latin has wheat and bread, Greek bread.
Both have Joseph send his brothers off, telling them not to quarrel on the way.
Both have them go up from Egypt to their father Jacob in Canaan.
Both have them tell Jacob that Joseph lives and rules Egypt, and Jacob not believe them; Latin adds he was like one waking from deep sleep, Greek that he was stunned.
Both have them relate everything and Jacob's spirit revive on seeing the wagons; Greek says they told what Joseph had said and the wagons were to carry him.
Both have Israel say it is enough that Joseph lives and he will go to see him before he dies.
Both have Israel set out with all he had to the Well of the Oath and sacrifice to his father Isaac's God; Latin says sacrifices (plural).
Both have God call "Jacob, Jacob" in a night vision; Latin has the reply "Here I am", Greek "What is it?".
Both have God say not to fear going down to Egypt, where He will make him a great nation; Latin "most mighty God of your father", Greek "God of your fathers".
Both promise to go down with him and bring him back, and that Joseph will close his eyes; Latin "bring you back", Greek "bring you up at last".
Latin says Pharaoh sent the wagons; Greek says Joseph sent them. Both have the sons carrying their father and families.
Both have them take their possessions from Canaan and Jacob enter Egypt with all his seed; Greek says "they took", Latin has Jacob taking them.
Both list his sons, grandsons, daughters and all descendants; Greek names sons' daughters explicitly.
Both introduce the names of Israel's sons who entered Egypt, with Reuben firstborn.
Both list Reuben's four sons; only name spelling differs.
Both list Simeon's six sons, including Shaul son of the Canaanite woman; only name spelling differs.
