Both list Levi's sons as Gershon, Kohath and Merari.
Latin gives Perez's sons as Hezron and Hamul; Greek gives Hezron and Jemuel.
Both list four sons of Issachar, starting with Tola and Phua; the third and fourth names (Job, Shimron / Jasoub, Zambram) are spelled differently.
Both list Zebulun's three sons; only name spelling differs.
Both say these are Leah's sons born in Mesopotamia of Syria with Dinah, thirty-three souls in all.
Both list seven sons of Gad; the names are spelled differently.
Both list Asher's four sons, their sister Serah, and Beriah's two sons; some names are spelled differently.
Both say these are Zilpah's sons, given by Laban to Leah, sixteen souls in all.
Both give Rachel's sons as Joseph and Benjamin.
Greek adds Manasseh's son Machir, Machir's son Gilead, and the sons of Ephraim and a grandson; Latin ends with Manasseh and Ephraim.
Latin lists ten sons of Benjamin; Greek lists three sons and makes the rest sons or grandsons of Bela and Gera.
Latin totals Rachel's descendants as fourteen persons; Greek totals eighteen souls.
Both give Hushim as Dan's son.
Both list Naphtali's four sons; only name spelling differs.
Both say these are Bilhah's sons, given by Laban to Rachel, seven souls in all.
Both give sixty-six souls entering Egypt with Jacob, not counting his sons' wives.
Latin sends Judah to announce him and have Joseph meet him in Goshen; Greek has the meeting near Heroopolis in the land of Rameses.
Both have Joseph harness his chariot, meet his father, fall on his neck and weep; Latin says the same place (Goshen), Greek Heroopolis.
Both have Israel say he can die now that he has seen Joseph alive; Latin adds he will die happy.
Both have Joseph say he will tell Pharaoh that his brothers and father's household from Canaan have come.
Both have Joseph describe them as shepherds who brought their livestock, herds and all they have.
Both anticipate Pharaoh calling them and asking their occupation.
Both tell them to answer that they have been shepherds / herdsmen from youth, to live in Goshen, since Egyptians detest / abominate shepherds; Greek names Gesem of Arabia.
Both have Joseph tell Pharaoh that his father, brothers, flocks and goods have come from Canaan and are in Goshen.
Both have Joseph present five of his brothers to Pharaoh; Latin says the youngest five, Greek five from among them.
Both have Pharaoh ask their work and them answer they are shepherds, as were their fathers.
Both have them say they came to sojourn for lack of pasture in the Canaan famine; Latin asks to be allowed in Goshen, Greek states they will live there.
Greek adds Pharaoh's order to settle them in Gesem and appoint capable men over his livestock, plus a narrative of their arrival; Latin has only "Your father and brothers have come".
Latin adds Goshen and the appointment of capable men over Pharaoh's livestock; Greek has only "settle your father and brothers in the best of the land" here.
Both have Joseph bring his father before Pharaoh, and Jacob bless him.
Both have Pharaoh ask how many are the days / years of his life.
Both have Jacob answer that his sojourning is 130 years, few and hard, short of his fathers' years.
Both have Jacob bless Pharaoh and go out.
Both have Joseph give his father and brothers a possession in the best of the land, Rameses, as Pharaoh commanded.
Both have Joseph provide for his father, brothers and household according to each one; Latin says sustained them with food, Greek allotted grain.
Both say food was lacking and famine was severe, especially in Egypt and Canaan; Latin says throughout the whole world, Greek in all the land.
Both have Joseph collect all the silver for the grain and bring it to Pharaoh's house; Greek adds that he allotted grain to them.
Both have the Egyptians come when the silver was spent, asking for bread so they do not die before him.
Both have Joseph offer bread in exchange for livestock if their silver is gone.
Both have Joseph give food in exchange for their horses, sheep, oxen and donkeys, sustaining them that year.
Both have them return the next year saying money and livestock are gone and only their bodies and land remain; Greek adds a plea not to be wiped out.
Greek adds buying them "for bread" and sowing so as to "live"; Latin adds the rhetorical question "Why should we die before your eyes?" and offers service to the king rather than slavery.
Both say Joseph bought all Egypt's land for Pharaoh amid the famine; Latin says each sold his property and he subjected it, Greek says the land became Pharaoh's.
Latin continues the verse 20 sentence about all peoples from border to border; Greek has Joseph enslaving the people across Egypt. Subjected / enslaved differs slightly.
Both exempt the priests' land and supply their allowance; Latin says the king had given them the land and they were not compelled to sell, Greek says Joseph did not buy it.
Latin has Joseph say Pharaoh now possesses them and their land; Greek has him say he has bought them and their land today for Pharaoh. Both then tell them to sow.
Both give a fifth to the king and leave four parts for seed and food for households; Latin adds "so that you may have produce".
Latin: "our preservation is in your hand," asking the lord to look on them and promising glad service; Greek: "you have saved us," stating they found favor and will be slaves.
Both establish the fifth to the king as a standing rule to this day, excepting the priests' land; Greek names Joseph as establishing it, Latin says it became law.
Both have Israel dwelling in Goshen, multiplying greatly; Latin has singular he possessing the land, Greek has they inheriting holdings there.
Both give seventeen years in Egypt and a total of 147; Greek names Jacob, Latin uses a pronoun.
Both give Jacob's request to Joseph, oath gesture and plea for mercy and truth not to be buried in Egypt; wording differs only slightly.
Both have Jacob asking to be buried with his fathers and Joseph agreeing; Latin says "from this land" and "tomb of my ancestors," Greek says "out of Egypt" and "their tomb."
Latin has Israel worship God turning toward the head of his bed; Greek has him bow in worship upon the top of his staff.
Both report to Joseph that his father is ill and that he took Manasseh and Ephraim and went; Greek names Jacob and adds "Behold."
Both tell the old man that Joseph is coming and he gathers strength and sits up; Latin says "the old man," Greek names Jacob and Israel.
Both recount God's appearing at Luz in Canaan and blessing; Latin says "God Almighty," Greek says "my God."
Both give the promise to multiply him and give the land as an everlasting possession; Latin "multitude of peoples" and Greek "assemblies of nations" differ in wording.
Both claim Ephraim and Manasseh as Jacob's own, like Reuben and Simeon; Greek adds "in Egypt" after "I came to you."
Both say later children will be Joseph's and called by their brothers' names in their inheritances.
Latin adds that it was springtime; Greek adds "of Syria" and the horse-course of Chabratha. Both have Rachel dying on the way to Ephrath, buried by the road, which is Bethlehem.
Both have Israel seeing the boys and asking who they are; Latin has a pronoun, Greek names Joseph's sons.
Both have Joseph say they are his sons given by God here, and Jacob ask for them to be brought for blessing.
Both say Israel's eyes were dim and he kissed and embraced them; Greek adds that Joseph brought them near.
Both have Israel say he was not deprived of seeing Joseph and God has also shown him his offspring.
Latin has Joseph bow face to the ground himself; Greek says "they bowed," with faces to the ground, after Joseph removed them from his knees.
Both place Ephraim toward Israel's left and Manasseh toward his right, and bring both near; only wording differs.
Both have Israel crossing his hands, right on younger Ephraim and left on Manasseh.
Latin: the fathers "walked" in God's sight; Greek: they "pleased" God. Both call God the one who nourished Jacob from youth to this day.
Both ask the angel who rescued him from evils to bless the boys, with the names called upon them; Latin says "rescued" and Greek "delivers."
Both have Joseph displeased at the right hand on Ephraim and trying to move it to Manasseh.
Both have Joseph protest that Manasseh is the firstborn and ask that the right hand be placed on his head.
Manasseh "shall multiply" in Latin but "be exalted" in Greek, and "peoples" versus "a people"; both say the younger brother will be greater.
Both give the blessing "May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh" and Ephraim set before Manasseh.
Both have Israel say he is dying but God will be with them and bring them back to their fathers' land.
Greek names Shechem as the portion given to Joseph; Latin gives only "one portion." Both say it was taken from the Amorites by sword and bow.
Both have Jacob call his sons to gather so he may tell what will befall them in the last days.
Both call the sons of Jacob to gather and hear Israel their father.
Latin praises Reuben as first in gifts and greater in authority; Greek rebukes him as hard to bear and stubbornly self-willed. "Sorrow" versus "children" also differs.
Latin: poured out like water, may you not increase; Greek: overflowed in insolence, do not boil over. Both charge him with defiling his father's bed.
Latin calls Simeon and Levi "warring instruments of iniquity"; Greek says they carried out injustice by their own choice.
Latin: they killed "a man" and undermined "a wall," and "my glory" is not in their assembly; Greek: they killed men and hamstrung a bull, and "my inward being" is not to rest on their conspiracy.
Both curse their wrath as stubborn and their anger as harsh, and both say he will divide and scatter them in Jacob and Israel.
Both have Judah praised by his brothers and his father's sons bowing; Latin has one hand on enemies' necks, Greek has hands on enemies' backs.
Latin: Judah went up "to the prey" and lies like a lion and a lioness; Greek: he went up "from a shoot" and lay like a lion and a cub.
Both have Judah binding his colt to the vine and washing his robe in wine; Latin has colt and she-donkey with "O my son," Greek has foal, donkey's colt and a tendril.
Latin: his eyes are more beautiful than wine; Greek: his eyes are joyful from wine. Both say his teeth are whiter than milk.
Both say Zebulun will dwell by the sea, at a haven for ships, extending to Sidon.
Latin calls Issachar a strong donkey lying between the boundaries; Greek says he desired what is good and rested between the inheritances.
Latin: he became a servant under tribute and the land was "excellent"; Greek: he became a tiller of the soil and the land was fertile. Both say he saw rest was good.
Both say Dan will judge his people; Latin "like another tribe in Israel," Greek "as one of the tribes of Israel."
Both make Dan a serpent by the road biting the horse's heel so the rider falls back; Latin adds "horned snake" while Greek says "lying in wait."
Both have Jacob say he awaits the Lord's salvation.
Latin has Gad, armed, fighting; Greek has a raiding band raiding Gad while he raids at their heels. The subject of the action differs.
Both say Asher's bread is rich and he will provide delicacies for kings / rulers.
Latin: Naphtali is a deer set free giving beautiful words; Greek: a spreading tree yielding beauty in its fruit.
Latin: Joseph is a growing, beautiful son, and daughters ran over the wall; Greek: a grown son, envied, with "my youngest son, return to me."
Both say Joseph was attacked and envied by archers; Latin says they provoked, quarreled and envied, Greek says they plotted, reviled and pressed him hard.
Latin: his bow rested in strength and he is the shepherd, stone of Israel; Greek: their bows were shattered and the sinews of their arms slackened. Both credit the Mighty One of Jacob.
Both speak of the God of his father blessing with heaven above and breasts and womb; Latin has the "deep lying below," Greek has "the earth that holds all things."

Latin: father's blessings strengthened by his fathers until the desire of the hills comes, on the one consecrated among his brothers; Greek: father's and mother's blessing prevailed over the mountains, on the brothers he led.
Both call Benjamin a ravenous wolf; Latin has him eat prey in the morning and divide spoil in the evening, Greek has him still eat in the morning and distribute food toward evening.
Both say the father spoke and blessed each; Latin calls them the twelve tribes of Israel, Greek says Jacob's twelve sons.
Both have Jacob ask to be buried with his fathers in the cave in Ephron's field; Latin calls it the "double cave" here, Greek only later. Gathered / added differs in wording.
Greek adds a further clause about the holding of the field and the cave acquired from the sons of Heth, and has "double cave" here; Latin has Abraham buying the field with the cave.
Both name Abraham's, Isaac's and Leah's burial there; Latin says Leah lies buried and the first burial is left as "him," Greek names Abraham and has Jacob say "I buried Leah."
Both say that when he finished charging his sons he drew his feet onto the bed, died and was added to his people.
Both have Joseph fall on his father's face, weeping and kissing him.
Both have Joseph command his servants to prepare his father; Latin says physicians with spices, Greek says embalmers and adds that they prepared Israel.
Both give forty days for embalming and seventy days of Egypt's mourning.
Both have Joseph address Pharaoh's household after mourning to ask them to speak to Pharaoh; Latin "household," Greek "officials," and Greek adds "on my behalf."
Both give Joseph's request to go up and bury his father in the tomb he dug in Canaan, then return; Latin includes "See, I am dying."
Both have Pharaoh tell Joseph to go up and bury his father as he was made to swear.
Both have Pharaoh's elders and the elders of Egypt go with Joseph; Greek adds Pharaoh's servants and names Joseph burying his father.
Both have Joseph's household and brothers going, leaving flocks and herds in Goshen; Latin adds "except the little ones," Greek adds his paternal household.
Both say chariots and horsemen went with him and the company was very great.
Both have them come to the threshing floor of Atad beyond the Jordan and mourn seven days; Latin says they held funeral rites, Greek says he mourned his father.
Both report the Canaanites' remark and the place named Mourning of Egypt; Greek adds "beyond the Jordan."
Latin: Jacob's sons did as he had commanded; Greek: his sons did this for him and buried him there.
Both have the sons carry him to Canaan and bury him in the double cave Abraham bought from Ephron opposite Mamre.
Both have Joseph return to Egypt with his brothers and all who accompanied him after burying his father.
Both have the brothers, seeing their father dead, fear Joseph will remember the wrong and repay all the evil they did.
Latin: they sent him a message that his father had commanded them; Greek: they came to Joseph saying their father gave an oath-bound charge.
Both have the brothers relay the father's plea to forgive their sin and ask pardon as servants of his father's God; Joseph weeps. Latin frames it as a direct appeal, Greek as a message to Joseph.
Latin has the brothers bow facedown to the ground; Greek omits the bowing. Both have them call themselves Joseph's slaves.
Latin: "Can we resist God's will?"; Greek: "I belong to God." Both begin "Do not fear."
Latin: God turned the evil to good to exalt Joseph and save many peoples; Greek: God planned good to bring about what is happening, feeding many people.
Both have Joseph promise to provide for them and comfort them; Latin says "your little ones" and spoke kindly and gently, Greek says "your households" and spoke to their hearts.
Both give 110 years, Ephraim's children to the third generation and Machir's sons born on Joseph's knees; Greek adds that he lived with his brothers.
Both have Joseph tell his brothers God will visit them and bring them up to the land sworn to the fathers; Latin says "after my death," Greek "I am about to die."
Both have Joseph make them swear to carry his bones from there; Greek ties carrying the bones to the time of God's visitation and names the sons of Israel.
Both have Joseph die at 110 and be prepared for burial and placed in a coffin in Egypt.
Both introduce the names of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt with Jacob, each with his household.
Both list Reuben, Simeon, Levi and Judah.
Latin gives the total from Jacob's thigh as seventy; Greek gives seventy-five. Both note Joseph was already in Egypt.
Both say Joseph, all his brothers and that whole generation died.
Both say Israel's sons multiplied and grew very strong; Latin says they filled the land, Greek says the land multiplied them.
Both say a new king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph.
Both have the king tell his people that Israel's people are numerous and stronger than they are.
Both propose dealing shrewdly with Israel lest they multiply, join enemies in war and leave the land; Latin says "oppress" and "defeat us," Greek says "deal craftily" and "make war against us."
Greek adds a third city, On, the City of the Sun, and calls the cities fortified; Latin says storage cities (tabernaculorum) and names only Pithom and Rameses.
Both say the more they were oppressed, the more Israel multiplied; Greek adds the Egyptians' loathing here, which Latin places in verse 13.
Latin: the Egyptians hated Israel and afflicted them with contempt; Greek: they oppressed them by force. The hatred is in Greek verse 12.
Both describe bitter labor in clay and brick and every task in the field; Greek adds "by force" and says the work was in the plains.
Both have the king of Egypt speak to the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah.
Both give the order to kill boys at birth and preserve girls.
Both say the midwives feared God, disobeyed the king and kept the boys alive.
Both have the king summon the midwives and ask why they kept the boys alive.
Latin adds that the Hebrew women know how to give birth themselves; Greek adds "And they bore children" and names Pharaoh as addressed. Both say they give birth before the midwives arrive.
Both say God dealt well with the midwives and the people multiplied and grew very strong.
Latin: God established households for the midwives; Greek: the midwives established households for themselves. Both give their fear of God as the reason.
Both have Pharaoh order every male thrown into the river and every female preserved; Greek specifies those born to the Hebrews.
Both have a man of Levi take a wife from his own tribe; Latin says he "went out" after this, Greek says she was one of Levi's daughters.
Both have her conceive, bear a son and hide him three months because he was beautiful; Latin has "she hid," Greek "they hid."
Both have the mother make a basket, coat it with bitumen and pitch, and put the child in it by the riverside.
Both have his sister stand watching from a distance to see what would happen.
Both have Pharaoh's daughter come to bathe, see the basket among the reeds and send her servant to fetch it.
Both have her open it, see the weeping child, take pity and say he is one of the Hebrew children.
Both have the child's sister offer to call a Hebrew woman to nurse him.
Both have Pharaoh's daughter say "Go" and the girl call the child's mother.
Both have Pharaoh's daughter hire the mother to nurse him for wages; Latin adds that she handed him over when grown, which Greek gives in the next verse.
Both have the child become Pharaoh's daughter's son and be named Moses because she drew him out of the water; Greek adds that he was brought to her when grown.
Both have Moses, grown, go out to his brothers and see an Egyptian striking a Hebrew.
Both have Moses look around, see no one, strike the Egyptian and hide him in the sand.
Both have Moses see two Hebrews fighting the next day and ask the wrongdoer why he strikes his neighbor.
Both give the man's retort about Moses as ruler and judge and the Egyptian killed yesterday, and Moses' fear that the matter is known.
Both have Pharaoh seek to kill Moses, and Moses flee to the land of Midian and sit by a well.
Both have the priest of Midian's seven daughters drawing water for their father's flocks; Greek names the father Jethro.
Both have shepherds drive the daughters away and Moses rescue them and water their sheep.
Both have the daughters return to their father Reuel, who asks why they came back so quickly.
Both have the daughters say an Egyptian rescued them from the shepherds and drew water and watered the sheep.
Both have the father ask where the man is and tell them to call him to eat bread.
Both have Moses settle with the man and take Zipporah as wife; Latin says Moses swore to live with him, Greek says the man gave her.
Latin adds a second son, Eliezer, with the explanation of his name; Greek has only Gershom and "I am a sojourner in a foreign land."
Both say the king of Egypt died after many days and Israel's groaning and cry because of labor rose to God.
Both say God heard their groaning and remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
Latin: the Lord looked on Israel and "acknowledged" them; Greek: God looked on them and "became known to them."
Both have Moses tend Jethro's sheep and come to Horeb; Latin adds driving the flock to the interior and calls it the mountain of God.
Latin says the Lord himself appeared in the flame from the bush; Greek says an angel of the Lord appeared.
Both have Moses decide to go and see the great sight of the bush not being consumed.
Both have the Lord call "Moses, Moses" from the bush; Moses' reply differs: Latin "Adsum" (Here I am), Greek "What is it?"
Both tell Moses not to come near, to remove his sandals, for the place is holy ground.
Both have God identify himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and Moses afraid to look; Latin says he hid his face, Greek says he turned it away.
Both have the Lord say he has seen his people's affliction and heard their cry because of taskmasters; Greek adds "for I know their pain," which Latin has in verse 8.
Greek lists seven nations including the Girgashites; Latin lists six without them. Otherwise both promise deliverance into a good, spacious land flowing with milk and honey.
Both say the cry of Israel has reached God and he has seen how the Egyptians oppress them.
Both have God send Moses to Pharaoh to bring his people out of Egypt; Greek adds "king of Egypt" and "land of."
Both have Moses ask who he is to go to Pharaoh and bring Israel out; Greek adds "king of Egypt" and "land of Egypt."
Both promise "I will be with you" and a sign on this mountain; Latin says you will "sacrifice" to God there, Greek says you will "serve" God.
Both have Moses ask what to say when Israel asks the name of the God of their fathers.
Both have God tell Moses to say the Lord God of the fathers sent him; this is his name forever and memorial to all generations.
Both tell Moses to gather the elders and say God has visited them and seen what happened in Egypt.
Greek lists seven nations including the Girgashites; Latin lists six without them. Both promise to bring them out of affliction to a land flowing with milk and honey.
Both have Moses and the elders go to the king to ask for a three-day journey to sacrifice; Latin has "the Lord, the God of the Hebrews," Greek "the God of the Hebrews," naming Pharaoh.
Both say God knows the king of Egypt will not let them go except by a strong hand.
Both say God will stretch out his hand and strike Egypt with wonders, after which the king will release them.
Both say God will give the people favor with the Egyptians so they do not leave empty-handed.
Both have each woman ask her neighbor and lodger for silver, gold and clothing, to put on children and despoil the Egyptians.
Latin has Moses state they will not believe him and will say the Lord did not appear; Greek makes it conditional ("if they do not believe"), ends with "what shall I say to them?" and says "God."
Both have the Lord ask what is in Moses' hand, and he answers a staff.
Both have the staff thrown to the ground, becoming a snake, and Moses fleeing.
Both have the Lord tell Moses to grasp the snake by the tail, and it becomes a staff in his hand.
Both give the purpose: that they may believe the Lord, the God of their fathers, has appeared to him.
Both have Moses put his hand into his bosom / cloak and bring it out like snow; Latin adds "leprous."
Both have the hand put back and drawn out restored to the color of his flesh.
Both say that if they do not believe the first sign, they will believe the latter sign.
Both say if they do not believe the two signs, Moses is to pour river water on dry ground and it becomes blood.
Both have Moses plead that he is not eloquent, with a slow tongue; Latin says since yesterday and the day before, Greek says never capable, before or since.
Both have the Lord ask who made the mouth, the deaf and blind, and say it is he; Latin says "mute and deaf," Greek "hard of hearing or deaf," and adds "God."
Both have God promise to teach Moses what to say; Latin "I will be in your mouth," Greek "I will open your mouth."
Both have Moses ask God to send another; Latin "send whom you will send," Greek "appoint another capable person."
Both have the Lord angry, pointing to Aaron the Levite who will meet him and rejoice; Latin says Aaron is eloquent, Greek says he will speak for you.
Both have Moses put God's words in Aaron's mouth; Latin: God will be in both mouths and show what to do; Greek: God will open both mouths and teach them.
Both say Aaron will speak to the people for Moses, be his mouth, and Moses will stand to him in matters of God.
Both tell Moses to take the staff for the signs; Greek identifies it as the one that was turned into a serpent.
Both have Moses ask Jethro to return to his brothers in Egypt to see if they live, and Jethro bid him go in peace / health.
Greek begins with the statement that after many days the king of Egypt died, which Latin lacks here; otherwise both have the Lord tell Moses in Midian to return since those seeking his life are dead.
Both have Moses take wife and sons and return to Egypt with the staff of God; Latin sets them on a donkey, Greek on beasts of burden.
Both have the Lord tell Moses to do all the wonders before Pharaoh, who will be hardened and not release the people.
Both give the message to Pharaoh: Israel is my firstborn son.
Latin: "Release my son"; you refused; I will kill your firstborn. Greek: "Let My people go"; if you refuse, I will kill your firstborn. Son / people and past refusal / condition differ.
Latin says the Lord met him at the lodging place and sought to kill him; Greek says an angel of the Lord did.
Latin: Zipporah says "You are a bridegroom of blood to me"; Greek: "The blood of my child's circumcision has stopped." The words of her declaration differ.
Latin: he let him go after she said "bridegroom of blood" because of the circumcision; Greek: he went away from him because she said the blood of the circumcision has stopped.
Both have the Lord send Aaron to meet Moses in the wilderness, meeting at the mountain of God and kissing.
Both have Moses tell Aaron all the Lord's words and the signs he had commanded.
Both have them gather the elders of Israel.
Both have Aaron speak all the Lord's words to Moses and perform the signs before the people.
Both say the people believed, learned that God had visited them and seen their affliction, and bowed in worship; Latin says they "heard," Greek says they "rejoiced."
Both give the demand to release the people to go into the wilderness; Latin says "sacrifice to Me," Greek says "hold a feast for Me."
Both have Pharaoh ask who the Lord is, say he does not know him, and refuse to release Israel.
Both have them say God called them to a three-day journey to sacrifice, lest evil befall; Latin says "plague or sword," Greek says "death or slaughter."
Both have the king ask why Moses and Aaron draw the people from their work and tell them to go back to their burdens.
Both have Pharaoh note the numerous people and deny rest; Latin asks "how much more if you give them rest," Greek says "Let us not give them rest."
Both have Pharaoh command the taskmasters and the people's officers; Latin says overseers and adds "that day," Greek says scribes.
Both say straw is no longer to be given for bricks; they must gather it themselves.
Both impose the same brick quota, not reduced, since they are idle and cry out to go sacrifice.
Both order heavier work so they pay no heed to false / empty words.
Both have the taskmasters and officers tell the people that Pharaoh will no longer give straw.
Both tell them to gather straw wherever they can find it, with no reduction in their work.
Both say the people scattered through the land of Egypt to gather straw / stubble.
Both have the taskmasters press them to complete each day's work as when straw was supplied.
Both have Israel's officers flogged over the unfinished brick quota; Latin says "yesterday or today" and Pharaoh's taskmasters, Greek says the quota "including today's" and calls them scribes.
Both have Israel's officers cry to Pharaoh asking why he treats his servants this way.
Both complain that no straw is given yet bricks are demanded and they are flogged; Latin says the people are treated unjustly, Greek says "you will wrong your own people."
Both have Pharaoh call them idle, which is why they say to go and sacrifice.
Both tell them to go and work: no straw, but the quota of bricks must be delivered.
Both say Israel's officers saw they were in trouble because their daily bricks were not to be reduced.
Both have them meet Moses and Aaron as they leave Pharaoh; Latin says Moses and Aaron stood opposite, Greek says they were coming to meet them.
Both have them ask the Lord / God to look and judge, since Moses and Aaron made their smell foul before Pharaoh and put a sword in his hand.
Both have Moses return to the Lord and ask why he afflicted / harmed the people and why he sent him.
Both have Moses say Pharaoh has harmed the people since he spoke in God's name, and God has not rescued them.
Both say Pharaoh will let them go and drive them out by a strong hand; Latin has "mighty hand," Greek "uplifted arm."
Both introduce God speaking to Moses: "I am the Lord."
Both say God appeared to the patriarchs without making his name known; Latin says "God Almighty" and names Adonai, Greek says "their God" and the name Lord.
Both say God made a covenant to give them Canaan, the land where they sojourned as strangers.
Both say God heard Israel's groaning under the Egyptians and remembered the covenant; Latin says "My covenant," Greek "your covenant," and the Egyptians "oppressed" versus "enslave."
Both promise to bring them out, deliver them from slavery and redeem them with an uplifted arm and great judgments; Latin has "prison of labor," Greek "domination," and Greek adds "Go, say."
Both say God will take them as his people, be their God, and they will know he brought them out of Egyptian oppression.
Both say God will bring them into the land he swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and give it as a possession / inheritance.
Both say Moses told Israel but they did not listen because of discouragement and hard labor.
Both tell Moses to go in to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, so that he lets Israel leave his land.
Both have Moses say Israel did not listen to him, so how will Pharaoh; Latin says "uncircumcised in lips," Greek says "ineloquent."
Both have the Lord charge Moses and Aaron regarding Pharaoh so that Israel is sent out of Egypt; Latin also names a command to the children of Israel.
Both list Reuben's sons Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron and Carmi; Greek closes with "the kindred of Reuben," which Latin places in verse 15.
Both list Simeon's sons; Latin opens with Reuben's clans and calls Shaul's mother a Canaanite woman, Greek a Phoenician woman.
Both name Levi's sons Gershon, Kohath and Merari and give Levi's life as 137 years.
Both name Gershon's sons Libni and Shimei by their families.
Both name Kohath's sons Amram, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel; Latin gives Kohath's life as 133 years, Greek as 130.
Both name Merari's sons Mahli and Mushi, and these as Levi's families.
Greek adds their sister Miriam among Amram's children and gives his age as 132; Latin gives Aaron and Moses only and 137 years.
Latin names three sons of Uzziel (Mishael, Elzaphan, Sithri); Greek names two (Elzaphan and Sithri).
Both have Aaron marry Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, who bore Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.
Both name Korah's sons Assir, Elkanah and Abiasaph.
Both have Eleazar marry one of Putiel's daughters, who bore Phinehas, and conclude with the heads of the Levite families.
Both identify Aaron and Moses as those the Lord told to bring Israel out of Egypt by their companies / forces.
Both identify Moses and Aaron as those who spoke to Pharaoh to bring Israel out of Egypt.
Both have the Lord say "I am the Lord" and tell Moses to speak to Pharaoh all that he says.
Both have Moses ask how Pharaoh will listen to him; Latin says his lips are uncircumcised, Greek says he is weak-voiced.
Both have the Lord make Moses as God to Pharaoh, with Aaron his prophet.
Both tell Moses to speak all that is commanded and Aaron to speak to Pharaoh to let Israel leave his land.
Both have God harden Pharaoh's heart and multiply signs and wonders in Egypt.
Both say Pharaoh will not listen and God will lay his hand on Egypt and bring Israel out; Latin says "army" and "very great judgments," Greek says "with My power and great vengeance."
Both say the Egyptians will know he is the Lord by his hand over Egypt bringing Israel out; Latin speaks of what he has done, Greek of when he stretches out his hand.
Both say Moses and Aaron did as the Lord commanded.
Both give Moses as eighty and Aaron as eighty-three when speaking to Pharaoh.
Both introduce the Lord speaking to Moses and Aaron.
Both tell Aaron to throw down his staff before Pharaoh to become a snake / dragon; Greek adds the ground and Pharaoh's attendants.
Both have Moses and Aaron do as commanded and the staff become a snake / dragon before Pharaoh and his servants; Latin says Aaron "took" it, Greek says he "threw" it.
Both have Pharaoh call the wise men and sorcerers, who do the same by Egyptian incantations.
Both have each throw down a staff becoming serpents / dragons, and Aaron's staff swallows theirs.
Both say Pharaoh's heart was hardened and he did not listen as the Lord said; Latin "hardened," Greek "grew strong."
Both say Pharaoh's heart is heavy and he will not let the people go.
Both tell Moses to meet Pharaoh at the river in the morning, holding the staff that turned into a serpent.
Both give the demand to release the people into the wilderness and note Pharaoh has not listened; Latin says "sacrifice," Greek says "serve."
Both say the Lord will strike the river's water with the staff and it will turn to blood.
Both say the fish will die and the water stink; Latin says the Egyptians will suffer drinking it, Greek says they will be unable to drink it.
Both have Aaron stretch out his hand over Egypt's waters to turn them to blood, in wood and stone; Latin gives this as part of the command, Greek as narrated fact.
Both have Moses and Aaron strike the river before Pharaoh and his servants, and it turned to blood.
Both say the fish died, the river stank, the Egyptians could not drink, and blood was throughout Egypt.
Both say the Egyptian sorcerers did the same, and Pharaoh's heart was hard so he did not listen.
Both say Pharaoh turned and went into his house, taking no notice even of this.
Both say all the Egyptians dug around the river for drinking water since they could not drink the river's water.
Both have the Lord tell Moses to demand Pharaoh release his people; Latin says "sacrifice to Me," Greek says "serve Me."
Both say if Pharaoh refuses, God will strike all his territory with frogs.
Both describe frogs coming into houses, bedrooms, beds, servants' houses and ovens; Latin adds the remnants of food, Greek says dough.
Both say the frogs will come upon Pharaoh, his people and his servants.
Both tell Aaron to stretch out over the rivers and marshes to bring up frogs; Greek specifies the staff in his hand.
Both say Aaron stretched out his hand over Egypt's waters and the frogs came up and covered the land.
Both say the sorcerers did the same and brought frogs up over Egypt.
Both have Pharaoh ask Moses and Aaron to pray for removal of the frogs and promise to let the people sacrifice.
Both have Moses ask Pharaoh to set the time to pray, so the frogs leave and remain only in the river.
Both have Pharaoh say "Tomorrow" and Moses agree so Pharaoh will know God's uniqueness; Latin "none like the Lord our God," Greek "no other besides the Lord."
Both say the frogs will leave Pharaoh, his houses, servants and people and remain only in the river.
Both have Moses cry to the Lord about the frogs after leaving Pharaoh; Latin says the promise he had made, Greek says the appointed limit Pharaoh had set.
Both say the Lord did as Moses said and the frogs died in houses, villages and fields.
Both say the frogs were gathered in great heaps and the land stank.
Both say Pharaoh, seeing relief, made his heart heavy and did not listen, as the Lord had said.
Both have Aaron strike the dust to produce gnats throughout Egypt; Greek specifies the gnats come on people and four-footed animals.
Both have Aaron strike the dust, and the gnats come on people and animals and from all the dust of Egypt.
Both say the sorcerers tried to bring forth gnats but could not, and the gnats were on people and animals.
Both have the sorcerers say "This is the finger of God," yet Pharaoh's heart is hardened and he does not listen.
Both tell Moses to rise early and confront Pharaoh at the water with the demand to release the people; Latin says "sacrifice to Me," Greek says "serve Me in the wilderness."
Both threaten flies upon Pharaoh, his servants, people and houses; Latin says "every kind of fly" of different kinds, Greek says dog-flies.
Both set Goshen apart so there are no flies there; the closing differs: Latin "I am the Lord in the midst of the land," Greek "the Lord of all the earth."
Both have God set a distinction between his people and Pharaoh's, with the sign to occur tomorrow.
Both say the Lord did so and a great swarm of flies came into Pharaoh's and his servants' houses and ruined the land.
Both have Pharaoh tell Moses and Aaron to sacrifice to their God within the land.
Both have Moses say it cannot be done because the Egyptians would stone them for sacrificing what they hold abominable.
Both have Moses propose a three-day journey into the wilderness to sacrifice as the Lord commanded.
Both have Pharaoh agree to let them sacrifice in the wilderness if they do not go far, and ask for prayer.
Both have Moses promise to pray so the flies leave tomorrow, and warn Pharaoh not to deceive again.
Both say Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to God / the Lord.
Both say the Lord did as Moses said and removed the flies so that not one remained.
Both say Pharaoh made his heart heavy this time also and did not release the people.
Both have the Lord send Moses with the demand to release the people; Latin says "sacrifice to Me," Greek says "serve Me."
Both open the warning: if Pharaoh still refuses and holds the people.
Both threaten a very grievous plague on the livestock; Latin says the Lord's hand is on fields and animals, Greek says on livestock in the plains with a great mortality.
Both have God distinguish Israel's property from Egypt's so nothing of Israel's perishes; Latin says possessions, Greek says livestock.
Both have the Lord appoint a time: tomorrow he will do this in the land.
Both say all the Egyptians' livestock died the next day but none of Israel's.
Both say none of Israel's livestock died and Pharaoh's heart grew heavy; Latin says Pharaoh sent to see, Greek says he saw.
Both have Moses scatter handfuls of ashes / soot from a furnace toward heaven before Pharaoh; Greek adds his attendants.
Both say the dust will cause boils and blisters on people and animals throughout Egypt; wording of the dust and the blisters varies.
Both have ashes / soot scattered toward heaven by Moses, causing boils on people and animals; Latin says they took it and stood before Pharaoh, Greek says he took it.
Both say the sorcerers could not stand before Moses because of the boils on them and throughout Egypt.
Both say the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart and he did not listen, as the Lord had told Moses.
Both repeat the morning command to stand before Pharaoh and demand release; Latin says "sacrifice to Me," Greek says "serve Me."
Both say God will send all his plagues this time upon Pharaoh, his servants and people, that he may know none is like him.
Both say God will stretch out his hand and strike Pharaoh and his people with death / plague so they are removed from the earth.
Latin: "I have set you in place" to show his strength; Greek: "you were preserved" for this purpose. Both add that his name be proclaimed through the earth.
Both ask whether Pharaoh still refuses to release the people; Latin "hold back" and Greek "act against My people."
Both announce very heavy hail tomorrow such as Egypt has never had since its founding.
Both warn Pharaoh to gather his livestock lest people and animals in the fields die; Latin says those not gathered, Greek says those who do not enter a house.
Both say those among Pharaoh's servants who feared the Lord's word brought their animals into houses; Latin also mentions their servants.
Both say those who disregarded the Lord's word left their animals in the fields; Latin also mentions their servants.
Both have the Lord tell Moses to stretch his hand toward heaven so hail falls on people, animals and plants in Egypt.
Both have thunder and hail from the Lord and fire / lightning across the earth; Latin says Moses stretched his staff, Greek says his hand.
Both say hail mingled with fire, greater than ever in Egypt since it became a nation.
Both say the hail struck people and animals, every plant and shattered the trees throughout Egypt.
Both say only in Goshen, where Israel's sons were, no hail fell.
Both have Pharaoh confess he has sinned, the Lord is righteous, and he and his people are wicked / ungodly.
Both have Pharaoh ask for prayer so the thunder and hail cease and he will let them go; Greek adds "fire" and "for me."
Both have Moses promise to spread out his hands and the thunder will cease so Pharaoh knows the earth is the Lord's; Latin says no more hail, Greek says no more hail and rain.
Both have Moses say he knows Pharaoh and his servants do not yet fear the Lord.
Both say the flax and barley were struck; Latin says the barley was green and the flax had formed seedpods, Greek says barley was standing ready and flax setting seed.
Both say the wheat and spelt were not struck because they were late crops.
Both have Moses leave the city and spread his hands to the Lord, and the thunder, hail and rain ceased.
Both have Pharaoh see the storm cease and sin again; Greek adds that he made his and his attendants' hearts heavy, which Latin has in verse 35.
Both say Pharaoh did not release Israel as the Lord had said; Latin says the hearts of Pharaoh and his servants were heavy and hardened, Greek says only Pharaoh's heart was hardened.
Both have the Lord say he has hardened Pharaoh's and his servants' hearts for the sake of the signs; Latin says to perform them in Pharaoh, Greek says they will come upon them in succession.
Both give the aim of telling descendants what signs God performed and knowing he is the Lord; Latin says he "crushed" the Egyptians, Greek says he "mocked" them.
Both ask how long Pharaoh will refuse and demand release of the people; Latin says "submit to Me" and "sacrifice," Greek says "show Me reverence" and "serve."
Both warn that if Pharaoh refuses to release the people, locusts come tomorrow into all his territory.
Both say the locusts will cover the land and devour what the hail left, including the trees.
Both say the locusts will fill the houses of Pharaoh, his servants and all Egypt as never seen by the fathers, and Moses went out.
Both have Pharaoh's servants ask how long this trouble will last and urge sending the men to worship their God, since Egypt is ruined; Latin asks "Do you not see," Greek "Do you wish to know."
Both have Moses and Aaron brought back and Pharaoh ask who will go; Latin says "sacrifice to the Lord your God," Greek says "serve your God."
Both list who will go, including elders, sons, daughters, flocks and herds, for the Lord's festival; Latin says "little ones," Greek says "young men."
Latin: Pharaoh says he will release them as surely as the Lord is with them, since they plot evil; Greek: he asks whether he should also send their household, as evil lies before them.
Both have Pharaoh refuse, allow only the men to go and drive them out; Latin says "sacrifice," Greek says "serve God."
Both have the Lord tell Moses to stretch out his hand for locusts to devour what the hail left; Greek adds the fruit of the trees.
Latin: a scorching wind brings the locusts after Moses stretches his staff over Egypt; Greek: a south wind after Moses raises his staff toward heaven.
Both say the locusts settled throughout Egypt in unprecedented numbers, never to be matched.
Both say the locusts covered the land and devoured all vegetation and fruit the hail left, leaving nothing green.
Both have Pharaoh hurriedly call Moses and Aaron and confess he has sinned against the Lord and against them.
Both have Pharaoh ask for forgiveness this once and for prayer to remove this death.
Both say Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to the Lord / God.
Both have a very strong wind lift the locusts into the Red Sea, leaving none; Latin says a west wind, Greek a wind from the sea.
Both say the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart and he did not release Israel.
Both have the Lord tell Moses to stretch his hand toward heaven for darkness that can be felt.
Latin has dreadful darkness over the land; this Greek reading has darkness, gloom and a tempest. Both date it to three days.
Latin says no one moved from his place; Greek adds three days and says no one rose from his bed. Both give Israel light where they lived.
Latin says sacrifice to the Lord and only sheep and herds remain; Greek says serve the Lord your God, and your household goes. Latin has parvuli (little ones).
Both have Moses demanding sacrifices and burnt offerings to offer to the Lord our God; the order of the offerings and the purpose clause differ slightly.
Both say all livestock go with them and not a hoof remains, since they are needed for worship and the offering is not known until arrival; the wording is looser in Latin.
Both say the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart and he was unwilling to let them go; refused / unwilling is only English wording.
Both have Pharaoh telling Moses to leave and not see his face again, on pain of death on the day he appears; wording differs only slightly.
Latin has Moses agree it will be as Pharaoh said, and he will not see his face; Greek says you have spoken and he will not appear before his face.
Both announce one more plague and release; Greek adds that Pharaoh will drive them out altogether, with everything, while Latin says he will compel them to depart.
Latin says ask friend and neighbor for silver and gold articles; Greek adds speaking secretly in the people's hearing and also asking for clothing.
Both say the Lord gave the people favor and Moses was very great. Greek adds that they lent to them; Latin has the favor as future and names Moses before Pharaoh's servants and the people.
Both give the Lord's words about midnight; Latin says He will go out into Egypt, Greek says enter the midst of Egypt, and Greek names Moses as speaker.
Both say every firstborn in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh's on the throne to the servant woman's at the mill, and all the animals' firstborn.
Both announce a great cry throughout Egypt such as never was and never will be again.
Both say not a dog will make a sound among Israel, so that the distinction between Egyptians and Israel is known; Latin says you may know the wonder, Greek says see how wonderfully.
Both have servants bowing and telling Moses to go out. Greek adds that Moses went out from Pharaoh in anger, which Latin places in the next verse; Latin says we will depart, Greek I will go out.
Latin begins with Moses leaving Pharaoh exceedingly angry (Greek has this at the end of 11:8); Latin says many signs be done, Greek has the Lord multiplying His signs and wonders.
Both say Moses and Aaron did the wonders and the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart; Latin says wonders that are written, Greek says all these signs and wonders in Egypt.
Both say the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt; Greek's 'saying' is only a speech marker.
Both call this month the beginning of months and the first of the year; Latin says first among the months, Greek says first month of the year for you.
Both command taking a lamb or sheep on the tenth day by households; Greek adds one sheep for each household, and Latin has lamb (agnum) where Greek has sheep.
Both say a small household joins its nearest neighbor and counts persons for the portion; Latin says sufficient to eat the lamb, Greek says each person's portion reckoned.
Latin has the lamb be a one-year male and adds that a young goat may also be taken; Greek says take it from the lambs or the kids. Both require unblemished.
Both say keep it until the fourteenth day and the whole assembly slaughters it toward evening; sacrifice / slaughter is only English wording.
Both say they take some of the blood and put it on the doorposts and lintel of the houses where they eat it.
Latin has unleavened bread with wild lettuces; Greek has bitter herbs. Both have the meat roasted over fire that night.
Both forbid raw or water-boiled meat and require roasting, with head, feet and inner parts; Latin says feet and entrails, Greek legs and inner parts.
Greek adds that they shall not break a bone of it; Latin lacks this clause. Both say none remains until morning and leftovers are burned.
Latin glosses Phase as 'transitus' (passing over) and calls it the Lord's Passover; Greek lacks the gloss. The dress and haste instructions agree.
Both have the Lord passing through Egypt that night and striking every firstborn; Latin says execute judgments on the gods of Egypt, Greek says execute vengeance.
Latin has the Lord pass over them; Greek has Him shelter them. Both say the blood is a sign and no destroying plague will fall on them.
Both make the day a memorial and a feast to the Lord for all generations; Latin ends 'everlasting observance', Greek 'perpetual statute' and repeats celebrate.
Latin says no leaven in houses on the first day; Greek says remove leaven from the houses from the first day. Both threaten that person perishing or being destroyed from Israel.
Both make the first and seventh days holy with no work except food preparation; Greek says no servile work and what must be done for each person.
Latin says observe the unleavened bread and leading out your army; Greek says keep this commandment and bring out your host. Both end with a perpetual observance.
Both fix unleavened bread from the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month until the evening of the twenty-first.
Both say no leaven for seven days, and whoever eats leavened is cut off from the assembly of Israel, stranger or native; perish / be destroyed is only English wording.
Both have Moses calling the elders to take an animal or sheep per family and slaughter the Passover; Greek says council of elders, Latin says animal.
Both command dipping a bunch of hyssop in the blood at the threshold, marking the lintel and doorposts, and staying inside until morning.
Both say the Lord passes through to strike, sees the blood, and does not let the destroyer enter; Latin adds 'and harm you', Greek says 'to strike'.
Both command keeping this word as a statute for you and your children forever.
Both say when you enter the land the Lord gives, as promised, keep this observance; Latin says ceremonies (plural), Greek says this service.
Both give the children's question about this observance; religious observance / service is only English wording.
Latin calls it the sacrifice of the Lord's passing over, when He passed over the houses; Greek says He sheltered the houses. Both end with the people bowing in worship.
Both say Israel did as the Lord commanded Moses and Aaron; Greek states it twice (did so, so they did).
Both have the Lord striking every firstborn at midnight, from Pharaoh's to the captive woman's; Latin says in prison, Greek says in the pit.
Both say Pharaoh, his servants and the Egyptians rose in the night, and a great cry arose because every house had someone dead.
Latin has Pharaoh say sacrifice to the Lord; Greek has serve the Lord your God. The call to rise and leave is parallel.
Both have Pharaoh telling them to take sheep and cattle and bless him; Latin adds 'as you requested' (ut petieratis).
Both have the Egyptians pressing the people to leave quickly because they feared death; Latin says 'we will all die', Greek 'we are all dying'.
Both say the people took dough before it was leavened and carried it on their shoulders in garments; Latin says bound in cloaks, Greek kneaded batches wrapped in garments.
Both say Israel did as Moses commanded and asked the Egyptians for silver, gold and clothing; Latin adds 'much' clothing (plurimam).
Both say the Lord gave the people favor and they lent to them; Latin says they despoiled the Egyptians, Greek says they plundered them.
Both give about 600,000 men on foot from Rameses to Succoth; Latin says besides little ones (parvulis), Greek says apart from the household company.
Both have a mixed multitude going up with them, with flocks and herds; Latin says innumerable and animals of diverse kinds, Greek says great and very many livestock.

Both say they baked unleavened cakes from the dough because the Egyptians drove them out. Latin adds that the dough could not be leavened for lack of delay; Greek says no provisions had been prepared.
Latin says on that very day the Lord's army left, after these things were completed; Greek says after the four hundred and thirty years, with no mention of the same day.
Both call it a night observed or kept vigil for the Lord for Israel's generations; Latin says when He led them out, Greek says to bring them out.
Both have the Lord speaking to Moses and Aaron and barring any foreigner from the Passover; Latin says observance (religio), Greek says law.
Latin speaks of a purchased slave who is circumcised and then eats; Greek speaks of a household slave or one bought with money, and says you shall circumcise him.
Both bar the outsider and hired worker from eating it; Latin says stranger (advena), Greek says resident alien.
Both require eating in one house, taking none of the meat outside, and not breaking a bone.
Both say the whole assembly or congregation of Israel shall keep it; keep / observe is only English wording.
Latin says a foreigner joining the settlement has every male circumcised first, then is like a native; Greek says a sojourner comes to observe it and he approaches after circumcision.
Both give one law for the native and the sojourner or settler living among them.
Both say Israel did as the Lord commanded Moses and Aaron; Greek states it twice.
Both say the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt that day; Latin says by their companies (turmas), Greek says with their host.
Both command consecrating every firstborn of person and animal; Latin says all of them are Mine, Greek says it is Mine.
Both have Moses telling them to remember the day they left slavery by a strong hand; Latin says you shall eat no leavened bread, Greek says no leaven shall be eaten.
Both say today you go out in the month of new crops or new grain; crops / grain is only a nuance.
Latin names five peoples (Canaanite, Hittite, Amorite, Hivite, Jebusite); Greek names seven, adding the Girgashites and Perizzites. Both have the oath and milk and honey.
Latin says unleavened bread for seven days; Greek says six days. Both put the festival of the Lord on the seventh day.
Both say unleavened bread for seven days with no leaven seen with you or in your territory; Latin phrases it as one prohibition, Greek as two.
Latin has the son told 'This is what the Lord did for me'; Greek has 'It is because of this that the Lord God acted for me'.
Both say it is a sign on the hand and a memorial before the eyes, so the Lord's law is in your mouth, since He brought you out with a strong hand.
Both command keeping this observance or law at the appointed time, year after year.
Both have the Lord bringing you into the land of the Canaanites as He swore and giving it to you; Latin adds 'and to you' with your fathers, Greek adds 'your God'.
Both command setting apart for the Lord whatever opens the womb among the males and livestock; the sentence structure differs.
Latin says if the donkey is not redeemed with a sheep, kill it; Greek says if you do not exchange it, redeem it. The human firstborn is redeemed in both.
Both give the son's question and the answer that the Lord brought them out of Egypt with a strong hand; strong / mighty is only English wording.

Both recount Pharaoh's refusal, the death of Egypt's firstborn, and the sacrifice of male firstborn with redemption of sons; Latin says Pharaoh was hardened (induratus), Greek says stubbornly refused.

Both make it a sign on the hand and a reminder before the eyes, because of the strong hand that led out of Egypt; Latin says something hung between your eyes, Greek a fixed reminder, and Latin says led us, Greek you.
Both say God did not lead them by the near Philistine road, fearing they would return to Egypt on seeing war; Greek quotes God's words, Latin reports His reasoning, and Latin says 'although near'.
Latin says Israel went up armed (armati); Greek says they went up in the fifth generation. Both have the wilderness road by the Red Sea.
Both say Moses took Joseph's bones because Joseph had made Israel swear to carry them; God / the Lord visiting is only English wording.
Both have departure from Succoth and camp at Etham; Latin says at the far edge of the wilderness, Greek says beside the wilderness.
Both have the pillar of cloud by day and fire by night to show the way; Latin has the Lord going before and guiding at both times, Greek says God led them.
Both say the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not fail before the people.
Latin names Pi-hahiroth as the camp site opposite Baal-zephon; Greek says opposite the settlement. Both place it between Migdol and the sea.
Latin has Pharaoh say Israel is hemmed in by the land; Greek has him say to his people that they are wandering in the land. Both say the wilderness shut them in.
Both have the Lord hardening Pharaoh's heart so he pursues, being glorified through Pharaoh and his army, and the Egyptians knowing He is the Lord.
Both report the people fled and Pharaoh and his servants changed their minds, asking why they released Israel from serving; Latin says 'What have we chosen to do', Greek 'What have we done'.
Both say Pharaoh harnessed his chariot or chariots and took all his people; Latin uses singular currum, Greek plural, and Greek names Pharaoh.
Both have six hundred chosen chariots with the army's commanders; Latin adds every other chariot in Egypt, Greek says all the Egyptians' horse force.
Both have the Lord hardening Pharaoh's heart so he pursued Israel, who went out with a high hand; Greek adds his attendants, and Latin says 'but they had gone out'.
Both say the Egyptians found Israel camped by the sea. Latin adds they followed the tracks of those ahead and names Pi-hahiroth; Greek adds horsemen and says opposite the settlement.
Both have Israel seeing the Egyptians behind them, being afraid and crying to the Lord; Greek adds the Egyptians camped, and names the sons of Israel again.
Both have the people asking Moses whether there were no graves in Egypt that he brought them to die; the closing question differs in wording (why did you choose / what have you done).
Both recall the earlier request to be left to serve the Egyptians and say serving them is better than dying in the wilderness.
Latin has Moses say do not fear and see the Lord's mighty deeds; Greek says take courage and see salvation from God. Both say the Egyptians will never be seen again.
Both have the Lord asking why Moses cries out and telling Israel to set out.
Both command lifting the staff, stretching out the hand over the sea and dividing it so Israel can go through on dry ground.
Both have the Lord hardening hearts so the Egyptians pursue, and being glorified in Pharaoh, his army, chariots and horsemen; Latin says horsemen, Greek horses, and Greek says 'Behold'.
Both say the Egyptians will know the Lord when He is glorified in Pharaoh, his chariots and his horsemen or horses.
Both say the angel of God and the pillar of cloud moved from before the camp to behind it.
Latin says the cloud was dark yet lit up the night, so the camps could not approach each other; Greek says darkness and gloom, and they did not mingle all night.
Latin has a strong, scorching wind driving the sea back; Greek has a violent south wind. Both have Moses stretching out his hand and the water divided.
Both say Israel entered the midst of the dry sea with the water a wall on the right and left.
Both say the Egyptians with Pharaoh's cavalry, chariots and riders pursued them into the midst of the sea.
Latin says the Lord slew their army; Greek says He threw the Egyptians' camp into confusion. Both have Him looking on in the pillar of fire and cloud at the morning watch.
Latin has the Lord overturn the chariot wheels so they were carried into the deep; Greek has Him bind the axles and drive them with force. The Egyptians' cry to flee is the same.
Both have the Lord telling Moses to stretch out his hand so the waters return on the Egyptians, chariots and riders; Latin is purpose clause, Greek a command.

Latin has the waters meet the fleeing Egyptians and the Lord engulf them; Greek says the Egyptians fled beneath the water and the Lord shook them into the sea. Both have the water returning at daybreak.
Both say the waters returned and covered the chariots, riders and Pharaoh's army, and none survived; Latin says not one survived, Greek says not one remained.
Both say Israel went through the midst of the sea on dry ground with the water a wall on each side.
Both say the Lord delivered Israel that day from the Egyptians' hand. Greek adds Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore; Latin has this at the start of 14:31.
Latin begins with the Egyptians dead on the seashore (in Greek this is 14:30) and has the people believing the Lord and Moses; Greek says trusted God and His attendant Moses.
Both have Moses and Israel singing the song, horse and rider thrown into the sea; Latin says sang to the Lord and He has been gloriously exalted, Greek says to God and gloriously glorified.
Latin opens with the Lord as my strength and my praise; Greek instead has 'a helper and shelterer'. Both then say salvation and 'my God, my father's God' to glorify and exalt.
Latin says his chosen commanders sank in the Red Sea; Greek says He drowned his chosen mounted officers. Pharaoh's chariots and army cast into the sea agree.
Latin has the depths covering them; Greek has God covering them with the sea. Both say they went down into the deep like a stone.
Both praise the Lord's right hand; exalted / glorified and struck / shattered the enemy are close in sense, with Greek plural enemies.
Both say in the abundance of glory the adversaries were overthrown or shattered, and wrath devoured them like stubble.
Latin has the waters gathered and a flowing wave standing still; Greek has the water parted and congealed like a wall. Both tie it to the breath of the Lord's fury or anger.
Both give the enemy's boast to pursue, overtake and divide spoils; Latin ends 'I will draw my sword; my hand will kill them', Greek ends 'my hand shall rule'.
Both say the sea covered them and they sank like lead in mighty waters; Latin says Your breath blew, Greek says You sent out Your wind.
Latin asks who is like You among the mighty, fearsome and praiseworthy; Greek asks among the gods, glorified among the holy ones, wonderful in glories. Both end with doing wonders.
Both say You stretched out Your hand and the earth devoured or swallowed them; Greek adds right hand.
Latin says the Lord guided the redeemed people in mercy and carried them in strength; Greek says in righteousness and comforted them. Both end at the holy dwelling.
Latin says the peoples rose up and were enraged; Greek says nations heard and grew angry. Both have anguish seizing the inhabitants of Philistia.
Latin has Edom's chiefs troubled, Moab's mighty men trembling, and Canaan rigid; Greek has Edom's leaders hurried, Moab's rulers trembling, and Canaan melting away.
Both ask that fear fall on them and they become stone-like until the people pass; Latin says motionless as stone, Greek turned to stone, and possessed / acquired differs.
Both have the people brought in and planted on the mountain of inheritance, at the Lord's dwelling and sanctuary made by His hands; Latin says firmest dwelling, Greek says prepared dwelling.
Both say the Lord reigns forever and beyond; Greek has 'forever and ever, and beyond' and a present verb, Latin a future.
Both say Pharaoh's force entered the sea and the Lord brought the waters over them while Israel walked on dry ground; Latin says Pharaoh the horseman, Greek says Pharaoh's horses.
Both have Miriam the prophetess taking a tambourine or timbrel, with all the women following with dances.
Both give the same song; Latin says she led their singing without naming her here, Greek names Miriam, and horse and rider is worded slightly differently.
Both have Moses leading Israel from the Red Sea into the wilderness of Shur, three days without finding water.
Both say Marah's water was bitter and could not be drunk; Latin has Moses name it Marah, that is bitterness, Greek says the place was named Bitterness.
Both say the people grumbled or murmured against Moses, asking what they would drink.
Both have Moses crying to the Lord, who shows him wood that turns the waters sweet; there He gave ordinances and tested them.
Both give the promise that if Israel obeys, none of the Egyptian diseases will come on them, for the Lord is their healer.
Both say they came to Elim with twelve springs and seventy palms and camped by the water.
Both say they journeyed from Elim to the wilderness of Sin, between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month.
Both say the whole congregation grumbled against Moses and Aaron; Latin adds 'in the wilderness'.
Both have the longing to have died in Egypt and the charge of being brought to kill the multitude by hunger; Latin phrases the charge as a question, Greek as a statement.
Both have the Lord raining bread from heaven, a daily gathering, and a test of whether they walk in His law.
Both say on the sixth day they prepare what they bring in, twice the daily amount.
Both have Moses and Aaron telling Israel that in the evening they will know the Lord brought them out of Egypt.
Both promise seeing the Lord's glory in the morning and ask what we are; Latin says He has heard your murmuring, Greek says when He hears it.
Both say meat in the evening and bread in the morning, and that the complaint is against the Lord/God; Latin says He heard complaints against Him, Greek against us.
Both have Moses telling Aaron to bid the congregation draw near before the Lord/God, for He has heard their murmuring.
Both say that as Aaron spoke they looked toward the wilderness and the Lord's glory appeared in a cloud.
Both have the Lord promising meat in the evening and bread in the morning, so they will know He is the Lord their God.
Both have quail covering the camp at evening; Latin says dew lay around the camp, Greek says the dew was subsiding, running into the next verse.
Latin says the fine thing was as though crushed with a pestle, like frost; Greek says like white coriander, like frost. Both say it lay on the wilderness surface.
Both have Israel asking what it is and Moses calling it the Lord's bread; Latin gives the Hebrew word 'Manhu' with its meaning, Greek gives only 'What is this?'.
Both command gathering an omer per person according to the number of persons in the tent; Latin says as much as suffices to eat, Greek says each for those belonging to him.
Both say Israel did so and gathered, some more and some less.
Latin has each gather according to what he could eat; Greek has each gather for those of his household. Both say the omer measure left no excess or lack.
Both say they did not listen to Moses, some left it until morning and it bred worms and stank, and Moses was angry or embittered.
Both say they gathered each morning as much as each needed, and it melted when the sun grew hot.
Both say that on the sixth day they gathered twice the amount, two omers each, and the leaders reported it to Moses.
Both have Moses repeating the Lord's word about tomorrow's Sabbath rest and setting aside what remains; Latin says do the needed work and cook what is to be cooked, Greek says bake and boil.
Both say it did not spoil or stink and no worm was in it; Latin says they did as Moses commanded, Greek specifies that they left some until morning.
Both have Moses telling them to eat today since it is the Lord's Sabbath, and it will not be found in the field.
Both say gather for six days, and on the seventh, the Sabbath, there will be none.
Both say some of the people went out on the seventh day to gather and found none.
Both have the Lord asking Moses how long they will refuse to keep or heed His commandments and law.
Both say the Lord gave the Sabbath and double food on the sixth day, and no one leaves his place on the seventh; Latin says remain where you are, Greek says stay in your houses.
Both have Israel naming it Man or Manna, like white coriander seed; Latin says its taste was like fine flour with honey, Greek says like a cake with honey.
Both have Moses commanding that an omer be filled and kept for generations so they may see the bread of the wilderness; Latin says 'I fed you', Greek says 'you ate'.
Latin has Aaron take one vessel; Greek has him take one golden jar. Both put an omer of manna in it before the Lord/God to keep for generations.
Latin says Aaron placed it in the tabernacle to be preserved; Greek says he set it before the Testimony to keep. Both say this was as the Lord commanded Moses.
Latin says they ate manna until they reached the borders of the land of Canaan; Greek says until they reached the region of Phoenicia. Forty years is the same.
Latin says an omer is a tenth of an ephah; Greek says it is a tenth of the three measures.
Both say Israel set out from the wilderness of Sin by stages at the Lord's word and camped at Rephidim, where there was no water.
Both have the people demanding water and Moses asking why they contend and test the Lord; Latin says quarreled, Greek says reviled.
Both say the people thirsted and grumbled against Moses, asking why he brought them out of Egypt to kill them, their children and the animals with thirst.
Both have Moses crying to the Lord, asking what to do with this people since they will almost stone him.
Both have the Lord telling Moses to go before the people with some elders and take the staff with which he struck the river.
Both have the Lord standing on the rock at Horeb and water coming out when it is struck; Latin says Moses did so before the elders of Israel, Greek before the sons of Israel.
Both name the place for Israel's testing of the Lord with 'Is the Lord among us or not?'; Latin names it Testing, Greek names it Testing and Reviling.
Both say Amalek came and fought Israel at Rephidim.
Both have Moses telling Joshua to choose men and fight Amalek, while he stands on the hilltop with God's staff; Greek says capable men and take your stand.
Both say Joshua did as Moses said against Amalek while Moses, Aaron and Hur went up to the hilltop.
Both say Israel prevailed when Moses raised his hands and Amalek when he lowered them; Latin adds 'a little' (paululum).
Both have the stone, Aaron and Hur supporting his hands until sunset; Latin says his hands did not tire, Greek says they remained supported.
Both say Joshua routed Amalek and his people by the sword.
Both have the Lord telling Moses to write this in a book as a memorial in Joshua's hearing, for He will blot out Amalek's memory from under heaven.
Latin names the altar 'The Lord is my exaltation'; Greek names it 'The Lord is my Refuge' and says it was an altar to the Lord.
Latin has 'the hand is of the Lord's throne' and the Lord's war against Amalek; Greek has the Lord fighting with a hidden hand. Both continue from generation to generation.
Latin says Jethro heard what God did for Moses and Israel his people; Greek mentions only what the Lord did for Israel. Both add the exodus from Egypt.
Both have Jethro taking Moses' wife Zipporah after she had been sent back; Greek names Jethro as subject and says 'after she had been sent away'.
Both name Gershom for the father's words about being a stranger in a foreign land; Latin says 'her two sons' and 'the father said', Greek says 'his' and 'Moses had said'.
Both name Eliezer, explained by the father's God being his helper and rescuing him from Pharaoh; Latin says from Pharaoh's sword, Greek from Pharaoh's hand.
Both have Jethro coming with Moses' sons and wife to him in the wilderness at the mountain of God.
Latin has Jethro send word to Moses that he is coming; Greek has it reported to Moses that Jethro is coming. Both name the wife and two sons with him.
Both have Moses meeting his father-in-law, bowing and kissing him, and greeting him; Latin adds 'words of peace', and Greek adds that he brought him into the tent.
Both have Moses recounting what the Lord did to Pharaoh and the Egyptians, the hardship on the way, and the deliverance; Greek adds 'from Pharaoh's hand and the Egyptians' hand'.
Both have Jethro reacting to the good the Lord did in delivering Israel from the Egyptians; Latin says rejoiced, Greek says amazed and adds Pharaoh's hand.
Both have Jethro blessing the Lord for delivering the people from the hand of the Egyptians and Pharaoh; Latin says 'delivered you' and repeats the thought, Greek says 'His people'.
Both have Jethro knowing the Lord is greater than all gods; Latin says because they acted arrogantly against them, Greek says because they attacked them.
Both have Jethro bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices to God and Aaron and the elders eating bread before God; Latin says offered, Greek says took, and Greek says eating with Jethro.
Both have Moses sitting to judge the people from morning until evening; Latin says the next day, Greek says after the next day.
Both have Jethro asking why Moses sits alone while all the people wait from morning until evening; Latin says wait, Greek says stand before you.
Both have Moses telling Jethro the people come to him to seek God's judgment.
Both have Moses saying that in a dispute he judges between them and instructs them in God's commands and laws.
Both have Moses' father-in-law saying that what Moses is doing is not good or not correct.
Both warn that Moses and the people will be worn out and cannot bear it alone; Latin says foolish labor, Greek says unbearable exhaustion.
Both have Jethro urging Moses to listen to his counsel, with God's presence, and represent the people before God.
Both have Moses instructing the people and showing them the way and work; Latin says ceremonies and manner of worship, Greek says God's ordinances and law.
Latin says men who hate greed, with truth in them; Greek says righteous men who hate arrogance. Capable God-fearing men and rulers of thousands to tens agree.
Both have them judging at all times, bringing weighty matters to Moses and judging small cases themselves to lighten his burden.
Latin says Moses will fulfill God's command and sustain His instructions; Greek says God will strengthen him and he will be able to stand. Both end with the people going home in peace.
Both say Moses listened to his father-in-law and did all he suggested.
Both have Moses choosing capable men from all Israel and appointing them leaders of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens.
Both say they judged at all times, bringing the weighty matters to Moses and judging the lighter ones themselves.
Both say Moses sent his father-in-law away and he went to his own land.
Both say that in the third month after leaving Egypt, on that day, they came to the wilderness of Sinai.
Both say they set out from Rephidim, came to the wilderness of Sinai and camped opposite the mountain.
Both have Moses going up and the Lord/God calling from the mountain with a message for the house of Jacob; Latin says Moses went up to God, Greek says to God's mountain.
Both have the Lord reminding them of what He did to the Egyptians and how He carried them on eagles' wings to Himself.
Both say if they obey His voice and keep His covenant they will be His special people out of all nations, for all the earth is His.
Both call them a holy nation; Latin says a priestly kingdom, Greek says a royal priesthood.
Both have Moses calling the elders and setting before them all the words the Lord commanded.
Both have all the people answering together that they will do all the Lord has said; Greek adds 'and we will obey', which Latin lacks.
Latin has the Lord coming in the darkness of a cloud; Greek has Him coming in a pillar of cloud. Both aim for the people to hear and believe Moses forever.
Latin tells Moses to go and consecrate the people for two days and wash their clothes; Greek adds a command to go down and solemnly warn them.
Both say be ready for the third day, when the Lord will descend on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people.
Both tell Moses to set bounds around the people, forbidding going up or touching the mountain, on pain of death.
Latin says they may ascend when the trumpet begins to sound; Greek says when the sounds, trumpets and cloud leave the mountain. The penalty of stoning or darts is the same.
Both have Moses coming down to the people, consecrating them, and their washing their clothes.
Both tell them to be ready for the third day and not approach women; Latin says your wives, Greek says a woman.
Both have thunder, lightning, a dense or dark cloud, a loud trumpet, and a frightened people on the third day; Latin adds the morning dawning and the cloud covering the mountain.
Both have Moses bringing the people out of the camp to meet God, standing at the foot of the mountain.
Latin ends with the whole mountain terrifying; Greek ends with all the people greatly astonished. Smoke like a furnace and descent in fire agree.
Both have the trumpet growing stronger, and Moses speaking with God answering him; Greek adds 'with a voice', and Latin says the trumpet was prolonged.
Both have the Lord descending to the top of Mount Sinai and calling Moses up.
Both have God telling Moses to warn the people lest many perish; Latin says cross the boundaries to see the Lord, Greek says come near God to gaze and a multitude fall.
Latin warns that the Lord may strike the priests unless they consecrate themselves; Greek warns that the Lord may depart from them.
