Both have Moses saying the people cannot go up Mount Sinai because of the Lord's warning to set the mountain apart; Latin adds the command to set boundaries around it.

Both have the Lord sending Moses down to come up with Aaron, while priests and people may not approach; Latin says cross the boundaries lest He kill them, Greek says force their way lest He destroy some.
Both say Moses went down to the people; Latin says he told them everything, Greek says he spoke to them.
Both say the Lord spoke all these words; 'saying' is only a speech marker.
Both give the Lord's self-identification as the God who led or brought Israel out of Egypt, the house of slavery.
Both forbid having other gods; Latin says foreign gods before Me, Greek says no other gods except Me.
Both forbid making a carved image or idol, or a likeness of anything in heaven, earth or the waters below.
Both forbid worship and service, with the jealous Lord visiting fathers' sins on children to the third and fourth generation; Latin adds 'mighty' and says worship, Greek says bow down.
Both say the Lord shows mercy to thousands who love Him and keep His commands or ordinances.
Both forbid taking the Lord's name in vain, since the Lord will not hold guiltless anyone who does.
Both say remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy.
Both say to labor six days and do all your work.

Both forbid all work on the seventh day for household, servants and animals; Greek lists ox, beast of burden and livestock, and says the sojourner among you, where Latin has the stranger within your gates.
Both ground the Sabbath in the Lord making heaven, earth and sea in six days and resting; Latin says He blessed the Sabbath day, Greek says the seventh day.
Both command honoring father and mother for long life in the land the Lord gives; Greek adds 'that it may go well with you' and calls the land good.
Both forbid false witness against your neighbor; speak / bear is only English wording.
Latin lists house, wife, servants, ox, donkey and all his things; Greek puts the wife first and adds the field and any livestock, with a beast of burden in place of the donkey.
Both have the people seeing the sounds or lights, trumpet and smoking mountain, and standing far off afraid; Latin says terrified and shaken with fear.
Both have the people asking Moses to speak so that God does not speak, lest they die; Latin adds 'and we will listen' (audiemus).
Both have Moses telling them not to fear, for God came to test them so that fear of Him would keep them from sin.
Both have the people standing far off while Moses goes to the darkness where God was; Latin says approached, Greek says entered.
Both have the Lord telling Moses to remind Israel that He spoke to them from heaven; Greek adds 'house of Jacob' and 'announce'.
Both forbid making gods of silver or gold for yourselves.
Both command an earthen altar with burnt and peace offerings of sheep and cattle, and the Lord coming to bless; Latin says where my name is remembered, Greek says where I name My name.
Both forbid building a stone altar of cut stones because a blade defiles it; Latin has 'if you raise a blade', Greek says 'you have laid your blade'.
Both forbid going up to the altar by steps, lest nakedness be exposed.
Both introduce the judgments or ordinances to be set before them.
Both say a Hebrew slave serves six years and goes free in the seventh without payment.
Latin says he leaves with the clothing he entered with, his wife with him if he had one; Greek says if he came in alone he goes out alone, and his wife goes out if she came with him.
Both say a wife given by the master and her children stay with the master; Latin has him leave with his clothing, Greek has him go out alone.
Both have the slave declaring love for his master, wife and children and refusing to go free.
Both have the master bringing him before the judges or God's tribunal, to the door and doorpost, piercing his ear and making him a slave forever.
Both say a daughter sold as a servant does not go free as female slaves do.
Latin has the master release her if she displeases him; Greek has him redeem her. Both bar selling her to a foreign people.
Both say if she is betrothed to his son, she is treated by the custom or ordinance for daughters.
Both require provision for the first woman if he takes another; Latin lists marriage, clothing and the price of chastity, Greek lists necessities, clothing and conjugal companionship.
Both say if he does not do these three things, she goes free without payment.
Latin makes the penalty for striking a person with intent to kill; Greek makes it for striking someone who then dies.
Both cover a killing where God delivered the person into his hands and a place of refuge is provided; Latin says he did not lie in wait, Greek says he did not act willingly.
Both order the deliberate killer taken from the altar to die; Latin says killed deliberately and by treachery, Greek adds that he takes refuge.
Both say whoever strikes his father or mother shall surely die.
Latin punishes stealing and selling a person; Greek limits it to kidnapping one of the sons of Israel, adds oppressing him, and says the kidnapper is found holding him.
Both say whoever curses or reviles his father or mother shall surely die.
Both describe men quarreling, one striking the other with a stone or fist, and the victim surviving but confined to bed.
Both say if the victim rises and walks outside with a staff, the striker is free but pays for lost work and medical costs.
Both treat a slave dying under the rod as a punishable offense; Latin says the master is guilty of a crime, Greek says the death shall be avenged by justice.
Both say if the slave survives a day or two there is no penalty because the slave is his property; Latin says no punishment, Greek says the death is not avenged.
Both say a slave struck in the eye and blinded goes free in return for the eye.
Both free a slave whose tooth is knocked out; Greek adds 'in compensation for their tooth'.
Both say an ox that gores a man or woman to death is stoned, its flesh uneaten, and the owner cleared.
Both cover a goring ox known from the past, with the owner warned and failing to restrain it, so the ox is stoned and the owner dies.
Both say if a ransom is imposed on the owner, he pays whatever is demanded for his life.
Both apply the same ruling to a goring of a son or daughter; Latin says it is subject to the same sentence, Greek says he is dealt with by this ordinance.
Both fine the owner thirty units of silver paid to the slave's master and stone the ox; Latin says shekels, Greek says didrachmas.
Both cover an uncovered pit into which an animal falls; Latin has an ox or donkey, Greek a calf or donkey.
Both make the pit's owner pay and give him the dead animal; Latin says repay the value of the animals, Greek says give silver to the animal's owner.
Both say if one ox kills another, they sell the live ox and divide the price and the dead animal.
Both cover an ox known to gore whose owner failed to restrain it: he repays ox for ox and keeps the dead animal.
Both set the penalty for stealing and killing or selling an ox/calf or sheep at five oxen/calves and four sheep.
Both say a thief caught breaking in and killed leaves the killer without bloodguilt; Latin adds digging through the house.
Both say that after sunrise the killing is guilty and a penniless thief is sold for the theft.
Both require double restitution when the live stolen animals are found with him; Latin lists ox, donkey and sheep, Greek says 'from donkey to sheep'.
Both require restitution for grazing damage; Greek adds a second case, where the whole field is grazed and the best of field and vineyard is paid.
Both make whoever kindled a fire liable for the damage to thorns and crops; Latin says stacks of grain, Greek says a threshing floor or a plain.
Both have goods left with a neighbor being stolen and the thief repaying double if found; Greek says stolen from the man's house.
Both have the householder come before the judges or God and swear he did not take his neighbor's property; Greek speaks of deposit and dishonesty.
Both bring the dispute before the judges or God and have the convicted party repay double; Latin says if they judge against him, Greek says whoever is convicted.
Both cover an animal left with a neighbor that dies, is injured or is captured with no witness.
Both settle the matter by an oath of innocence which the owner accepts, with no restitution; Greek says 'an oath by God'.
Both say if it was stolen he must repay the owner.
Both excuse repayment if a beast killed it and he brings the remains; Greek says he shows the owner the prey.
Both require restitution for a borrowed animal injured or dead in the owner's absence; Greek adds 'taken captive'.
Both excuse repayment if the owner is present; Latin adds 'especially if hired for its wages', Greek says if it was hired it is reckoned against its hire.
Both say if a man seduces an unbetrothed virgin and lies with her, he pays the marriage payment and takes her as wife.
Both say if the father refuses, silver is paid according to a virgin's marriage payment; Greek says the seducer pays the father.
Both forbid letting sorcerers live.
Both command death for anyone who lies with an animal.
Both say whoever sacrifices to gods other than the Lord alone shall be put to death.
Both forbid afflicting the stranger or resident alien, for you were strangers in Egypt.
Both forbid harming or mistreating a widow or orphan.
Both say if they are harmed and cry out, the Lord will hear their cry.
Both say the Lord's wrath will kill them by the sword, leaving their wives widows and their children orphans.
Both forbid pressing a poor person and charging interest on a loan; Latin says one of My poor people, Greek says the poor brother beside you.
Both say a garment taken in pledge must be returned before sunset.
Both give the reason that it is his only covering, nothing else to sleep in, and the Lord hears his cry since He is merciful.
Both forbid reviling gods/judges and speaking ill of the people's ruler or rulers; Latin has singular ruler, Greek plural rulers.
Latin commands not delaying tithes and firstfruits; Greek speaks only of the firstfruits of the threshing floor and winepress. The firstborn sons are given in both.
Both treat firstborn animals the same way, seven days with the mother and given on the eighth; Latin says cattle and sheep, Greek says calf, sheep and beast of burden.
Both call them holy to the Lord and tell them to throw to the dog(s) flesh not slaughtered by them; Latin says flesh already tasted by beasts, Greek says taken by wild animals.
Both forbid accepting a false report and joining a wicked person as a false witness; Latin says join hands, Greek says agree with an unjust person.
Both forbid following the crowd to do evil or perverting justice with the majority; Latin says deviate from truth, Greek says exclude justice.
Both forbid favoring a poor person in judgment; Latin says have pity (misereberis), Greek says show partiality.
Both command returning an enemy's wandering ox or donkey/beast of burden.
Both command helping lift the fallen load of an enemy's donkey or beast of burden.
Both forbid perverting a poor person's judgment.
Both forbid killing the innocent and righteous; Latin gives the reason 'I reject the wicked', Greek adds not acquitting the ungodly for bribes.
Both forbid accepting gifts, which blind the wise and corrupt the words of the righteous.
Both forbid afflicting a resident alien or stranger, since you know their soul and were strangers in Egypt.
Both say in the seventh year leave the land to rest for the poor, with the wild animals eating the rest, and do likewise with vineyard and olive grove.
Both command six days of work and rest on the seventh so the ox, beast, slave's son and stranger are refreshed.
Both command keeping all He said and not letting other gods' names be heard from your mouth; Latin forbids swearing by their name, Greek forbids calling it to mind.
Both say three times a year they keep a feast or festivals to the Lord.
Both command the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days at the month of new crops/grain in memory of coming out of Egypt, and not appearing empty-handed.
Both command the harvest feast of firstfruits and the feast at the year's end when produce is gathered; Greek names it the Feast of Completion.
Both say all males shall appear before the Lord your God three times a year.
Both forbid offering sacrificial blood with leaven and leaving the fat until morning; Greek adds an opening clause about God driving out nations and enlarging borders.
Latin forbids boiling a young goat in its mother's milk; Greek says a lamb. The firstfruits command is the same.
Both have the Lord sending His angel to guard them and bring them to the prepared place; Latin says place, Greek says land, and Latin adds going before.
Both command heeding the angel because the Lord's name is in or on him; Latin says he will not pardon sin, Greek says he will not yield before you.

Greek adds a long passage (keep My covenant, treasured people, royal priesthood, holy nation, words to speak to Israel) and repeats the conditional; Latin has only the single promise to be enemy to Israel's enemies.
Latin lists six peoples; Greek adds the Girgashites and has Amorites listed; Latin God will crush (conteram), Greek destroy. Both promise the angel going before.
Worship / bow down, works / practices, statues / pillars differ in wording; both forbid serving their gods and command breaking down their cult objects.
Latin blessing is purposed (ut benedicam) on bread and water; Greek blesses bread, wine, and water. Latin removes sickness; Greek turns it away.
Both promise no one unfruitful or barren in the land and a full number of days.
Latin: kill every people and make enemies turn their backs; Greek: throw nations into confusion and make adversaries fugitives. Latin says My terror; both send terror ahead.
Latin names Hivite, Canaanite, Hittite; Greek adds Amorites. Both send hornets to drive them out before Israel enters.
Both refuse to drive them out in one year lest beasts multiply; wilderness / desolate and beasts / animals of the land differ slightly.
Both: little by little drive them out until Israel increases and possesses / inherits the land.
Same borders; Latin ends with 'the river', Greek names it the great River Euphrates. Delivery of inhabitants and driving out agree.
Both bar them from the land lest Israel sin; Latin joins serving their gods to the sin and calls it certainly a stumbling block, Greek makes it a conditional.
Latin 'also said' and addresses worship to the group (you will worship); Greek has them bow down to the Lord from a distance. Same company named.
Both: Moses alone approaches, others do not, people do not go up; Latin says people not ascend with him, Greek with them.
Latin people answer 'we will do'; Greek adds 'and obey'. Latin judgments / Greek ordinances; Latin the Lord, Greek God.
Both: Moses writes the words and builds an altar and twelve pillars / stones for the tribes; Greek repeats Moses as subject.
Young bulls / calves and peace offerings / sacrifice of well-being are wording differences; both have young men offering burnt and peace offerings.
Latin puts half the blood into bowls; Greek pours it into bowls. Remaining half poured upon / against the altar.
Both: Moses reads the covenant book to the people, who say they will do everything and be obedient.
Both: Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders of Israel went up; 'council of elders' is wording only.
Latin: God did not lay hand on those who withdrew; they saw God and ate. Greek: none of the chosen men missing; they appeared in God's place and ate.
Latin: tablets, law and commandments written so that Moses may teach them; Greek: written to establish law for them. Purpose of the writing differs.
Latin: Moses and Joshua rise, Moses ascending; Greek: Moses rises with Joshua and they go up the mountain of God. Joshua's role is stated differently.
Latin: he tells the elders to wait and refer disputes to Aaron and Hur; Greek: 'they said' and let a disputant approach them. Same instruction.
Greek has Moses and Joshua going up; Latin mentions only Moses. Cloud covers the mountain in both.
Latin glory dwelt (habitavit) on Sinai and called from midst of darkness; Greek glory descended and called Moses from within the cloud.
Both: the Lord's glory looked like blazing fire on the summit before Israel.
Both: Moses enters the cloud, goes up the mountain, and stays forty days and nights.
Latin: tell Israel to take firstfruits for Me, received from the willing; Greek: Moses receives firstfruits from the willing-hearted and repeats 'My firstfruits'.
Both list gold, silver, bronze; Greek names them 'the firstfruit offering' where Latin says what you must receive.
Both list blue, purple, double / twice-dyed scarlet, fine linen, goats' hair.
Rams' skins dyed red and acacia / decay-resistant wood agree; Latin violet-colored skins, Greek blue skins.
Latin lists lamp oil, spices for anointing oil, and incense; Greek has no corresponding clause.
Latin onyx stones and gems for ephod and breastpiece; Greek sardius and engraving stones for shoulder-piece and full-length robe.
Latin: they make the sanctuary and I will dwell in their midst; Greek: you make it and I will appear among you.
Both: make the tabernacle and all its furnishings according to the pattern shown; Greek adds 'on the mountain'.
Same wood and dimensions; Greek calls it an ark of testimony.
Both overlay with pure gold inside and out with a gold molding around; Greek says twisted moldings, Latin molding on top around.
Four gold rings, two on each side; Latin places them at the four corners, Greek on the four sides.
Both: make poles of acacia / decay-resistant wood and overlay with gold.
Both: put the poles through the rings on the ark's sides to carry it.
Both say the poles stay in the rings; Latin adds that they are never taken out and speaks of 'them', Greek names the carrying poles in the ark's rings.
Both: put into the ark the testimony I will give; Latin singular testimony, Greek plural testimonies.
Both: a cover of pure gold, two and a half cubits by a cubit and a half; atonement / propitiatory cover is wording.
Latin cherubim of hammered gold on either side of the oraculum (place of divine speech); Greek cherubim of worked gold at the sides of the propitiatory cover.
Both: one cherub on each side; Greek adds 'of the propitiatory cover' and repeats the instruction.
Latin cherubim cover the sides and shelter the oraculum, facing toward the cover; Greek wings spread above, overshadowing the cover. Latin adds the cover covering the ark.
Greek adds placing the propitiatory cover on top of the ark before putting the testimonies in; Latin only says the testimony is placed in it.
Latin 'I will give commands' and speak; Greek 'I will make Myself known' and speak. Same place between the cherubim, same subject.
Latin table of acacia wood; Greek table of pure gold. Dimensions agree.
Latin first overlays the table with purest gold and then makes a gold rim; Greek mentions only twisted gold moldings around it.
Latin: openwork molding four fingers high and a second small gold molding; Greek: rim a handbreadth wide and a twisted molding around it.
Both: four gold rings for the table's legs; Latin 'corners, one by each leg', Greek 'four parts of its legs'.
Both: rings beneath the molding / rim hold the poles so the table can be carried.
Both: poles of acacia / decay-resistant wood overlaid with gold for carrying the table; purest / pure is wording.
Same four sets of vessels of pure gold; Latin censers and drink-offering vessels, Greek incense cups and libation vessels.
Both: bread of presentation / of the Presence on the table before Me always.
Both: a lampstand of worked pure gold with stem, branches, cups / bowls, knobs, and lilies from it.
Both: six branches, three from each side.
Latin gives three nut-shaped cups with knob and lily on each of the branches; Greek states it for one branch and extends it to all six.
Four nut-shaped cups on the lampstand itself in both; Latin has knobs and lilies for each, Greek places them on one branch.
Latin: knobs under pairs of branches in three places; Greek: a knob under two branches and a knob under four branches.
Both: knobs and branches of one piece with the lampstand, wholly worked of pure gold.
Both: seven lamps set on the lampstand; Latin to shine in front, Greek to shine from one face.
Both: snuffers of pure gold; Latin adds vessels for the extinguished snuffings, Greek has supports.
Both: a talent of pure gold; Latin the whole lampstand with utensils, Greek 'all these utensils'.
Both: see that you make it according to the pattern shown on the mountain.
Latin curtains varied with embroidered work; Greek curtains with cherubim, the work of a weaver. Ten curtains and colors agree.
Both: each curtain twenty-eight by four cubits, all of one measure.
Both: five curtains joined together and the other five likewise.
Both: blue loops for joining the curtains; Latin on sides and ends, Greek at the edge of each curtain at the joining.
Both: fifty loops, set opposite one another; Latin on each side of a curtain, Greek on each of the two sets.
Both: fifty gold fittings joining the curtains into one tabernacle; Latin rings, Greek clasps.
Both: eleven goats' hair coverings over the tabernacle.
Both: each thirty by four cubits, all the same measure.
Both: five joined apart and six apart, sixth doubled at the front; Latin front of the roof, Greek front of the tabernacle.
Both: fifty loops on the edge of each of the two sets; Greek specifies the middle curtain, Latin one covering and the other.
Both: fifty bronze clasps joining the loops so the covering becomes one.
Both: the surplus half curtain covers the back of the tabernacle; Greek adds tucking under the surplus and repeats the covering clause.
Both: a cubit on each side from the excess length covers the tabernacle's sides.
Both: a covering of red-dyed rams' skins with another over it; Latin violet-colored skins, Greek blue skins.
Both: make upright boards / posts of acacia (decay-resistant) wood for the tabernacle; boards / posts is wording.
Both: each ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide.
Latin two joints on the sides connecting board to board; Greek two tenons fitted opposite each other. Same instruction for all boards / posts.
Latin puts the twenty boards on the south side; Greek puts the twenty posts on the north side.
Both: forty silver bases, two under each board / post; Latin cast them, Greek make them.
Latin puts the second side of twenty boards to the north; Greek puts it to the south.
Both: forty silver bases, two under each board / post.
Both: six boards / posts for the back of the tabernacle; Latin western side, Greek rear toward the sea.
Both: two more boards / posts for the corners at the back of the tabernacle.
Latin: boards joined from bottom to top by one fastening; Greek: equal below and equal at the tops at one joining. Corner boards handled alike in both.
Both: eight boards / posts with sixteen silver bases, two for each.
Both: five bars of acacia (decay-resistant) wood for the boards / posts on one side.
Both: five bars for the other side and five for the rear (western / sea) side.
Latin bars pass through the middle of the boards from end to end; Greek speaks of the middle bar passing through the posts from one side to the other.
Both: overlay boards / posts with gold, make gold rings for the bars, and cover the bars with gold.
Both: erect the tabernacle according to the pattern / plan shown on the mountain.
Latin veil woven with embroidery and beautiful patterns; Greek veil with cherubim, the work of a weaver. Colors and materials agree.
Both: veil on four gold-overlaid acacia pillars / posts with gold capitals and silver bases; Latin hangs it before them, Greek places it on them.
Both: ark of the testimony inside the veil, which divides the holy place from the holy of holies; Latin adds hanging the veil by rings.
Latin places the atonement cover on the ark in the Holy of Holies; Greek screens the ark with the veil there.
Both: table outside the veil, lampstand opposite on the south side, table on the north.
Both: a screen of blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, embroiderer's work; Latin specifies it for the tabernacle entrance.
Both: five gold-overlaid posts with gold capitals and bronze bases for the screen; Latin specifies acacia wood, Greek has the bases cast.
Both: an altar of acacia (decay-resistant) wood, five cubits square, three cubits high.
Latin: horns at the four corners and the altar overlaid with bronze; Greek: horns of one piece with it, and the horns covered with bronze.
Latin lists ash pots, tongs, forks, and firepans; Greek lists a rim, its cover, bowls, meat forks, and firepan. All utensils of bronze in both.
Both: a bronze net-like grating with four bronze rings; Latin at its four corners, Greek on its four sides.
Latin places the rings beneath the altar's ledge (arulam); Greek beneath the altar's grating. Grating reaches halfway up in both.
Both: poles of acacia (decay-resistant) wood overlaid with bronze; Latin specifies two poles and bronze plates.
Both: poles through the rings along the altar's sides for carrying.
Latin: hollow and empty inside, not solid; Greek: hollow, with boards. Both follow the pattern shown on the mountain.
Latin places the south hangings on the southern side facing south; Greek places them on the side toward the southwest. Hundred cubits in both.
Both: twenty pillars / posts and twenty bronze bases; Latin silver capitals with engraved fittings, Greek silver rings and braces.
Latin puts the hundred-cubit hangings on the north side; Greek on the east side. Greek describes the silver details differently.
Both: west / sea side width of fifty cubits of hangings, ten pillars / posts, and as many bases.
Latin gives the east width as fifty cubits; Greek gives the south side width of fifty cubits and adds ten posts and ten bases.
Both: fifteen-cubit hangings on one side with three pillars / posts and three bases; Latin says length, Greek says height.
Both: fifteen-cubit hangings on the other side with three pillars / posts and bases; Latin extent, Greek height.
Both: a twenty-cubit gate screen of blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen on four pillars / posts and bases; Latin long, Greek high.
Both: all pillars / posts around the court silver-covered, with silver capitals and bronze bases.
Both: court of a hundred cubits by fifty, five cubits high, of fine linen with bronze bases; Greek phrases the dimensions as 'hundred by hundred' and 'fifty by fifty'.
Both: all utensils and the court's pegs of bronze; Latin adds 'for every use and ceremony' and Greek 'all the tools'.
Both: Israel brings pure beaten olive oil so the lamp burns continually; Latin beaten with a pestle, Greek free of sediment, for the light.
Both: Aaron and sons tend the lamp before the Lord as a perpetual statute; Latin 'set it in place, shine until morning', Greek 'burn it from evening to morning'.
Both: bring Aaron and his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar from Israel to serve as priests.
Both: make holy garments for Aaron; Latin for glory and beauty, Greek for honor and glory.
Both: speak to the skilled whom God filled with a spirit of understanding to make Aaron's holy garments; Greek adds 'for the sanctuary', Latin says he is consecrated to minister.
Both list breastpiece, ephod / shoulder-piece, robe, tunic, turban, and sash; garment names differ (fitted linen tunic / tasseled tunic).
Both: take gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen; twice-dyed / yarn is wording.
Latin makes the ephod of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and linen; Greek names only spun fine linen, in skilled embroidered weaving.
Latin two joined edges at the top, forming one; Greek two shoulder-pieces joined to one another at the sides.
Both: the woven work of the same gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and linen; Greek says it is made as one piece with the shoulder-pieces.
Latin takes two onyx stones; Greek takes two emerald stones. Names of Israel's sons engraved in both.
Both: six names on one stone and six on the other, in birth order / according to generations.
Latin adds that the stones are enclosed and surrounded by gold; Greek has no such clause and likens the engraving to a seal.
Both: stones as a memorial, Aaron bearing the names before the Lord on his shoulders; Latin sets them on either side of the ephod, Greek on the shoulders of the shoulder-piece.
Latin makes gold hooks; Greek makes small rosettes of pure gold.
Latin two linked little chains attached to the hooks; Greek two braided ornaments intertwined with flowers, set on the rosettes in front.
Both: a breastpiece / oracle-piece of judgment in embroidered work like the ephod, of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and linen.
Both: square and doubled, a span long and a span wide.
Both: four rows of stones, first row sardius, topaz, emerald; Greek adds weaving a fabric set with them.
Both: second row carbuncle, sapphire, jasper.
Both: third row ligure, agate, amethyst.
Both: fourth row chrysolite, onyx, beryl in gold settings; the order of onyx and beryl is reversed and Greek adds 'bound in gold'.
Both: twelve stones each engraved with the name of one of the twelve tribes.
Both: chains of pure gold for the breastpiece; Latin linked chains, Greek braided chains.
Latin has two gold rings at the upper ends of the breastpiece; Greek has no corresponding ring instruction.
Latin joins the gold chains to the rings at the edges; Greek has no matching clause here.
Latin attaches the chain ends to two hooks on the ephod; Greek has no matching clause here.
Latin makes two more gold rings at the breastpiece's lower edges facing the ephod; Greek has no corresponding clause.
Latin makes two further gold rings for the ephod's lower sides; Greek has no corresponding clause.
Latin binds breastpiece to ephod with a blue cord so they cannot separate; Greek has no corresponding clause.
Both have Aaron bearing the names on the breastpiece of judgment; Latin says 'everlasting', while Greek adds placing the braided ornaments, chains, and rosettes.
Latin places Teaching and Truth on the breastpiece; Greek places Manifestation and Truth. Aaron carries Israel's judgment on his chest before the Lord in both.
Both: a robe entirely blue; Latin the robe of the ephod, Greek a full-length under-robe.
Both: head opening in the middle with a woven border so it does not tear; Greek adds a seam woven as one piece with it.
Latin pomegranates of blue, purple, scarlet with bells between; Greek adds fine linen and gold pomegranates, with bells between them all around.
Latin alternates a gold bell and a pomegranate; Greek has a gold pomegranate with a bell and a floral ornament beside it.
Both: the sound is heard as he enters and leaves the sanctuary, so he does not die; Latin adds that Aaron wears the robe in his ministry.
Both: a plate of pure gold engraved or stamped; Latin 'Holy to the Lord', Greek 'The Lord's consecrated thing'.
Both fasten the plate with blue material so it rests on the turban / headband; Greek adds 'at the front of the headband'.
Latin: Aaron bears the iniquities of the offerings and the Lord is appeased; Greek: Aaron removes the sins of the holy things, and it is acceptable before the Lord.
Latin: fit the tunic closely with fine linen; Greek: the tunics' tassels shall be of fine linen. Linen turban and embroidered sash agree.
Both: tunics, sashes, and turbans for Aaron's sons; Latin glory and beauty, Greek honor and glory.
Both: clothe Aaron and his sons and consecrate them as priests; Latin consecrates hands, Greek adds anointing and filling their hands.
Both: linen undergarments covering the nakedness of the flesh from waist to thighs.
Both: worn on entering the tent or approaching the altar so they do not die; a perpetual statute for Aaron and his descendants; Latin 'guilty of iniquity', Greek 'bring sin on themselves'.
Both: consecrate them as priests; take a calf / young bull from the herd and two unblemished rams.
Latin lists unleavened loaves, an oiled cake, and wafers; Greek lists only loaves mixed with oil and wafers. All from fine wheat flour.
Both: put them in one basket and present them with the calf / young bull and two rams.
Both: bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tent of testimony and wash them with water.
Latin dresses Aaron in the linen tunic, robe, ephod, and breastpiece fastened with the sash; Greek names tunic, shoulder-piece, oracle-piece, fastened to the shoulder-piece.
Both: turban / headband on his head and the holy plate upon it.
Both: pour anointing oil on his head; Latin adds that by this rite he is consecrated, Greek says to anoint him.
Both: bring his sons and clothe them in tunics; Latin also girds them with a sash here, Greek places sashes in the next verse.
Both: sashes and head coverings, perpetual priesthood, and consecrating their hands; Latin 'after you have ordained their hands' runs into the next verse.
Both: bring the bull / calf to the tent entrance and Aaron and sons lay hands on its head; Greek repeats the location and adds 'before the Lord'.
Both: slaughter it before the Lord at the entrance of the tent of testimony.
Both: blood on the altar's horns with the finger; remaining blood poured at the altar's base.
Both: the fat of the entrails, the liver lobe, two kidneys and their fat, burned on the altar.
Both: burn the flesh, skin, and dung outside the camp, for it is a sin offering.
Both: take one ram; Aaron and his sons lay hands on its head.
Both: slaughter it and pour its blood around / against the altar.
Both: cut the ram in pieces, wash entrails and feet, and put them with the pieces and the head.
Both: offer the whole ram on the altar as a pleasing aroma to the Lord; Latin 'sweetest aroma of the victim', Greek names it a whole burnt offering.
Both: take the other ram; Aaron and his sons lay hands on its head.
Both put blood on the right ear, hand, and foot; Latin names thumbs and toes and adds pouring blood around the altar, which Greek does not here.
Both sprinkle blood and oil on Aaron, his sons, and garments; Greek adds that they become holy and pours the blood against the altar, while Latin breaks off mid-sentence.
Latin includes the ram's tail and the fat over the vitals; Greek has no tail. Other fat, kidneys, and right foreleg / shoulder agree.
Latin takes a round loaf, an oiled cake, and a wafer; Greek takes one oiled loaf and one wafer from the unleavened basket.
Both: put all on the hands of Aaron and his sons before the Lord; Latin consecrates by lifting, Greek sets apart as a dedicated portion.
Both: receive them and burn on the altar as a pleasing aroma before the Lord; Latin 'most sweet aroma', Greek names the altar of burnt offering.
Both: the breast of the ram of consecration, lifted / set apart before the Lord, as Moses' portion; wording of the lifting differs.
Both consecrate the breast and the shoulder / foreleg from the consecration ram; Greek adds 'for Aaron and his sons' and calls it the contribution.
Both: a perpetual portion for Aaron and his sons from Israel's peace / well-being sacrifices; Latin calls them firstfruits, Greek a contribution to the Lord.
Both: Aaron's holy garments pass to his sons after him for anointing and consecrating their hands.
Both: the son who succeeds him and enters the tent wears them seven days; Latin 'appointed high priest', Greek 'succeeds as priest'.
Both: take the ram of consecration and cook / boil its flesh in a holy place.
Both: Aaron and his sons eat the flesh and the bread in the basket at the tent entrance.
Latin gives the purpose as an appeasing sacrifice and consecrated hands; Greek says they eat what sanctified them. An outsider may not eat in both.
Both: leftover flesh or bread until morning is burned with fire and not eaten because it is holy / consecrated.
Both: do everything commanded for Aaron and his sons, consecrating their hands for seven days.
Latin offers a sin-offering bull every day for expiation; Greek offers the calf on the day of purification. Altar purified and anointed in both.
Both: seven days of purifying the altar; it is most holy and whatever touches it is sanctified.
Both: two year-old lambs daily, continually; Greek adds 'without blemish' and 'a continual offering'.
Both: one lamb in the morning and the other in the evening.
Both: a tenth of fine flour with a quarter hin of beaten oil, and a quarter hin of wine as libation, for each lamb.
Both: the evening lamb offered as in the morning, as a pleasing aroma; Greek adds 'an offering to the Lord'.
Both: perpetual sacrifice at the tent entrance before the Lord; Latin 'where I will appoint to speak', Greek 'where I will make Myself known to speak'.
Latin: God gives commands there and the altar is sanctified in His glory; Greek: God appoints Himself there and is Himself sanctified in His glory.
Both: God consecrates the tent, the altar, and Aaron with his sons to serve as priests.
Latin: I will dwell in the midst of Israel; Greek: I will be called upon among them. Both add 'and be their God'.
Both say Israel will know the Lord their God who brought them out of Egypt; Latin 'to dwell among them' and repeats the title, Greek 'to be called upon among them and to be their God'.
Both: make an incense altar of acacia (decay-resistant) wood.
Both: square, a cubit by a cubit, two cubits high, with horns of one piece with it.
Both: overlay grating, sides, and horns with pure gold and make a gold rim around; Latin little molding, Greek twisted rim.
Both: two gold rings beneath the rim as holders for carrying poles; Greek adds 'on its two flanks, on the two sides'.
Both: poles of acacia (decay-resistant) wood overlaid with gold.
Both place the altar opposite the veil by the ark, where God speaks to Moses; Latin adds 'before the atonement cover that covers the testimony', which Greek lacks.
Both: Aaron burns incense each morning when tending the lamps; Latin 'sweetly fragrant', Greek 'finely ground compounded'.
Both: incense burned in the evening when the lamps are set / lit, continually before the Lord throughout the generations.
Both: no other incense, offering, sacrifice, or libation on the altar.
Both: once a year Aaron makes atonement on its horns with sin-offering blood, perpetually; most holy to the Lord. Greek repeats 'once a year'.
Both: each gives a ransom for his life at the census; Latin so no plague is among them, Greek so no downfall.
Both: half a shekel / didrachma, twenty obols, offered to the Lord; Latin 'measure of the temple', Greek 'holy didrachma'.
Both: everyone counted from twenty years up gives; Latin 'the ransom', Greek 'the contribution to the Lord'.
Both: the rich give no more and the poor no less than half; Greek adds the purpose 'to make propitiation for your lives'.
Both: the money goes to the tabernacle's work as a memorial before the Lord and for propitiation of their lives.
Both: a bronze basin with its base for washing, placed between the tent and the altar, with water put in.
Both: Aaron and his sons wash their hands and feet from it.
Latin: washing before entering the tent or approaching the altar to offer incense; Greek: washing before the tent so they do not die, and altar service with burnt offerings.
Latin: lest they die, an everlasting statute; Greek repeats the washing of hands and feet and the entering-the-tent clause before the perpetual statute.
Both: the Lord spoke to Moses; Greek's 'saying' is the Latin dicens in the next verse.
Both: five hundred shekels of choice myrrh, half as much cinnamon, and two hundred fifty of fragrant cane.
Latin: five hundred shekels of cassia; Greek: five hundred sanctuary shekels of iris. A hin of olive oil in both.
Both: a holy anointing oil, a perfumer's compound; Greek adds 'It shall be holy anointing oil.'
Both: anoint the tent and the ark; Latin 'ark of the covenant', Greek 'ark of the testimony'.
Latin anoints the table, its vessels, lampstand, utensils, and incense altars; Greek names only the lampstand and its utensils and the incense altar here.
Latin ends with the burnt-offering altar and all furnishings in general; Greek names the altar's utensils, the table, and the basin and its base.
Both: consecrate them as most holy; whoever touches them is sanctified.
Both: this anointing oil is holy throughout their generations; Latin 'holy to Me', Greek 'holy anointing oil for you'.
Both: not applied to human flesh, no imitation made, and it is holy and holy to you.
Latin penalizes one who compounds its like and gives it to an outsider; Greek penalizes one who makes anything like it or gives any to an outsider.
Both: take stacte, onycha, fragrant galbanum, and clear frankincense in equal weights.
Both: a perfumer's blended incense, pure and holy; Latin addresses Moses singly, Greek says 'they shall make them'.
Both: grind fine and place some before the testimony where God appears / makes Himself known; Greek places it before the testimonies in the tent. Most holy in both.
Both forbid making this composition for themselves; Latin 'holy to the Lord', Greek 'a holy thing to you for the Lord'.
Both: whoever makes its like to enjoy its fragrance perishes from among his people.
Both: the Lord has called Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, of Judah, by name.
Both: filled with the Spirit of God / a divine Spirit of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge for every work.
Greek adds blue, purple, scarlet yarn, and fine linen to the gold, silver, and bronze that Latin names; Latin says 'devise whatever can be fashioned'.
Latin lists marble, gems, and various woods; Greek has stone, woodworking crafts, and every kind of work.
Latin names Oholiab son of Ahisamach of Dan as companion; Greek names Eliab. Wisdom given to the skilled in both.
Both list the tent, the ark, the cover on it, and the furnishings; covenant / testimony labels are swapped between tent and ark.
Both list table and utensils and the pure lampstand with utensils; Latin names the incense altar's utensils, Greek names 'the altars'.
Both include the basin and its base; Latin adds utensils of the burnt-offering altar here, which Greek covers in the preceding list.
Both: the holy / ministering garments for Aaron and his sons for priestly service.
Both: the anointing oil and incense for the sanctuary, made as commanded; Latin 'incense of spices', Greek 'compounded incense'.
Both: keep My Sabbath as a sign so they know the Lord sanctifies them; Latin singular, Greek plural Sabbaths.
Both: keep the Sabbath; profaning means death and working means being cut off; Greek says holy 'to the Lord'.
Both: six days of work, the seventh a holy rest to the Lord, and death for working on it.
Both: Israel keeps and celebrates the Sabbath throughout their generations as an everlasting covenant.
Both: a perpetual sign between God and Israel since the Lord made heaven and earth in six days; Latin 'ceased from work', Greek 'rested and ceased'.
Both: after finishing speaking on Sinai, God gave Moses two stone tablets of the testimony written by God's finger.
Both: the people gather against Aaron over Moses' delay and ask for gods to go before them.
Latin has earrings from wives, sons, and daughters; Greek only from wives and daughters.
Both: the people bring the earrings to Aaron; Latin 'did what he commanded', Greek 'took off the earrings from their ears'.
Latin: they declare 'These are your gods'; Greek: Aaron says it. Tool of fashioning (casting / engraving tool) and 'led out / brought up' also differ.
Both: Aaron builds an altar before the calf and announces a feast / festival of the Lord tomorrow; Latin adds 'like a herald'.
Latin: the people rise and offer burnt and peace offerings; Greek: Aaron (he) rises early and offers. People eat, drink, and play in both.
Both: the Lord sends Moses down because his people have sinned; Latin 'sinned', Greek 'acted lawlessly' and adds 'Hurry away from here'.
Both: quickly turned from the way, made a calf, worshiped and sacrificed to it, and said 'These are your gods'; Latin 'molten'.
Latin has the Lord saying again that the people are stiff-necked; Greek has no corresponding declaration.
Both: leave Me so My anger destroys them, and I will make you a great nation; Latin adds 'wrath may blaze'.
Both: Moses asks why the Lord's anger burns against the people He led out with great strength; Latin 'mighty hand', Greek 'uplifted arm'.
Both: do not let the Egyptians say He led them out to kill them in the mountains; Latin 'cunningly', Greek 'with evil intent'.
Both recall Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob / Israel, to whom God swore, with offspring like the stars and the land forever; wording of the quotation differs.
Both: the Lord is appeased regarding the harm / calamity He had spoken against His people.
Both: Moses comes down with the two tablets written on both sides; Greek adds that they are stone.
Both: the tablets are God's work and the writing is God's engraved writing.
Both: Joshua hears the people shouting and tells Moses there is a sound / cry of war in the camp.
Latin: not the shout of those urging battle or flight, but the voice of singers; Greek: not a song of victory or defeat, but a wine-song.
Both: Moses sees the calf and the dancing, grows angry, and shatters the tablets at the mountain's foot.
Both: he burns the calf, grinds it fine, scatters it on the water, and makes Israel drink it.
Both: Moses asks Aaron what the people did to him that he brought so great a sin on them.
Both: Aaron asks Moses not to be angry; Latin says the people are inclined to evil, Greek says 'this people's impulse'.
Both: the people asked Aaron to make gods to go before them, not knowing what happened to Moses.
Both: the people gave Aaron their gold, he threw it in the fire, and the calf came out; Latin asks who has gold, Greek tells them to take off gold ornaments.
Latin: Aaron stripped the people naked to their shame among enemies; Greek: Aaron scattered them, to their enemies' delight.
Both: Moses at the camp gate calls whoever is the Lord's to join him, and the Levites gather.
Both: each takes his sword and goes gate to gate killing; Latin lists brother, friend, and neighbor, Greek brother, neighbor, and nearest one.
Both: Moses says they have consecrated / filled their hands to the Lord at the cost of son and brother, so a blessing is given.
Both: Moses tells the people they sinned greatly and will go up to the Lord; Latin 'to see if I can plead', Greek 'to make propitiation'.
Both: Moses returns and says the people sinned and made gold gods; Latin adds 'Either forgive them this guilt', which Greek places in the next verse.
Both: if not forgiven, blot me out of Your book; Greek states the forgiveness condition here ('if You will forgive... but if not').
Both: whoever has sinned against the Lord is blotted out of His book.
Both: lead the people, My angel goes before you, and I will punish their sin; Latin 'day of vengeance', Greek 'day I visit'.
Both: the Lord struck the people over the calf Aaron made; Latin 'for the guilt of', Greek 'because of the making'.
Both: go up from this place to the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to be given to their offspring.
Latin sends an angel to drive out Canaanite, Amorite, Hittite, Perizzite, Hivite, Jebusite; Greek omits the Canaanite and adds the Girgashites.
Both: a land flowing with milk and honey, but God will not go up lest He destroy a stiff-necked people on the way.
Latin: the people mourn and none puts on his usual ornaments; Greek: they mourn in mourning clothes.
Latin: going up among them for a moment would destroy them; Greek: beware another blow. Remove ornaments to know / show what God will do.
Both: Israel removes its ornaments from Mount Horeb onward; Greek adds splendid clothing.
Both: Moses pitches the tent outside the camp; Latin names it the Tabernacle of the Covenant for those with a question, Greek Tent of Testimony for those seeking the Lord.
Both: the people stand at their tent entrances watching Moses until he enters; Latin watch his back, Greek watch him go.
Both: when Moses enters the tent, the pillar of cloud descends at the entrance and God speaks with him.
Both: all see the cloud and worship at their tent entrances; Latin 'stood and worshiped', Greek 'rose and bowed down'.
Both: the Lord speaks to Moses face to face as to a friend; Joshua son of Nun stays in the tent.
Latin: 'I know you by name'; Greek: 'I know you above all'. Moses complains in both that he is not told whom God sends.
Latin: show me Your face to know You and look on this people; Greek: reveal Yourself to see You with understanding and know the nation is Yours.
Both promise rest and that God goes before Moses; Latin 'My face will go before you', Greek 'I Myself will go'.
Both: if You do not go before / with us, do not lead us out; Latin 'us', Greek 'me'.
Both: God's going with them is how favor is known and they are glorified above all peoples; wording of the rhetorical question differs.
Latin: 'I know you by name'; Greek: 'I know you above all'. God grants Moses' request because he found favor in both.
Both: Moses says, 'Show me Your glory.'
Latin: God shows all goodness and proclaims the name of the Lord; Greek: God passes before in His glory and speaks His name. Mercy clause agrees.
Both: you cannot see My face, for no human can see it and live.
Both: there is a place beside Me and you shall stand on the rock.
Both: when My glory passes, I will set you in the cleft of the rock and shelter you with My hand until I pass.
Both: God removes His hand, Moses sees His back, but His face cannot be seen.
Both: cut two stone tablets like the first and God will write the former words; Greek adds 'come up to Me on the mountain' here.
Both: be ready in the morning, go up Mount Sinai, and stand with / before God on the summit.
Both: no one goes up or is seen on the mountain, and flocks and herds do not graze near it.
Both: Moses cuts two tablets and goes up Sinai as commanded, carrying them; Latin rises in the night, Greek early.
Latin: the Lord descends and Moses stands with Him, invoking the Lord's name; Greek: the Lord descends, stands beside him, and calls on the name.
Latin has Moses speaking as the Lord passes ('Sovereign Lord God, merciful...'); Greek has the Lord Himself proclaiming. Speaker differs.
Latin: no one is innocent of himself and God repays fathers' iniquity; Greek: God does not cleanse the guilty and brings the fathers' lawlessness on descendants.
Both: Moses quickly bows to the ground and worships.
Both: if I have found favor, go with us, for the people are stiff-necked; Latin 'take away and possess us', Greek 'You shall take away... we shall be Yours'.
Latin: God makes a covenant in everyone's sight and works fearsome signs; Greek: establishes a covenant with Moses and does marvelous, glorious things.
Latin drives out six peoples including the Canaanite; Greek lists seven, adding the Girgashites. Greek is a present 'I am driving out'.
Both warn against alliances with the land's inhabitants; Latin 'friendships that bring ruin', Greek 'covenant, a stumbling block'.
Greek adds burning their gods' carved images with fire; Latin has altars, statues, and groves only.
Both: do not worship another god, for the Lord, Jealous by name, is a jealous God.
Both: no covenant with the inhabitants, lest they prostitute themselves to their gods and invite you to eat sacrifices; Greek adds that they sacrifice to them.
Both warn against taking their daughters for your sons; Greek adds giving your daughters to their sons.
Both: do not make molten / cast-metal gods for yourself.
Both: keep Unleavened Bread seven days in the month Israel left Egypt; Latin 'month of new crops... springtime', Greek 'month of new grain' twice.
Both: every male that opens the womb is the Lord's; Latin says among cattle and sheep, Greek specifies firstborn calf and sheep.
Latin: an unredeemed donkey's firstborn is killed; Greek: if a beast of burden is not redeemed, pay its value. Sons redeemed and empty hands forbidden in both.
Both: six days of work and rest on the seventh; Latin ceasing plowing and reaping, Greek rest at sowing and harvest.
Both keep the Feast of Weeks at wheat harvest; Latin's second festival is when everything is stored at year's end, Greek's is Ingathering at mid-year.
Both: all males appear before the Lord three times a year; Latin adds 'almighty'.
Both: God drives out nations and enlarges borders so no one threatens the land; Latin 'plot against', Greek 'desire'.
Both: no blood of the sacrifice with leaven and no Passover sacrifice left until morning.
Latin forbids boiling a young goat in its mother's milk; Greek forbids offering a lamb in its mother's milk. Firstfruits clause agrees.
Both: write these words, for by them God made a covenant with Moses and Israel.
Both: forty days and nights, no bread or water, and he wrote the ten words of the covenant on the tablets.
Latin: Aaron and Israel's sons saw Moses' horned face; Greek: Aaron and Israel's elders saw the skin of his face glorified. Both fear to approach.
Both have Moses call them and Aaron and the leaders return; Greek says "all" the leaders and names Moses, Latin has neither.
Both say all Israel came and he commanded them all that the Lord gave on Sinai; heard from / spoken to is only wording.
Both have him put a veil over his face when he finished speaking; Greek only names Moses.
Both have him remove the veil on entering before the Lord until he came out, then tell Israel what was commanded.
Latin says the face was horned and he covered it whenever speaking to them; Greek says it was glorified and the veil stays until he enters to converse with God.
Both have the assembly gathered and Moses state what the Lord commanded; commanded / said is only wording.
Both give six days of work, a holy seventh-day Sabbath rest to the Lord, and death for working on it.
Greek adds the closing "I am the Lord"; Latin has only the prohibition on kindling fire on the Sabbath.
Both have Moses address the whole assembly and introduce the Lord's command; commanded / appointed is wording.
Latin says to set apart firstfruits, offered by the willing and ready in spirit; Greek says take an offering, brought by whoever welcomes it in heart. Gold, silver, bronze agree.
Both list blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen and goats' hair; twice-dyed / double-spun is only wording.
Both list rams' skins dyed red, blue/violet skins and acacia (Greek "decay-resistant") wood.
Latin adds oil for the lamps, ointment and sweet incense; the Greek has no corresponding entry here.
Latin has onyx stones and gems for the ephod and breastpiece; Greek has sardius and engraving stones for the shoulder-piece and full-length robe.
Both call every skilled / wise person to come and make what the Lord commanded.
Both list tabernacle furnishings, but items differ: Latin has rings, framework, pegs and bases; Greek has side curtains, stretching cords, bars and pillars.
Both list ark, poles, atonement cover and veil; Greek calls it the ark of the testimony, Latin adds the veil spread before it.
Latin adds the table's poles and the bread of presentation; Greek has only the table and its utensils.
Latin adds the lamps and oil to feed the flames; Greek has only the lampstand for light and its utensils.
Latin lists altar of incense, poles, anointing oil, spice incense and entrance screen; Greek has only the incense and anointing oil.
Latin adds the bronze grating, poles, basin and base of the burnt-offering altar; Greek has only the altar and its utensils.
Both have the court hangings and pillars; Latin adds bases and the entrance screen, Greek adds the emerald stones.
Latin lists the pegs and cords of the tabernacle and court; the Greek has no separate entry for them.
Latin gives sanctuary garments and Aaron's and his sons' vestments for priesthood; Greek lists the holy robes and tunics and adds anointing oil and compounded incense.
Both say the whole assembly of Israel left Moses' presence; multitude / congregation is wording.
Both say the willing-hearted brought offerings to the Lord for the tabernacle work, its service and the holy garments.
Items and givers differ: Latin has men with women giving bracelets, earrings, rings, armlets; Greek has men bringing from the women seals, earrings, rings, chains, bracelets.
Latin lists blue, purple, scarlet, linen, goats' hair, red and violet skins; Greek names only fine linen, blue skins and red rams' skins.
Both have silver and bronze offered and wood brought; Latin says acacia wood for various uses, Greek decay-resistant wood for the work of preparation.
Both have skilled women spinning and giving blue, purple, scarlet and fine linen.
Latin has them give goats' hair freely; Greek has the skilled women spin the goats' hair.
Latin has leaders offering onyx stones and gems for ephod and breastpiece; Greek has emerald stones and stones for the shoulder-piece and oracle-piece.
Latin has spices and oil for lamps, ointment and incense; Greek has compounds, anointing oil and compounded incense, with no lamp oil.
Both have the willing men and women bringing offerings for the work the Lord commanded through Moses; Latin adds that all Israel dedicated voluntary offerings.
Both have Bezalel son of Uri son of Hur of Judah called by name; Latin says the Lord, Greek says God.
Both say he is filled with God's Spirit, wisdom, understanding, knowledge; Latin adds "every skill", Greek says knowledge of all things.
Both give skill to work gold, silver and bronze; Latin says devise and carry out the work, Greek says design in every craft.
Both speak of working stone and wood and every skilled work.
Names differ: Latin has Oholiab son of Ahisamach, Greek has Eliab; Greek adds that the Lord put it in his mind to teach.
Latin has both instructed to work as woodworkers, weavers and embroiderers and to devise new things; Greek has them filled with wisdom for all the sanctuary work.
Both have Bezalel and the wise workers doing the Lord's work; Latin names Oholiab, Greek names Eliab.
Both have Moses calling the wise and willing workers; Greek names Bezalel and Eliab and says God gave knowledge, Latin says them and the Lord gave wisdom.
Both have the workers receiving the Israelites' gifts and more offerings arriving every morning; Latin says Moses handed them over, Greek says they received them from Moses.
Latin says the craftsmen were compelled to come; Greek says they came, each according to the work he was doing.
Both have the workers telling Moses the people bring more than needed; Greek adds "for the work the Lord commanded".
Latin has a herald forbidding man or woman to offer more; Greek has the proclamation forbid working for the sanctuary firstfruits, and the people restrained.
Both say what was supplied was sufficient with some left over; superabundarent / left over is wording.
Latin describes ten curtains of twisted linen, blue, purple and scarlet in patterned work; Greek says only that they made ten curtains.
Both give each curtain as twenty-eight cubits by four, all alike.
Latin joins the curtains five and five; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin makes blue loops on the curtain edges; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin has the loops facing and joined; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin has fifty gold rings clasping the curtain loops into one tabernacle; Greek has gold rings for the tent and bronze rings for the court and covering.
Latin makes eleven goats' hair coverings for the roof; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin gives the covering dimensions (thirty by four cubits); the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin joins the coverings five and six separately; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin makes fifty loops on each covering edge; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin makes fifty bronze clasps to join the coverings into one; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin makes coverings of red rams' skins and violet skins; the Greek has no corresponding clause.
Latin makes upright acacia boards for the tabernacle; the Greek has no corresponding board account.
Latin gives board size (ten cubits by one and a half); the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin gives each board two joints; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin places twenty boards on the south side; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin gives forty silver bases, two per board; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin makes twenty boards for the north side; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin gives forty silver bases for the north boards; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin makes six boards for the west side; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin adds two corner boards at the back; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin joins the corner boards bottom to top; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin totals eight boards with sixteen silver bases; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin makes five acacia bars for one side; the Greek has no corresponding bar count.
Latin makes five bars for the other side and five for the west; the Greek has no corresponding bar count.
Latin adds a middle bar running corner to corner; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin overlays the framework with gold on cast silver bases; Greek overlays the pillars with silver and the veil pillars with gold, adding gold hooks. Gold rings and bars agree.
Both make the veil of blue, purple, scarlet and fine linen; Latin says skilled varied weaving, Greek says woven cherubim.
Both set four gold-overlaid acacia pillars on silver bases; Greek adds cast capitals for the tent, doorway and court gate, and silver hooks.
Both make the entrance screen of blue, purple, scarlet and linen; Latin says embroidered work, Greek says woven cherubim.
Both give five pillars with gold-covered capitals and bronze bases; Greek also mentions rings and bands.
Latin gives the ark's acacia wood, dimensions and inner and outer gold; Greek says only that Bezalel made the ark.
Latin makes a gold molding around the ark; Greek instead has the pure-gold overlay inside and outside, with no molding.
Both cast four gold rings for the ark, two on each side.
Both have the poles made and overlaid with gold; Latin names acacia wood, Greek calls them carrying poles.
Both have the poles used in the rings to carry the ark; Latin says he inserted them, Greek says the rings were wide enough for them.
Latin adds the cover's dimensions and the gloss "oraculum"; Greek says only that he made the gold propitiatory cover above the ark.
Both make two gold cherubim; Latin specifies hammered gold and placing them either side of the cover.
Both place one cherub at each end of the propitiatory cover.
Both have the cherubim's wings covering the propitiatory cover; Latin adds that they face each other and look toward it.
Latin makes the table of acacia wood with stated dimensions; Greek makes it of pure gold, set before God.
Latin covers the table with gold and adds a gold rim; the Greek has no separate rim clause.
Latin adds an openwork gold molding and a second molding on the rim; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Both cast four rings for the table; Latin places them at the four corners by the legs, Greek has two on each side.
Both have the rings and poles for carrying the table; Latin places the rings opposite the molding.
Both make the table's poles and overlay them with gold.
Both make the table's gold vessels for drink offerings; the lists of dishes, bowls, cups, censers and ladles differ in naming.
Latin describes the hammered lampstand with branches, cups, knobs and lilies; Greek gives a solid shaft with branches on both sides, without the cups, knobs and lilies.
Both give three branches on each side of the lampstand; Latin counts six branches, Greek speaks of shoots extending from them.
Latin gives three nut-shaped cups with knobs and lilies per branch; Greek describes nut-shaped lamp supports, fittings and a seventh solid-gold fitting.
Latin adds four nut-shaped cups on the shaft with knobs and lilies; the Greek has no corresponding clause here.
Latin places knobs beneath each pair of the six branches; the Greek has no corresponding clause here.
Latin says knobs and branches were one piece of hammered pure gold; Greek states solid gold only in its earlier verse.
Both make seven gold lamps with snuffers/tongs and trays for the lampstand.
Latin gives the lampstand's weight as a talent of gold; the Greek has no corresponding total.
Latin makes the acacia incense altar with dimensions and horns; the Greek has no corresponding construction here.
Latin overlays the incense altar with pure gold; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin adds a gold molding and two rings per side for carrying poles; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Latin makes the altar's poles of acacia covered with gold; the Greek has no corresponding detail.
Both make the holy anointing oil and the incense of spices, by a perfumer's work.
Latin makes the burnt-offering altar of acacia wood, five by five by three cubits; Greek makes a bronze altar from the bronze censers of Korah's rebels.
Latin adds the altar's horns and bronze plating; the Greek has no corresponding clause.
Both make the altar's bronze utensils; Latin lists pots, tongs, forks, hooks, firepans, Greek lists firepan, base, bowls and meat forks.
Both make a bronze net-like grating beneath, reaching the altar's midpoint; Latin calls it a grating with a ledge, Greek an attachment.
Both have four rings for carrying poles; Latin casts them at the grating's corners, Greek puts them on the attachment's sides.
Latin makes the poles of acacia and covers them with bronze; the Greek has no separate pole clause.
Latin inserts the poles and says the altar was hollow, made of boards; the Greek has no corresponding clause.
Both make the bronze basin from the women's mirrors; Greek adds the fasting women, the day of erection and the priests' washing.
Latin puts the courtyard's linen hangings on the south side, a hundred cubits long; Greek says southwest hangings, a hundred by a hundred.
Latin gives twenty bronze pillars and bases with silver capitals and engraved fittings; Greek gives only twenty pillars and twenty bases.
Both give the north side matching the south, with twenty pillars and bases; Greek states the hundred by hundred measure.
Both give fifty-cubit hangings and ten pillars with bases on the west; Latin adds bronze pillars, silver capitals and engraved fittings.
Both give the east side as fifty cubits of hangings.
Both give fifteen cubits of hangings with three pillars and bases on one side.
Both give the other side as fifteen cubits, three pillars and three bases, with the gate between.
Both say all the court's hangings were of twisted / spun fine linen.
Both give bronze bases and silver-covered capitals and pillars; Latin adds engraved fittings, Greek names silver hooks.
Both make the gate screen of blue, purple, scarlet and linen, twenty cubits long and five high; Greek adds five cubits breadth.
Both give four pillars with bronze bases and silver capitals; Latin adds engraved fittings, Greek adds silver hooks and silvered pillars.
Both make the pegs of the tent and court of bronze.
Both introduce the tabernacle's inventory under Ithamar for the Levites' service; Latin says furnishings counted, Greek says arrangement appointed.
Both say Bezalel of Judah did as the Lord commanded; Latin adds his grandfather Hur.
Latin joins Oholiab as Bezalel's companion, skilled in wood, weaving and embroidery; Greek names Eliab, who directed the woven and embroidered work.
Gold total is twenty-nine talents and 730 shekels in Latin but 720 shekels in Greek; Greek also calls it the firstfruits gold.
Latin gives the 603,550 enrolled men here; Greek gives the silver total of 100 talents and 1,775 shekels and carries the enrollment to its next verse.
Latin gives the hundred talents of silver for the bases; Greek gives the half-shekel per head and the 603,550 enrolled.
Latin casts a hundred bases from the hundred talents; Greek casts a hundred capitals for the tent and the veil.
Latin uses the 1,775 shekels for the pillars' capitals and silver covering; Greek uses them for the pillars' hooks and for gilding the capitals.
Bronze total differs: Latin has seventy-two thousand talents and 400 shekels, Greek seventy talents and 1,500 shekels.
Both cast the entrance bases, the bronze altar part and utensils; Greek adds all the tent's equipment and calls the grating an attachment.
Both list the court's bases, its gate bases and the pegs of the tent and court.
Both have the holy garments for Aaron made as the Lord commanded Moses; Greek names the skilled craftsmen and the remaining blue, purple and scarlet.
Both make the ephod / shoulder-piece of gold, blue, purple, scarlet and fine linen.
Both have the gold plates cut into threads to be woven with the coloured materials.
Both have joined sections on either side; Latin speaks of edges joined at the top, Greek of joined shoulder sections.
Latin adds a sash of the same colours; Greek describes the woven work made by itself from the same materials, with no sash.
Both make two engraved stones set in gold with Israel's names; Latin says onyx, Greek says emerald.
Both place the stones on the shoulders / sides of the ephod as a memorial for Israel.
Both make the breastpiece / oracle-piece like the ephod, of gold, blue, purple, scarlet and linen.
Both make it square, doubled and a span.
Both set four rows of stones; the first is sardius, topaz, emerald.
Both give the second row as carbuncle, sapphire, jasper.
Both give the third row as ligure, agate, amethyst.
Both give chrysolite, onyx and beryl enclosed in gold; the order of onyx and beryl differs.
Both have twelve stones engraved with the twelve tribes' names.
Both make linked / braided chains of pure gold for the breastpiece.
Both make two gold rings for the breastpiece's sides; Latin adds two hooks, Greek two gold rosettes.
Both attach gold chains / braids to the rings; Latin hangs them from the rings onto hooks at the ephod's corners.
Latin has the front and back fitted so ephod and breastpiece fasten to each other; Greek puts the braids on the rosettes and shoulders facing forward.
Latin binds the pieces to the sash with a blue cord through rings; Greek makes two more gold rings at the oracle-piece's rear edge.
Latin makes the ephod's robe entirely blue; Greek here places two gold rings on the shoulders, with the robe following later.
Latin makes the robe's head opening and woven border; Greek here fastens the oracle-piece to the shoulder-piece with blue cord.
Latin adds pomegranates on the lower hem; Greek here has the entirely blue woven robe beneath the shoulder-piece.
Latin places gold bells among the pomegranates on the robe's hem; this Greek verse instead describes the robe's head opening and its border.
Latin has a gold bell and pomegranate adorning the high priest at his ministry; this Greek verse makes the coloured pomegranates on the hem.
Latin makes woven linen tunics for Aaron and his sons; this Greek verse makes gold bells set between the pomegranates.
Latin makes linen headdresses with little crowns; this Greek verse has a gold bell and pomegranate on the robe's hem.
Latin makes linen undergarments; this Greek verse makes the woven linen tunics for Aaron and his sons.
Latin makes the sash of twisted linen and colours; this Greek verse lists turbans, headband and linen undergarments.
Latin makes the gold plate inscribed "Holy to the Lord"; this Greek verse makes the sashes.
Latin fastens the plate to the headdress with a blue cord; this Greek verse makes the gold plate and its inscription.
Latin says all the tabernacle work was completed; this Greek verse puts the blue band on the plate.
Latin lists the tabernacle parts brought to Moses; this Greek verse says Israel did as commanded and made utensils from the remaining gold.
Latin lists the ram-skin and violet coverings brought; this Greek verse says they brought the robes, tent, bases, bars and pillars.
Latin lists the veil, ark, poles and atonement cover; this Greek verse lists the skin coverings.
Latin lists the table with vessels and the bread; this Greek verse lists the ark and its poles.
Latin lists the lampstand, lamps and oil; this Greek verse lists the table, utensils and bread.
Latin lists the gold altar, ointment and incense; this Greek verse lists the lampstand, lamps and oil.
Latin lists the screen at the tabernacle entrance; this Greek verse lists the altar, anointing oil and incense.
Latin lists the bronze altar, basin, court hangings and pillars; the Greek has no corresponding entry in this position.
Both list the court's screen, pegs and equipment; Latin adds cords and the statement that no utensil was missing, Greek adds the court's hangings, pillars and tent utensils.
Both speak of the priestly garments for Aaron and his sons in the sanctuary.
Latin says Israel brought the garments as the Lord commanded; Greek says Israel made all the equipment as the Lord commanded Moses.
Both have Moses seeing the work done as the Lord commanded and blessing them; Greek repeats that they had done it so.
Both command erecting the tabernacle on the first day of the first month; at the new moon is only wording.
Both command placing the ark and screening it with the veil.
Both command bringing in the table with its arrangement and the lampstand with its lamps.
Both place the gold incense altar before the ark and a screen at the entrance.
Both place the altar of burnt offering at the entrance of the tabernacle.
Latin sets the basin between altar and tabernacle and fills it with water; the Greek has no corresponding command.
Latin has the courtyard and its entrance enclosed with hangings; Greek has the tent set about and everything around it sanctified.
Both anoint the tent and its furnishings with the anointing oil to make them holy.
Both anoint the burnt-offering altar and its utensils; Greek adds that the altar becomes most holy.
Latin anoints the basin and its base and consecrates everything as most holy; the Greek has no corresponding clause.
Both bring Aaron and his sons to the doors and wash them with water.
Both clothe and anoint Aaron and his sons for priesthood forever; Greek spells out Aaron's robes, the sons' tunics and "throughout their generations".
Both say Moses did everything the Lord commanded.
Both date the tabernacle's erection to the first day of the first month of the second year; Greek adds "after they came out of Egypt".
Both have Moses erecting the tabernacle with bars and pillars; Latin adds boards and bases, Greek has capitals.
Both have the covering spread over the tabernacle as the Lord commanded.
Both put the testimony in the ark with poles beneath; Latin adds the place of divine speech set above it, which the Greek lacks.
Both bring the ark in and hang the veil before it as the Lord commanded.
Both place the table on the north side outside the veil.
Both have the bread of presentation set before the Lord as commanded.
Both place the lampstand on the south side of the tent; Latin adds opposite the table.
Both set the lamps in place before the Lord as commanded.
Both place the gold altar in the tent opposite the veil.
Both have incense of spices / compounded incense burned on the altar as commanded.
Latin places the screen at the tabernacle entrance; the Greek has no corresponding clause here.
Both place the altar of burnt offering at the entrance; Latin adds Moses offering burnt offering and sacrifices on it as commanded.
Latin sets the basin between the tabernacle and altar and fills it with water; the Greek has no corresponding clause here.
Latin has Moses, Aaron and his sons washing hands and feet; the Greek has this material earlier, not here.
Latin says the washing was when entering the tent or approaching the altar; the Greek has this material earlier, not here.
Both have the court erected around the tent and altar and the work finished; Latin adds the screen drawn across its entrance.
Both say Moses could not enter because of the cloud and the Lord's glory; Latin has the majesty shining forth, Greek the tent filled with glory.
Latin has Israel set out by their companies when the cloud leaves; Greek has them set out with their belongings when it rises.
Both have Israel staying put while the cloud stays; Latin says they remained in the same place, Greek says they did not set out until the day it rose.
Both have the cloud by day and fire by night in sight of all Israel; Latin says the Lord's cloud and encampments, Greek says a cloud and journeys.
Both have the Lord calling Moses and speaking to him from the tent of testimony.
Both address Israel about offerings from cattle or flock; Latin says sacrificial victims, Greek says gifts.
Both require an unblemished male burnt offering from the cattle at the tent door; to obtain favor / acceptable differs in wording.
Both have the calf slaughtered before the Lord and Aaron's sons pouring the blood around the altar.
Both have the burnt offering skinned and cut into pieces.
Both have fire and wood prepared on the altar; Greek names the priests as doing it.
Both have the cut parts and head arranged on the altar wood; Latin says what adheres to the liver, Greek says suet.
Both wash the entrails and legs and burn all on the altar as a fragrant aroma to the Lord.
Greek adds that he lays his hand on the animal's head; Latin has no such clause. Sheep or goats / lambs and kids otherwise agree.
Both slaughter it on the altar's north side and have Aaron's sons pour the blood around the altar.
Both divide the animal and place the parts on the altar wood; Latin says what adheres to the liver, Greek says suet.
Both wash the entrails and feet and burn all on the altar as a pleasing fragrance.
Both give the bird offering from turtledoves or pigeons.
Latin twists back the head, opens the wound and lets the blood run on the altar's edge; Greek pinches off the head, places it on the altar and drains the blood at the base.
Both throw the crop with feathers beside the altar on the east, at the ash place.
Both break the bird open by its wings without dividing it and burn it on the altar wood as a fragrant offering.
Both give a fine flour offering with oil and frankincense poured and placed on it.
Both bring it to Aaron's sons, who take a handful of flour, oil and all the frankincense as the memorial portion.
Both give the remainder to Aaron and his sons as most holy.
Both give oven-baked unleavened loaves / cakes mixed with oil and wafers spread with oil.
Both give an unleavened fine-flour offering mixed with oil, prepared in a pan / on a griddle.
Both break it into pieces and pour oil on it.
Both give a fine-flour and oil offering from a cooking vessel; Latin names a griddle, Greek a hearth.
Both have the offering brought to the priest; Latin has it placed in his hands, Greek says he approaches the altar.
Both have the priest take the memorial portion and burn it on the altar as a pleasing fragrance.
Both give what remains to Aaron and his sons as most holy among the Lord's offerings.
Both forbid leaven and honey in offerings to the Lord.
Both allow them only as firstfruits and forbid placing them on the altar for a fragrant aroma.
Both require salt of the covenant on every offering; season / bring is only wording.
Both give a roasted, crushed firstfruits offering; Latin specifies green ears roasted in fire and crushed like meal, Greek says new roasted groats.
Both pour oil and place frankincense on the firstfruits offering.
Both have the priest burn a memorial portion of grain, oil and all the frankincense.
