Both give an unblemished male or female peace offering / sacrifice of deliverance from the cattle before the Lord.
Both have the hand laid on the head, slaughter at the tent door and the priests pouring the blood around the altar.
Both present the fat covering the inner organs; Latin says fat within the organs generally, Greek says fat on the belly.
Both present the two kidneys with their fat and the liver lobe / membrane.
Both have the priests burn these on the altar wood as a pleasing fragrance; Greek places them on top of the burnt offerings.
Both give an unblemished male or female peace offering from the flock.
Both cover offering a lamb before the Lord.
Both have the hand laid on its head, slaughter at the tent entrance and the blood poured around the altar.
Latin offers the fat and the whole tail; Greek offers the fat and the unblemished loin removed with the lower-back muscles, and the belly fat.
Both list the kidneys with their fat and the liver lobe / membrane; Latin also repeats the belly fat and organs.
Both have the priest burn these on the altar; Latin calls it food for the fire, Greek a fragrant aroma.
Both cover a goat offered before the Lord.
Both have the hand laid on the head, slaughter at the tent entrance and the blood poured around the altar.
Both offer the fat covering the belly and the inner organs to the Lord.
Both list the two kidneys with their fat and the liver lobe / fat.
Both have the priest burn it on the altar as a fragrant offering; all the fat is the Lord's.
Both give a perpetual ordinance in all dwellings forbidding eating fat or blood.
Both address sins done unintentionally against what the Lord's commandments forbid.
Both have an anointed priest's sin bringing guilt on the people and an unblemished calf; Greek says high priest and adds "for the sin he has committed".
Both bring the calf to the tent door, lay a hand on its head and slaughter it before the Lord.
Both bring some of the calf's blood into the tent; Greek adds that the anointed priest's hands have been consecrated.
Both dip a finger in the blood and sprinkle it seven times before the veil.
Both put blood on the incense altar's horns and pour the rest at the burnt-offering altar's base.
Both remove all the fat of the sin-offering calf covering the inner parts.
Both list the two kidneys with their fat and the liver lobe / fat.
Both remove it as from the peace-offering calf and burn it on the altar.
Both list the calf's hide, flesh, head, extremities / feet, entrails and dung.
Both carry it outside the camp to a clean place of ashes and burn it on wood.
Both cover the whole congregation sinning in ignorance; Greek adds that the matter escapes their notice and they incur guilt.
Both have the sin become known and a calf brought to the tent door; Greek specifies an unblemished calf from the cattle.
Both have the elders lay their hands on the calf's head and slaughter it before the Lord.
Both have the anointed priest bring some of the blood into the tent.
Both dip a finger in the blood and sprinkle it seven times before the veil.
Both put blood on the altar's horns in the tent and pour the rest at the base of the burnt-offering altar.
Both remove all the fat and burn it on the altar.
Both repeat the earlier calf procedure and end with the priest interceding; Latin says the Lord will be gracious, Greek says propitiation is made and sin forgiven.
Both carry the calf outside the camp and burn it as the first calf, as the congregation's sin offering.
Both cover a ruler who sins unintentionally against what the Lord forbids.
Both have the sin become known and an unblemished male goat / kid brought.
Both lay a hand on its head and slaughter it where burnt offerings are slaughtered, as a sin offering.
Both put blood on the horns of the burnt-offering altar and pour the rest at its base.
Both burn all the fat as with peace offerings; the priest makes atonement and he is forgiven.
Both cover a common person who sins unintentionally against what the Lord forbids.
Both have the sin become known and an unblemished female goat / kid brought.
Both lay a hand on the sin offering's head and slaughter it at the burnt-offering place.
Both put blood with the finger on the altar's horns and pour the rest at its base.
Both remove all the fat as from a peace offering and burn it for a pleasing fragrance; he is forgiven.
Both give an unblemished female sheep as the sin offering.
Both lay a hand on its head and slaughter it where burnt offerings are slaughtered.
Both put blood with the finger on the altar's horns and pour the rest at its base.
Both remove all the fat as in the peace offering and burn it on the altar, with forgiveness; Latin says a ram's fat, Greek a sheep's.
Both cover a witness who hears an oath and, not reporting what he saw or knew, bears his sin.
Both cover touching an unclean thing such as a beast-killed carcass; Latin adds forgetting and being guilty, Greek gives a longer list and continues the sentence.
Both cover touching human uncleanness unknowingly and later becoming liable.
Both cover a rash oath to do evil or good, forgotten and later recognized.
Latin says he shall repent of the sin; Greek says he shall confess the sin in the matters he sinned.
Both require a female lamb or goat from the flock with the priest's intercession; Greek adds forgiveness and the offense wording.
Both allow two turtledoves or pigeons, one for sin and one for burnt offering, if he cannot afford a sheep.
Both have the priest offer the sin bird first without severing the head; Latin twists it back toward the wings, Greek pinches it at the neck.
Both sprinkle blood on the altar's side and drain the rest at its base, as a sin offering.
Both burn the second bird as a burnt offering; the priest makes atonement and he is forgiven.
Both allow a tenth of an ephah of fine flour with no oil or frankincense for a sin offering.
Both have the priest take a handful and burn the memorial portion on the altar.
Both have the priest make atonement, with forgiveness, and keep the remainder.
Latin prices the ram at two shekels by the sanctuary weight; Greek says only it is valued in silver shekels by the sanctuary shekel.
Both require restitution plus a fifth to the priest, who atones with the ram.
Both cover unwitting sin against the Lord's commands; Latin has him recognize his iniquity, Greek has him bear the sin.
Both bring an unblemished ram for atonement of unwitting sin; Latin says by assessment of the sin, Greek says valued in silver.
Latin says he transgressed against the Lord by mistake; Greek says he has indeed committed an offense before the Lord.
Both say the Lord spoke to Moses, saying.
Both cover denying a deposit or wronging a neighbor; Latin adds extortion by force, Greek adds a partnership and robbery.
Both cover finding a lost thing and denying it with a false oath.
Latin has only "when convicted of the offense"; Greek continues with the duty to return the plunder, deposit or lost thing.
Both require full repayment plus a fifth to the owner; Greek adds that the swearing was unjust and that he repays on the day he is convicted.
Both require an unblemished ram valued to match the offense; Latin has him give it to the priest, Greek has him bring it to the Lord.
Both have the priest make atonement before the Lord and the man forgiven for all he did.
Both say the Lord spoke to Moses, saying.
Both give the law of the burnt offering: it stays on the altar all night until morning with the fire kept burning.
Both have the priest in linen tunic and undergarments remove the ashes and place them beside the altar.
Both have him change garments and carry the ashes outside the camp to a clean place; Latin adds that they are burned down to fine ash.
Both keep the altar fire burning, with wood added each morning, the burnt offering laid on it and the peace-offering fat burned above.
Both say the fire on the altar burns continually and is never put out.
Both give the law of the grain offering presented by Aaron's sons before the Lord at the altar; Latin adds the accompanying drink offerings.
Both have the priest take a handful of flour with oil and the frankincense and burn it as a memorial.
Both have Aaron and his sons eat the remainder unleavened in a holy place in the courtyard.
Latin gives the reason for no leaven as a part being burned for the Lord; Greek says it is not baked leavened because the Lord has given it to them as their portion.
Both limit eating to the males of the priests, as a perpetual ordinance, and whatever touches it is made holy.
Both say the Lord spoke to Moses, saying.
Both give the tenth of an ephah of flour as the continual offering, half morning and half evening.
Both prepare it with oil on a pan / griddle as a fragrant offering; Latin has it fried and offered hot, Greek has it brought in rolled pieces.
Both have the priest who succeeds the father prepare it; Latin adds that all of it is burned on the altar, Greek that it is a perpetual law fully performed.
Both say a priest's own grain offering is wholly burned and not eaten.
Both say the Lord spoke to Moses, saying.
Both give the sin offering law: slaughtered before the Lord where the burnt offering is, most holy.
Both have the offering priest eat it in a holy place in the tabernacle court.
Both say whatever touches its flesh is made holy and a blood-sprinkled garment is washed in a holy place.
Both break an earthenware cooking vessel and scour and rinse a bronze one.
Both let every priestly male eat it as most holy.
Both forbid eating a sin offering whose blood is brought into the tent; it is burned with fire.
Both give the law of the guilt / offense offering as most holy; Greek specifies the ram.
Both slaughter it where the burnt offering is slaughtered and pour the blood around the altar.
Latin offers the tail and the fat covering the organs; Greek offers all the fat, including the loin, and the fat on the inner parts.
Both list the two kidneys with their fat and the liver lobe / membrane.
Latin has the priest burn them as the Lord's fire offering for guilt; Greek says he offers them up as an offering for an offense. Burn / offer up differs slightly.
Both let every priestly male eat the meat in a holy place because it is most holy; only word order differs.
Both give one law for sin and guilt offerings, belonging to the offering priest; Greek adds that he makes propitiation with it.
Both give the burnt-offering skin to the offering priest; Greek adds "a person's" offering and repeats the burnt offering.
Both give oven, pan and griddle-type offerings to the offering priest; Latin specifies fine flour and lists gridiron and pan, Greek hearth and griddle.
Both say oil-mixed or dry offerings go to all Aaron's sons in equal shares.
Both give the law of the peace / deliverance sacrifice offered to the Lord; only English wording differs.
Latin lists unleavened loaves, wafers, cooked fine flour and oil-mixed cakes; Greek lists fine-flour loaves, wafers and mixed fine flour, without cakes or unleavened loaves.
Both add leavened loaves with the thanksgiving / praise peace sacrifice; Latin phrases it as the victim sacrificed for peace offerings.
Both set one portion aside for the Lord, belonging to the priest who pours the blood; Latin calls it firstfruits, Greek a set-apart portion from all his gifts.
Both require eating on the same day with nothing left until morning; Greek adds that the meat belongs to the offerer.
Both allow a vow or voluntary offering to be eaten on the day and on the next day.
Both burn with fire whatever remains until the third day.
Both void the offering if eaten on the third day and make the eater bear guilt; Latin says offering is invalid, Greek not accepted or credited, and a defilement.
Both forbid meat touched by uncleanness, to be burned, and allow the clean to eat.
Both say an unclean person eating the Lord's peace-offering meat shall perish from his people.
Both cut off the one who touches uncleanness and eats the meat; Greek specifies unclean four-footed animals and abominations and names the sacrifice.
Both forbid eating the fat of sheep, cattle and goats; only the order of animals differs.
Both allow other uses of the fat of animals found dead or torn; Greek adds that it must not be eaten.
Both cut off whoever eats the fat of the offered animal; Latin says fat to be burned for the Lord, Greek fat from livestock offered to the Lord.
Both forbid eating blood of birds or livestock; Greek adds "in any of your dwelling places".
Both say any person who eats blood shall perish from his people.
Both address Israel about the peace offering; Latin says the offerer brings its accompanying offerings (libamenta), Greek that he brings his gift from the sacrifice.

Both forbid the raven and its kind.

Both give the purpose of distinguishing clean from unclean and what may and may not be eaten.

Both have the item washed and isolated for another seven days.

Both have the fat of the sin offerings burned on the altar.
Both have the man who sends away the goat wash, bathe and then enter the camp.
Both have the sin-offering calf and goat carried outside the camp and burned with skins, flesh and dung.
Both have whoever burns them wash, bathe and then enter the camp.
Both set a perpetual ordinance for the tenth day of the seventh month to humble themselves and do no work, native or foreigner.
Both say that on this day expiation / propitiation is made to cleanse them from all sins before the Lord.
Both call it a rest and require humbling oneself by perpetual ordinance; Greek says a Sabbath of Sabbaths.
Both have the anointed and consecrated successor-priest make atonement, wearing the holy linen robe.
Both have him make expiation for the sanctuary, tent, altar, priests and all the people.
Both set a yearly ordinance of atonement for Israel's sins; Latin adds that he did as the Lord commanded Moses, Greek ties the once-a-year rule to the Lord's direction.
Both have Moses speak to Aaron, his sons and all Israel about what the Lord commanded.
Latin binds any man of the house of Israel; Greek also binds the newcomers attached to Israel, and says calf where Latin says ox.
Both make the one who slaughters without bringing it to the tent entrance guilty of blood and cut off; Greek adds that the offering is a burnt or deliverance offering and repeats the charge.
Both require Israel to bring slaughtered sacrifices to the priest at the tent door as peace / deliverance offerings.
Both have the priest pour the blood on the altar at the tent door and burn the fat as a fragrant aroma.
Latin forbids sacrificing to demons with whom they have prostituted themselves; Greek forbids sacrificing to vain things after which they prostitute themselves.
Both address any Israelite or resident foreigner who presents a burnt offering or sacrifice.
Both cut off the one who does not bring it to the tent door to offer to the Lord.
Both have the Lord set His face against any Israelite or foreigner who eats blood and destroy him from his people.
Both say no Israelite or resident foreigner may eat blood.
Both command pouring out the blood of a hunted permitted animal or bird and covering it with earth; hunting wording is English only.
Latin says life is "in" the blood; Greek says life is the blood. Both forbid eating blood on pain of destruction.
Both require washing and bathing and uncleanness until evening for anyone, native or foreigner, who eats an animal found dead or torn.
Latin: not washing garments and body; Greek adds bathing the body in water. Iniquity / lawless deed is a nuance of wording.
Both give the same instruction to speak to Israel: I am the Lord your God.
Both forbid the customs of Egypt and Canaan and walking in their ordinances; custom / practice is English wording.
Both command keeping and walking in the Lord's judgments and precepts; commands / ordinances is only wording.
Both forbid approaching a close relative to uncover nakedness; the Lord seals the command.
Both forbid uncovering the nakedness of father and mother, since she is the mother.
Both forbid uncovering a father's wife because it is the father's nakedness.
Both forbid uncovering a sister, of father or mother, born at home or abroad.
Both forbid uncovering a son's daughter or daughter's daughter, as it is one's own nakedness.
Latin says the father's wife's daughter was borne to your father; Greek puts it as sister by the same father and repeats the prohibition.
Both forbid the father's sister, who is the father's close kin; flesh / relative is wording.
Both forbid the mother's sister, who is the mother's close kin; flesh / relative is wording.
Latin says the uncle's wife is joined to you by marriage; Greek says only that she is your relative.
Both forbid uncovering a daughter-in-law, the son's wife; shame / nakedness is wording.
Both forbid uncovering a brother's wife, as it is the brother's nakedness.
Latin says your wife and the grandchildren are her flesh and the act incestuous; Greek says a woman, they are your relatives, and it is impiety.
Latin forbids taking the wife's sister as rival while the wife lives; Greek words it as a woman in addition to her sister.
Both forbid approaching a menstruating woman; Latin speaks of her uncleanness being uncovered, Greek of uncovering her nakedness.
Both forbid lying with a neighbor's wife; Latin says mingling of seed defiles, Greek says to emit semen and be defiled through her.
Latin names the idol Moloch and the name of your God; Greek has serving a ruler and the holy name.
Both forbid a man lying with a male as with a woman, as an abomination.
Both forbid bestiality for man and woman; Latin calls it a wicked act, Greek detestable, and describes the animal and act in different terms.
Both warn against defilement like the nations being driven out; Greek adds a causal clause that the nations became defiled, Latin leaves it to the next verse.
Latin: I will visit the land's wickedness so it vomits its inhabitants (future); Greek: the land became defiled, I repaid them, the land became indignant (past).
Both command keeping the laws and avoiding abominations, native and resident alike; ordinances and judgments / commands and settler / newcomer vary.
Both say the earlier inhabitants did all these abominations and defiled the land.
Latin: take care lest the land vomit you out as it did the earlier nation; Greek: lest it become indignant with you as with the nations.
Both say whoever does any of these abominations shall be cut off from among his people.
Both command keeping the Lord's charge and not doing what those before did; Latin gives separate imperatives, Greek links them with so that.
Both command reverence for father and mother and keeping the Lord's sabbaths.
Turn to / follow idols and cast-metal / cast gods differ slightly; both forbid idolatry.
Latin: peace offering to obtain favor; Greek: sacrifice of deliverance offered so as to be acceptable. Both introduce the peace-offering rule.
Both allow eating on the day of sacrifice and the next, and burning leftovers on the third day.
Latin: eating after two days makes one profane and guilty of impiety; Greek: the sacrifice is unfit and not accepted.
Both say the eater bears sin for profaning the Lord's holy thing and is cut off from his people.
Both forbid reaping the field completely; Latin adds not gathering leftover ears, Greek not gathering what falls.
Both leave vineyard gleanings for the poor and the stranger; Latin names fallen grapes and clusters, Greek forbids gleaning again.
Both forbid stealing and lying; Latin says none shall deceive his neighbor, Greek that none shall defraud him.
Latin forbids swearing falsely by My name; Greek forbids swearing by it for an unjust cause. Closing formula differs slightly (the Lord / the Lord your God).
Latin forbids defrauding the neighbor and oppressing him by force; Greek forbids wronging him or seizing his property. Wages not remaining overnight agrees.
Both forbid cursing the deaf and placing an obstacle before the blind, and command fear of the Lord.
Both forbid injustice in judgment and partiality to poor or powerful; judge the neighbor justly.
Latin forbids being a slanderer or whisperer and standing against a neighbor's blood; Greek forbids acting deceitfully in the nation and conspiring against his blood.
Latin adds rebuking him openly and says brother throughout; Greek says reprove the neighbor. Heart / mind is wording; both avoid bearing sin.
Latin forbids sowing a field with diverse seed; Greek says vineyard. Other prohibitions (mixed livestock, two-material garment) correspond.
Latin: both shall be beaten but not die; Greek: there shall be an inquiry concerning them, and they shall not die. Different legal outcome.
Both require a ram as offering for the offense, brought to the entrance of the tent of testimony.
Latin has the priest pray for him and favor restored; Greek has the priest make propitiation with the ram. Both end with forgiveness of the sin.
Greek adds that the Lord gives the land and that the fruit is unpurged for three years; Latin lacks the three-year term and speaks of removing foreskins.
Both say the fourth-year fruit is holy / consecrated and praiseworthy to the Lord.
Both permit eating in the fifth year; Latin speaks of gathering the produce, Greek says the produce will be increase for you.
Latin forbids eating with blood and observing dreams; Greek forbids eating on the mountains and observing birds. Divination by omens is common.
Both forbid altering the hair and beard; Latin says cutting hair in a circle and shaving, Greek making a sisoe and spoiling the beards.
Both forbid cutting the body for the dead and tattoo marks; Latin adds "figures", Greek says tattooed letters.
Both forbid prostituting a daughter lest the land be defiled; Latin: filled with guilt, Greek: land prostitutes itself and is filled with lawlessness.
Both command keeping the sabbaths and revering what is holy; Latin has "sanctuary", Greek "holy things".
Both forbid turning to mediums and diviners and being defiled; magicians / spirit-mediums and diviners / enchanters vary in wording.
Both command rising before the gray head, honoring the elder, and fearing God.
Latin forbids reproaching the foreigner who dwells among you; Greek forbids oppressing the newcomer who comes to you.
Both treat the foreigner as native, love him as yourself, and recall being foreigners in Egypt.
Both forbid injustice in judgment and in measures; Latin lists rule, weight, measure, Greek measures, weights, scales.
Latin names balance, weights, modius and sextarius; Greek names scales, weights and a chous. Both demand just measures and cite the exodus.
Both command keeping all the Lord's commands / law and judgments and doing them.
Latin names the idol Moloch; Greek says a ruler. Both prescribe death by stoning for giving offspring.
Latin: gave to Moloch, defiled the sanctuary, profaned My holy name; Greek: gave to a ruler, profaned the name of those consecrated to Me.
Latin has the people negligent and despising the command, sparing the one who gave to Moloch; Greek has them overlooking him who gave to a ruler.
Latin: those who agreed to prostitute themselves with Moloch; Greek: after rulers. Face set against the man and his kin agrees.
Both have God set His face against the person who turns to mediums and diviners; Latin says kill, Greek destroy.
Latin: sanctify yourselves and be holy because I am the Lord; Greek: be holy because I the Lord am holy.
Both command keeping and doing the Lord's commands; I am the Lord who sanctifies you.
Both prescribe death for cursing father or mother; blood upon him / guilty is the same consequence.
Both prescribe death for adulterer and adulteress; Latin joins another's wife and neighbor's spouse, Greek offers them as alternatives.
Both prescribe death for both parties who lie with the father's wife; stepmother / father's wife is wording.
Both prescribe death for both who lie with a daughter-in-law; wicked act / acted impiously is wording.
Both prescribe death for both men lying together as with a woman; forbidden act / abomination is wording.
Both condemn taking a woman and her mother and burning them; Latin says burned alive with them, Greek burn him and them.
Both prescribe death for the man and killing the animal; Latin says beast or livestock, Greek a four-footed animal.
Both prescribe death for the woman and the animal in bestiality; lies beneath / approaches to be mounted is wording.
Both condemn marrying a sister and mutual exposure, with destruction and bearing sin; Latin says they uncovered each other, Greek that he uncovered his sister.
Both condemn intercourse during menstruation with both cut off; Latin says she opened the fountain of her blood, Greek says he exposed her fountain and she uncovered the flow.
Both forbid uncovering the aunt's nakedness; Latin says he exposed the shame of his own flesh and both bear iniquity, Greek says he exposed his kinship.
Latin specifies the wife of a paternal or maternal uncle and that both bear sin; Greek speaks of a female relative. Dying childless agrees.
Both condemn taking a brother's wife and childlessness; Latin calls it unlawful, Greek an uncleanness, and Greek says die childless.
Both command keeping the laws and judgments lest the land vomit / be indignant at them; Latin adds the land they are about to enter and inhabit.
Both forbid walking in the nations' ordinances because they did these things and God abhorred them.
Both promise their land as inheritance, flowing with milk and honey, and that God separated them; Latin: other peoples, Greek: all nations.
Both command separating clean from unclean animals and birds and not defiling oneself; Latin says God showed them unclean, Greek says He set them apart.
Both command holiness because God is holy and He separated them to be His; Greek adds the Lord your God.
Both prescribe death by stoning for a man or woman who is a medium or diviner.
Both command priests, sons of Aaron, not to defile themselves for the dead among their people.
Both permit defilement only for near kin: father, mother, son, daughter and brother.
Both extend the exception to a virgin sister not married to a man.
Latin: not even for a ruler of his people; Greek: not suddenly among his people so as to profane himself.
Latin forbids shaving head and beard and cutting flesh; Greek specifies a bald patch for a dead person, the beard's edge, and incisions.
Both command holiness, not profaning God's name, since they present the Lord's offerings; Latin adds bread of their God, Greek says gifts of their God.
Both forbid priests to marry a prostitute / profaned woman or a divorced / expelled woman, because of holiness to God.
Latin: they offer the bread of the Presence and are holy; Greek: he shall sanctify him since this man presents gifts of the Lord. Holy as the Lord is holy agrees.
Both burn a priest's daughter who dishonors her father; Latin says found in sexual misconduct, Greek says profaned by prostituting herself.
Both forbid the high priest to uncover his head or tear his garments; Latin adds hands consecrated and clothed in holy garments, Greek says consecrated to wear the garments.
Both forbid the high priest to enter where there is a dead person or be defiled even for his father or mother.
Both forbid leaving the holy place because of the anointing oil; Latin: lest he profane the Lord's sanctuary, Greek: profane what is consecrated to God.
Both command marrying a virgin; Greek adds from his own kin.
Both forbid widow, divorced / expelled, defiled and prostitute and require a virgin of his own people; Greek makes the wife "only a virgin" in the same verse.
Latin: not mingle his lineage with the common people; Greek: not profane his offspring among his people. The Lord sanctifies him in both.
Both bar a blemished descendant of Aaron from offering; Latin says bread, Greek gifts, and Greek says approach to present.
Latin lists blind, lame, small / large / crooked nose; Greek lists lame, blind, mutilated nose and cut-off ear.
Both list a man with a broken foot or hand.
Latin lists inflamed eyes, a white spot in the eye and a hernia; Greek lists a skin spot, diseased eyelashes and a single testicle. Hunchback and scab agree.
Both bar a blemished descendant of Aaron from presenting offerings and bread / gifts; Greek repeats that he has a blemish.
Both allow him to eat the offered food; Greek names the most holy things and portions of the holy things, Latin the bread offered in the sanctuary.
Both bar him from the veil / curtain and altar because of his blemish; Latin says defile My sanctuary, Greek says profane the holy place of his God.
Latin adds that Moses spoke everything that had been commanded; the Greek reading lacks that clause.
Both: the Lord spoke to Moses, saying; also / and is only wording.
Both tell Aaron's sons to take care with Israel's holy offerings; Latin says not profane the name of the consecrated things, Greek My holy name.
Both say an unclean man approaching the holy things shall be destroyed; Greek adds throughout your generations and says from Me rather than before the Lord.
Both bar leprous or discharging descendants of Aaron from the holy things until cleansed; Latin specifies touching uncleanness from the dead, Greek uncleanness of a person.
Both include touching an unclean creeping creature; Greek adds a human being who defiles through any uncleanness.
Both: unclean until evening and no eating of holy things until he has washed his body in water; Greek names the one who touches these things.
Both say at sunset he is clean and may then eat the holy things as his food / bread.
Both forbid eating an animal found dead or torn by beasts and being defiled by it.
Both command keeping the Lord's commands to avoid sin and death; Latin says dying in the sanctuary by defiling it, Greek dying through them by profaning them.
Both bar an outsider, a priest's lodger and a hired worker from eating the holy things.
Both allow a person the priest has bought and those born in his house to eat; Greek adds purchased with silver.
Both bar a priest's daughter who marries outside from the holy portions; Latin says any man of the people, Greek an outsider, and the food named differs slightly.
Both let a widowed or divorced childless priest's daughter return to her father's house and eat his food; no outsider may eat.
Both require a man who eats holy things in ignorance to add a fifth and give it to the priest.
Both forbid defiling / profaning the holy things the Israelites offer to the Lord.
Both warn that eating the holy things brings the guilt of an offense; I am the Lord who sanctifies them.
Both address Aaron, his sons and Israel about vow and freewill whole burnt offerings; Latin says offering or fulfilling vow, Greek pledges and voluntary choices.
Both require unblemished males from cattle, sheep or goats; Latin says to be offered by you, Greek to be acceptable for you.
Both forbid offering a blemished animal because it will not be acceptable.
Both require an unblemished peace offering from cattle or sheep; Greek adds the vow or voluntary offering or at your festivals.
Latin lists blind, injured, scarred, swellings, scaly, eruption; Greek lists blind, crushed, tongue cut, warts, severe scab, eruptions.
Latin: such an animal may be offered as a freewill offering but not for a vow; Greek: it may be slaughtered for yourself, not accepted for the vow.
Both forbid offering animals with crushed, bruised, cut or removed testicles, and doing so in your land.
Both reject offerings from a foreigner's hand because blemished; Latin names bread of your God and anything else, Greek gifts of your God.
Both require seven days under the mother and acceptance from the eighth day.
Both forbid slaughtering a cow or sheep and its young on the same day.
Both introduce an offering sacrificed so as to be acceptable; Latin says thanksgiving offering, Greek a vow of rejoicing.
Both require eating it the same day and leaving nothing until morning.
Both command keeping and doing the Lord's commandments; Latin adds the closing I am the Lord, the Greek reading lacks it.
Both forbid profaning His holy name so He is sanctified among Israel; Greek says the name of the Holy One.
Both say the Lord brought them out of Egypt to be their God; Greek is a relative clause.
Both: the Lord spoke to Moses, saying.
Both speak of the Lord's feasts to be proclaimed holy; Greek calls them holy convocations and adds these are My festivals.
Both give six days of work and a holy sabbath rest with no work in all dwellings; Greek calls it a holy convocation.
Both give the Lord's holy feasts to be proclaimed / celebrated at their proper times.
Both date the Passover to the fourteenth day of the first month; Latin says at evening, Greek between the evenings.
Both give the feast of Unleavened Bread on the fifteenth day, eating unleavened bread seven days.
Both make the first day holy with no laborious / servile work; celebration / convocation is wording.
Both have offerings seven days and a seventh day with no laborious work; Latin says fire offering and holier day, Greek whole burnt offerings and holy convocation.
Both command bringing the firstfruits of the harvest to the priest on entering the land; Latin says sheaves, Greek a sheaf.
Both require an unblemished year-old lamb / sheep as burnt offering the day the sheaf is brought / consecrated.
Both give two tenths of fine flour with oil, a fragrant offering, and a quarter hin of wine.
Both forbid eating new grain until the offering is brought; Latin lists bread, roasted meal and porridge, Greek bread and roasted fresh grain.
Both count seven full weeks from the day after the sabbath on which the sheaf was brought.
Both count fifty days to the day after the seventh week and then offer a new sacrifice.
Both bring two firstfruits loaves of two tenths of fine flour baked leavened; Latin says from all your dwellings, Greek from your dwelling.
Both give seven year-old lambs, one calf and two rams as burnt offering; Greek calls the rams unblemished and names the drink offerings.
Both give a goat for sin and two year-old lambs as peace offering; Greek adds that the lambs go with the firstfruits loaves.
Both have the priest present the lambs with the loaves before the Lord and keep them for himself; Greek adds that they are holy to the Lord.
Both proclaim the day, forbid servile / laborious work, and make it a perpetual ordinance; Latin says most holy and of great celebration, Greek a holy convocation.
Both forbid reaping to the edge and gleaning, leaving it for the poor and foreigner; wording of the reaping prohibition differs.
Both set a rest and memorial of trumpets on the first day of the seventh month, called holy.
Both forbid servile / laborious work and require a whole burnt offering to the Lord.
Both set the Day of Atonement on the tenth day of the seventh month: holy day, afflict / humble yourselves, burnt offering.
Both forbid work on this day of propitiation, for the Lord to be gracious to you.
Both say anyone who does not afflict / humble himself that day shall be cut off from his people.
Both cut off the person who works; Latin has God say I will blot him out, Greek says that person shall perish.
Both forbid all work and make it a perpetual ordinance throughout generations and dwellings.
Both make it a sabbath, with humbling and observance from evening to evening; Greek calls it a Sabbath of Sabbaths and places the ninth day differently.
Both set the Feast of Tabernacles on the fifteenth day of the seventh month for seven days.
Both make the first day holy with no servile / laborious work.
Both have seven days of burnt offerings and a holy eighth day without work; Latin calls it a gathering and an assembly, Greek a closing observance.
Both state these are the Lord's feasts with burnt and drink offerings for each day; Greek says holy convocations and sacrifices.
Both add these offerings to the Sabbaths, gifts, vows and freewill offerings.
Both celebrate seven days from the fifteenth of the seventh month after gathering the produce, with rest on the first and eighth days.
Greek adds branches of the chaste tree and the seven days of rejoicing; Latin lacks them. Fruit, palm fronds, leafy branches and willows agree.
Both make it a seven-day perpetual ordinance celebrated in the seventh month; verse division only.
Both have all native Israelites dwell in booths / tents for seven days.
Both give the reason: descendants will learn / see that God made Israel dwell in booths when leaving Egypt.
Both say Moses spoke the Lord's feasts to the children of Israel.
Both command bringing pure olive oil for lamps continually; Latin says to you, purest and clear, Greek to Me, pure beaten oil.
Both have the lamps tended outside the veil from evening to morning; Latin names Aaron, Greek Aaron and his sons.
Both place the lamps on the pure lampstand before the Lord; Latin says always, Greek until morning.
Both take fine flour and make twelve loaves of two tenths each.
Both set the loaves in two rows of six on the pure table before the Lord.
Greek adds salt with the frankincense on the loaves; Latin has only pure frankincense as a memorial of the offering.
Both set the bread before the Lord each sabbath as a perpetual covenant; Latin says replaced, Greek set continually.
Both give the bread to Aaron and his sons to eat in a holy place, most holy, a perpetual ordinance.
Both: the son of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian father quarreled / fought with an Israelite man in the camp.
Both have him bring a curse on the Name and be taken to Moses; Latin says blasphemed the Name, Greek pronounced the Name. Mother's name agrees.
Both put him in custody awaiting the Lord's decision; Latin: until they learned the command, Greek: to judge him by the command.
Both: the Lord spoke to Moses; saying is carried into the next Latin verse.
Both: bring the blasphemer outside the camp, hearers lay hands on his head, all stone him.
Both say a man who curses his God bears / incurs sin.
Latin: whoever blasphemes the Lord's name dies, repeated; Greek: whoever names the Lord's name dies. Citizen / foreigner both covered.
Both prescribe death for one who strikes and kills a human being.
Both require life for life when an animal is struck; Greek states the animal dies, Latin speaks of giving a replacement.
Both give the principle that what a man did to his neighbor shall be done to him.
Both give fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, and the same injury inflicted.
Latin adds that one who strikes an animal gives another, and that one who strikes a human is punished; Greek has only a human who dies, put to death.
Both require one judgment for foreigner and native, since I am the Lord your God.
Both say Israel brought the blasphemer / one who cursed outside the camp, stoned him, and did as the Lord commanded.
Both say that on entering the land a sabbath is kept; Latin has you keep the sabbath, Greek has the land rest.
Both allow sowing the field and pruning the vineyard for six years and gathering produce.
Both make the seventh year a sabbath rest for the land, with no sowing or pruning.
Both forbid reaping what grows of itself and gathering the grapes in the year of rest; Latin: first grapes as vintage, Greek: grapes of your consecration.
Both make the produce food for you, slaves, hired worker and resident foreigner.
Both give the produce as food for livestock; Latin says beasts and livestock, Greek livestock and wild animals.
Both count seven weeks of years, totalling forty-nine years.
Both sound a trumpet throughout the land on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Propitiation.
Both make the fiftieth year a jubilee without sowing, reaping what grows of itself, or gathering the firstfruits; Latin says jubilee, Greek signal of release.
Both make the year holy and have them eat the produce directly; jubilee holiness versus signal of release is a difference of expression.
Both return each to his possession in the jubilee / year of release.
Both forbid wronging a neighbor in buying and selling; Latin adds reckoning by years from the jubilee here, Greek places that in the next verse.
Both price by the number of harvests; Greek also includes the years after the signal, which Latin gives in the previous verse.
Both raise or lower the price with the number of remaining years, since a number of harvests is sold.
Both forbid oppressing one's fellow and command fear of God; Latin says fellow tribesmen, Greek neighbor.
Both promise dwelling in the land in safety if they do and keep the statutes and judgments.
Both promise the land will yield its fruit, eaten to fullness without fear.
Both pose the question of what to eat in the seventh year without sowing or gathering.
Both promise a blessing in the sixth year producing three years' harvest.
Both sow in the eighth year and eat old produce until the ninth year when the new comes in.
Both forbid selling land in perpetuity since the land is the Lord's and they are foreigners with Him.
Both secure redemption of the land; Latin says sold subject to redemption, Greek says you shall provide ransom for the land.
Both let a kinsman redeem a poor brother's sold property; Latin says if the relative wishes it, Greek says the nearest kinsman shall ransom.
Both cover a man with no kinsman who can find the redemption price; Greek adds that he prospers by his hand.
Both reckon the time since the sale and repay the balance to the buyer to recover the possession; Latin reckons harvests, Greek years.
Latin: the buyer keeps it until the jubilee year; Greek: until the sixth year of release. Reversion to the original owner agrees.
Both give a year to redeem a house sold in a walled city.
Both make the walled-city house permanent to the buyer and his generations, not released at the jubilee.
Both treat unwalled-village houses like fields; Latin returns them at the jubilee if unredeemed, Greek calls them always redeemable and released.
Both make Levite houses in their cities always redeemable; Greek adds redeemable by the Levites and cities of possession.
Both return unredeemed Levite houses at the jubilee because they are the Levites' possession; Greek frames it as whoever ransoms from the Levites.
Both forbid selling the fields around the Levite cities, their perpetual possession.
Both command supporting a poor brother as a foreigner and sojourner so that he lives with you.
Both forbid taking interest or increase from a brother and command fear of God so he may live with you; Greek adds I am the Lord.
Both forbid lending money at interest or taking an increase on food / produce.
Both forbid treating a poor brother who is sold as a slave; Latin says oppress with slaves' servitude, Greek says serve as a household slave.
Both treat him as a hired worker and settler / lodger working until the jubilee / year of release.
Both have him go out with his children and return to his kin and ancestral possession.
Both say they are the Lord's servants, brought out of Egypt, not to be sold as slaves.
Both forbid oppressing him and command fear of God; Latin: by power, Greek: wear him down with toil.
Both allow male and female slaves from the surrounding nations; Greek adds that you may acquire them from there.
Both allow slaves from resident foreigners; Latin includes those born in your land, Greek the sons of lodgers and their relatives, who become possession.
Both leave them to descendants permanently and forbid oppressing Israelite brothers; Latin by power, Greek by wearing them down with toil.
Latin: the poor brother sells himself to the foreigner or anyone of his family; Greek: to the foreigner or lodger, a foreigner by birth.
Both give a right of redemption after the sale, by one of his brothers.
Latin lists uncle, cousin, blood relative and relative by marriage; Greek lists father's brother, his son and a close blood relative from his tribe.
Both count the years from sale to the jubilee / release and price it like a hired worker's pay; Greek adds year by year.
Both: if many years remain, the redemption payment is proportionally larger.
Both: if few years remain, he calculates with the buyer by years and repays; Latin repays the remaining years, Greek his ransom.
Both treat him as a hired worker and forbid harsh treatment in your sight; Latin credits earlier wages, Greek says year by year.
Both: if not redeemed, he goes out in the jubilee / year of release with his children.
Both say Israel are the Lord's servants brought out of Egypt; Greek adds household slaves and I am the Lord your God.
Both forbid idols, carved images, pillars and stones for worship; Latin opens with I am the Lord and repeats it, Greek has it once at the end.
Both command keeping the sabbaths and revering the sanctuary / holy things; I am the Lord.
Both give the condition of walking in and keeping the commands; Latin adds the rain promise here, Greek in the next verse.
Both promise produce and fruit from trees; Greek adds the rain in its season here, Latin gave it in the previous verse.
Both: threshing reaches the vintage and vintage the sowing, eating bread to satisfaction, dwelling securely.
Both promise peace, sleep without fear, harmful beasts removed, and no sword / war through the land.
Both: pursue enemies and they fall before you; Greek adds in slaughter.
Both: five pursue a hundred, a hundred pursue ten thousand, enemies fall by the sword.
Both: God will look on them, increase them, and establish His covenant.
Both: eat the old stores and clear out the old for the new.
Latin: I will place My tabernacle among you; Greek: My covenant. Reject / abhor is wording.
Both recall the exodus and the breaking of Egypt's yoke; Latin says chains of the neck, walk upright, Greek bond of the yoke and boldness.
Both: if you do not obey Me and do not do My commandments.
Both describe rejecting the laws and judgments and breaking the covenant; Latin says despise, Greek says your soul is indignant at them.
Latin: want and burning fever; Greek: distress, scab and jaundice. Seed sown in vain and eaten by enemies agrees.
Latin: they fall and are subjected to haters; Greek: haters pursue them. Both end with fleeing when no one pursues.
Both: if still disobedient, discipline sevenfold for your sins.
Both: crush pride and make the sky like iron and the earth like bronze.
Both: land and trees yield nothing; Latin: your labor is spent in vain, Greek: your strength in vain.
Both: continued opposition brings a sevenfold increase; Latin says plagues, Greek says seven blows.
Both send wild beasts to devour them and their livestock and desolate the roads; Latin reduces everything to a few, Greek makes you few.
Both: if even after these things they are not disciplined but walk in opposition to Him.
Both: God will walk against them and strike seven times for their sins; Latin says in opposition, Greek in contrary anger, and Greek says in return.
Both bring the avenging sword, flight to cities, and delivery to enemies; Latin sends pestilence, Greek sends death.
Both have ten women bake in one oven and give bread back by weight, eating without being filled; Latin breaks the staff of bread, Greek afflicts with scarcity of bread.
Both: if after these things they do not obey and walk against / crookedly toward God.
Both: God walks against them in contrary anger; Latin chastises with seven plagues, Greek disciplines seven times.
Both: they will eat the flesh of their sons and daughters.

Both give twelve silver dishes, twelve silver bowls and twelve golden incense vessels offered by the leaders at the altar's dedication.
Both give 130 shekels per dish, 70 per bowl, and 2,400 sanctuary shekels of silver in all.
Both give twelve incense vessels full of incense totalling 120 shekels of gold.
Both total twelve bulls, rams and lambs for burnt offering with libations, and twelve goats for sin; Latin 'oxen', Greek 'young bulls'.
Both total 24 bulls and sixty each of rams, goats and lambs; Greek adds 'unblemished' and 'after the filling of his hands'.
Both have Moses hear the voice from above the mercy seat between the cherubim; Latin says he entered 'to seek the oracle', Greek 'to speak with Him'.
Latin adds the lampstand set on the southern side and the lamps facing north toward the table of the Presence; Greek only says the seven lamps shine from one side toward the front of the lampstand.
Latin has Aaron place the lamps on the lampstand; Greek has him light the lamps from one side toward the lampstand's front.
Latin describes hammered gold with a central shaft and branches; Greek describes solid gold with stem and lilies, entirely solid.
Both command taking the Levites from among Israel and purifying them.
Both purify them with purification water, a full-body shave and washed clothes.
Both take a bull with its fine-flour offering and a second bull for sin; Greek makes the second a year-old young bull.
Both bring the Levites before the tabernacle and assemble the whole congregation.
Both have Israel lay hands on the Levites before the Lord; Latin 'when they are before the Lord', Greek 'bring the Levites before the Lord'.
Both have Aaron present the Levites as a gift from Israel; Latin 'to serve in His ministry', Greek 'to perform the works of the Lord'.
Both have the Levites lay hands on the bulls, one for sin and one for burnt offering; Latin 'supplication', Greek 'propitiation', and the offerer is 'you' vs 'he'.
Both stand the Levites before Aaron and his sons and offer them to the Lord; Greek also stands them before the Lord.
Both separate the Levites from Israel so they are the Lord's.
Both have the Levites enter the tent to serve and be purified and given to the Lord; Latin adds 'given as a gift' here, which the Greek has in the next verse.
Both say the Levites are taken in place of the firstborn; Greek begins with the 'given as a gift' clause that the Latin has in the previous verse.
Both say every firstborn of Israel is the Lord's, human and animal, consecrated when Egypt's firstborn were struck.
Both say the Lord took the Levites in place of all the firstborn of Israel.
Latin has the Levites pray so no plague falls on the people if they approach the sanctuary; Greek has them make propitiation and no one among Israel approach the holy things.
Both say Moses, Aaron and the congregation did for the Levites what the Lord commanded; Greek adds 'So the sons of Israel did for them'.
Both have the Levites purified and clothes washed, and Aaron present them before the Lord; Latin 'prayed', Greek 'made propitiation'.
Both have the Levites then enter their service before Aaron and his sons, as the Lord commanded; Latin states the purpose 'that purified they enter'.
Both set the Levites' service from twenty-five years old and upward in the tabernacle.
Both have them cease service at fifty.
Latin has the older Levites assist their brothers, keeping charge but not working; Greek says 'their brother shall minister' in the Tent, keeping charge with no work.
Both date the Lord's word to the first month of the second year after leaving Egypt, in the wilderness of Sinai.
Both ask Israel to keep the Passover at its appointed time; Latin 'let them keep it', Greek 'tell them to observe it'.
Both fix the fourteenth day at evening with its ordinances; Greek says 'first month' for 'this month' and adds 'at the proper times'.
Both say Moses told Israel to keep the Passover.
Latin has them keep it at Mount Sinai at evening on the fourteenth; Greek says 'in the wilderness of Sinai' and has no evening, adding 'at the beginning'.
Both have men unclean through a corpse unable to keep the Passover that day and approaching Moses and Aaron; Greek repeats 'that day'.
Both have the unclean men ask why they should miss offering to the Lord at its appointed time; Latin 'deprived', Greek 'must we fail'.
Both have Moses tell them to wait for the Lord's command; Latin 'I will consult', Greek 'I will hear'.
Both allow one unclean by a corpse or on a distant journey to keep the Passover; Latin 'in your nation', Greek 'among you or your generations'.
Both fix the second month, fourteenth day at evening, with unleavened bread; Latin 'wild lettuces', Greek 'bitter herbs'.
Both forbid leaving any until morning or breaking a bone, and require the Passover rite / law.
Both cut off the clean, non-traveling person who fails to keep the Passover at its time; he bears his sin.
Both give the same law for the stranger and the native; Latin 'foreigner and sojourner', Greek 'newcomer'.
Both have the cloud cover the tent the day it was erected, with fire-like appearance at evening until morning; Greek adds 'the House of Testimony'.
Both say the cloud covered it by day and a fire-like appearance by night, continually.
Both have Israel set out when the cloud lifted and camp where it stood.
Both tie camping and setting out to the Lord's command while the cloud stays; Latin is past tense and adds pitching the tabernacle and 'remaining in the same place'.
Both say if the cloud stays many days Israel keeps the Lord's charge and does not set out; Latin is past tense, Greek 'shall'.
Both tie camping and setting out to the Lord's command for as many days as the cloud is over the tent; Latin 'pitched / took down', Greek 'camp / set out'.
Latin has them depart at daybreak if the cloud left, and strike tents if it left after a day and a night; Greek says they set out by day or by night.
Latin gives two days, a month or longer, and moving camp as soon as it withdrew; Greek mentions only a month of days of camping.
Latin adds that at the Lord's word they pitched their tents; Greek has only setting out by command, with the charge kept through Moses.
Both command two hammered silver trumpets to summon the congregation and set the camp in motion.
Both have the trumpets blown and the whole congregation gather at the tent door.
Both say one blast brings the leaders and heads of Israel to Moses.
Both have the eastern camps move first at the signal; Latin specifies a longer, broken blast.
Greek adds third and fourth signals for the sea and north camps and puts the second at the southwest; Latin has the second for the south and the rest 'likewise'.
Both call for gathering the people with a plain blast, not a signal; Latin says 'simple blast, not broken ringing'.
Both give the priests, Aaron's sons, the trumpets as a perpetual statute for generations.
Latin has them go to war from their land against enemies; Greek has them go to war in their land against opponents. Both give a trumpet signal, being remembered and delivered.
Latin names a banquet (epulum), feast days and new moons; Greek has days of gladness, festivals and new moons. Trumpets, offerings, remembrance and closing formula agree.
Both date the cloud's lifting from the tabernacle / Tent of Testimony to the twentieth day of the second month of the second year; lifted / rose is only wording.
Companies (turmas) versus equipment for how Israel set out; settled versus stood for the cloud in the wilderness of Paran.
Latin has them move camp first at the Lord's command (imperium) through Moses; Greek says they set out first by the Lord's voice. Command / voice differs slightly.
Both have Judah first under Nahshon son of Amminadab; Greek adds the formation of the camp and says he was over the army, where Latin says leader.
Both name Nethanel son of Zuar as leader of Issachar; leader / over the army is only wording.
Both name Eliab son of Helon as leader of Zebulun; leader / over the army is only wording.
Latin narrates the tabernacle taken down and Gershon and Merari departing; Greek gives it as future / instruction. Same persons and action.
Both have Reuben set out under Elizur son of Shedeur; Latin adds companies and their order, Greek speaks of the camp's formation and army.
Both name Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai as leader of Simeon; leader / over the army is only wording.
Gad's leader is Eliasaph son of Duel in Latin but son of Reuel in Greek; otherwise parallel.
Latin has the Kohathites carrying the sanctuary while the tabernacle is carried until they reach the place of erection; Greek has the Tent erected before they arrive.
Both have Ephraim set out under Elishama son of Ammihud; Latin says by companies, Greek speaks of the camp's formation and army.
Both name Gamaliel son of Pedahzur as leader of Manasseh; leader / over the army is only wording.
Both name Abidan son of Gideoni as leader of Benjamin; leader / over the army is only wording.
Both have Dan set out last under Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai; Latin says by companies, Greek speaks of the camp's formation and army.
Both name Pagiel son of Ochran as leader of Asher; leader / over the army is only wording.
Both name Ahira son of Enan as leader of Naphtali; leader / over the army is only wording.
Camps and departures by companies (Latin) versus armies setting out with their force (Greek); both summarize Israel's order of march.
Both have Moses invite Hobab to come along; kinsman / relative by marriage, and promised / spoken good, differ slightly, and Greek quotes the Lord's words about the place.
Hobab refuses in both; Latin says he will return to the land where he was born, Greek to his land and his kindred.
Latin gives Hobab's knowledge of where to camp and the role of guide; Greek gives his having been with them in the wilderness and the role of elder.
Latin promises to give Hobab whatever is best of the wealth the Lord hands over; Greek promises only to treat him well with whatever good the Lord does.
Both describe a three-day journey from the mountain with the ark going ahead to find a camping place; providing / scouting is only wording.
Cloud over them by day as they traveled (Latin) versus overshadowing them when they set out from the camp (Greek); verse numbered differently.
Same prayer at the ark's setting out; Latin adds from Your presence (a facie tua) where Greek simply has flee.
Latin asks the Lord to return to the multitude of Israel's army; Greek asks Him to turn back, thousands and myriads in Israel.
Latin has the people grumbling as if pained by hardship and the fire devouring the camp's outskirts; Greek has them grumbling evil things and the fire consuming a part of the camp.
Both have the people cry out, Moses pray, and the fire die down; wording only.
Both name the place Burning because the Lord's fire blazed against / among them; active / passive naming is only wording.
Both have the mixed crowd craving meat and Israel weeping; Latin has them join the crowd, and Who will give / feed us meat differs slightly.
Both recall the fish eaten free in Egypt, with cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic.
Both say the soul / life is dried up and the eyes see only manna; Greek adds now.
Manna is like coriander seed in both, but Latin gives its color as bdellium where Greek gives its appearance as crystal.
Both describe gathering, grinding, pounding and cooking manna; Greek has cakes baked in ashes with a pleasant taste, Latin little cakes tasting of oiled bread.
Both say the manna fell with / on the dew on the camp at night.
Both have Moses hearing the weeping, the Lord's great anger; Latin says the matter seemed unbearable to Moses, Greek that it was evil in his sight.
Moses' complaint is parallel; afflicted / treated badly, servant / attendant, and burden / onrush of the people differ in nuance.
Both have Moses ask whether he conceived and bore the people that he should carry them like a nurse to the land sworn to the fathers.
Both ask where Moses can get meat for the people who weep and demand it.
Both have Moses say he cannot bear / carry this people alone because the burden / matter is too heavy.
Both ask the Lord to kill Moses so he is spared misery; Latin puts it as if the Lord sees fit otherwise, Greek as if this is how He treats him.
Both have seventy elders gathered to stand with Moses; Latin calls them elders and leaders of the people, Greek elders and their scribes, and Latin specifies the entrance of the tabernacle.
Both have the Lord come down, take of Moses' spirit and put it on them to share the burden; Latin states a purpose, Greek states plain future acts.
Both tell the people to prepare and promise meat; Latin has consecrate and we were well off, Greek purify and things are good for us, with Greek repeating meat to eat.
Both say the meat will last not one, two, five, ten or twenty days; days is only repeated in Greek.
Both give a whole month until it comes out the nostrils; rejected / disobeyed the Lord and nausea / bilious sickness are slightly different expressions.
Both give six hundred thousand on foot and the promise of meat for a month; Greek phrases it as the people among whom Moses is, and the Lord's earlier saying.
Both ask whether flocks and herds, and the sea's fish / food, could suffice; fish versus food of the sea differs slightly.
Is the Lord's hand powerless / will it not suffice is parallel; Latin says My word will be fulfilled in deed, Greek whether My word overtakes you or not.
Both have Moses tell the people the Lord's words and station seventy elders around the tabernacle / tent.
Both have Eldad and Medad left in the camp with the spirit upon them, enrolled but not at the tent; Greek adds here that they prophesied in the camp.
Both have a young man report that Eldad and Medad prophesy in the camp; Latin adds that this was while they were prophesying.
Joshua son of Nun, Moses' servant, asks Moses to stop them in both; Latin adds at once, and chosen from among many versus chosen attendant.
Both have Moses and the elders of Israel return to the camp; only word order differs.
Both have a wind from the Lord bringing quail from the sea, a day's journey around the camp, two cubits high; Latin says they flew in the air, Greek that they were cast upon the camp.
Both have the people gather quail for a day, night and day, least ten cors; Latin has them dry the quail around the camp, Greek cool them in cooling places.
Both have the meat still between their teeth when the Lord's anger struck the people with a great plague.
Both name the place Graves of Craving where the craving people were buried, then the journey to Hazeroth.
Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses over his Ethiopian wife; Greek adds that he had married an Ethiopian woman.
Same question whether the Lord spoke only through / to Moses and not to them; Latin leaves the Lord's hearing as a lead-in to the next verse, Greek ends the sentence.
Both have the Lord immediately summon the three to the tabernacle / Tent; Latin says alone, and Greek adds that the three came out.
Both have the Lord descend in the pillar of cloud, stand at the entrance, and Aaron and Miriam called forward.
Both introduce the prophet and revelation by vision and dream / sleep; Latin offers vision or dream, Greek vision and sleep, and phrases the prophet differently.
Moses is distinguished as the Lord's faithful servant in all His house; Latin says most faithful, Greek faithful.
Both say the Lord's anger was against them and He departed.
Both have the cloud withdraw and Miriam leprous as snow, with Aaron seeing her; white is explicit only in Latin.
Both have Aaron beg Moses not to lay the sin on them, as committed foolishly / ignorantly.
Both plead that she not be like one dead or a stillborn child with half her flesh consumed; Latin says already devoured by leprosy, Greek that it consumes.
Both have Moses cry out to the Lord to heal her.
Same spitting-in-the-face comparison and seven days outside the camp; Latin says she is called back, Greek that she shall enter.
Latin has Miriam shut out until she is called back; Greek has her set apart until she is cleansed.
Both have the people depart from Hazeroth and camp in the wilderness of Paran.
Both say the Lord spoke to Moses, saying; Latin adds there.
Both order men sent to examine Canaan, one leader from each tribe; Greek adds the ancestral families and says the land is being given as a possession.
Moses sends them from Paran at the Lord's command in both; Latin leads into the list of names, Greek adds that all were leaders and gives the names next.
Reuben's representative is Shammua (Latin Sammua) in Latin but Salamiel in Greek; father Zaccur agrees.
Simeon's Shaphat is the same man in both; father's name is Huri in Latin and Souri in Greek, a spelling variation.
Both name Gaddi son of Susi from Joseph's tribe, of Manasseh; branch / sons is only wording.
Naphtali's representative Nahbi is the son of Vophsi (Latin Vapsi) in Latin but of Iabi in Greek.
Gad's representative is Geuel son of Machi in Latin but Gaddiel son of Machi in Greek; father agrees.
Both say these are the names of the men Moses sent to examine the land, and that he renamed Hoshea son of Nun Joshua.
Both have Moses send them into Canaan and tell them to go up; Latin says through the southern region and into the mountains, Greek by this wilderness and into the hill country.
Both tell them to see what the land and its people are like, strong or weak, few or many.
Both ask whether the land is good or bad and whether the cities are walled or unwalled.
Both ask about the soil and trees and urge them to bring fruit; Latin says rich or barren, wooded or not, and that first ripe grapes were in season, Greek says rich or neglected and spring days.
Both have them explore from the wilderness of Zin / Sin to Rehob / Raab; Latin ends at the entrance to Hamath, Greek at the entrance to Ephaath.
Both reach Hebron with the sons / families of Anak and note its founding before Tanis; Latin says they went up through the south, Greek through the wilderness.
Both have them cut a branch with a cluster of grapes, carried with pomegranates and figs; Latin has two men carrying it on a pole, Greek on carrying poles.
Both explain the place name from the cluster; Latin gives the Hebrew name Nehelescol with its meaning, Greek simply says they named it Ravine of the Cluster.
Both have the explorers return after forty days of exploring the land.
Both have them come to Moses, Aaron and the whole assembly at Kadesh in Paran, report, and show the land's fruit.
Both report the land flowing with milk and honey; Latin adds that this can be known from the fruits, Greek says this is its fruit.
Both report strong people, large fortified cities and the descendants of Anak; very strong versus bold is a slight difference.
Both list peoples living in the south, mountains and by the sea and Jordan; Greek includes the Hivites, which the Latin list lacks.
Caleb quiets the people and urges going up to possess the land; Latin specifies the grumbling against Moses, Greek has him speak before Moses with emphatic assurance.
The other men refuse to go up because the people are stronger; Greek adds an emphatic denial and much stronger.
Both have the spies give a bad report that the land devours its inhabitants and its people are huge; disparaged / brought dismay differs slightly.
Both mention giants and being like locusts / grasshoppers; Latin calls them monstrous men of giant stock among Anak's sons, Greek adds and indeed so we were before them.
Both say the whole congregation raised its voice and wept all that night.
Latin verse ends at saying; the wish to have died in Egypt or the wilderness appears here only in the Greek, and in Latin falls in the next verse.
Latin includes the wish to die in Egypt or the wilderness and a sword and captivity fear; Greek has the Lord bringing them to fall in war and plunder, with the wish in its previous verse.
Both have Moses and Aaron fall on their faces before the whole assembly of Israel.
Both have Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh, among the explorers, tear their clothes.
Both have them tell the whole assembly that the land they explored is exceedingly good.
Both promise the Lord will bring them into a land flowing with milk and honey; gracious versus chooses us differs slightly.
Both say do not rebel and do not fear because the Lord is with us; Latin says their protection has departed, Greek that their season has passed.
Both have the assembly threaten stoning and the Lord's glory appear over the tent; Latin says they sought to overwhelm them, Greek that they said to stone them, and Greek adds in a cloud.
Both have the Lord ask how long this people will reject Him despite the signs; speak against / provoke differs slightly.
Latin has the Lord strike with pestilence and make Moses ruler over a greater nation; Greek strikes with death and makes Moses and his father's house a greater, more numerous nation.
Moses warns that Egypt will hear; Latin phrases it as a question that continues into the next verse, Greek states it and adds by Your strength.
Both say the inhabitants have heard that the Lord is among this people, seen face to face, with the cloud and pillars of cloud and fire.
Both speak of destroying the people as one man and what will be said; Greek names the nations who have heard His name as speakers.
Both give the charge that the Lord could not bring them to the sworn land and so killed them in the wilderness.
Both ask that the Lord's power be exalted as He said / swore; might versus strength and swore versus spoken differ slightly.
Both ask forgiveness for the people's sin according to the Lord's great mercy, as from Egypt until now.
Latin has the Lord say He has forgiven; Greek has Him say He is gracious to them, both according to Moses' word.
Both say the Lord lives and His glory fills the earth; Greek adds that His name lives, with no counterpart in the Latin.
Both speak of men who saw His glory and signs and tested Him ten times; Greek says this tenth time and this wilderness.
Both say the unbelievers shall not see the land; Greek adds that their children who do not know good or evil will be given it, which the Latin lacks.
Both promise Caleb, who had a different spirit and followed the Lord, entry to the land he saw, with his offspring inheriting it.
Both name Amalek and the Canaanites in the valley and tell Israel to turn tomorrow toward the wilderness by the Red Sea road.
Latin has the Lord hear the complaints made against Him; Greek has Him hear grumbling that Israel directed against Moses and Aaron.
Both have the Lord swear by His life to do to them just as they spoke in His hearing.
Both say they will fall in the wilderness, those counted from twenty years up who grumbled; Latin says corpses, Greek limbs, and Greek adds their entire registration.
Both exclude them from the land sworn with a raised hand, except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.
Latin has the little ones brought in to see the land that displeased them; Greek has the children brought in to inherit the land they rejected.
Both say their bodies shall fall in the wilderness; corpses (Latin) versus limbs (Greek), and Greek says this wilderness.
Latin has the children wandering forty years and bearing unfaithfulness until the fathers' corpses are consumed; Greek has them living as herders, bearing prostitution, until your limbs are consumed.
Both reckon a day for a year over forty years of bearing sins; Latin says know My vengeance, Greek the fury of My anger.
Both have the Lord affirm He has spoken and will do this to the wicked assembly that rose against Him; Latin says waste away, Greek consumed.
Latin says the spies caused the whole multitude to grumble against Moses; Greek says the spies themselves grumbled against the land before the congregation.
Both have the men who slandered the land die before the Lord; Latin says struck down, Greek in the plague.
Both say Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh alone lived of the men who went to explore.
Both say Moses spoke these words to all Israel and the people mourned greatly.
Both have them rise early, go up the mountaintop and confess they have sinned and will go up to the place the Lord spoke of.
Both have Moses ask why they transgress the Lord's word, since it will not prosper.
Both warn them not to go up since the Lord is not with them; Latin gives lest you fall, Greek and you will fall.
Both warn that Amalek and the Canaanites are before them, they will fall by the sword, and the Lord will not be with them because they turned from Him.
Both have them go up the mountaintop while the ark and Moses stay in camp; Latin says blinded, Greek that they forced their way.
Both have Amalek and the Canaanites come down and strike them as far as Hormah / Erman; Greek adds that they then returned to the camp.
Both tell Moses to speak to Israel about entering the land of their dwellings that the Lord gives.
Both list burnt offering or sacrifice, to fulfill a vow or freely or at festivals, as a fragrant aroma to the Lord from cattle or sheep.
Latin gives lamb and ram together two tenths of flour and a third of a hin of oil; Greek gives the lamb one tenth and a quarter hin, and only the ram two tenths and a third hin.
Both cover a burnt offering or sacrifice from cattle for a vow or peace / deliverance offering.
Both prescribe three tenths of fine flour mixed with half a hin of oil for each ox / calf.
Both prescribe half a hin of wine as a drink offering, a fragrant offering to the Lord.
Latin briefly applies the rule to each animal and to natives and foreigners; Greek adds a long passage on resident aliens and an enduring law. Both close with the opening of the next command.
Both say that when they eat the land's bread they set apart a portion for the Lord; firstfruits (Latin) versus contribution (Greek).
Both compare giving from food or dough with the threshing floor; Latin says firstfruits from food, Greek the first of the dough, a loaf as contribution.
Both command a gift to the Lord from the prepared food / first of the dough; Greek adds throughout your generations.
Both open the case of erring and failing to keep all the commandments the Lord spoke to Moses.
Both refer to the Lord's command through Moses from the day He began onward; Greek adds throughout your generations.
Latin has the multitude forget to do it and offer a bull and goat; Greek has it done unintentionally out of the congregation's sight, with an unblemished calf and male goat.
Both have the priest atone for the congregation, forgiven because of unintentional sin, with an offering brought; pray / make propitiation differs slightly.
Both say forgiveness extends to the whole people and the resident aliens because the sin was unintentional.
Both say one person who sins unknowingly offers a year-old female goat for sin.
Latin adds that the person will obtain pardon and be forgiven; the Greek verse ends with the priest making propitiation and gives no forgiveness clause.
Both give one law for natives and resident aliens who act unintentionally.
Both address the person who acts arrogantly, native or foreign; Latin gives the cause as rebellion against the Lord, Greek as provoking God, and its destruction clause begins here.
Both say he despised / treated as worthless the Lord's word and will be cut off, bearing his sin.
Both say Israel in the wilderness found a man gathering wood on the Sabbath.
Both have the finders bring him to Moses, Aaron and the whole assembly.
Both put him in custody because it was not decided what to do with him.
Both have the Lord order the man put to death by the whole assembly stoning him; Latin adds outside the camp here, Greek in the next verse.
Both have the assembly take him outside and stone him as the Lord commanded; Latin states that he died, Greek repeats outside the camp.
Both introduce a further word of the Lord to Moses.
Both command tassels / fringes on garment corners with a blue cord / thread; Greek adds throughout your generations.
Both say seeing the fringes should prompt remembering the commandments and not following their thoughts and eyes; Latin says straying, Greek prostituting yourselves, and Greek adds and do them.
Both say they are to remember and do the commandments and be holy to their God.
Both say the Lord brought them out of Egypt to be their God; Greek repeats I am the Lord your God at the end.
Both list Korah, Dathan, Abiram and On; Greek makes Korah the one who spoke, while Latin continues into the next verse for the verb.
Both have 250 leaders of the assembly rising against Moses; Latin says summoned by name at council, Greek summoned to the council and men of renown.
Both quote Enough for you, the whole assembly is holy, the Lord among them; Latin says why exalt yourselves above, Greek why rise up against the Lord's congregation.
Both say Moses heard and fell on his face.
Latin has Moses say the Lord will make known His own in the morning; Greek says God has already looked upon and known His own and brought them near.
Both tell Korah and his company to take censers / fire pans.
Both have fire and incense before the Lord tomorrow and the chosen man holy; Latin says you exalt yourselves greatly, Greek let that suffice for you.
Both have Moses tell Korah to listen, sons of Levi.
Both ask whether it is too little that God set the Levites apart to serve and stand before the people; separated from all the people versus distinguished from Israel's congregation.
Both say God brought Korah and his Levite brothers near; Latin's question runs on into the next verse, Greek ends with whether they seek the priesthood.
Both say they have gathered against God and ask who Aaron is that they grumble against him.
Both have Moses summon Dathan and Abiram, who refuse to come.
Both quote them asking if it is too little to bring them from a land of milk and honey to die in the wilderness and also rule them.
Latin has them say Moses has indeed brought them into such a land and ask if he would gouge out their eyes; Greek makes it a conditional that even so he would gouge out those men's eyes.
Both have Moses angry and asking the Lord to disregard their offering, having wronged none of them; Latin says not taking even a donkey, Greek no desirable possession.
Both order Korah's company and Aaron before the Lord tomorrow; Latin says to stand separately, Greek to consecrate and be ready.
Both have each man take a censer / fire pan with incense, 250 in all, and Aaron his own.
Both have Moses and Aaron stand at the tent entrance; Greek describes each man taking fire and incense, where Latin only says when they had done this.
Both have the assembly gathered against them at the entrance and the Lord's glory appear; Greek names Korah as the gatherer.
Both tell them to separate from the congregation so that the Lord may consume them at once.
Both have them fall on their faces and plead to the God of spirits and all flesh about one man's sin; Latin calls Him most mighty God, Greek God, God.
Both introduce a word of the Lord to Moses.
Latin tells the people to separate from the tents of Korah, Dathan and Abiram; Greek tells them to withdraw from Korah's congregation, without naming Dathan and Abiram.
Both have Moses go to Dathan and Abiram with Israel's elders.
Both tell the people to withdraw from the tents of these men and touch nothing of theirs lest they be destroyed with their sins; wicked / stubborn and caught up / perish differ slightly.
Both have Dathan and Abiram stand at their tent entrances with wives and children; Latin says all their company, Greek their baggage.
Both have Moses say the proof that the Lord sent him is that these deeds are not from himself.
Both say that if they die the common death of all people, the Lord has not sent Moses.
Both say that as Moses finished speaking the ground beneath them split open.
Both have the earth open and swallow the rebels; Latin says with their tents and possessions, Greek with their households, all Korah's people and their livestock.
Both say they went down alive to the underworld / Hades, the earth covered them, and they perished from the assembly.
Both say all Israel around them fled at their cry for fear the earth would swallow them.
