Both say fire went out from the Lord and consumed the 250 men offering incense.
Both introduce a word of the Lord to Moses (Greek numbers this as 17:1).
Both command Eleazar to take up the censers from the burned and scatter the fire; Greek specifies bronze and strange fire, and its sentence runs on into the next verse.
Both have the censers of the sinners hammered into plates for the altar as a sign; Latin adds the reminder for Israel to see, Greek calls them a covering for the altar.
Both have Eleazar take the bronze censers of those burned and apply them as plating for the altar.
Both give the reminder that no outsider outside Aaron's line may offer incense lest he become like Korah and his group.
Both have Israel grumble the next day against Moses and Aaron: You have killed the Lord's people.
Both have the assembly rise against Moses and Aaron, the cloud cover the tent and the glory appear; Greek has them rush to the tent and then come before it, Latin has them flee in.
Both introduce a word of the Lord; Latin addresses Moses alone, Greek Moses and Aaron.
Both have the Lord tell them to withdraw from the assembly so that He destroys it, and they fall on their faces.
Both have Moses tell Aaron to take the censer with altar fire and incense and hurry to make atonement because wrath has gone out and the plague begun.
Both have Aaron run into the assembly, where the plague had begun, and offer incense.
Both have Aaron stand between the dead and the living and the plague stop.
Both give 14,700 dead of the plague, besides those who died through Korah.
Both have Aaron return to Moses at the tent entrance after the plague stopped.
Both tell Moses to take twelve staffs, one from each leader of a tribe / ancestral house, each marked with the man's name.
Both have Aaron's name written for Levi, with one staff for each tribe.
Both have the staffs placed in the tent before the testimony, where the Lord will speak with / make Himself known to Moses.
Both say the chosen man's staff will sprout and the Lord will remove Israel's grumbling against Moses.
Both say Moses placed the staffs before the Lord in the tent of testimony.
Both find Aaron's staff for Levi sprouted with blossoms and nuts / almonds; Latin has Moses return alone and gives more detail of buds and leaves, Greek has Moses and Aaron enter.
Both have Moses bring out the staffs, the people look, and each take his own.
Both have Aaron's staff kept as a sign for the rebels so their grumbling ceases; Latin adds lest they die as a purpose, Greek states they shall not die.
Both say they did as the Lord commanded; Latin names Moses alone, Greek Moses and Aaron.
Israel tells Moses they are consumed and lost; Greek adds a third exclamation, utterly spent.
Both say anyone who approaches / touches the Lord's tent dies and ask whether they must all perish; approach versus touch differs slightly.
Both charge Aaron, his sons and his father's house with bearing the sins of the sanctuary / holy things and of the priesthood.
Both have the Levites brought to join and minister to Aaron while he and his sons serve before the tent of testimony.
Both have the Levites keep charge of the tent but not approach the holy vessels or altar, so that neither they nor Aaron die.
Both have the Levites join Aaron and keep charge of the tent, with no outsider approaching.
Both charge Aaron's house with the sanctuary and altar so that no wrath comes on Israel.
Both say the Levites are a gift to the Lord for the tent ministries; Latin says the Lord gave them to Aaron, Greek that He took them.
Both charge the priests with the altar and inside the veil and decree death for an outsider; Greek adds that the ministry is a gift of the priesthood.
Both give Aaron charge of the firstfruits and the consecrated things as a perpetual ordinance; Latin says for the priestly office, Greek as a share of honor and to your sons after you.
Both assign to Aaron and his sons the most holy offerings, including sin and guilt offerings.
Both say it is eaten in the holy place by males only, as consecrated to them.
Both give the firstfruit offerings to Aaron, his sons and daughters as a perpetual right, for the clean in his house to eat.
Both give Aaron the firstfruits of oil, wine and grain that Israel gives the Lord; Latin stresses the best (optima) of them, Greek every firstfruit.
Both give the first produce of the land brought to the Lord to Aaron, for the clean in his house to eat.
Both give Aaron what Israel devotes by vow; Latin says rendered by vow, Greek placed under a vow of devotion.
Both give the firstborn of man and beast to Aaron, with human firstborn and unclean animals redeemed; Latin phrases redemption as taking a price, Greek as ransom.
Both set redemption from one month old at five shekels by the sanctuary shekel of twenty obols.
Both forbid redeeming firstborn ox, sheep or goat, since they are holy, with blood poured on the altar and fat burned as a pleasing fragrance.
Both give the meat to Aaron, like the breast and right shoulder / foreleg of the presented portion.
Both give the holy offerings to Aaron, his sons and daughters as a perpetual ordinance, a covenant of salt.
Both say Aaron has no inheritance or share in the land because the Lord is his portion.
Both give Levi all Israel's tithes as a possession for their service in the tent of testimony.
Both say Israel shall no longer approach the tent and incur a deadly sin.
Both have the Levites alone serve at the tent and bear offenses, with no inheritance among Israel; Latin says bear the people's sins and adds a lasting ordinance more fully.
Both give the tithes to the Levites in place of an inheritance; Latin says they are content with the tithes for their needs, Greek that the Lord therefore said they receive no allotment.
Both tell the Levites to give the Lord a tenth of the tithe they receive from Israel.
Both say the gift will be reckoned as from threshing floor and winepress; Latin as an offering of firstfruits, Greek as grain and a removed portion.
Both tell the Levites to give a portion of all they receive to Aaron the priest as the Lord's portion.
Latin requires the offering from the tithes to be the best and choicest; Greek only says to remove a portion for the Lord from all gifts.
Latin says offering the finest and best will be counted as threshing-floor and winepress firstfruits; Greek says when they remove the firstfruit it is reckoned to the Levites as produce.
Both permit the Levites and their households to eat it anywhere as payment for service in the tent.

Latin warns they must not sin by keeping the best portions for themselves, lest they defile the offerings and die; Greek says no sin is incurred when they remove the firstfruit, and they must not profane the holy things.
Both command a red, unblemished heifer never yoked; Latin adds of full age, and states this is the sacrificial rite, Greek the provision of the law.
Both give the heifer to Eleazar to be slaughtered outside the camp; Latin has him do it in everyone's sight, Greek has them take it to a clean place and slaughter it before him.
Both have Eleazar sprinkle its blood seven times toward the tent entrance; Latin specifies dipping his finger.
Both have the heifer burned whole with skin, flesh, blood and dung; Latin says in everyone's sight, Greek before him.
Both have the priest throw cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet into the burning heifer.
Both have the priest wash his clothes and body, then enter the camp, unclean until evening.
Both have the one who burned it wash his clothes and body and be unclean until evening.
Both have a clean man gather the ashes and store them outside the camp for water of sprinkling; Latin says it was burned for sin, Greek that it is a means of purification.
Both have the one handling the ashes wash his clothes and be unclean until evening, and a perpetual ordinance for Israel and sojourners; carried versus gathers differs.
Both say whoever touches a dead human is unclean seven days.
Both require purification on the third and seventh days, or the person is not clean.
Both say touching a dead body without sprinkling defiles the Lord's tent, and the person is cut off from Israel and stays unclean.
Both give the law for a death in a tent / house making entrants and contents unclean seven days; tent versus house and vessels versus everything differ slightly.
Both say an open vessel with no fastening is unclean.
Both say touching in the open a slain or dead person, a bone or a grave makes one unclean seven days.
Both mix ashes of the burnt offering with water in a vessel; Latin says for sin and fresh water, Greek for purification and living water.
Both have a clean man sprinkle the tent / house, vessels and people with hyssop; Greek adds sprinkling those who touched a bone, slain person, dead person or tomb.
Both have the clean person sprinkle on the third and seventh days, and the purified wash and be unclean until evening.
Both say the unpurified person shall be cut off for defiling the Lord's sanctuary, the water not having been sprinkled on him.
Both make it a perpetual ordinance, with the sprinkler washing his clothes and anyone touching the water unclean until evening.
Both say whatever the unclean person touches becomes unclean, and the one touching it is unclean until evening.
Both place Israel in the wilderness of Zin at Kadesh in the first month, where Miriam died and was buried.
Both say there was no water and the people gathered against Moses and Aaron.
Both have the people wish they had died with their brothers before the Lord; Latin says turning to rebellion, Greek that they reviled Moses.
Both ask why Moses brought the Lord's assembly into the wilderness to die with their animals.
Both complain of being brought from Egypt to a barren place with no figs, vines, pomegranates or water.
Both tell Moses to take the staff, assemble the people with Aaron, and speak to the rock so it gives water for people and animals.
Both say Moses took the staff from before the Lord as commanded.
Both have Moses address the assembly before the rock and ask if he can bring water; Latin says rebels and unbelievers, Greek disobedient, and Greek has Moses and Aaron assemble them.
Both have Moses strike the rock twice with the staff and abundant water come out for the people and animals.
Both name the water for Israel's quarrel with the Lord and His being shown holy; contradiction / dispute and disputed / reviled differ slightly.
Both have Moses send messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom, speaking as your brother Israel about the hardship.
Both recount the fathers going down to Egypt, a long stay, and Egyptian oppression.
Both recount crying to the Lord, an angel bringing them out, and their being at Kadesh at the edge of Edom's territory.
Both promise to pass without touching fields, vineyards or wells and keep to the road; Latin adds a request to pass, and public road / royal road and wells / cistern differ.
Both have Edom refuse passage and threaten to come out against Israel armed / in war.
Latin has Israel say they will keep to the beaten road and pay a fair price; Greek has them pass alongside the mountain and pay its price.
Both have Edom refuse again and come out against Israel with a large, strong force.
Both say Edom refused passage through his territory so Israel turned away.
Both have Israel leave Kadesh for Mount Hor; Latin adds here that Hor is at the borders of Edom, while Greek has it in the next verse.
The Lord speaks at Mount Hor; Latin addresses Moses alone, Greek Moses and Aaron, and places the Edom border in this verse.
Latin says Aaron shall not enter because he did not believe the Lord's word at the waters of contradiction; Greek addresses both and says because you provoked Me at the Water of Reviling.
Both tell Moses to take Aaron and his son up Mount Hor; Greek names Eleazar and adds before the whole congregation.
Both tell Moses to strip Aaron of his garments, clothe Eleazar, and let Aaron die there.
Both say Moses did as commanded and took them up Mount Hor before the whole assembly.
Both have Eleazar clothed, Aaron die on the summit and Israel mourn thirty days; Latin says by families, Greek the house of Israel, and Greek says Aaron was released.
Latin has the Canaanite king of Arad dwelling in the south, Israel on the explorers' road, and plunder taken; Greek has him by the wilderness, the road of Atharim, and captives taken.
Both have Israel vow that if given the people they will destroy them; Greek says devote them and their towns, Latin destroy their cities.
Both have the Lord hear and deliver the Canaanites, with Israel destroying them and naming the place; Latin gives the name Hormah with its meaning, Greek only the meaning.
Both depart Mount Hor toward the Red Sea around Edom with the people discouraged; Latin adds hardship as well as the journey.
Both have the people speak against God and Moses about dying in the wilderness with no bread or water and disgust at the food.
Both have serpents sent that bit and killed many; Latin calls them fiery serpents, Greek deadly serpents.
Both have the people confess their sin and ask Moses to pray for removal of the serpents, and he prayed for them.
Both say Israel set out and camped at Oboth.
Latin names the camp as Iye-abarim; Greek names it Achel-gai on the farther side, after setting out from Oboth, both facing Moab to the east.
Both have Israel move on to the wadi / ravine of Zered.
Both place the camp at the Arnon in the wilderness, the border between Moab and the Amorites.
Latin quotes the Book of the Wars of the Lord saying He will do at the Arnon wadis as at the Red Sea; Greek quotes a book about a war of the Lord setting Zoob and the Arnon torrents ablaze.
Latin describes the cliffs of the wadis sloping to rest at Ar by Moab's borders; Greek says He appointed the torrents for the settlement of Er, beside Moab's borders.
Both give the well where the Lord told Moses to gather the people for water; Latin says a well appeared there, Greek that they went to it.
Both have Israel sing a song at the well; Latin has the song address the well to spring up, Greek has Israel call on others to lead the singing for it.
Latin says leaders and chiefs dug the well with the lawgiver and staffs; Greek says rulers dug it and kings of nations hewed it in their kingdom. Both continue to Mattanah / Manthanain.
Both list the stages from Mattanah / Manthanain to Nahaliel and Bamoth.
Both place a valley in Moab's land near the height overlooking the wilderness; Latin names Pisgah, Greek the Hewn Height, and Greek has them go there.
Both send messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites; Latin says Israel sent them, Greek Moses sent them with words of peace.
Both ask passage without turning into fields or vineyards or drinking well water, on the king's / royal road; Greek adds we will travel by the road.
Both have Sihon refuse passage, gather his people, go into the wilderness and fight Israel at Jahaz.
Both have Israel strike Sihon and take land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and Ammon; Latin gives the reason as strong defense on Ammon's border, Greek as Jazer being Ammon's border.
Both have Israel take all his cities and settle in the Amorite cities, Heshbon and its surrounding towns.
Both say Heshbon was Sihon's city, taken from Moab's king, up to the Arnon; Greek adds from Aroer.
Both introduce a saying calling to Heshbon to build Sihon's city; proverb versus those who speak in riddles.
Both say fire went out from Heshbon; Latin has it devour Ar of Moab and the Arnon's heights' inhabitants, Greek consume as far as Moab and swallow the Arnon's pillars.
Both lament Moab, people of Chemosh, with sons in flight and daughters captive to Sihon; Latin says He (Chemosh) has given them, Greek that they were handed over.
Latin says their yoke perished from Heshbon to Dibon and they reached Nophah and Medeba; Greek says their offspring perish and women kindled more fire against Moab.
Both say Israel settled in the Amorites' land; Greek says in all the Amorite towns.
Both have Moses send men to Jazer, who take its villages and drive out the inhabitants.
Both have them go up the road to Bashan, where Og comes out with all his people to battle at Edrei.
Both have the Lord tell Moses not to fear Og, delivered into his hand, to be treated as Sihon was.
Both have Israel strike Og, his sons and people and take his land; Latin says to utter destruction, Greek until no survivors remained.
Both have Israel camp by the Jordan opposite Jericho; Latin says in the plains of Moab, Greek on the western side of Moab.
Both say Balak son of Zippor saw all Israel had done to the Amorites.
Both say Moab feared Israel; Latin says they could not withstand its assault, Greek that Israel was numerous and distressed Moab.
Both have the warning to Midian's elders that Israel will consume everything around like an ox / calf eating the grass; Latin has Balak speak and mentions his kingship, Greek has Moab speak.
Latin places Balaam among the sons of Ammon by the river; Greek has him at Pethor by the river in the land of his people. Message about Israel agrees.
Both ask Balaam to curse a stronger people, hoping to strike and expel it; Latin says perhaps I may, Greek if we can strike some of them.
Both have the elders of Moab and Midian come to Balaam with divination fees and relay Balak's words.
Both have Balaam tell them to stay the night; Latin ends with God coming, while Greek ends with the Moabite officials staying.
God asks about the men with Balaam; Greek includes God's coming here, which Latin put in the previous verse, and the question wording differs.
Both have Balaam answer that Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, sent them.
Both give Balak's message to curse the people that covers the land; Greek adds encamped next to me, and drive away in battle versus strike and drive out.
Both forbid Balaam to go or curse the people because they are blessed; Latin 'Do not go' and Greek 'You shall not go' are only English wording.
Latin tells the leaders to go back to 'your land'; Greek says 'to your lord'. Latin 'the Lord' forbids; Greek 'God' does not permit.
Both report Balaam's refusal to Balak; Greek adds that the officials of Moab rose and came, and says 'unwilling' where Latin says 'refused'.
Both have Balak send more and higher-ranking officials; Latin 'nobiliores' (more distinguished) and Greek 'more honored' are close, and Greek names Balak as subject.
Both give Balak's message not to hesitate to come; Greek adds the polite 'I ask you' and Latin has 'Do not delay'.
Latin 'I am ready to honor you' and Greek 'I will honor you richly' differ slightly in emphasis; both promise whatever Balaam asks and call him to curse.
Both refuse a houseful of silver and gold; Latin 'alter the word... to speak more or less' and Greek 'transgress... do anything small or great by my own intention' differ in nuance.
Both ask the men to stay the night to learn what the Lord will say; Latin 'I ask you' versus Greek 'Now you also remain' is a change of tone.
Both have God tell Balaam to go with the men and do only what he is told; 'provided that' versus 'But' is English wording.
Both have Balaam rise, saddle his donkey and go; Latin 'with them' while Greek says 'with the officials of Moab'.
Greek adds that God grew angry 'because he went'; Latin simply says God was angry. The angel stands against Balaam in both, with two servants.
Both have the donkey see the armed angel and turn into the field; Latin 'standing' versus Greek 'opposing', and Greek names the staff Balaam strikes with.
Latin has the angel in a narrow passage between two walls; Greek has him in the furrows of the vineyards with a fence on either side.
Both have the donkey press against the wall and crush the foot; Latin 'struck' and Greek 'whipped' differ slightly, and Greek names Balaam and the angel.
Both have the angel move on to a narrow place with no turning right or left; Latin 'stood in the way' and Greek 'went farther' differ slightly.
Latin 'collapsed' and Greek 'crouched' differ; Latin says Balaam beat her sides 'still harder', Greek only that he beat her with his staff.
Both have the donkey speak after the mouth is opened; Latin 'Lord' versus Greek 'God', and 'these three times' versus 'this third time'.
Both have Balaam wish for a sword; Latin adds 'you deserved it' and 'If only I had', where Greek says 'If I had... I would have stabbed you already'.
Latin 'always ridden' and Greek 'from your youth' differ; the donkey's question also differs, Latin asking if she ever did the like, Greek if she acted from deliberate disregard.
Both have Balaam's eyes opened and him bowing before the angel; Latin 'Lord opened' versus Greek 'God uncovered', and 'Immediately' appears only in Latin.
Both have the angel rebuke Balaam for striking the donkey; Latin 'perverse and contrary to me' and Greek 'not fitting before me' differ in wording.
Both say the donkey's turning aside saved Balaam; Greek adds that she saw the angel and turned away 'this third time', and says 'preserved' where Latin has 'would have lived'.
Both have Balaam confess sin from ignorance and offer to turn back; Greek names the angel and adds 'in the road', and 'displeases you' versus 'does not please you'.
Both send Balaam on with the men, speaking only what he is told; Latin 'nothing except what I command' versus Greek 'the word that I tell you', and Greek names Balak's officials.
Both have Balak go out to meet Balaam at a Moabite town on the Arnon border; Greek states Balak heard Balaam had arrived, Latin 'when Balak heard this'.
Both have Balak complain that Balaam did not come; Latin asks if he cannot 'reward' him for coming, Greek asks if he is unable to 'honor' him.
Both have Balaam say he has come and can speak only what God puts in his mouth; the Greek's extra 'Am I now able to say anything?' is phrasing.
Latin has them come to a city at the farthest boundary of Balak's kingdom; Greek has them come to 'towns of farmsteads'.
Latin has Balak slaughter oxen and sheep and send gifts; Greek has him sacrifice sheep and calves and send portions.
Latin leads Balaam to the 'heights of Baal' where he sees the outermost part of the people; Greek brings him to 'Baal's pillar' and shows him a part of the people.
Both have Balaam order seven altars with seven bulls/calves and seven rams; Latin 'as many' for the number is only wording.
Both have the offerings made on the altars; Latin has 'they together placed' a bull and a ram, Greek has Balak himself offering on each altar.
Greek adds that Balak stood by his sacrifice and Balaam went on to inquire of God; Latin omits this. Latin 'commands' versus Greek 'shows' also differs.
Both have God meet Balaam and Balaam report the altars and offerings; Latin adds that he went swiftly, and 'erected' versus 'prepared' differs.
Both have God put a word in Balaam's mouth and tell him to return to Balak and speak; 'Lord'/'God' and 'these things'/'thus' are wording.
Both have Balaam find Balak with the officials of Moab; Latin has one 'burnt offering', Greek has 'whole burnt offerings' in the plural.
Greek adds that God's Spirit came upon Balaam; Latin has no such clause. Latin 'Aram' versus Greek 'Mesopotamia', and the curse commands are worded differently.
Both ask how he can curse whom God has not cursed; Latin pairs God/Lord in the opposite order from Greek, and Latin has 'By what right' where Greek repeats 'Why'.
Both have Balaam see the people from the heights and say they dwell alone, not reckoned among the nations; Latin 'highest rocks' and 'him' versus Greek 'tops of mountains' and 'them'.

Latin counts Jacob's 'dust' and the number of Israel's offspring, and wishes to die the death of the righteous; Greek has measuring Jacob's offspring, counting clans, and wishing his own offspring be like theirs.
Both have Balak protest that he called Balaam to curse his enemies and Balaam has blessed them; wording of the opening question differs only in English.
Both have Balaam say he can speak only what God directs; Latin 'what the Lord commands' versus Greek 'what God puts in my mouth', framed as taking care.
Both have Balak take Balaam to another place from which he sees only part of Israel and tell him to curse from there.
Latin has a high place on Mount Pisgah where Balaam builds the altars; Greek has a lookout in a field at the 'Hewn Height' and Balak making the offering.
Both tell Balak to stand by his offering; Latin 'while I go to meet Him' versus Greek 'while I go to inquire of God'.
Both have the Lord/God meet Balaam, put a word in his mouth and send him back to Balak to speak; 'these things'/'these words' is wording.
Both have Balaam find Balak by his offering and Balak ask what the Lord said; Greek says 'all the officials' and Latin 'the leaders'.
Both open the oracle by calling Balak to stand and hear; Latin 'Stand... listen' versus Greek 'Rise... Listen as a witness'.
Latin says God is not a man 'to lie' or 'to change'; Greek says 'to be deceived' and 'to be threatened'. The closing questions parallel each other.
Both have Balaam say he was brought to bless; Latin 'I cannot prevent the blessing' versus Greek 'I will bless and certainly will not reverse it'.
Both deny augury and divination in Jacob and Israel; Latin 'what God has done' (past) versus Greek 'what God will accomplish' (future).
Both compare the people to a rising lion that does not rest until it devours prey and drinks blood; Latin 'lioness' versus Greek 'lion cub', 'lie down' versus 'sleep'.
Both have Balak say neither curse nor bless; Greek adds 'for me' and 'at all' for emphasis.
Both have Balaam recall he must do whatever God says; Latin 'whatever God commanded me, I would do' versus Greek 'I must do the word that God speaks'.
Both have Balak offer another place; Latin 'Perhaps it will please God' versus Greek 'If it pleases God', and Greek adds 'for me'.
Both have Balak lead Balaam to the summit of Peor toward the wilderness; Latin 'faces' versus Greek 'extends toward', and Greek names Balak and Balaam.
Both repeat the order for seven altars with seven bulls/calves and seven rams; Greek 'for me here' and Latin 'as many' are wording.
Both have Balak do as Balaam said and offer a bull/calf and a ram on each altar; plural versus singular offerings per altar is wording.
Both say Balaam saw it pleased the Lord to bless Israel, did not seek omens/augury as before, and turned his face to the wilderness.
Both have Balaam see Israel by tribes with God's Spirit upon him; Latin 'dwelling in tents' and 'rushed upon him' versus Greek 'encamped' and 'came within him'.
Latin calls Balaam the man 'whose eye is closed'; Greek calls him the man 'who sees truly'. Both introduce his oracle as son of Beor.
Latin has him behold the Almighty's vision, falling with his eyes opened; Greek has a vision of God 'in sleep' with eyes uncovered. 'Words' versus 'oracles' also differs.
Both exclaim over how beautiful Jacob's dwellings are; Latin 'tabernacles' versus Greek 'houses', with 'tents' in both.
Both give the four comparisons: valleys, gardens by rivers, tents pitched by the Lord, cedars by water; Latin 'irrigated gardens' versus Greek 'shaded wooded valleys'.
Latin has water flowing from his bucket and his king removed because of Agag; Greek has a man coming from his offspring to rule many nations, his kingdom higher than Gog.
Both say God brought him out of Egypt; Latin 'strength like a rhinoceros', breaking bones, piercing with arrows; Greek 'glory like a one-horned beast', sucking out fat, shooting with missiles.
Both compare him to a resting lion and bless those who bless him; Latin 'lioness' versus Greek 'lion cub', and Latin says cursers are 'reckoned' under a curse.
Both have Balak angrily clap his hands and complain of blessing three times; Latin 'enemies' versus Greek 'enemy', and Greek 'thoroughly blessed'.
Both have Balak send Balaam away, saying the Lord has deprived him of honor; Latin 'Return' versus Greek 'flee', and Latin 'honor' versus Greek 'glory'.
Both have Balaam ask Balak whether he did not tell the messengers sent to him.
Both repeat that a houseful of silver and gold cannot make him exceed the Lord's word; Latin 'good or evil from my own heart' versus Greek 'evil or good on my own'.
Both have Balaam say he will counsel what this people will do to Balak's people in the last days; Greek adds 'Come' and says 'returning to my place' where Latin has 'to my people'.
Latin repeats the man 'whose eye is closed'; Greek the man 'who sees truly'. Latin adds that he took up his oracle 'again'.
Latin has him know the Most High's teaching and see the Almighty's visions, falling with eyes open; Greek has knowledge from the Most High and a vision of God 'in sleep'.
Latin has Edom as his possession with Seir's inheritance falling to its enemies; Greek has Edom and Esau, his enemy, both becoming an inheritance.
Both have one rising from Jacob to destroy the survivors of a city; Latin adds that he 'rules', which the Greek omits.
Both have Balaam see Amalek and say it is first among the nations and will perish; Latin 'its latter end' versus Greek 'their offspring'.
Both have Balaam see the Kenite(s) and say their dwelling is strong even if they set their nest in the rock.
Latin asks how long the Kenite chosen from the stock of Cain can remain before Asshur captures him; Greek speaks of a nest of craftiness belonging to Beor and Assyrians capturing.
Greek adds that Balaam saw Og, and has 'Alas, alas'; Latin has only that he took up his oracle again. Both ask who will live when God does these things.
Latin has them come in triremes from Italy to overcome the Assyrians and devastate the Hebrews; Greek has one coming from the Kitians' hand to afflict Asshur and the Hebrews.
Both have Balaam return to his place and Balak go home; Latin adds that Balak returned 'by the way he had come'.
Both have Israel at Shittim committing sexual immorality with Moab's daughters; Latin 'At that time' and 'fornicatus est' versus Greek 'profaned themselves by engaging in sexual immorality'.
Both have the women invite the people to sacrifices, where they eat and worship; Latin 'their gods' versus Greek 'their idols', and Greek names the people as subject.
Both say Israel was initiated into Baal of Peor and the Lord became angry; Greek 'with Israel' and 'the worship of' are clarifying English.
Latin has the leaders hanged on gibbets in the sun so His fury turns away; Greek has them made a public example before the Lord in the sunlight.
Latin has Moses address Israel's judges to kill neighbors who were initiated; Greek addresses the tribes and orders each to kill his own kinsman.
Latin has an Israelite go in to a Midianite prostitute; Greek has him bring his brother to the Midianite woman. Latin 'tabernacle's entrance' versus Greek 'Tent of Testimony'.
Both have Phinehas see this, rise from the congregation and take a weapon; Latin 'dagger' versus Greek 'lance in his hand'.
Latin has Phinehas follow the man into a brothel and pierce them through the genitals; Greek has him go into the 'furnace' and stab the woman through her womb.
Both give twenty-four thousand dead; Greek states they died in the plague, Latin that they were killed.
Both have the Lord speak to Moses; 'said' and 'spoke... saying' is wording only.
Both say Phinehas turned away God's wrath through zeal so Israel was not consumed; Latin 'moved with My zeal against them' versus Greek 'zealous with My zeal among them'.
Both have the Lord give Phinehas a covenant of peace; Latin 'say to him... the peace of My covenant' and Greek 'a covenant of peace' agree.
Both give Phinehas and his offspring an everlasting covenant of priesthood because he was zealous for his God and atoned for Israel.
Both name the slain Israelite Zimri son of Salu, a leader of a Simeonite clan or ancestral house.
Both name the Midianite woman Cozbi daughter of Zur; Latin calls Zur a 'most distinguished leader of the Midianites', Greek a ruler of the nation of Ommoth, an ancestral house of Midian.
Greek adds a command 'Speak to the sons of Israel, saying:' which Latin does not have here; Latin only has the Lord speaking to Moses.
Both command striking the Midianites; Latin 'Let the Midianites know you as enemies' versus Greek 'Be hostile to the Midianites'.
Both give the reason: Midian's hostility through deceit over Peor and Cozbi their sister, killed on the day of the plague; Latin adds 'schemes' and 'sacrilege of Phogor'.
Latin dates the command to after the blood of the guilty was shed; Greek says after the plague. Latin adds that Eleazar is Aaron's son.
Both order a census of men twenty and over fit for war; Latin 'households and clans' versus Greek 'ancestral houses', and Greek says 'whole congregation'.
Both place Moses and Eleazar by the Jordan opposite Jericho; Latin's sentence runs on into the next verse, Greek ends with 'saying' and names Araboth of Moab.
Both say from twenty years upward as the Lord commanded; Latin ends 'This is their number', Greek says 'These are the sons of Israel who came out of Egypt'.
Both list Reuben as firstborn with Hanoch and Pallu and their families; the naming style differs only in English.
Both list Hezron and Carmi with their families.
Both give Reuben's total as forty-three thousand seven hundred thirty.
Both give Eliab as Pallu's son; Latin 'The son' singular versus Greek 'The sons' plural.
Both name Nemuel, Dathan and Abiram and the rising against Moses and Aaron; Latin calls Dathan and Abiram 'leaders of the people', Greek 'summoned members of the congregation'.
Both have the earth swallow Korah and the fire consume two hundred fifty; Greek says the earth swallowed 'them and Korah', Latin 'a great wonder' versus 'a sign'.
Both say Korah's sons did not die; Latin links it to the wonder as a purpose clause, Greek states it plainly.
Both list Simeon's sons Nemuel, Jamin and Jachin with their families.
Both list Zerah and Shaul with their families.
Both give Simeon's total as twenty-two thousand two hundred.
Both list Gad's sons Zephon, Haggi and Shuni with their families; Greek's LXX numbering note is a verse reference only.
Both list Ozni with his family; the second son is Latin 'Her' (Eri) but Greek 'Addi'.
Both list Arod and Areli/Ariel with their families; the spelling differs only.
Both give Gad's total as forty thousand five hundred.
Both say Judah's sons Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan.
Both list Judah's sons with their families: Perez and Zerah agree; Latin 'Sela' (Shelah) versus Greek 'Shelon'.
Both give Perez's sons Hezron and a second son with his family; the second name is spelled Hamul in Latin and Iamun in Greek.
Both give Judah's total as seventy-six thousand five hundred.
Both list Issachar's sons Tola and Puah (Puvah) with their families.
Both list Jashub and Shimron with their families.
Both give Issachar's total as sixty-four thousand three hundred.
Both list three sons of Zebulun with families; Sered agrees, while Latin Elon and Jalel (Jahleel) appear as Allon and Allel in Greek.
Both give Zebulun's total as sixty thousand five hundred.
Both give Machir and Gilead with their clans; Latin says Machir was born from Manasseh, Greek lists him among Manasseh's sons.
Both list Gilead's sons with clans; Latin first son Jezer is Ahiezer in Greek, and Helek agrees.
Both list Asriel (Esriel) and Shechem with their families.
Both list Shemida and Hepher with their families; Latin Semida appears as Symaer in Greek, and Hepher agrees.
Both say Zelophehad, son of Hepher, had only daughters and name them Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah.
Both give Manasseh's total as fifty-two thousand seven hundred.
Latin lists three sons of Ephraim, Shuthelah, Becher and Tahan; Greek lists only Shuthelah and Tanach, so Becher is missing.
Both give Shuthelah's son and his family; Latin names him Eran, Greek names him Eden.
Both give Ephraim's total as thirty-two thousand five hundred; Greek adds the closing note about Joseph's sons that Latin places at the start of the next verse.
Both list Benjamin's first three sons with families; Latin begins with the note about Joseph's sons and spells the names Ashbel and Ahiram, Greek Asyber and Iachiran.
Latin lists two sons, Shupham and Hupham, with families; Greek lists only Sophan.
Both give Bela's sons as Ard/Adar and Naaman with their families; the first name is spelled differently.
Both give Benjamin's total as forty-five thousand six hundred.
Both give Dan's single son with his clan; the name is Shuham in Latin and Sami in Greek.
Both say all the clan numbered sixty-four thousand four hundred.
Both list Asher's three sons with families; Latin Jemna (Imnah) versus Greek Jamin, and Ishvi and Beriah agree.
Both list Heber and Malchiel with their families as Beriah's sons.
Both give the name of Asher's daughter as Serah/Sarah.
Both give Asher's total as fifty-three thousand four hundred.
Both list Naphtali's sons with families; Latin Jesiel (Jahzeel) versus Greek Asiel, and Guni agrees.
Both list Jezer and Shillem with their families.
Both give Naphtali's total as forty-five thousand four hundred.
Both give the total of Israel as six hundred one thousand seven hundred thirty.
Both say the land is divided among these according to the number of names.
Both say the larger group receives more and the smaller less, each according to its count.
Both divide the land by lot; Latin 'among the tribes and families' versus Greek 'according to the names of their ancestral tribes'.
Both have the lot decide the share of larger and smaller groups; Latin 'whatever falls by lot' versus Greek 'you shall divide by the lot'.
Both list Levi's sons Gershon, Kohath and Merari with families; Latin opens 'This is also the number'.
Latin names five Levite families including the Mahlites; Greek names four, omitting Mahli. Both then say Kohath fathered Amram.
Latin says Jochebed 'was born to Levi in Egypt'; Greek says she 'bore these to Levi in Egypt'. Both give Aaron, Moses and Miriam as her children.
Both list Aaron's sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.
Greek adds that Nadab and Abihu died 'in the wilderness of Sinai'; Latin lacks the place. Both say they offered alien fire before the Lord.
Both give twenty-three thousand males from a month old, not registered with Israel and given no allotment; Latin phrases the possession as 'with the others'.
Both say this is the census by Moses and Eleazar the priest in the plains of Moab by the Jordan opposite Jericho; wording differs only in English.
Both say none of those counted earlier by Moses and Aaron in the wilderness of Sinai was among these.
Both say the Lord had said they would die in the wilderness and none remained except Caleb and Joshua.
Both name Zelophehad's lineage and five daughters; Latin ends 'son of Manasseh, who was Joseph's son', Greek 'of the clan of Manasseh among the sons of Joseph'.
Both have the daughters stand before Moses and Eleazar at the tent entrance; Latin 'all the leaders of the people' versus Greek 'the rulers, and the whole congregation'.
Both give the daughters' plea, the Lord's ruling that they inherit among their father's kin, and the law for a man without a son; Latin puts the plea as a question, 'kinsmen' versus 'brothers'.
Both give the inheritance to the brother(s) if there is no daughter; Latin 'his brothers shall be his successors' versus Greek 'you shall give the inheritance to his brother'.
Both pass the inheritance to the father's brother(s) if there are no brothers; Latin plural versus Greek singular.
Latin makes the nearest relatives heirs and calls this 'sacred... perpetual law'; Greek gives it to the nearest relative of his tribe and calls it 'a rule of judgment'.
Latin names Mount Abarim and the land to be given; Greek says the mountain on the farther side, identifies it as Mount Nebo, and names the land of Canaan.
Both say Moses will join his people as Aaron did; Greek adds that Aaron was gathered 'at Mount Hor', which Latin does not say.
Both blame Moses for failing to show the Lord holy at the waters in Zin; Latin 'offended Me... contradiction', Greek 'transgressed My word... resisted'.
Both say Moses answered the Lord; 'answered' versus 'said to the Lord' is wording.
Both ask the Lord, God of spirits of all flesh, to set a man over the multitude; Latin 'provide' versus Greek 'appoint', and Greek reads 'spirits and of all flesh'.
Both ask for a man to go out and come in before them, lead them out and in, so the Lord's people are not like sheep without a shepherd.
Both have the man stand before Eleazar and the whole assembly; Greek adds instruction before the congregation, where Latin has commands in the next verse.
Both have Moses give him a share of his glory so Israel obeys him; Latin also says 'give him commands in everyone's sight', which in Greek appears in the previous verse.
Latin has Eleazar consult the Lord for him; Greek has the man stand before Eleazar while they ask for the judgment of the manifestations. Both say Israel goes out and in at his word.
Both say Moses did as the Lord commanded and stood Joshua before Eleazar and the whole assembly.
Latin has Moses lay hands on Joshua and repeat everything the Lord commanded; Greek has him lay hands on him and present him as commanded.
Both have the Lord speak to Moses; 'also said' versus 'spoke... saying' is wording.
Both command Israel to present the offerings at the appointed times; Latin lists offering, bread and incense, Greek lists gifts, donations and offerings, 'at My festivals'.
Both prescribe two unblemished year-old lambs daily as a continual burnt offering; Greek adds an extra 'Say to them'.
Both prescribe one lamb in the morning and the other at evening.
Both prescribe a tenth of an ephah of fine flour with oil and a quarter hin; Latin says 'purest oil', Greek 'worked with oil'.
Both call this the continual burnt offering of pleasing fragrance from Mount Sinai; Latin 'you offered', Greek 'instituted'.
Both give a quarter hin of drink offering per lamb in the holy place; Latin says 'wine', Greek 'strong drink'.
Both have the second lamb offered at evening with its sacrifice and libation as a fragrant offering; Latin spells out 'the whole rite of the morning sacrifice'.
Both prescribe on the Sabbath two unblemished year-old lambs, two tenths of fine flour with oil, and a libation.
Both make this the Sabbath offering on every Sabbath alongside the continual offering; Greek states it is 'in addition to' the continual offering and its libation.
Both prescribe at the new moons two bulls/calves, one ram and seven unblemished year-old lambs.
Both prescribe three tenths of fine flour with oil per bull/calf and two tenths per ram.
Latin gives 'a tenth of a tenth' of fine flour per lamb; Greek gives a tenth of an ephah. Both call it a fragrant offering to the Lord.
Both give wine libations of half a hin per bull/calf, a third per ram, a quarter per lamb, as the monthly offering through the year.
Both add one male goat for sin with the continual burnt offering and its libation.
Both date the Lord's Passover to the fourteenth day of the first month.
Both make the fifteenth day a festival with unleavened bread for seven days.
Both make the first day holy with no work; Latin 'revered and holy' and 'servile work' versus Greek 'holy appointed assembly' and 'laborious work'.
Both prescribe burnt offerings of two bulls/calves, one ram and seven unblemished year-old lambs.
Both prescribe fine flour with oil: three tenths per bull/calf and two tenths per ram.
Latin gives 'a tenth of a tenth' of flour for each of the seven lambs; Greek gives a tenth of an ephah for each lamb.
Both add one male goat for sin to make atonement for the people.
Both say these are besides the continual morning burnt offering; Greek's added 'which is a continual whole burnt offering' only repeats the term.
Both repeat the offerings daily for seven days as a pleasing fragrance to the Lord; Latin 'food for the fire' versus Greek 'a gift, an offering', and Greek adds the libation.
Both make the seventh day holy with no work; Latin 'most solemn and holy' and 'servile work' versus Greek 'holy summoned assembly' and 'laborious work'.
Both mark the day of new produce at the weeks with no work; Latin 'firstfruits' and 'revered and holy' versus Greek 'new sacrifice' and 'holy appointed assembly'.
Both prescribe a burnt offering of two bulls/calves, one ram and seven unblemished year-old lambs.
Both prescribe fine flour with oil: three tenths per bull/calf and two per ram.
Latin gives 'a tenth of a tenth' per lamb, Greek a tenth of an ephah; both add a male goat for sin besides the continual offering, and Greek adds 'to make propitiation for you'.
Both make the first day of the seventh month holy with no work, a day of trumpet signal; Latin 'revered and holy' and 'trumpet blasts' versus Greek 'holy appointed assembly' and 'signaling'.
Both prescribe one bull/calf, one ram and seven unblemished year-old lambs as a burnt offering.
Both prescribe fine flour with oil: three tenths for the bull/calf and two tenths for the ram.
Both add a male goat for sin for atonement; Latin 'for the people's atonement' versus Greek 'to make propitiation for you'.
Both place this besides the new moon and continual burnt offerings with their grain and drink offerings; Latin adds 'the same ceremonies', Greek 'according to their prescription'.
Both make the tenth day holy with self-denial and no work; Latin 'afflict your souls' and 'servile work' versus Greek 'humble yourselves' and 'no work'.
Both prescribe one bull/calf, one ram and seven unblemished year-old lambs as a pleasing burnt offering.
Both prescribe fine flour with oil: three tenths for the bull/calf and two tenths for the ram.
Latin gives 'a tenth of a tenth' of flour for each of the seven lambs; Greek gives one-tenth for each lamb.
Both add a male goat for sin besides the continual burnt offering; Latin mentions what is usually offered for guilt, Greek 'the sin offering of propitiation' and adds 'to make propitiation for you'.
Both make the fifteenth day of the seventh month holy, with no work and a festival to the Lord for seven days.
Both prescribe thirteen bulls/calves, two rams and fourteen unblemished lambs; Greek adds 'On the first day' to place the offering.
Both prescribe fine flour with oil: three tenths per bull/calf of the thirteen and two tenths per ram of the two.
Latin gives 'a tenth of a tenth' of flour for each of the fourteen lambs; Greek gives one-tenth for each lamb.
Both add a male goat for sin besides the continual burnt offering with its grain and drink offerings.
Both prescribe for the second day twelve bulls/calves, two rams and fourteen unblemished lambs.
Both require the grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams and lambs; Latin says to present them 'duly', Greek 'according to their number, as prescribed'.
Both add a male goat for sin besides the continual burnt offering with its grain and drink offerings.
Both prescribe for the third day eleven bulls/calves, two rams and fourteen unblemished lambs.
Both require the grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams and lambs; Latin says to present them 'duly', Greek 'according to their number, as prescribed'.
Both add a male goat for sin besides the continual burnt offering with its grain and drink offerings.
Both prescribe for the fourth day ten bulls/calves, two rams and fourteen unblemished lambs.
Both require the grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams and lambs; Latin says to present them 'duly', Greek 'according to their number, as prescribed'.
Both add a male goat for sin besides the continual burnt offering with its grain and drink offerings.
Both prescribe for the fifth day nine bulls/calves, two rams and fourteen unblemished lambs.
Both require the grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams and lambs; Latin says to present them 'duly', Greek 'according to their number, as prescribed'.
Both add a male goat for sin besides the continual burnt offering with its grain and drink offerings.
Both prescribe for the sixth day eight bulls/calves, two rams and fourteen unblemished lambs.
Both require the grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams and lambs; Latin says to present them 'duly', Greek 'according to their number, as prescribed'.
Both add a male goat for sin besides the continual burnt offering with its grain and drink offerings.
Both prescribe for the seventh day seven bulls/calves, two rams and fourteen unblemished lambs.
Both require the grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams and lambs; Latin says to present them 'duly', Greek 'according to their number'.
Both add a male goat for sin besides the continual burnt offering with its grain and drink offerings.
Both set the eighth day with no work; Latin calls it 'most solemn' and 'servile work', Greek 'a closing festival' and 'laborious work'.
Both prescribe one bull/calf, one ram and seven unblemished year-old lambs as a pleasing burnt offering.
Both require the grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams and lambs; Latin says to present them 'duly', Greek 'according to their number'.
Both add a male goat for sin besides the continual burnt offering with its grain and drink offerings.
Both say these are offered at the festivals, apart from vows and freewill offerings of burnt, grain, drink and peace (salvation) offerings.
Both say Moses told the Israelites everything the Lord had commanded him.
Both have Moses speak to the leaders of the tribes of Israel with 'This is the word the Lord has commanded'.
Both say a vow or oath must be kept; Latin 'a man' and 'fulfill what he promised' versus Greek 'any person', adding a self-imposed restriction and 'not profane his word'.
Both begin the case of a young woman vowing in her father's house; Latin goes on to the father's silence binding her vow, which Greek carries into the next verse.
Both end with the vow standing; Latin says she must fulfill what she promised, Greek completes the father-silent condition so her vows and restrictions stand.
Greek adds 'The Lord will cleanse her' after the father's refusal; Latin has no such clause here. Both void the vows when the father objects.
Latin has a woman with a husband who makes a vow; Greek has a woman who becomes a man's wife while earlier vows are upon her.
Both bind the wife if her husband hears and does not object that day; Latin says she is 'bound' and must render, Greek says her vows 'stand'.
Both void her vows if the husband objects at once; Latin 'the Lord shall be gracious to her' versus Greek 'the Lord will cleanse her'.
Both say a widow's or divorced woman's vow binds her; 'render' versus 'remain against her' is wording.
Both introduce a wife's vow and oath made in her husband's house; Latin states it as a single case, Greek as a vow or a restriction with an oath.
Both say that if the husband hears, stays silent and does not object, her vow stands and she must render it.
Both release her if her husband cancels the vow at once; Latin 'the Lord shall be gracious to her' versus Greek 'the Lord will cleanse her'.
Both let the husband decide on a vow to humble herself; Latin names fasting or abstinence and 'at his discretion', Greek says he may establish or cancel it.
Both bind her if the husband stays silent past the day he hears; Latin 'postponing his decision to another day', Greek 'remains silent from day to day'.
Both say a husband who objects later bears the guilt; Latin has him bear 'her iniquity', Greek has him bear 'his sin'.
Both close the laws between husband and wife and between father and daughter in her youth in his house.
Both command vengeance on the Midianites for Israel, after which Moses will be gathered to his people.
Both have Moses call men to arms against Midian to exact the Lord's vengeance; Greek adds 'to draw up for battle before the Lord'.
Both command a thousand men from each tribe of Israel to be sent to war.
Both say a thousand from each tribe, twelve thousand, were equipped for battle; Greek adds 'from the thousands of Israel'.
Both send them with Phinehas, the holy vessels and the trumpets; Greek adds Phinehas's descent from Aaron and 'with their force', Latin that Moses entrusted them to him.
Greek adds 'as the Lord had commanded Moses'; Latin instead says they 'defeated' the Midianites. Both say they killed every male.
Both name the five kings of Midian and Balaam's death by the sword; Latin lists Rekem before Zur and ends with Reba, Greek ends with Robok and adds 'together with their slain'.
Both have them take the women, little ones/dependents, livestock and goods as plunder; Latin adds 'whatever they could possess', Greek 'their resources'.
Both have the Midianite towns burned; Latin lists cities, villages and strongholds, Greek towns, settlements and farmsteads.
Both say they took the plunder and all spoils, people and livestock.
Both bring the spoil to Moses, Eleazar and Israel at the camp in the plains of Moab; Latin separates the remaining equipment carried to the camp, Greek names captives, spoils and plunder.
Both have Moses, Eleazar and the leaders of the assembly go out to meet them outside the camp.
Both say Moses was angry with the army's leaders, the commanders of thousands and hundreds, returning from battle.
Both have Moses ask why they let the women live; Latin 'spared the women', Greek 'taken every female alive'.

Both blame the women for causing Israel to sin at Balaam's word over Peor, with the plague; Latin asks it as a question, 'deceived' and 'unfaithful' versus Greek 'turn away and disregard the Lord's word'.
Both command killing every male, including the little ones, and every woman who has known a man.
Both allow keeping the young women who have not known a man; Latin says 'keep for yourselves the girls and virgin females', Greek 'take alive all the female dependents'.
Greek adds that the purification applies to 'both you and your captives'; Latin has no such phrase. Both order seven days outside the camp and purification on the third and seventh days.
Both require purifying garments and articles of goat skin or hair and wood; Latin frames it as everything in the plunder, Greek lists covering, leather, goat material and wooden articles.
Both have Eleazar tell the men who fought that this is the ordinance of the law the Lord gave Moses.
Both list gold, silver, bronze, iron, lead and tin; Greek opens with 'Except for', Latin simply lists them.
Latin purifies by fire what withstands it and by water of purification what does not; Greek has fire-proof items cleansed and also purified with water, and the rest passing through water.
Both order washing clothes on the seventh day, after which they may enter the camp.
Both have the Lord speak to Moses.
Both have Moses, Eleazar and the leaders count the captured people and livestock; Greek specifies 'rulers of the congregation's ancestral houses'.
Both divide the plunder between the fighters and the rest of the people; Latin adds 'equally'.
Both set aside one in five hundred from the warriors for the Lord; the animals listed differ, Latin cattle, donkeys and sheep, Greek livestock, cattle, sheep and goats.
Both give the portion to Eleazar as the Lord's firstfruits; Greek says 'take it from their half', Latin gives the reason 'because these are the Lord's firstfruits'.
Both take one in fifty from the Israelites' half, people and animals, and give them to the Levites who keep charge of the Lord's tabernacle.
Both say Moses and Eleazar did as the Lord commanded.
Both give six hundred seventy-five thousand sheep; Latin calls it the plunder the army captured, Greek 'the surplus of the plunder'.
Both give thirty-two thousand women who had not known a man.
Both give the fighters' half as three hundred thirty-seven thousand five hundred sheep.
Both give the Lord's portion from the sheep as six hundred seventy-five.
Both give thirty-six thousand cattle with seventy-two for the Lord.
Both give thirty thousand five hundred donkeys with sixty-one for the Lord.
Both give sixteen thousand persons with thirty-two for the Lord.
Both have Moses give the Lord's portion to Eleazar as commanded; Latin 'number of the Lord's firstfruits', Greek 'levy for the Lord, God's contribution'.
Both say it came from the Israelites' half that Moses had separated from the fighters.
Both give the congregation's half as three hundred thirty-seven thousand five hundred sheep.
Both have Moses take one in fifty and give it to the Levites as commanded; Greek specifies 'from the people and livestock'.
Both have the commanders of thousands and hundreds approach Moses; Latin ends with 'said', Greek carries the speech into the next verse.
Both report the officers counted their fighting men and not one is missing.

Both bring gold articles as gifts to the Lord for the men; Latin lists anklets, bracelets, rings, armlets and necklaces, Greek armlets, bracelets, rings, wrist and hair ornaments, 'make supplication' versus 'make propitiation'.
Both have Moses and Eleazar receive the gold; Latin 'in its various forms', Greek 'every article worked by hand'.
Both give the gold from the commanders as sixteen thousand seven hundred fifty shekels.
Both say the fighters kept the plunder each for himself.
Both have the gold brought into the Tent of Testimony as a memorial before the Lord.
Both say Reuben and Gad had very much livestock and saw Jazer and Gilead suitable for animals; Latin 'immense wealth of animals' versus Greek 'great multitude'.
Both have them approach Moses, Eleazar and the leaders and speak.
Both list the same towns from Ataroth to Beon; Sebam/Sibmah is only spelling.
Latin says the Lord 'struck' the land before Israel; Greek says the Lord 'handed over' the land. Both call it good for livestock.
Both ask that the land be given as a possession and that they not be made to cross the Jordan.
Both have Moses ask whether their brothers go to battle while they sit here.
Both ask why they discourage Israel from crossing; Latin 'undermine... so that they do not dare', Greek 'turn aside the minds'.
Both recall the fathers did the same when sent from Kadesh-barnea to explore the land.
Both say the spies went to the Valley/Ravine of the Cluster, looked over the land and discouraged Israel from entering; 'undermined' versus 'turned away' the heart.
Both say the Lord swore in anger; Greek adds 'fiercely' and 'on that day'.
Greek adds that these men 'know evil and good'; Latin has no such clause. Both bar the men from twenty years up from the land because they did not follow Him.
Latin calls Caleb 'the Kenizzite' and says both fulfilled God's will; Greek calls him 'the one set apart' and says Joshua followed the Lord.
Both have the Lord's anger keep Israel in the wilderness forty years until the evil generation was consumed; Latin 'led it around', Greek 'whirled them about'.
Both say they have risen in their fathers' place to add to the Lord's fury; Latin 'offspring and pupils of sinful men', Greek 'a band of sinful men'.
Both warn the Lord will leave the people in the wilderness; Latin says they will cause the death of all, Greek says they will act lawlessly against the congregation.
Both propose folds for livestock and towns for their dependents; Latin adds 'fortified' cities and 'shelters', Greek adds 'here'.
Both pledge to go armed ahead of Israel while their dependents stay in walled towns; Latin adds 'everything we possess', Greek 'advance guard'.
Both pledge not to return home until Israel has its inheritance; Greek says 'each been allotted'.
Both give up claims across the Jordan because they have their share on the east; Latin 'seek nothing', Greek 'not inherit further among them'.
Both have Moses say: if you do what you promise, go equipped before the Lord to war.
Both say every armed man crosses the Jordan until the Lord overthrows His enemies.
Greek adds 'then afterward you may return'; Latin has no such clause. Both say they will be blameless before the Lord and Israel and keep the land.
Both warn that failing to do so is sin that will overtake them; Latin 'sin against God' and 'your sin will overtake you', Greek 'recognize your sin when evils overtake you'.
Both tell them to build towns for their dependents and folds for their livestock and fulfill what they said.
Both have Gad and Reuben say they are servants who will do as their lord commands.
Both say their dependents, wives and livestock will stay in the towns of Gilead.
Both say all the servants will go armed to war as the lord says.
Both name Eleazar, Joshua and the heads of the tribes; Latin 'gave instructions... saying to them', Greek 'appointed over them'.
Both say that if Gad and Reuben cross armed before the Lord and the land is subdued, Gilead is given to them.
Greek adds that their dependents, wives and livestock are brought across and that they inherit in Canaan; Latin only says they receive places to dwell among them.
Both have Gad and Reuben answer that they will do as the Lord says to His servants.
Latin has them say they already received their possession beyond the Jordan; Greek has them ask that their possession be given on this side of the Jordan.
Both have Moses give Gad, Reuben and half of Manasseh the kingdoms of Sihon and Og with their land and cities.
Both say the sons of Gad built Dibon, Ataroth and Aroer.
Latin lists Atroth, Shophan, Jazer and Jogbehah; Greek names only Shophar and Jazer, omitting Atroth and Jogbehah, and adds 'raised them up'.
Both say they built Beth-nimrah and Beth-haran as fortified cities with folds for livestock.
Both say the sons of Reuben built Heshbon, Elealeh and Kiriathaim.
Latin includes Nebo and says names were changed; Greek omits Nebo and says Baal-meon was 'surrounded with defenses'. Both mention Sibmah and naming the towns.
Latin has the sons of Machir devastating Gilead; Greek has a son of Machir taking it. Number and verb (devastated / took) differ; both destroy the Amorite inhabitant.
Both say Moses gave Gilead to Machir son of Manasseh, who settled there; land of Gilead and dwelt / settled are only wording.
Both have Jair taking the villages and naming them for himself; Latin also gives the Hebrew name Havoth Jair, and its / their settlements differs slightly.
Nobah / Nabau and the resulting name (Nobe / Naboth) differ in form, and Latin has the name given to Kenath alone while Greek names the settlements; the event is the same.
Both introduce the stages / stations of Israel's departure from Egypt under Moses and Aaron; companies / force is only wording.

Latin says Moses recorded the camp sites, changed at the Lord's command; Greek says he recorded departures and stations by the Lord's word and adds a closing sentence about the stations of their journey.
Both give departure from Rameses on the fifteenth day of the first month, the day after Passover, with a high hand before the Egyptians.
Latin has the Egyptians burying the firstborn the Lord struck; Greek says all their dead, namely every firstborn in Egypt. Both note vengeance on their gods.
Both have them camp at Succoth; Greek restates that they set out from Rameses.
Latin has them come to Etham at the farthest edge of the wilderness; Greek has them camp at Bouthan, a part of the wilderness. Place name and description differ.
Pi-hahiroth / mouth of Eiroth differ in form; both place the camp facing Baal-zephon and Migdol.
Both cross the sea and journey three days; Latin names the wilderness of Etham and Marah, Greek gives Bitternesses (the same place by meaning).
Both reach Elim with twelve springs and seventy palms; Greek adds that they camped beside the water.
Both camp by the Red Sea after leaving Elim; Latin ends with the departure from the Red Sea that Greek places at the start of the next verse.
Both camp in the wilderness of Sin after the Red Sea; the departure clause is carried in the previous Latin verse.
Dophkah / Raphaka differ in form and came / camped is wording; both move on from the wilderness of Sin.
Both depart and camp at Alush; Dophkah / Raphaka is only a name form.
Both camp at Rephidim where the people had no water to drink.
Both depart from Rephidim and camp in the wilderness of Sinai.
Both go from Sinai to the Graves of Craving / Desire; craving / desire and came / camped are wording.
Both depart from the Graves and camp at Hazeroth.
Both go from Hazeroth to Rithmah; came / camped is only wording.
Both depart from Rithmah and camp at Rimmon-perez.
Libnah / Lemonah differ in form; both move on from Rimmon-perez.
Rissah / Dessah differ in form; both record a camp after leaving the previous station.
Kehelathah / Makellath differ in form; both record the next station after Rissah / Dessah.
Latin camps at Mount Shepher; Greek at Shaphar without 'Mount'. Same station, differing name form.
Both leave Shepher / Shaphar and reach Haradah.
Both depart from Haradah and camp at Makheloth.
Tahath / Kataath differ in form; both depart from Makheloth to the next station.
Both go from Tahath / Kataath to Terah / Tarath; only name forms differ.
Both go from Terah / Tarath to Mithkah.
Hashmonah / Zalmonah differ in form; both depart from Mithkah to the next station.
Both go from Hashmonah / Zalmonah to Moseroth.
Bene-jaakan / Banaia differ in form; both depart from Moseroth to the next station.
Both reach Mount Gidgad / Gadgad after leaving the previous station.
Both camp at Jotbathah after leaving Gidgad / Gadgad.
Both go from Jotbathah to Abronah.
Both go from Abronah to Ezion-geber.
Greek adds a stage: from Ezion-geber to the wilderness of Sin, then to Paran, that is Kadesh. Latin goes directly to the wilderness of Zin, that is Kadesh.
Both camp at Mount Hor after leaving Kadesh; Latin says at the farthest border of Edom, Greek only near the land of Edom.
Both have Aaron go up at the Lord's command and die in the fortieth year, fifth month, first day; Latin names Mount Hor here, Greek in the next verse.
Both give Aaron's age as 123; Greek names Aaron again and adds that he died on Mount Hor.
Latin places the king of Arad in the south and says Israel had come into Canaan; Greek says he lived in the land of Canaan and heard as Israel was entering.
Both depart from Mount Hor and camp at Zalmonah.
Punon / Phino differ in form; both move on to the next station after Zalmonah.
Both depart from Punon / Phino and camp at Oboth.
Latin has Iye-abarim at the borders of the Moabites; Greek has Gai on the other side at the borders of Moab. Place name differs in form.
Both depart from Iye-abarim / Gai and camp at Dibon-gad.
Both go from Dibon-gad to Almon / Gelmon-diblathaim; only the name form differs.
Both reach the mountains of Abarim opposite Nebo.
Latin has them cross to the plains of Moab; Greek has them camp on the western side of Moab. Both place it by the Jordan opposite Jericho.
Both camp from Beth-jeshimoth to Abel-shittim; Latin says in the level places of the Moabites, Greek beside the Jordan on the western side of Moab.
Both say the Lord spoke to Moses there; Greek spells out the place (western Moab, by the Jordan opposite Jericho) and adds 'saying'.
Both tell Moses to speak to Israel about crossing the Jordan into Canaan; Latin is a conditional 'when you cross', Greek a statement 'you are crossing'.
Both order destruction of the inhabitants and of pillars, idols and high places; the items are listed in different order and wording (statues / cast idols, high places / lookout places).
Both give the land as a possession and tell them to settle in it; Latin says 'clearing the land', Greek repeats 'destroy all who inhabit the land'.
Both divide the land by lot, larger portions for larger groups; Greek adds that it falls 'wherever his name comes out', and wording of tribes and families differs.
Both warn that surviving inhabitants will trouble Israel; nails and spears / splinters and missiles are different images of the same irritation.
Both say the Lord will do to Israel what He had planned to do to the inhabitants.
Both command Israel about the borders of Canaan; Latin says it falls to them by lot, Greek says it is their inheritance with its boundaries.
Both begin the southern boundary at the wilderness of Zin / Sin beside Edom and the Salt Sea; Latin says south and east, Greek southwest.
Latin has the border reach the settlement Addar; Greek has Arad. Ascent of Scorpions / Akrabin and the direction of Kadesh-barnea are also worded differently.
Both run the boundary from Azmon to the Wadi of Egypt and end at the Great Sea.
Both make the Great Sea the western boundary; Latin begins and ends it there, Greek calls it the sea boundary.
Both start the northern boundary at the Great Sea; Latin reaches the highest mountain, Greek says to measure a line beside 'the mountain'.
Both run to Hamath and the borders of Zedad / Sarada; Greek words it as measuring a line toward the entrance to Hamath.
Both extend the northern boundary to Ziphron / Dephrona and Enan / Hazar-enan.
Both mark the eastern boundary from Enan to Shepham.
Latin descends from Shepham to Riblah opposite the spring of Daphnim; Greek has Arbela and Bela and the eastern ridge of the sea. Place names and landmarks differ.
Both bring the boundary to the Jordan and end at the Salt Sea, closing the land's surrounding borders.
Both have Moses tell Israel to divide the land by lot among nine and a half tribes; Greek names Manasseh and says the Lord prescribed it to Moses.
Both name Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh; Latin says by families and clan numbers, Greek by ancestral houses, and Greek states 'received their allotments' here.
Both say the two and a half tribes received land across the Jordan opposite Jericho to the east; Greek adds 'from the south'.
Both say the Lord spoke to Moses.
Both name Eleazar and Joshua; Latin says they divide the land, Greek says they obtain it as an inheritance for the people.
Latin lists one leader from each tribe among the men; Greek commands Israel to take one ruler from each tribe to allot the land.
Both introduce the names, beginning with Caleb son of Jephunneh of Judah.
Both give a Simeonite son of Ammihud; the name differs (Shemuel / Salamiel).
Both give Benjamin's leader as Elidad / Eldad son of Chislon; only the name form differs.
Both name Dan's leader as a son of Jogli / Egli; the personal name differs in form (Bukki / Bakchir) and Greek adds 'the ruler'.
Both give Manasseh's leader as Hanniel; the father's name differs in form (Ephod / Ouphi) and Greek adds 'the ruler'.
Both give Ephraim's leader as Kemuel; the father's name differs in form (Shiphtan / Sabatha) and Greek adds 'the ruler'.
Both give Zebulun's leader as Elizaphan son of Parnach; 'the ruler' is only added wording.
Both give Issachar's leader as Paltiel son of Azzan / Oza; leader / ruler is only wording.
Both give Asher's leader as a son of Shelomi; the personal name differs in form (Ahihud / Achior).
Both give Naphtali's leader as Pedahel; the father's name differs (Ammihud / Benammihud).
Both say these are the men the Lord commanded to divide the land of Canaan among Israel; divide / distribute is only wording.
Both say the Lord spoke to Moses by the Jordan opposite Jericho; Latin says the plains of Moab, Greek the western side of Moab, and Greek adds 'saying'.
Both command Israel to give the Levites from their possessions; Latin's object (cities) comes in the next verse, and Greek also adds the outlying lands here.
Both give cities to live in and surrounding lands for livestock; Latin says flocks and beasts of burden, Greek livestock and all four-footed animals.
Both measure two thousand cubits on each side with the town in the middle; Greek says southwestern for the south and 'outside the town', Latin names the sea as the west.
Both give the Levites six refuge cities for the killer plus forty-two other towns.
Both total forty-eight towns for the Levites with their surrounding lands.
Both take more towns from tribes with more and fewer from those with less, according to inheritance.
Both say the Lord spoke to Moses.
Both introduce the instruction at the crossing of the Jordan into Canaan; Latin 'when you cross' is conditional, Greek 'you are crossing' a statement.
Both have Israel set apart towns as refuges for the one who killed unintentionally.
Both protect the refugee from the avenging kinsman until he stands before the assembly for judgment.
Both set three refuge cities beyond the Jordan and three in Canaan, for Israelites and foreigners, for the unintentional killer; Latin runs verses 13 to 15 together.
Both say that striking with iron and causing death makes him a murderer who shall be put to death.
Both give a stone as the weapon and the same death penalty; Latin says he throws it, Greek that he strikes with a stone in his hand capable of killing.
Both treat a death by wood as murder with the same penalty; Greek specifies a wooden object in his hand.
Both have the avenging kinsman put the murderer to death on meeting him.
Both describe pushing out of hatred or throwing from ambush; Greek adds that the person dies, which Latin completes in the next verse.
Both condemn a deadly blow struck in enmity, with the kinsman killing the murderer; Latin says 'enmity', Greek 'wrath', and Greek repeats the death sentence.

Both free the unintentional killer and return him to the refuge city until the high priest dies; Greek adds the case of a stone falling on him unseen, and describes the congregation's judgment in more detail.
Both treat the killer found outside the boundaries of his refuge city.
Both say the avenger who kills him outside the refuge city is without guilt.
Both say he must stay in the city until the high priest dies, after which he may return to his own land.
Both make this a standing ordinance in all dwellings; Latin says lasting (sempiterna), Greek an ordinance of judgment throughout your generations.
Both require witnesses for punishing a killer and forbid condemnation on one witness's testimony.
Both forbid accepting a ransom from the killer, who must die.
Latin says exiles may in no way return before the high priest's death; Greek forbids accepting a ransom to let the refugee live in the land again before then.
Both forbid polluting the land with blood, which can be expiated only by the blood of the one who shed it.
Latin promises the possession will be cleansed while the Lord dwells among them; Greek forbids defiling the land in which He dwells. Both end with the Lord dwelling among Israel.
Latin has the family heads speak before the leaders of Israel; Greek has them speak before Moses, Eleazar the priest and the rulers of the ancestral houses.
Both say the Lord commanded Moses to divide the land by lot and to give Zelophehad's inheritance to his daughters.
Both say that if the daughters marry into another tribe their allotment passes to that tribe, diminishing the original inheritance.
Both say the inheritance would pass to another tribe; Latin specifies the jubilee, the fiftieth year of release, confusing the lots, while Greek says only 'if the release comes'.
Moses speaks at the Lord's command; Latin says the tribe has spoken rightly, Greek has him say 'thus speaks the tribe' without the verdict.
Both let the daughters marry whom they wish within limits; Latin says men of their own tribe, Greek from their father's clan.

Latin applies the rule to all men and women marrying within tribe and clan; Greek applies it to daughters who inherit, marrying within their father's clan. Both keep inheritance from passing between tribes.
Both have the five daughters marry their paternal cousins; the order of names differs (Mahlah first in Latin, last in Greek) and Greek names them as Zelophehad's daughters.
Both say they married within the family of Manasseh son of Joseph, so the inheritance stayed in their father's tribe.
Both close the book at Moab by the Jordan opposite Jericho; Greek lists commandments, ordinances and judgments, Latin commands and judgments, and the place wording differs.
Both give an eleven-day journey from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea by the Mount Seir road.
Both date Moses' address to the fortieth year, eleventh month, first day, according to all the Lord commanded.
Both place Moses' address after the defeat of Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan; struck down / defeating is only wording.
Both say that beyond the Jordan in Moab Moses began to explain the law.
Both report the Lord's word at Horeb that they had stayed long enough at the mountain.
Both send them to the Amorite hill country and the lands as far as the Euphrates; the regions are listed differently (Greek adds Arabah, southwest) and Lebanon / Anti-Lebanon differs.
Both give the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; Latin has 'He said' and the Lord in the third person, Greek speaks as 'I'.
Both open Moses' recollection of the time he said he could not bear them alone; Greek carries the saying here, Latin in the next verse.
Both say the Lord multiplied them as the stars of heaven; Latin includes 'I cannot bear you alone', which Greek has in the previous verse.
Both pray the Lord will increase them and bless them as He promised; Latin says add many thousands to their number, Greek a thousandfold.
Both say Moses cannot bear their burden and disputes alone; Greek asks it as a question and names trouble, resistance and disputes, Latin affairs, burden and disputes.
Both ask for wise, knowledgeable men to be appointed leaders; Latin adds men of proven conduct, Greek adds discerning, and Moses' appointment is stated as purpose or promise.
Both record the people answering that what Moses proposed was good.
Both appoint commanders of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens; Latin adds that they instruct the people, Greek instead adds recording officials for the judges.
Both command the judges to hear and judge justly, including the foreigner; Greek frames it as disputes between brothers and the newcomer with him.
Both forbid partiality, treat small and great alike, and refer hard cases to Moses; Latin says 'accept no one's person', Greek 'do not shrink back before anyone'.
Both say Moses commanded them everything they were to do.
Both describe the journey from Horeb through the great terrible wilderness to Kadesh-barnea as the Lord commanded.
Both say they reached the Amorite hill country the Lord is giving; Latin says 'give us', Greek 'give you'.
Both tell them to go up and possess the land without fear; Latin says the Lord told 'your fathers', Greek that the God of your fathers told 'you'.
Both have all the people propose sending men to examine the land and report the road and the cities.
Both say the proposal pleased Moses and twelve men were taken, one per tribe; sent / selected differs slightly.
Both have the men go up to the Valley of the Cluster and examine the land.
Both have them bring fruit and report that the land the Lord is giving is good.
Both say the people would not go up against the Lord's word; Latin says 'distrusting', Greek 'refused and disobeyed'.
Both quote the grumbling that the Lord hated them and brought them out of Egypt to hand them over to the Amorites.
Latin says the messengers frightened them and the people are taller; Greek says 'your brothers' and that the nation is stronger. Latin Anakim / Greek sons of giants.
Both have Moses tell them not to fear or be afraid.
Both say the Lord who goes before them will fight as in Egypt; Greek says 'fight against them alongside you'.
Latin says the Lord carried them as a man carries his little son; Greek says He nurtured them as a man nurtures his son.
Both say that even so the people did not trust the Lord.
Both have the Lord going ahead, choosing a camp place, guiding by fire by night and cloud by day; Latin says 'pillar of cloud' and 'went ahead', Greek 'goes ahead'.
Both say the Lord heard their words, was angered and swore.
Both say none of this generation will see the good land sworn to their fathers; Latin calls the generation 'most wicked'.
