Both except Caleb and give him the land he walked on; Latin says he followed the Lord, Greek that he remained devoted to the Lord's concerns.
Latin adds that the people's punishment is not surprising since the Lord was also angry with Moses; Greek lacks this clause. Both report the Lord's refusal that Moses enter.
Both say Joshua son of Nun will enter and Moses is to strengthen him; Latin says he will divide the land by lot, Greek that he will cause Israel to inherit it, and Latin adds 'encourage'.
Latin adds the people's claim that their little ones would be taken captive, which Greek lacks. Both say the children who do not know good and evil will enter and possess the land.
Both tell them to turn and go toward the wilderness by the Red Sea road; Latin says depart into the wilderness, Greek encamp in it.
Both have the people confess sin, promise to go up and fight, and arm themselves; Latin runs the thought into the next verse, Greek says they gathered and went up into the hill country.
Both have the Lord forbid them to go up because He is not with them; Latin warns lest they fall, Greek says they will not be crushed before their enemies.
Both say they did not listen and went up; Latin adds defying the command and swollen with pride, Greek says they transgressed the word and forced their way up.
Both have the Amorites of the hill country come out and chase them like bees from Seir to Hormah.
Both say they wept before the Lord and He did not listen; Latin says they returned and wept, Greek that they sat down and wept.
Both say they stayed at Kadesh a long time; Greek expresses it as many days, as many as they stayed.
Both have them set out toward the wilderness of the Red Sea as the Lord said and circle Mount Seir for a long time.
Both say they have circled the mountain long enough and are to turn north.
Both tell them to pass through the territory of their brothers the descendants of Esau, who will fear them; Greek adds that they will be exceedingly wary.
Both forbid fighting Esau's descendants, since Mount Seir is theirs and none of their land, not even a footstep, will be given.
Both tell them to buy food and water from them with money / silver.
Latin says the Lord knows their journey; Greek tells them to consider how they crossed the wilderness. Both say the Lord has been with them forty years and they lacked nothing.
Both pass Esau's descendants by the road from Elath / Ailon and Ezion-geber toward the wilderness of Moab; Latin calls it the plain road, Greek the Arabah road.
Latin says the Lord gave Ar to Lot's descendants; Greek says He gave Seir. Both forbid fighting Moab.
Both describe the Emim as the former inhabitants, a great people like the Anakim; Latin says powerful and tall, Greek numerous and strong.
Both reckon the Emim as giants / Rephaim like the Anakim, and say the Moabites call them Emim.
Both say the Horites lived in Seir until Esau's descendants destroyed them and settled there, as Israel did in its land.
Both involve crossing the Zered torrent; Latin says they arose to cross and came to it, Greek commands the crossing and says they passed through.
Both give thirty-eight years from Kadesh-barnea to the Zered, until the generation of fighting men had perished as sworn.
Both say the Lord's hand was against them until they perished from the camp.
Both say this was after all the fighting men had fallen.
Both say the Lord spoke to Moses.
Latin has them cross Moab's territory at the city of Ar; Greek has them pass through Moab's territory, Seir.
Both forbid fighting the Ammonites, whose land is given to Lot's descendants.
Both call it a land of giants / Rephaim, formerly inhabited by those the Ammonites call Zamzummim.
Latin calls the people tall as the Anakim, Greek stronger than you, like the Anakim. Both say the Lord destroyed them before the Ammonites; Greek adds 'to this day'.

Latin has the Lord doing for Esau's descendants what He did for the Ammonites, destroying the Horites and handing over their land; Greek says 'they' did it, wiping out the Horites and inheriting the land.
Both say the Cappadocians from Cappadocia destroyed the Hivites near Gaza and settled in their place.
Both command them to cross the Arnon, since Sihon of Heshbon and his land are given to them, and to begin possessing and fight.
Latin has the Lord say He will begin to put dread of Israel on the nations; Greek commands Israel to begin putting it. Latin adds trembling like women in labor.
Both say Moses sent messengers with peaceful words from Kedemoth to Sihon king of Heshbon.
Both promise to pass through by the road, turning neither right nor left; Latin speaks as 'we', Greek as 'I'.
Both ask to buy food and water for money; Latin asks only to be granted passage, Greek says he will only pass through on foot.
Both say Esau's descendants and the Moabites did likewise until crossing the Jordan; Latin gives Ar, Greek Aroer, and Latin says 'we' where Greek says 'I'.
Both say Sihon refused passage because the Lord hardened his spirit and made his heart stubborn so he would be handed over.
Both have the Lord say He has begun to hand Sihon and his land over, and to begin possessing it.
Both have Sihon and all his people come out to battle at Jahaz.
Both say the Lord handed Sihon over and Israel struck him, his sons and all his people.
Both say they captured all his cities and destroyed the inhabitants; Latin names men, women and little children, Greek women and children and says no one was left alive.
Both say only the livestock and the spoil of the cities were taken.
Both say from Aroer on the Arnon to Gilead no city escaped, and the Lord handed all over.
Both say they did not approach the Ammonites' land, the Jabbok, or the hill-country cities, as the Lord forbade.
Both have them go up the road to Bashan, where Og and his people came out to battle at Edrei.
Both have the Lord tell Moses not to fear Og, who is handed over with all his people and land, and to do as to Sihon.
Both say the Lord handed Og and all his people over and Israel struck them down; Latin says to complete destruction, Greek until none of his offspring remained.
Both give sixty cities, the region of Argob, and no town escaping; Latin says 'laying waste' where Greek says 'captured'.
Both describe the cities as walled with gates and bars; Latin adds countless unwalled towns, Greek adds very many cities of the Perizzites.
Both say they destroyed every city as with Sihon; Latin names men, women and little children, Greek women and children and 'in succession'.
Both say they took the livestock and spoil of the cities as plunder.
Both say they took the land from the two Amorite kings beyond the Jordan, from the Arnon to Hermon.
Both give the names for Hermon in other languages; Latin has the Sidonians say Sirion, Greek the Phoenicians say Sanior, and both give the Amorite name Senir.
Both list the cities of the plain, Gilead and Bashan as far as Salecah and Edrei, in Og's kingdom.
Both say Og alone remained of the giants / Rephaim and describe his iron bed nine by four cubits; Latin places it at Rabbah of the Ammonites, Greek in their citadel.
Both give the land from Aroer on the Arnon to half of Gilead to Reuben and Gad; Latin separates the possession from the gift of the cities.
Both give the rest of Gilead and all Bashan to half-tribe Manasseh and call it a land of giants / Rephaim.

Both say Jair took Argob to the borders of the Geshurites / Gargasi and Maacathites and named Havvoth-jair; Latin says he named Bashan, Greek the places in Bashan, and Latin adds the meaning Villages of Jair.
Both say Gilead was given to Machir.
Both give Reuben and Gad the land from Gilead to the Arnon, with its middle as boundary, and to the Jabbok.
Both give the plain, the Jordan and the Salt Sea below Pisgah on the east; place names differ in form (Chinnereth / Machanareth, wilderness / Arabah sea).
Both have Moses recall commanding armed men to go ahead of their brothers since the land is given as inheritance.
Both have wives, children and livestock remain in the cities already given.
Both say they stay until the Lord gives their brothers rest and they possess the land beyond the Jordan, then return.
Both have Moses command Joshua, reminding him of what the Lord did to the two kings and will do to all kingdoms.
Both say not to fear, because the Lord will fight for them.
Both say Moses prayed / pleaded with the Lord at that time.
Both praise the Lord's greatness and mighty hand; Latin states that no other god can match Him, Greek asks it as a question and adds the uplifted arm.
Both ask to cross and see the good land, hill country and Lebanon; Greek names Anti-Lebanon where Latin has Lebanon.
Both say the Lord, because of the people, did not hear Moses and told him to speak of it no more; Latin says He was angry, Greek that He disregarded him.
Both send Moses up to look in all directions but not cross the Jordan; Latin names Pisgah, Greek the Hewn Place, and the compass points are worded slightly differently.
Both have Moses command and strengthen Joshua, who will lead the people; Latin says he will divide the land Moses will see, Greek that he will cause them to inherit the land Moses has seen.
Both say they stayed in the valley by Peor; opposite the shrine / near the house is only wording.
Both urge Israel to hear and do the ordinances so as to live and possess the land; Greek adds 'multiply' and 'today'.
Both forbid adding to or taking from the word and command keeping the Lord's commandments.
Both say they saw what the Lord did at Baal-peor, wiping out all its followers from among them.
Both say those who held fast to the Lord are alive today.
Both say Moses has taught the ordinances as the Lord commanded, to be practiced in the land they will possess.
Both call the keeping of the commands their wisdom before the nations, who will call them a wise and understanding great nation.
Both say no great nation has its god so near; Latin states it with 'gods' near and God present to prayers, Greek asks it as a question about calling on Him.
Both ask what nation has such a law; Latin says renowned with rites, just judgments and law, Greek great with ordinances and judgments as righteous as the whole law.
Both tell them to guard their souls, not to forget what they saw, and to teach children and grandchildren.
Both recall the day at Horeb when the Lord told Moses to gather the people to hear and learn to fear Him; Greek adds 'the day of the assembly'.
Both describe the mountain burning to heaven; Latin adds cloud, while Greek adds fire, tempest and a loud sound to darkness and gloom.
Both say the Lord spoke from the fire and they heard a voice but saw no form; Greek adds 'only a voice'.
Both say He declared His covenant, the ten words, written on two stone tablets.
Both say the Lord commanded Moses to teach ordinances and judgments to practice in the land.
Both say they saw no likeness / form on the day the Lord spoke from the fire at Horeb; Greek adds 'on the mountain'.
Both warn against making a carved likeness of male or female; Latin says lest you be deceived, Greek lest you act lawlessly, and Greek adds 'any image'.
Both forbid a likeness of any animal on earth or bird flying under heaven.
Both forbid a likeness of creeping things on the earth and fish in the waters beneath the earth.
Latin says the Lord created the heavenly bodies to serve all the nations; Greek says He allotted them to the nations. Both warn against being led astray to worship them.
Both say the Lord took them out of Egypt's iron furnace to be His people of inheritance.
Both say the Lord was angry with Moses because of the people and swore he would not cross the Jordan or enter the good land.
Both have Moses say he will die in the land and not cross the Jordan, while Israel will cross and possess the good land.
Both warn not to forget the covenant or make a carved likeness; Latin says of anything the Lord forbade, Greek of anything about which He gave orders.
Both give the case of descendants making a likeness and provoking the Lord; Latin says they are deceived, Greek that they act lawlessly and remain long in the land.
Both call heaven and earth to witness that they will quickly perish from the land and not remain long.
Both say the Lord will scatter them among the nations, leaving them few in number.
Both say they will serve / worship gods of wood and stone made by hands, which cannot see, hear, eat or smell.
Both say they will find the Lord when seeking Him there with all their heart and soul; Latin states it as a proviso.
Both say that in the latter time, after these things overtake them, they will return to the Lord and hear His voice.
Both say the Lord is merciful and will not abandon or destroy them or forget the covenant sworn to their fathers.
Both ask whether anything like this has happened since God created humankind, from one end of heaven to the other.
Both ask whether a people has heard God speaking from the fire and lived; Greek calls Him the living God.
Both ask whether God ever took a people for Himself by trials, signs, wonders, war, mighty hand and outstretched arm, as in Egypt.
Both say this was so they would know the Lord is God and there is no other.
Both say God made His voice heard from heaven and showed His great fire on earth, speaking from the midst of it.
Both say He loved the fathers, chose their offspring and brought Israel out of Egypt by great power; Latin adds 'He went before you', Greek identifies the offspring as 'you'.
Both say God destroyed greater and stronger nations and gave their land as a possession.
Both say to know and consider that the Lord is God in heaven above and earth below, and there is no other.
Both tell them to keep the commandments so it goes well with them and their children and they live long on the land; Greek adds 'for all time'.
Both say Moses set apart three cities beyond the Jordan to the east.
Both give refuge for one who killed unintentionally without prior enmity; Latin says 'a day or two before', Greek 'previously hating him', and Greek says he could flee and live.
Both name Bezer for Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead for Gad and Golan in Bashan for Manasseh.
Both say this is the law Moses set before Israel.
Both list the testimonies, rites / ordinances and judgments spoken after leaving Egypt; Greek adds that they were spoken in the wilderness.
Both place it beyond the Jordan opposite Peor in Sihon's land; Latin says Moses struck him, Greek says Moses and the Israelites defeated him.
Both say they possessed the land of Sihon and Og, the two Amorite kings beyond the Jordan to the east.
Both give the extent from Aroer on the Arnon to Mount Sion, that is Hermon.
Both include the eastern plain beyond the Jordan; Latin ends at the sea of the wilderness and the foot of Pisgah, Greek at Asedoth, the hewn height.
Both have Moses summon Israel to hear, learn and practice the rites / ordinances and judgments.
Both say the Lord made a covenant at Horeb; Latin says with 'us', Greek with 'you'.
Both say the Lord spoke face to face on the mountain from the midst of the fire.
Both have Moses stand between the Lord and the people to declare His words, since they feared the fire.
Both forbid other / foreign gods before the Lord.
Both forbid a carved image or likeness of anything in heaven, earth or the waters beneath.
Both forbid bowing down to or serving them and describe the jealous God repaying fathers' sin to the third and fourth generation.
Both say He shows mercy to thousands who love Him and keep His commandments.
Both forbid taking the Lord's name in vain, and say such a one will not go unpunished.
Both say to labor six days and do all one's work.
Both forbid all work on the seventh day for household, slaves, animals and the foreigner so slaves may rest; Latin says within your gates, Greek residing among you.
Both recall slavery in Egypt and the strong hand and outstretched arm as the reason for Sabbath observance; Greek adds 'and keep it holy'.
Both command honoring father and mother so as to live long and have it go well in the land given.
Both forbid false testimony against a neighbor.
Both forbid coveting a neighbor's wife and goods; Greek repeats the prohibition for the house and adds 'any of his livestock'.
Both say the Lord spoke from the fire to the whole assembly, added nothing and wrote on two tablets; the accompanying phenomena differ (Latin cloud, Greek tempest and gloom).
Latin has the voice heard from the midst of the darkness; Greek from the midst of the fire. Both have the leaders and elders approach Moses; the Latin 'and said' leads into the next verse.
Both report the people saying the Lord showed His majesty / glory, they heard His voice from the fire, and a person can live when God speaks.
Both fear the great fire will consume them and that hearing the voice any longer means death; Latin asks 'why should we die?', Greek says 'let us not die'.
Both ask what mortal has heard the living God speak from the fire and lived.
Both have the people ask Moses to go near, hear all the Lord says, and tell them so they will listen and do it.
Both say the Lord heard the people's words and said everything they spoke was good.
Both express the wish that they had a heart / mind to fear Him and keep His commandments always, for their good forever.
Both tell Moses to send the people back; Latin says to their tents, Greek to their houses.
Both have the Lord tell Moses to stay with Him to receive the commandments, ordinances and judgments to teach the people for the land.
Both command doing what the Lord commanded without turning right or left.
Both command walking in the way the Lord commanded, for good and long days in the land; Latin says that they may live, Greek that He may give them rest.
Both say these are the commandments, rites / ordinances and judgments to be practiced in the land they are entering to possess.
Both give the purpose that they fear the Lord and keep all His commandments, for themselves, children and grandchildren, so days may be long.
Both urge Israel to hear and do so it goes well and they multiply, as promised in a land flowing with milk and honey.
Both say these words shall be in your heart; Greek adds 'and in your soul'.
Both tell them to teach / tell the words to their children and speak of them sitting, walking, lying down and rising.
Both bind the words as a sign on the hand; Latin says they hang and move between the eyes, Greek says it is to be immovable before the eyes.
Both say to write them at the house entrances; Latin says threshold and doors of the house, Greek doorposts of the houses and gates.
Both describe the Lord bringing them into the land sworn to the fathers with great cities they did not build.
Both warn not to forget the Lord after eating their fill and to fear and swear by Him; Latin says serve Him alone, Greek says worship Him and hold fast to Him. Latin runs verses 11 to 13 together.
Both forbid following the foreign / other gods of the surrounding nations.
Both say the Lord in their midst is a jealous God, lest His wrath destroy them from the face of the earth.
Both forbid testing the Lord as they did at the place of testing.
Both command keeping the Lord's commandments, testimonies and ordinances.
Both command doing what is pleasing and good so it goes well and they possess the good land sworn to the fathers.
Both say the Lord promised to remove their enemies before them; Latin says destroy, Greek says drive out.
Both have a son ask in time to come about the testimonies, ordinances and judgments the Lord commanded.
Both answer that they were Pharaoh's slaves and the Lord brought them out with a strong hand; Greek adds 'uplifted arm' and 'household' slaves.
Both say the Lord worked great and terrible signs and wonders against Pharaoh and his household before their eyes.
Both say He brought them out to bring them in and give the land sworn to their fathers.
Both say the Lord commanded them to practice all these ordinances and fear Him, for their good as today.
Both list the same seven nations stronger than Israel; Latin says many nations, far more numerous, destroyed, while Greek says great nations, numerous, removed.
Both command striking them down completely and making no covenant or mercy with them.
Both forbid intermarriage, giving or taking daughters for sons.
Both say they would turn the son away to serve other gods, provoking the Lord's wrath and swift destruction.
Both command overthrowing altars, breaking pillars, cutting down sacred groves and burning carved images.
Both say Israel is a holy people, chosen as His own people from all the peoples of the earth.
Both say the Lord chose them though they were the fewest, not for numbers; Latin says He 'joined' Himself to them, Greek that He 'preferred' them.
Both say He chose them because He loved them and kept His oath, redeeming them from Pharaoh's hand; Greek adds 'uplifted arm'.
Both say the Lord is God, faithful, keeping covenant and mercy for a thousand generations with those who love Him.
Latin says He repays those who hate Him immediately; Greek says He repays them to their face. Both say He does not delay.
Both command keeping and practicing the commandments, ordinances and judgments given today.
Both promise that if they keep these judgments the Lord will keep covenant and mercy sworn to their fathers.
Both promise love, multiplication and blessing on womb, land, grain, wine, oil, herds and flocks.
Both promise blessing and no barrenness among people or livestock; Latin says 'among all peoples', Greek 'above all peoples'.
Both promise removal of sickness and that Egypt's diseases fall on enemies instead of Israel.
Latin has them consume all the peoples; Greek has them consume the spoils of the nations. Latin says their gods would bring ruin, Greek that serving them would be a stumbling block.
Both give the objection that the nations are more numerous and ask how to destroy them; Latin has 'these nations', Greek 'this nation'.
Both say not to fear and to remember what the Lord did to Pharaoh and the Egyptians.
Both recall the signs, wonders, mighty hand and outstretched arm; Latin says plagues, Greek trials, and Greek says 'the Lord our God'.
Latin has those who flee and hide destroyed; Greek speaks of those left behind and hiding. Both have hornets sent until the survivors are gone.
Latin says do not fear; Greek says you shall not be wounded. Latin calls God great and terrible; Greek says great and mighty.
Latin adds 'part by part'; Greek adds that the land would become deserted before wild animals multiply. Both give the gradual-conquest reason.
Both have the Lord delivering the nations; Latin has them killed until utterly destroyed, Greek destroyed with great destruction until annihilated.
Latin has you wiping out their names from under heaven; Greek has their name perishing from that place. The agent and the extent differ.
Both command burning the images and not coveting the silver and gold; Greek specifies images of their gods, Latin 'of which they are made'.
Latin forbids bringing anything from an idol into the house; Greek forbids bringing an abomination. Latin's detest as filth differs from Greek's reject utterly.
Same command to keep every commandment so as to live, multiply and possess the land; Latin has 'take great care', Greek adds 'your God'.
Latin dates the wilderness journey to forty years; this Greek reading has no number. Otherwise both speak of affliction and testing to reveal the heart.
Both say clothing did not wear out and feet did not suffer; worn sore / calloused and 'fortieth year' / 'forty years' are slight variations.
Latin says the Lord has disciplined you (past, as a lesson to consider); Greek says the Lord will discipline you (future). Know / consider is slight.
Both call for keeping the commandments, walking in His ways and fearing Him; Latin states a purpose, Greek a direct command.
Latin has a land of rivers, waters and springs with deep sources; Greek has a good and extensive land with flowing water. 'Extensive' has no Latin counterpart.
Same list of crops; Latin 'olive groves' and 'oil' where Greek has only olive oil.
Both describe bread without lack, iron stones and copper from the hills; Latin adds abundance of all things, Greek says without poverty.
Both: eat, be satisfied, bless the Lord for the land; Latin is purpose ('excellent land'), Greek a future statement ('good land').
Both warn against forgetting the Lord and His commandments and judgments; Latin 'rites' (cæremonias) and 'neglect' where Greek says ordinances and failing to keep.
Same warning after eating, building houses and dwelling in them; beautiful / good houses differs slightly.
Latin has you acquiring herds, flocks, silver and gold; Greek says these have multiplied. Both speak of abundance.
Both warn against a proud heart forgetting the Lord who brought you from Egypt; lifted up / proud is wording.
Latin names serpents with scorching breath, scorpions and the dipsas, and streams from the hardest rock; Greek has biting serpents and a spring from sheer rock.
Latin says after afflicting and testing, He finally had mercy; Greek says He afflicted and tested in order to do you good in the latter days.
Both forbid saying my strength made this; Latin 'provided all this', Greek 'made this great wealth'; Latin is 'lest you say', Greek a direct prohibition.
Latin: He gave strength to fulfill His covenant. Greek: He gives strength to produce wealth and to establish His covenant. 'Wealth' is added in Greek.
Latin: serving and worshiping foreign gods; 'I warn you'. Greek: worship and bow down to other gods; 'I call heaven and earth to witness'.
Latin: the nations destroyed on your entering, you will perish if you disobey. Greek: nations being destroyed, you will perish because you did not listen.
Both announce crossing the Jordan to possess greater nations and walled cities; Latin 'enormous', Greek 'great', and Greek adds 'enter'.
Both describe a great, tall people, the sons of Anak; Greek adds 'numerous' and ends with the question 'Who can stand before the descendants of Anak?'
Latin: He crushes and quickly wipes them out. Greek: He destroys and turns them back, and you will destroy them. 'Quickly' is Latin only.
Both forbid claiming righteousness; the nations are destroyed for their wickedness. Latin states it as past, Greek as future.
Both: not for your righteousness but for their wickedness; Latin 'fulfill His word' and Greek 'establish His covenant' for the oath to the fathers.
Both say the land is not given for your righteousness since you are stiff-necked; Latin 'very stiff-necked' and 'excellent land' are intensified.
Both recall provoking the Lord from Egypt to this place; Latin says continually contended against Him, Greek kept disobeying.
Both: provoked at Horeb and the Lord wished to destroy you; Latin 'in anger', Greek 'was angry enough'.
Both give the ascent for the stone tablets, forty days and nights, and no bread or water; only English wording differs.
Latin adds 'from the midst of the fire' for the words spoken at the assembly; the Greek has no mention of fire.
Both: after forty days and nights the Lord gave the two stone tablets of the covenant.
Greek adds that the people 'acted lawlessly' and has the way 'commanded' rather than shown; Latin has no lawlessness clause.
Greek adds 'I have spoken to you once and twice'; Latin has 'again' only. Both call the people stiff-necked.
Both: let Me destroy them and blot out their name, and make you a greater nation; Greek adds 'more numerous'.
Both have Moses coming down the burning mountain with the two tablets in his hands; Latin calls them tablets 'of the covenant', Greek adds 'I turned'.
Both: you sinned, made a cast image and turned from the way; Latin names a calf and says 'quickly', Greek says 'image' and 'commanded'.
Both: Moses threw the tablets from his hands and broke them before the people; Greek adds he took hold of them first.
Both: forty days and nights without bread or water for the people's sins; Latin 'fell down', Greek 'pleaded a second time'.
Both: fear of the Lord's anger and His intent to destroy, and He heard me again; Latin 'I feared', Greek 'I am terrified'.
Both: the Lord was very angry with Aaron and Moses prayed for him; crush / destroy is only a nuance.
Both: Moses burned the calf, ground it to dust and threw it into the torrent; Latin 'sinful thing', Greek 'your sin'.
Same three places (Burning, Testing, Graves of craving / desire) where they provoked the Lord; Greek adds 'kept provoking' and 'your God'.
Both: sent from Kadesh-barnea to take the land, and they disobeyed; Latin 'despised the command' and 'would not listen', Greek 'disobeyed the word'.
Latin: rebellious from the day I (Moses) first knew you. Greek: disobeying from the day He (the Lord) became known to you. Who knows whom differs.
Both: forty days and nights pleading not to be destroyed; Latin 'as He had threatened', Greek 'because the Lord had said'.
Greek adds 'Lord, Lord, King of the gods' and a longer list: great strength, mighty hand, uplifted arm. Latin has the shorter 'Lord God' and 'strong hand'.
Greek adds 'to whom You swore by Yourself' after the patriarchs; Latin lacks it. Otherwise both ask God not to regard the people's stubbornness and sin.
Both give the feared taunt that the Lord could not bring them in and hated them; Greek frames it as 'because', Latin as a direct quotation.
Both: they are Your people and inheritance brought out by great strength and an outstretched arm; Greek adds 'out of Egypt'.
Both give the command to cut two tablets like the first, come up the mountain and make a wooden ark.
Both: the Lord will write the same words on the new tablets, and they are put in the ark; broke / shattered is wording.
Both: Moses made the ark, cut the tablets and went up; Latin names acacia wood (setim), Greek 'decay-resistant wood'.
Latin adds 'when the people assembled' after the ten words from the fire; this Greek reading lacks it. The rest agrees.
Both: came down and put the tablets in the ark as commanded; Latin says they are still there, Greek 'they were there'.
Place names differ: Latin Jaakan and Moserah; Greek 'Iakim' and 'Misadai'. Both record Aaron's death and Eleazar serving as priest.
Same stages (Gadgad, Jotbathah); Latin 'land of waters and torrents', Greek 'land of flowing torrents'.
Both: the Lord set apart Levi to carry the ark, stand before Him in service and bless in His name to this day.
Both: Levi has no share among his brothers because the Lord is his inheritance; Latin adds 'the Lord your God promised', Greek 'as He told him'.
Both: forty days and nights on the mountain, and the Lord heard and would not destroy you; Latin adds 'as before'.
Both: go before the people so they enter and possess the sworn land; Latin 'lead the people', Greek 'set out ahead of this people'.
Both ask what the Lord requires: fear, walk, love, serve with all heart and soul; Greek says 'all His ways'.
Both: keep the commandments and statutes for your good; Latin 'rites', Greek 'ordinances' and 'all that I command'.
Both: heaven, the heaven of heaven, the earth and all in it belong to the Lord your God.
Both: the Lord loved your fathers and chose their offspring from / above all nations; Latin 'bound Himself to', Greek 'preferred'.
Both: God of gods, Lord of lords, great, mighty and fearsome, showing no partiality and taking no bribes.
Both: justice for the orphan and widow, love for the foreigner; Greek also names the newcomer in the justice clause and says 'bread'.
Both command loving the foreigner / newcomer since you were strangers in Egypt.
Both: fear, serve, hold fast to Him and swear by His name; Latin adds 'Him alone'.
Both: He is your praise / boast and your God who did great things you saw; Latin 'terrible', Greek 'glorious'.
Both: seventy persons went down to Egypt, and the Lord has now multiplied you like the stars of heaven.
Both: love the Lord and keep His requirements always; Latin lists precepts, rites, judgments and commandments, Greek charges, ordinances and judgments.
Latin: know what your children do not know, as they did not see God's discipline. Greek: know that I am addressing you, not your children, who neither knew nor saw.
Both: the signs done in Egypt to Pharaoh and his land; Latin 'signs and works', Greek 'signs and wonders'.
Both: the Egyptian army overwhelmed in the Red Sea; Latin 'horses and chariots', Greek 'chariots and cavalry'.
Both continue the list of what the Lord did for you in the wilderness until you reached this place.
Both: Dathan and Abiram swallowed by the earth with households, tents and possessions; Latin 'among Israel', Greek 'in the midst of all Israel'.
Both say your eyes have seen the great works of the Lord; Greek adds 'all', 'for you' and 'today'.
Greek adds 'so that you may live and multiply' and 'crossing the Jordan'; Latin has only keeping the commandments to enter and possess the land.
Both: long life in the land sworn to the fathers and their offspring, flowing with milk and honey; live a long time / prolong your days.
Latin: seed sown and water channeled as in gardens. Greek: they sow seed and water it with their feet like a vegetable garden. The means of watering differs.
Both: a land of mountains and plains watered by rain from heaven; Latin 'waits for rain', Greek 'drinks the rain'.
Both: the Lord's eyes are on the land from the start of the year to its end; 'visits' / 'watches over' is a nuance.
Same condition of obeying and loving and serving with all heart and soul; Latin 'my commandments', Greek 'all His commandments' with 'diligently'.
Both: early and late rain and grain, wine and oil; Latin states purpose ('that you may gather'), Greek a promise ('you will bring in').
Both: grass / fodder for livestock and eating to satisfaction; Latin states purpose, Greek makes it a promise and leads into the next verse.
Latin: lest your heart be deceived and you turn away from the Lord. Greek: lest your heart grow expansive and you transgress. Both then mention serving other gods.
Both: the Lord's anger, heavens shut, no rain or produce, and swift perishing from the good land; tense is the main difference.
Both: put these words in heart and soul, as a sign on the hand and before the eyes; Greek adds 'immovable'.
Both: teach them to your children at home, on the road, lying down and rising; Latin 'meditate', Greek 'speak of them'.
Both: write them on the doorposts; Latin 'doors of your house', Greek 'of your houses and of your gates'.
Both: lengthened days for you and your children in the sworn land while heaven is over the earth; multiplied / long days.
Both: keep the commandments, love the Lord, walk in all His ways and cling to Him; Latin 'your God', Greek 'our God'.
Both: the Lord removes the nations and you take greater, stronger ones; destroy / drive out is a nuance.
Borders match except Latin names Lebanon and Greek names Anti-Lebanon; Greek also adds 'the Euphrates River' after 'the great river'.
Both: no one will stand against you, and the Lord will put dread and fear of you over all the land as He said.
Both: today I set before you a blessing and a curse.
Both: the blessing if you obey the Lord's commandments commanded today.
Both: curse if you disobey and turn to unknown gods; Greek says 'curses' and 'all that I command you today', Latin 'the way I now show you'.
Both: blessing on Mount Gerizim, curse on Mount Ebal; Latin 'where you are going to live', Greek 'crossing over to inherit'.
Greek is a question and places the site near 'the lofty oak'; Latin describes Canaanites in the plains opposite Gilgal beside a far-reaching valley.
Greek adds that the land is given 'as an allotment for all time' and 'dwell in it'; Latin says only to hold and possess it.
Both: take care to carry out the ordinances and judgments set before you today; Greek says 'all His ordinances'.
Both: the precepts and judgments to practice in the land given by the Lord all the days of your life; Latin 'is going to give', Greek 'gives as an allotment'.
Both command destroying the nations' worship places on mountains, hills and under leafy trees; overthrow / completely destroy is wording.
Latin burns the groves and smashes idols; Greek cuts down the groves and burns the carved images. Latin has them wipe out names; Greek says the name will perish.
Both: you shall not do so to the Lord your God.
Latin: the place chosen from all your tribes, where He dwells. Greek: the place chosen in one of your tribes, where His name is invoked.
Latin lists tithes among the offerings; the Greek list omits tithes. Otherwise both give burnt offerings, firstfruits, vows, gifts and the firstborn.
Both: eat and rejoice before the Lord, you and your households; Latin 'in which He has blessed you', Greek 'because He has blessed you'.
Both forbid doing as each person sees fit; Latin 'not as we do here', Greek 'not everything we do'.
Both: you have not yet come to the rest and possession the Lord is giving you.
Both: cross the Jordan, dwell in the land, rest from enemies and live without fear; Greek names the Lord as the one giving rest.
Both: bring offerings, sacrifices, tithes, firstfruits and vowed gifts to the chosen place; Greek 'invoked' where Latin has 'His name be there'.
Both: rejoice before the Lord with sons, daughters, servants and the Levite, who has no share; Latin 'feast', Greek 'rejoice', and 'in your cities' / 'at your gates'.
Both: take care not to offer your burnt offerings in every place you see.
Both: offer at the place the Lord chooses in one of your tribes and do all He commands; Latin 'sacrifices', Greek 'whole burnt offerings only'.
Both permit slaughtering and eating meat in your cities, clean and unclean alike, like gazelle and deer; Latin glosses unclean as blemished, Greek adds 'as much as you desire'.
Both: do not eat the blood; pour it on the ground like water.
Both list the tithes, firstborn, vows and firstfruits not to be eaten in your towns; Latin 'freewill offerings', Greek 'pledged offerings'.
Latin includes the Levite among those eating before the Lord and adds 'refresh'; Greek has the newcomer in the cities instead of the Levite.
Both: take care not to abandon the Levite as long as you live in the land.
Both: when the Lord enlarges your borders you may eat the meat you desire; Greek states the permission outright, 'as much as you desire'.
Both: if the chosen place is far, slaughter from your herds and eat in your cities; Greek adds 'that God gives you' and 'invoked'.
Both: eat as gazelle and deer are eaten; the clean and unclean may eat together.
Both forbid eating the blood because it is life; Latin 'blood stands for life', Greek 'blood is life'.
Both: pour the blood on the ground like water; Greek adds 'Do not eat it'.
Both: so that it goes well with you and your children for doing what pleases the Lord; Greek repeats 'do not eat it'.
Both: take your consecrated and vowed offerings to the chosen place; Greek adds 'for His name to be invoked there'.
Latin offers flesh and blood on the altar and pours blood on it; Greek prepares burnt offerings and pours the blood against the base of the altar.
Both: observe and hear all commands so it goes well with you forever; Latin 'when you do', Greek 'if you do' what is good.
Both: when / if the Lord destroys the nations and you possess and live in their land; wording of condition differs slightly.
Both warn against imitating the nations saying you will worship as they do; Latin 'inquire into their rites', Greek 'inquire after their gods'.
Both: do not do so to the Lord, for they did abominations burning sons and daughters; Latin 'offering and burning', Greek only 'burn'.
Both command doing what is commanded and not adding or taking away; Greek is numbered 13:1 and 'every word I command you today'.
Both: a prophet or dreamer arises and gives a sign or wonder; Latin 'predicts', Greek 'gives you'.
Both: the sign comes true and he urges serving unknown gods; Latin adds 'follow', Greek ties it to 'the sign or wonder he told you'.
Both: do not listen to that prophet, for the Lord is testing whether you love Him with all heart and soul; Latin 'make plain', Greek 'to know'.
Both: follow, fear, keep His commandments and hear His voice, and cling to Him; Latin adds 'serve Him', Greek lacks it.
Both: that prophet shall die for leading you from the Lord; Latin 'fabricator of dreams' and 'remove the evil', Greek 'remove the evil person'.
Both list the relatives and friend who secretly urge serving other gods; Latin 'loved as your soul', Greek 'equal to yourself'.
Both: gods of the surrounding nations, near or far, from one end of the earth to the other.
Both: do not yield, listen, spare or conceal him; Latin 'show mercy', Greek 'feel longing'.
Latin: kill him at once, your hand first. Greek: you must report him, and your hands are first to put him to death. Greek adds the reporting step.
Both: he shall be stoned to death for seeking to turn you from the Lord who brought you out of Egypt.
Both: all Israel will hear and fear and not do such a thing again; Latin 'like this', Greek 'such an evil thing among you'.
Both: if you hear people saying this in one of the cities the Lord gives you to live in.
Both: men have gone out and led the city astray to serve other gods; Latin 'sons of Belial', Greek 'lawless men'.
Both: inquire thoroughly, and if the report is true and the abomination done; Greek adds 'among you'.
Both: put the city's inhabitants to the sword and destroy it; Latin adds 'down to the livestock', Greek 'devoting it to destruction'.
Both: gather the spoil in the squares and burn it with the city for the Lord, never to be rebuilt; mound of ruins / uninhabited.
Both: nothing devoted to destruction in your hand, so the Lord turns from anger and multiplies you; Greek adds 'grant you mercy'.
Both: heed the Lord's voice, keep His commandments and do what pleases Him; Greek adds 'good'.
Latin forbids cutting yourselves and shaving bald for the dead; Greek forbids purification rites and a bald patch between the eyes for the dead.
Both: you are a holy people, chosen from all nations on earth as His own special people.
Both forbid eating forbidden food; Latin 'unclean things', Greek 'anything abominable'.
Both list cattle, sheep and goats as edible; Greek specifies a calf, a lamb and a young male goat.
Both: you may eat any animal with a divided hoof that chews the cud.
Both name the camel, hare and rock badger / hyrax as unclean for chewing the cud without dividing the hoof.
Both: the pig has a divided hoof but does not chew the cud and is unclean; do not eat or touch the carcasses.
Both: of water creatures, eat what has fins and scales.
Both: do not eat anything without fins and scales; it is unclean.
Both permit eating every clean bird.
Both list the eagle, griffon and sea eagle among birds not to be eaten.
Latin lists the ixion before the vulture and kite; the Greek list omits it. The vulture and kite 'after its kind' agree.
Both forbid every kind of raven.
Both name ostrich, owl and gull; Latin includes the hawk here, Greek places the hawk in the next verse.
Latin lists diving bird, purple swamphen, night raven; Greek lists diving bird, hawk, hoopoe, night-raven. Birds are arranged differently across verses 17 and 18.
Latin gives pelican, plover, hoopoe and bat; Greek gives pelican, plover, purple swamphen and bat. Different birds fall in this verse.
Both: winged crawling creatures are unclean and not to be eaten.
Both permit eating clean creatures; Greek specifies clean flying creatures, Latin 'everything clean'.
Latin gives the carcass to the foreigner within your gates or sells it; Greek distinguishes resident alien and foreigner. Latin kid versus Greek lamb in its mother's milk.
Both: set apart a tenth of the produce each year; Greek specifies the yield of your seed and field.
Both: tithe and firstborn eaten at the chosen place so you learn to fear the Lord; Latin 'you shall eat', Greek 'eat it... bring the tithes'.
Both: if the place is too far to carry the tithes because of the Lord's blessing; sentence structure differs.
Both: sell it for money / silver, carry it in your hand to the chosen place.
Both: spend the money on whatever you desire and eat and rejoice before the Lord with your household; Latin 'feast'.
Both include the Levite who has no share; Latin adds 'take care not to abandon him', Greek continues the sentence.
Latin: in the third year set apart another tithe. Greek: after three years bring out the whole tithe, stored that year in your cities.
Both: the Levite, newcomer / foreigner, orphan and widow eat and are satisfied so the Lord blesses your work; Latin 'within your gates', Greek 'in your cities'.
Latin sets the release in the seventh year; Greek says at seven-year intervals. Both command a remission.
Both: a creditor may not demand repayment from a neighbor or brother because the Lord's remission is proclaimed; Greek phrases it as a command to release the debt.
Both: you may demand payment from a foreigner but not from your brother.
Both: there will be no needy person among you because the Lord will bless you in the land given; Greek adds 'surely' and 'allotment to inherit'.
Both: the blessing depends on obeying the Lord's voice and keeping His commands; Latin adds 'as He promised' here, which Greek has in the next verse.
Both: you will lend to many nations and not borrow, and rule without being ruled; Greek opens with 'the Lord has blessed you as He told you'.
Both: if a brother is poor in your city, do not close your hand; Latin 'harden your heart', Greek 'withdraw your heart's affection'.
Both: open your hand to him and lend what he needs; Greek adds 'freely' and 'according to his lack'.
Both warn against a wicked thought that the year of release is near and refusing the poor brother, who will cry to the Lord; Greek 'great sin'.
Latin: give and do not act craftily in relieving his need. Greek: give freely without a grieving heart. Both promise the Lord's blessing.
Both: the poor will always be in the land, so open your hand to your poor brother; Greek adds 'freely'.
Both: a Hebrew brother or sister sold to you serves six years and is freed in the seventh.
Both: when you set him free, do not send him away empty-handed.
Both: give from your flocks and winepress as the Lord has blessed you; Latin 'threshing floor', Greek 'grain', and Greek adds 'generously'.
Both: remember you were slaves in Egypt and the Lord freed you; Greek 'household slave' and 'redeemed'.
Both: if the slave says he will not leave because he loves you and fares well; Latin 'I do not wish to leave', Greek 'I will not leave you'.
Both: pierce his ear with an awl at the door and do likewise for a female slave; Latin 'serve forever', Greek 'household slave permanently'.
Both: consecrate every male firstborn of cattle and sheep; do not work the firstborn ox or shear the firstborn sheep.
Both: eat it yearly with your household before the Lord at the chosen place.
Both: a blemished animal, lame or blind, is not to be sacrificed; Latin lists deformed or weak, Greek 'any serious defect'.
Both: eat it in your cities, clean and unclean alike, as gazelle or deer.
Both: do not eat the blood; pour it on the ground like water.
Latin adds 'the first month of spring' to the month of new produce; the Greek has only the month of new produce.
Both: sacrifice the Passover, sheep and cattle, at the chosen place; Latin 'name to dwell', Greek 'name to be invoked'.
Latin: you came out of Egypt in dread (pavore); Greek: in haste. Otherwise both give seven days of unleavened bread of affliction.
Both: no leaven seen in your borders for seven days, and no meat left until morning; Greek adds 'overnight'.
Both: you may not sacrifice the Passover in any of the cities the Lord gives you.
Both: sacrifice only at the chosen place in the evening at sunset, the time of leaving Egypt; Latin 'dwell', Greek 'invoked'.
Both: cook and eat at the chosen place and return in the morning; Latin 'tents', Greek 'houses'; Greek names boiling and roasting.
Greek adds a concluding celebration and an exception for work done for a person's needs; Latin calls it an assembly with no work.
Both: count seven weeks from first putting the sickle to the grain; Greek adds 'complete' and states the counting twice.
Latin: a freewill offering from your hand according to the Lord's blessing. Greek: celebrate according to your hand's ability, as the Lord has blessed you.
Both list the household, Levite, stranger, orphan and widow rejoicing at the chosen place; Latin 'dwell', Greek 'invoked'.
Both: remember you were a slave in Egypt and keep the commandments; Greek 'household slave'.
Both: celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles / Tents for seven days after gathering from threshing floor and winepress.
Both list the household, Levite, stranger, orphan and widow feasting; feast / rejoice and gates / cities are wording.
Both: seven days' feast at the chosen place with joy; Latin states the blessing as fact, Greek makes the rejoicing conditional on it.
Both: three yearly appearances at Unleavened Bread, Weeks and Tabernacles / Tent-pitching, not empty-handed; Latin phrased as statement.
Both: each gives according to the blessing the Lord gave; Latin 'what he has', Greek 'the ability of your hands'.
Both: appoint judges to judge justly tribe by tribe; Latin 'officers' at gates, Greek 'recording officials' in cities.
Both: no partiality or bribes, as bribes blind the wise; Latin 'change the words', Greek 'nullify' them.
Both: pursue justice so that you may live and possess the land the Lord gives you.
Both forbid planting a grove or tree by the Lord's altar; Greek adds 'that you make for yourself'.
Both forbid setting up a pillar the Lord hates; Latin 'hates' (present), Greek 'hated'.
Both forbid sacrificing a defective animal as an abomination; Latin 'sheep and ox', Greek 'calf or sheep'.
Both: a man or woman found in your gates doing evil and transgressing the covenant.
Both: going to serve and worship other gods, the sun, moon and host of heaven, which was not commanded.
Both: when it is reported, investigate thoroughly, and if true that the abomination was done in Israel.
Both: bring out the man or woman and stone them; Latin adds 'to the gates of your city', Greek adds 'they shall die'.
Both: death only on two or three witnesses, never on one.
Both: the witnesses' hand first, then all the people, removing the evil from among you.
Latin includes judging between one leprosy and another and judges disagreeing; Greek has injury from injury and a case beyond you. Go up to the chosen place.
Both: go to the Levitical priests and the judge of that time, who will declare the judgment; Latin 'consult', Greek 'after investigating'.
Both: do what they declare from the chosen place; Greek adds 'name invoked' and 'take great care to do everything legislated'.
Both: act according to the law and their decision, turning neither right nor left.
Both: whoever arrogantly refuses the priest and judge shall die and the evil be removed; Latin 'command' and 'decree', Greek 'refusing to listen'.
Both: all the people hear and fear; Latin 'swell with pride', Greek 'act impiously'.
Both: when you enter and settle the land and say you will appoint over you one like the surrounding nations; Latin 'king', Greek 'ruler'.
Both: appoint the one the Lord chooses from your brothers, not a foreigner; Greek states the command twice and gives the reason 'not your brother'.
Both forbid multiplying horses / cavalry and returning to Egypt; Latin ties it to relying on cavalry, Greek to multiplying cavalry.
Both: not many wives and not much silver and gold; Latin 'entice his heart', Greek 'his heart shall not turn aside'.
Both: he keeps it and reads it all his life to learn to fear the Lord; Latin 'words and rites', Greek 'commandments and ordinances' and practicing them.
Both: heart not lifted above his brothers, no turning right or left, so he and his sons reign long; Greek adds 'from the commandments'.
Both: the priests and Levites have no share with Israel and eat the Lord's offerings; Latin gives the reason, Greek calls the offerings their allotment.
Both: no portion among their brothers; the Lord is their inheritance as He told them.
Greek lists the arm, the jawbones and the stomach as the priest's portion; Latin names only the shoulder and the stomach.
Both: firstfruits of grain, wine, oil and of the wool; Latin 'a share of the wool', Greek 'first of the fleece'.
Latin: he and his sons minister forever. Greek: they minister and bless in His name 'among the Israelites'. Duration and the added blessing differ.
Both: a Levite leaves his city and comes to the chosen place; Latin 'longing for', Greek 'as his soul desires'.
Both: he ministers in the Lord's name like his fellow Levites who stand before the Lord.
Latin: he receives the same portion of food as the others apart from his paternal inheritance in his city. Greek: an allotted share apart from the sale of his family estate.
Both warn against copying the nations' abominations when you enter; Latin 'desire to imitate', Greek 'learn to practice'.
Both ban purifying children by fire, divination, omens and sorcery; Latin adds consulting dreams and soothsayers.
Both ban spells, mediums, and questioning the dead; Latin 'diviners', Greek 'observer of portents'.
Both: these things are an abomination and the Lord will destroy them; Greek says 'everyone who does these things'.
Both: be perfect before the Lord; Latin adds 'and without blemish'.
Both: the nations listen to augurs and diviners; Latin says you have been instructed otherwise, Greek says the Lord has not permitted this.
Both recall the request at Horeb not to hear the voice or see the fire lest they die; Latin 'my God', Greek 'our God'.
Both: the Lord said that everything they said is good / right.
Both: the Lord will raise up a prophet like Moses from their brothers, putting His word in his mouth.
Both: the Lord will exact retribution from whoever does not listen to the prophet's words in His name.
Both: a prophet who speaks in God's name unbidden, or in other gods' names, shall die; Latin 'corrupted by arrogance', Greek 'acts impiously'.
Both: the question in your heart of how to recognize a word the Lord has not spoken; Latin 'I', Greek 'we'.
Latin: the prophet invented it in pride, so do not fear him. Greek: he spoke impiously, so you shall not spare him. The response advised differs.
Both: when / if the Lord destroys the nations and you live in their cities and houses; Latin 'hand over', Greek 'giving'.
Both: set apart three cities in the land; Latin adds 'in the midst' and 'as a possession'.
Both: prepare the road and divide the land into three parts as a refuge for a killer; Latin adds 'equally'.
Both: the law for a killer who fled and lives, who struck his neighbor unknowingly without prior hatred.
Both: the woodcutting accident where the axe head flies off and kills a companion, who takes refuge in one of these cities.
Both: the relative may pursue in anger and kill an undeserving man; Latin 'driven by grief', Greek 'in the heat of anger'.
Latin adds that the three cities be at equal distances from one another; Greek simply commands setting apart three cities.
Both: when the Lord enlarges your borders as He swore and gives all the promised land.
Both: on keeping the commandments and loving the Lord, add three more cities; Latin states it as doubling the number.
Both: so that innocent blood is not shed in the land and no one is guilty of blood; Latin 'to possess', Greek 'as an allotment'.
Both: a man who hates his neighbor, lies in wait, strikes him dead and flees to one of these cities.
Both: the elders of his city send for him, take him from refuge and hand him to the avenger, and he dies; refuge is named only in Latin.
Both: show no pity and remove the guilt of innocent blood from Israel so it goes well with you; Latin 'do not pity', Greek 'let your eye show no pity'.
Both forbid moving a neighbor's boundary set by earlier generations / your fathers in the inheritance the Lord gives.
Both: one witness is not enough; every matter stands on two or three witnesses; Greek lists 'injustice, offense, or sin'.
Both: a lying / unjust witness accuses someone; Latin 'wrongdoing', Greek 'impiety'.
Both: the two parties stand before the Lord, the priests and judges of those days.
Both: careful examination finds the false witness lied against his brother; Greek names the judges as examiners.
Both: do to him what he planned to do to his brother, and remove the evil.
Both: the rest hear and fear and do not do such evil again; Greek adds 'among you'.
Both: no pity; life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.
Both: do not fear a larger army because the Lord who brought you from Egypt is with you; Latin 'cavalry and chariots', Greek 'horses, riders'.
Both: the priest speaks to the people as battle nears; Latin has him stand before the battle line, Greek has him approach.
Both: Hear Israel, you go into battle today; do not fear or retreat. Latin 'do not dread them', Greek 'be broken'.
Both: the Lord your God fights for you against your enemies to save you; Latin 'in your midst', Greek 'goes ahead with you'.
Both: the man with an undedicated new house returns home lest another dedicate it; Latin 'officers' to each division, Greek 'scribes'.
Both: the man who planted a vineyard goes home lest another have it; Latin 'not yet made common for all to eat', Greek 'not enjoyed'.
Both: a man betrothed but not yet married goes home lest another take her.
Both: the fearful man goes home lest he make his brothers' hearts afraid; Latin has more elaborate wording.
Latin: when the officers finish speaking, each prepares his ranks. Greek: the scribes appoint army commanders to lead the people.
Both: first offer peace to a city you approach to attack; Greek 'call its people out'.
Both: if the city opens, its people serve under tribute; Latin adds they are spared, Greek 'answer peacefully'.
Both: if the city makes war rather than yielding, besiege it; Latin 'refuses a covenant', Greek 'will not submit'.
Both: when the Lord hands the city over, strike every male with the sword.
Latin spares women, infants and livestock, then divides plunder among the army; Greek spares women and households but plunders the livestock and all in the city.
Both: do this to the far cities that are not among the nations' cities given to you.
Both: in the cities given you, let nothing living remain; Latin 'allow no one to live', Greek 'take nothing that breathes'.
Greek lists the Girgashites as a seventh nation and uses 'devote to destruction'; Latin names six nations and says 'kill with the sword'.
Both: lest they teach you their abominations done for their gods and you sin against the Lord.
Both forbid cutting down fruit trees in a siege because a tree is not a man; Latin states it, Greek asks a question.
Both: non-fruit trees may be cut down for siege works against the hostile city.
Greek adds that the slain person is 'lying in the open country'; Latin does not state where the body lies. Otherwise both give an unknown killer.
Both: elders and judges measure the distance to the surrounding cities.
Both: the nearest city's elders take a heifer never yoked or worked; Latin adds it never broke soil with a plow.
Latin: cut the heifer's neck in a rough, rocky valley; Greek: cut its sinews in a rough ravine. The act and terrain differ.
Latin: the priests judge every dispute and what is clean or unclean; Greek: every dispute and every injury is decided by their word.
Both: the elders of the nearest city wash their hands over the heifer killed in the valley; Greek adds 'entire' and 'head'.
Both: they declare their hands did not shed this blood and their eyes did not see it.
Both: be gracious to Israel whom You redeemed and clear the innocent bloodguilt; Greek adds 'from the land of Egypt'.
Both: you will be rid of innocent bloodguilt by doing what the Lord requires; Latin 'what the Lord commanded', Greek 'what is good and pleasing'.
Both: in war the Lord hands your enemies over; Latin says you take captives, Greek says you plunder their spoil.
Both: you see a beautiful woman among the captives / spoil and wish to take her as wife; Latin 'fall in love', Greek 'set your mind on her'.
Latin has the woman shave her hair and trim her nails; Greek has the man shave her head and trim her nails. The one acting differs.
Both: remove captive clothing, mourn parents one month, then marry; Latin 'sleep with her', Greek 'live with her as husband' and 'full month'.
Both: if she no longer pleases you, release her free and do not sell her; Latin 'oppress by force', Greek 'treat with contempt'.
Both: a man with two wives, one loved and one hated, and the hated wife's son is firstborn.
Both: he may not give the loved wife's son firstborn status over the hated wife's son; Greek adds that the hated wife's son is the firstborn.
Both: he must acknowledge the hated wife's son as firstborn with a double share, as the first of his children.
Both: a stubborn / disobedient son who will not heed father or mother even when disciplined; wording of the adjectives differs.
Both: they seize him and bring him to the city elders at the gate; Greek names father and mother, Latin 'gate of judgment'.
Both: the parents say their son disobeys and is given to excess; Latin 'revelry, luxury and feasting', Greek 'carouses and drinks to excess'.
Both: the city's men stone him, removing the evil, and Israel hears and fears; Latin 'all Israel', Greek 'the rest'.
Both: a man guilty of a capital offense is hung; Latin 'condemned and hung on a gibbet', Greek 'dies and you hang him on a tree'.
Both: do not ignore your brother's straying ox / calf or sheep but bring it back; Greek adds 'on the road' and 'restore them'.
Both: if the brother is not near or unknown, keep the animals in your house until he seeks them and return them.
Both extend the rule to the donkey, garment and anything lost; Latin 'as though someone else's', Greek repeats 'do the same'.
Both: do not ignore your brother's fallen donkey or ox / calf; help him raise it.
Both forbid cross-dressing as an abomination; Latin 'men's clothing', Greek 'a man's equipment'.
Both: if you find a nest with a mother and young or eggs, do not take the mother with the young.
Both: let the mother go and keep the young so it goes well and you live long.
Both: build a wall / rim around the roof so no one is killed in your house; Latin adds you would be guilty.
Both forbid sowing the vineyard with another seed lest the produce become consecrated.
Both: do not plow with an ox / calf and a donkey together.
Both forbid wearing wool and linen woven together.
Both: make fringes / tassels on the four corners of your cloak.
Both: a man marries and then hates his wife; Greek adds he lived with her as husband.
Both: he brings a false charge, claiming he did not find her a virgin; Latin 'sought grounds to dismiss her', Greek 'pretextual charges'.
Both: her parents take the proof of virginity to the elders at the gate; Latin 'signs', Greek 'evidence'.
Both: the father tells the elders he gave his daughter to this man who now hates her.
Both: the husband's accusation is answered by displaying the evidence of virginity before the elders; cloth / garment.
Both: the elders take the man and punish him; Latin 'beat', Greek 'discipline'.
Both fine him a hundred shekels, paid to the girl's father, for slandering an Israelite virgin; she stays his wife, never dismissed. Latin adds "of silver".
Both say the charge proves true and the girl's virginity is not found; accusation / charge is only wording.
Latin brings her outside the door; Greek to the doors of her father's house. Outrage in Israel vs folly among Israel's sons; evil vs evil person.
Latin simply says both shall die; Greek says the man is found lying with her and has both put to death, with an added agent.
Both describe a betrothed virgin found in the city by another man who lies with her.
Both bring the two to the city gate to be stoned: the girl for not crying out, the man for violating his neighbor's wife.
Latin says he alone shall die; Greek has "you" put only the man to death. Latin seizes her; Greek forces her.
Both spare the girl and compare the case to murder. Latin: a robber against his brother; Greek: a man against his neighbor.
Latin says she was alone in the countryside; Greek says he found her in the field. Both have her cry out with no rescuer.
Latin says the matter comes to judgment; Greek says he is discovered. Otherwise the same unbetrothed-virgin case.
Latin gives fifty shekels of silver; Greek fifty silver didrachmas. Both make her his wife, never to be sent away.
Both forbid taking one's father's wife or uncovering his covering; Greek repeats "father's".
Latin names a eunuch with crushed, cut testicles and severed penis; Greek says any man with crushed testicles or a severed organ. Both exclude from the assembly.
Latin adds "even to the tenth generation" and the term mamzer; Greek has only one born of a prostitute barred from the assembly.
Latin bars Ammonites and Moabites even after the tenth generation; Greek even to the tenth generation. Both say forever.
Both give refusal of bread and water and hiring Balaam. Latin adds "Syria" after Mesopotamia and has two "because" clauses.
Both say God would not heed Balaam and turned the curse into blessing out of love; Greek repeats "the Lord your God".
Latin: do not make peace or seek their good; Greek: do not address them with words of peace or advantage. Both: all your days, forever.
Both forbid abhorring an Edomite (your brother) or an Egyptian (you were a stranger in his land).
Both let their descendants enter the Lord's assembly in the third generation.
Latin goes out to battle against enemies; Greek goes out to encamp against them. Both: guard against every evil thing.
Both send the man unclean by night emission outside the camp; Greek adds "and shall not enter it".
Both: wash with water toward evening, return after sunset. Latin says he may not return until then; Greek says he washes his body.
Both require a place outside the camp; Latin states its purpose (relieving oneself), Greek only "where you may go out".
Both: a peg on the belt, dig and cover. Latin says cover excrement; Greek "unseemliness"; Greek has the dig and cover done with the peg.
Both say God walks in the camp to rescue you and deliver enemies; keep it holy. Latin begins with "where you relieved yourself"; enemies / enemy; abandon / turn away.
Both forbid returning a slave to his master; Latin says he fled to you, Greek that he joined you from his master.
Both let him live with you where he pleases without distress. Latin adds "in one of your cities"; Greek says live among you.
Latin bars only prostitute and fornicator among Israel's daughters and sons; Greek adds a second ban on initiation functionaries and initiates.
Both forbid bringing a prostitute's wages or a dog's price into the Lord's house for a vow, as an abomination.
Both forbid charging a brother interest on money, food or anything else lent.
Both allow interest from a foreigner but not a brother, that the Lord may bless all you do in the land.
Both say do not delay a vow, for the Lord will require it and delay is sin.
Both say declining to vow brings no sin.
Both say keep what passes your lips. Latin stresses willing, spoken promise; Greek calls it a vowed gift.
Both allow eating a neighbor's grapes but carrying none off. Latin: as many as you please, not carry away; Greek: until satisfied, put none in a vessel.
Both allow plucking ears by hand, not with a sickle. Latin says friend's grain; Greek neighbor's harvest.
Both: she leaves and becomes another man's wife.
Both: second husband hates her, gives a divorce certificate, sends her away, or dies. Greek adds "puts it in her hands".
Both bar the first husband from retaking her. Latin: she is defiled and abhorrent; Greek: that is an abomination. Sin / defile the land.
Both exempt a newly married man from war and duty, staying home a year to rejoice with his wife.
Both forbid taking a mill or upper millstone as pledge, since it takes a life. Latin lists lower and upper stones; Greek says mill and its upper stone.
Both make kidnapping and selling a fellow Israelite a capital crime. Latin adds receiving the price; Greek adds subjugating him.
Both tell him to follow the Levitical priests' teaching on leprosy. Latin warns against incurring the plague; Greek frames it as a case of leprosy.
Both forbid entering the neighbor's house to take a pledge for a debt.
Both say stand outside while the debtor brings it out. Latin says he brings what he has; Greek says the pledge.
Both say a poor man's pledge must not be kept overnight.
Return the pledge so he sleeps in his garment and blesses you. Latin: before sunset, righteousness before God; Greek: around sunset, an act of mercy.
Both forbid withholding wages from the poor, brother or foreigner. Latin adds "in your land"; Greek adds "wrongfully" and says within your cities.
Both require same-day pay before sunset, lest he cry out and sin result. Latin: he sustains his life by it; Greek: he places his hope in it.
Both say fathers and children are not put to death for each other; each dies for his own sin.
Latin forbids perverting justice for stranger and orphan, and separately taking a widow's garment; Greek includes the widow among those owed justice.
Both recall Egypt and rescue. Latin: you served; the Lord rescued. Greek: household slave; the Lord redeemed.
Both leave a forgotten sheaf for the foreigner, orphan and widow. Greek also lists the poor; Latin says let them take it.
Greek adds a closing reminder of slavery in Egypt and the command; the Latin verse ends with leaving olives for stranger, orphan and widow.
Both forbid gleaning the vineyard; what remains is for the foreigner, orphan and widow.
Both remind Israel of slavery in Egypt as the reason for the command.
Both have judges vindicate the righteous and condemn the wicked in a dispute.
Both have the guilty man beaten before judges in proportion to his offense. Latin has him lie down; Greek has him seated.
Both limit lashes to forty. Latin warns against your brother leaving horribly torn; Greek warns he would be disgraced.
Both forbid muzzling an ox as it threshes; Latin adds "on the threshing floor".
Both have the son carry the dead man's name so it is not erased from Israel. Latin says firstborn son; Greek says the child.
Both: she goes to the elders at the gate and says he will not raise up his brother's name. Latin adds "or take me as wife"; Greek adds "was unwilling".
Both: the elders summon and speak to him; he says he does not wish to take her. Latin says "immediately" and "wife"; Greek says his city's elders and that he stands.
Both: she removes his sandal, spits in his face and speaks. Greek says one sandal and names his brother's wife; wording of her declaration differs slightly.
Both name the house after the sandal removed. Latin says his household is called this; Greek says his name.
Both: a wife seizes the other man's private parts to rescue her husband. Latin: stronger man; genitals. Greek: the one striking; testicles; brother detail.
Both cut off her hand and show no pity.
Both forbid two different weights in your bag, large and small.
Both forbid two different measures in the house, large and small.
Both require a true and just weight and measure so you live long in the land.
Both say the Lord abhors whoever does these things and acts unjustly.
Both recall the attack on the weary rear of the company by one who did not fear God. Latin: met you; Greek: opposed you on the road.
Both command blotting out the name under heaven once rest is given. Greek names Amalek; Latin says "his name" and mentions subjecting nations.
Both: when you enter the land the Lord gives, possess it and settle in it.
Both: firstfruits in a basket to the chosen place. Latin: of all your produce; Greek: some of the produce of the land the Lord gives you.
Both: go to the priest and declare you have entered the promised land. Latin: before the Lord your God; Greek: to the Lord my God.
Both have the priest take the basket and set it before the altar.
Both say the Egyptians oppressed and burdened us. Latin: afflicted, persecuted, heavy burdens; Greek: mistreated, humiliated, hard labors.
Both: we cried to the Lord, God of our fathers, and He heard and saw our humiliation, toil and distress.
Both recall the exodus with strong hand, outstretched arm, signs and wonders. Latin says "great terror"; Greek says great visions and adds great strength.
Both: He brought us to this place and gave a land flowing with milk and honey.
Both offer the firstfruits and worship before the Lord. Greek adds that the land flows with milk and honey, and has the speaker address God directly.
Both: enjoy all the good the Lord gave you, your household, the Levite and the foreigner. Latin says feast; Greek says rejoice.
Both give the tithe in the third year to Levite, foreigner, orphan and widow. Latin calls it the year of tithes; Greek calls it the second tithe.
Both: sacred portion cleared from the house and given to the four groups, with no transgression or forgetting. Latin "as You ordered"; Greek "according to all the commands".
Both deny eating in mourning, using it while unclean, or for the dead. Latin says set aside or spent on a funeral; Greek says offered for unclean use or given to the dead.
Both ask God to look from heaven and bless Israel and the land. Latin: sanctuary and lofty dwelling; Greek: holy house; "given us" vs "gave them".
Both: today the Lord commanded you to keep these ordinances and judgments with all your heart and soul.
Both: you have chosen the Lord to walk in His ways and obey. Latin lists rites, commandments and judgments; Greek lists ordinances and judgments.
Both: the Lord has chosen you today as His own people, as He said, to keep all His commands.
Both set Israel above all nations and holy to the Lord. Latin: for His praise, name and glory; Greek: renowned, a boast and glorious.
Both: Moses and the elders command the people to keep the commandments given today.
Both: on crossing the Jordan, set up large stones and coat them with plaster / lime. Greek says "on the day" and "for yourself".
Both write the law on the stones on entering the land of milk and honey. Latin gives it as a purpose clause; Greek as a command and repeats "God of your fathers".
Both: when you cross the Jordan, set up the stones on Mount Ebal and coat them with lime / plaster.
Both: build an altar of stones on which no iron is used.
Both build the altar and offer burnt offerings. Latin says unshaped, unpolished rocks; Greek says whole stones.
Both: sacrifice, eat and rejoice before the Lord. Latin names peace offerings; Greek an offering of deliverance and adds "be satisfied".
Both: write the whole law on the stones very clearly.
Both: Moses and the Levitical priests tell Israel to listen, for today they are the Lord's people. Latin "attend and hear"; Greek "be silent and listen".
Both command obeying the Lord and doing His commands and ordinances.
Both list Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, Benjamin on Gerizim to bless.
Both list Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, Naphtali on Ebal for the curse. Latin adds "opposite them".
The Levites speak in a loud voice. Latin says to all the men of Israel; Greek to all Israel.
Both curse the maker of a carved or cast image set up in secret; people answer Amen / So be it.
Both curse the one who dishonors father or mother.
Both curse moving a neighbor's boundary.
Both curse misleading a blind person on the road.
Both curse perverting justice for the foreigner, orphan and widow.
Both curse lying with one's father's wife. Latin says "uncovers the covering of his bed"; Greek says he uncovers his father's covering.
Both curse lying with any animal.
Both curse lying with a sister, daughter of father or mother.
Both curse lying with a mother-in-law; Greek adds a further curse on lying with his wife's sister.
Both curse striking a neighbor. Latin says in secret (clam); Greek says treacherously.
Both curse taking a bribe to kill an innocent person.
Both curse the one who does not abide by and perform the words of this law.
Both promise setting Israel above all nations for obedience. Greek opens with a clause about crossing the Jordan into the land; Latin lacks it.
Both: all these blessings will come upon and overtake / find you if you obey.
Both: blessed in the city and blessed in the field.
Both bless womb, land, cattle and sheep. Latin also blesses the fruit of your livestock as a separate item, which the Greek list lacks.
Both bless your storehouses / granaries and your reserves.
Both bless you coming in and going out; Greek repeats "blessed".
Both: enemies fall before you, coming by one road and fleeing by seven.
Both: the Lord sends blessing on your storehouses and all you undertake in the land He gives.
Both establish Israel as His holy people if they obey and walk in His ways. Latin says He swore "to you"; Greek says to your fathers.
Both: the nations see the Lord's name called over you and fear you.
Both: the Lord makes you abound in good things, in womb, livestock and land, as sworn to your fathers.
Both open heaven's treasury for rain and have Israel lend but not borrow. Greek adds that Israel will rule many nations but not be ruled.
Both make you the head and not the tail, above and not below, if you obey and keep the commands.
Both: do not turn right or left nor follow and worship other gods.
Both: if you do not obey, all these curses overtake you. Latin adds "rites" beside the commandments.
Both: cursed in the city and cursed in the field.
Both curse your granary / storehouses and your reserves.
Both curse the fruit of the womb and land, the herds and flocks.
Both curse coming in and going out; Greek puts going out first.
Both: famine-like afflictions until quick destruction for forsaking Him. Latin includes rebuke on your work; Greek names consumption instead.
Both: until He consumes you from the land you enter. Latin fastens pestilence on you; Greek makes death cling to you.
Both strike with destitution, fever, chills and pursue until destruction. The remaining afflictions differ: Latin has burning heat, corrupt air; Greek has slaughter, wind blight, pallor.
Both: heaven over you bronze and the earth beneath iron.
Both turn rain to dust until you are destroyed. Latin says ashes fall from heaven; Greek says soil descends.
Both: fall before enemies, one road out, seven fleeing, scattered. Latin says fall; Greek says given over to slaughter.
Both: your corpse is food for birds and beasts, with no one to drive them off.
Both: Egyptian ulcer, scabs and itching, incurable. Latin describes the part by which excrement passes; Greek says the buttocks.
Both: struck with madness, blindness and derangement of mind.
Both: groping at noon like the blind, always wronged, no helper. Latin: you cannot direct your ways; Greek: He will not prosper them.
Both: take a wife but another has her; build a house and not live in it; plant a vineyard and not harvest.
Ox / calf slaughtered, donkey seized, sheep given to enemies with no helper. Latin says ox; Greek says calf.
Both: your sons and daughters given to another people while your eyes watch and your hand is powerless.
Both: an unknown people eat your produce and labors, and you are continually wronged and oppressed.
Both speak of the sights your eyes will see. Latin: stunned with terror; Greek: driven mad.
Both: a severe ulcer on knees and legs, incurable from sole to crown.
Both lead you to an unknown nation to serve other gods of wood and stone. Latin says your king; Greek says rulers.
