Both: you become a proverb and tale among the nations. Latin adds "ruined"; Greek adds "riddle".
Both: sow much, gather little, locust devours. Latin says into the land; Greek says into the plain.
Both: plant a vineyard but get no wine because worms ruin it. Latin: gather nothing; Greek: not rejoice in it.
Both: olive trees everywhere but no oil, since the olives fall away.
Both: sons and daughters taken captive. Latin: you will not enjoy them; Greek: they will not remain yours.
Both: blight consumes your trees and land's produce.
Both: the foreigner among you rises ever higher while you sink lower.
Both: he lends to you and you do not lend; he is the head and you the tail.
Both: the curses pursue and overtake you until you perish for disobedience; commandments and rites / commands and ordinances is wording.
Both: signs and wonders upon you and your offspring forever.
Both: you did not serve the Lord with joy and gladness of heart amid abundance.
Both: serve the enemy sent by the Lord in hunger, thirst and nakedness under an iron yoke. Latin says yoke and one enemy; Greek says collar and enemies.
Both: a nation from far away swooping like an eagle, whose language you cannot understand.
Both: a nation without respect for the old or mercy to the young. Latin "most brazen"; Greek "shameless in countenance"; little child / young.
Both: it devours your livestock offspring and produce, leaving no grain, wine, oil, herds or flocks until you perish.
Both: walls you trusted are brought down. Latin has you besieged within your gates; Greek says it afflicts you in all your cities.
Both: you will eat your own children's flesh in the distress the enemy inflicts.
Both: the pampered man begrudges his brother and the wife in his embrace. Greek adds the children left to him.
Both: he begrudges them a share of his children's flesh, having nothing else in the siege. Latin says gates; Greek says cities.
Both: the delicate woman begrudges husband and children. Latin names the flesh of son and daughter; Greek names husband, son and daughter as those she looks at begrudgingly.
Both: she secretly eats afterbirth and child for lack of all things. Latin says children born at the same hour; Greek says the child she bears.
Both: perform all the words of this law and fear His name. Latin: scroll, glorious and terrible; Greek: book, honored and wondrous.
Both: great and lasting plagues on you and your offspring. Latin says the Lord increases them; Greek says makes them extraordinary.
Both: Egypt's afflictions you dreaded return and cling to you.
Both: every sickness and plague not written in this book of the law, until He destroys you.
Both: you are left few though once countless as stars. Latin says "formerly were"; Greek says "instead of being".
Both: as the Lord once rejoiced to do you good, so He will rejoice to destroy you and remove you from the land.
Both: scattered among all peoples to serve unknown gods of wood and stone.
Both: no rest among the nations; fearful heart, failing eyes, wasting soul.
Both: your life hangs before you; you fear night and day without assurance of life.
Both: morning wish for evening, evening wish for morning, from heart's fear and what your eyes see.
Both: back to Egypt in ships, sold to enemies as slaves with no buyer. Latin says the Lord told you; Greek has the speaker say "I said".
Both: the words of the covenant made in Moab, besides the Horeb covenant.
Both: Moses summoned all Israel and recalled what the Lord did to Pharaoh, his servants and his land.
Both: the great trials, signs and wonders your eyes saw.
Both: to this day the Lord has not given a heart to understand, eyes to see, ears to hear.
Both: forty years in the wilderness; clothes and sandals did not wear out.
Both: no bread, wine or strong drink, so you know the Lord is your God. Latin has God speak ("I am"); Greek says "He is".
Both: Sihon and Og came out to battle and were struck down.
Both: their land given to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh. Latin says "we gave"; Greek has "I gave" as an allotment.
Both: keep and perform the words of this covenant so you understand all you do.
Both gather all Israel before the Lord. Latin lists leaders, tribes, elders, teachers; Greek lists tribal leaders, elders, judges, court scribes.
Latin sets the woodcutters and water carriers apart ("exceptis"); Greek includes everyone from woodcutter to water carrier. Wives, children and foreigner appear in both.
Both: enter the Lord's covenant made today. Latin adds the oath; Greek speaks of His curses.
Both: He establishes you as His people and is your God, as sworn to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob.
Both: made not with you alone. Latin says covenant and oaths; Greek says covenant and curse.
Both include those not present. Latin says "present and absent"; Greek adds "here today before the Lord your God".
Both: you know how we lived in Egypt and passed through the nations.
Both: you saw their abominations and idols of wood, stone, silver and gold. Latin adds "filthy things" and that they worshiped them.
Both warn of anyone turning from the Lord to serve other gods and of a bitter root. Latin is a prohibition ("our God"); Greek asks questions ("your God").
Both: he blesses himself in his heart despite following his own heart. The closing purpose differs: Latin, the drunken consumes the thirsty; Greek, the sinner destroys the guiltless with him.
Both: God will not forgive; anger and jealousy against that man, the written curses cling, his name erased from under heaven.
Both single him out from all Israel according to the covenant curses. Latin says destruction; Greek says calamities.
Both: the next generation and distant foreigners will speak on seeing the land's plagues and diseases.
Both: sulfur and salt, unsown and without green growth, like Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim.
Both: the nations ask why the Lord did this to the land and why such great anger.
Both: they abandoned the covenant made at the exodus. Greek adds "their fathers' God".
Both: they served and worshiped gods they did not know, not allotted to them.
Both: the Lord's anger burned against the land, bringing all the written curses.
Both: the Lord cast them out of their land in great anger into another land, as now.
Both: hidden things belong to the Lord, revealed things to us and our children, to do the law.
Both: blessing and curse come upon you among the scattered nations. Latin says moved by repentance of heart; Greek says you receive it into your heart.
Both: return and obey with all heart and soul. Latin adds "you and your children"; Greek has no such phrase.
Latin: the Lord restores you from captivity; Greek: the Lord heals your sins. Both add mercy and regathering from the nations.
Both: though scattered to heaven's far edge, the Lord gathers you from there. Greek says one end of heaven to the other and repeats "take you".
Both: bring you into the fathers' land and make you more numerous. Latin has "take up" and "blessing"; Greek says "do you good".
Both: the Lord turns these curses on your enemies and those who hate and persecute you.
Both: you will return, obey the Lord, and do all the commands given today.
Both: prosperity in works, womb, livestock and land, and the Lord rejoices over you as over your fathers. Latin adds "generous supply of everything"; abound / care greatly.
Both: if you obey and return with all your heart and soul. Latin says precepts and rites; Greek says commands, ordinances and judgments.
Both: the command is not far from you. Latin: not beyond you; Greek: not excessively burdensome.
Both: not in heaven, so you need not ask who will ascend and bring it that we may hear and do it.
Both: not beyond the sea, so no need to ask who will cross and fetch it. Latin adds "make excuses"; Greek says He makes it audible.
Both: today I set before you life and death, good and evil.
Both: love the Lord, walk in His ways, keep His judgments, live and multiply in the land. Latin as purpose clause with rites; Greek as a conditional on obeying.
Both: if your heart turns away and you are led to worship other gods.
Both: you will perish and not live long in the land across the Jordan.
Both call heaven and earth to witness life and death, blessing and curse, and urge choosing life. Greek says witnesses "against you".
Both: love, obey and hold fast to the Lord to dwell in the land. Latin says He Himself is your life; Greek says this (obeying and clinging) is your life.
Latin: Moses went and spoke all these words to Israel; Greek: Moses finished speaking them. Same audience and words.
Both: Moses is 120, can no longer go out and come in, and the Lord forbade him to cross the Jordan.
Both: the Lord goes before you and destroys the nations; Joshua goes before you as the Lord said.
Both: the Lord will do to them as to Sihon and Og, the Amorite kings. Greek adds "beyond the Jordan".
Latin: when He hands these peoples over, treat them as commanded (future); Greek: the Lord handed them over (past).
Both: be strong, do not fear, the Lord will not abandon you. Latin calls Him your guide; Greek says He goes ahead with you, among you.
Both: Moses charges Joshua before Israel to be strong. Latin: you will bring them in and divide it by lot; Greek: you enter ahead and give it as an inheritance.
Both: the Lord goes with you, will not abandon you; do not fear.
Both: Moses wrote this law and gave it to the Levite priests who carry the ark and to the elders.
Both: after seven years, in the year of release, at the Feast of Tabernacles / Booths; Greek notes "that day".
Both: when all Israel appears at the chosen place, read the law in their hearing.
Both: assemble men, women, little ones and the foreigner within your gates to hear, learn, fear the Lord and keep the law.
Both: their children who do not know shall hear and fear the Lord all their days in the land.
Both: Moses' death is near; call Joshua to the Tent of Testimony. Latin says stand in the tent; Greek says stand beside its doors.
Both: the Lord appears at the tent in a cloud. Latin: He appears in the pillar at the entrance; Greek: He descends and stands, and the pillar stands beside the doors.
Both: Moses sleeps with his fathers; the people prostitute themselves after foreign gods and break the covenant. Latin adds "to live in".
Both: anger, abandonment, hidden face, devouring, evils find them, and they say God is not with them. Latin "hide"; Greek "turn"; Greek "the Lord my God".
Both: God hides his face that day because of their evils and foreign gods. Latin "hide and conceal"; Greek "turn away".
Both: write the song, teach Israel, let it be a witness. Latin: keep by memory and sing; Greek: put it in their mouth.
Both: land of milk and honey, then fat and satisfied they turn to foreign gods and break the covenant. Latin: dishonor Me; Greek: provoke Me and "good land".
Both: the song stands as witness, not forgotten; God knows what they do before the land. Latin: thoughts, after evils; Greek: wickedness, oath to fathers.
Both: Moses wrote the song and taught it to Israel; Greek adds "that day".
Latin: the Lord commands Joshua and says "I will be with you". Greek: Moses commissions him, saying the Lord will be with him. Different speaker.
Both: when Moses finished writing the law in a book.
Both: he commanded the Levites who carry the ark of the covenant.
Both: place the book beside the ark as a witness against you.
Both: I know your stubbornness and stiff neck; you provoked the Lord while I lived, how much more after my death.
Both: gather the leaders to hear the words, with heaven and earth as witnesses. Latin names elders and teachers; Greek names tribal leaders, elders, judges and court scribes.
Both: after my death you will act wickedly, turn from the way, and calamities will meet you for provoking the Lord.
Both: Moses spoke the words of the song to the end before the whole assembly.
Both call heaven to hear and the earth to hear the words of his mouth.
Both liken the words to rain and dew. Latin has droplets upon the green growth; Greek has a snowstorm on vegetation and words "awaited".
Both: ascribe greatness / majesty to our God. Latin "I will invoke" the Lord's name; Greek "I proclaimed".
Both: God's works and ways, faithful, without injustice, just. Perfect / true works and a different closing: "just and upright" vs "righteous and holy is the Lord".
Both: a crooked generation that sinned. Latin: not His children in filth; Greek: blemished children, not His own.
Both: is this how you repay the Lord, foolish people; is He not your father who made and created you.
Both: remember days of old; ask your father and elders and they will tell you.
Both: the Lord's portion is His people, Jacob His inheritance. Greek adds the name Israel; Latin gives it as a statement.
Latin: He found him in a desert of horror and vast solitude; Greek: He sustained him in a thirsty, waterless wilderness. Both: led around, taught, guarded as the pupil of his eye.
Both liken God to an eagle carrying its young. Latin: stirring young to fly and hovering, carried on shoulders; Greek: sheltering the nest, yearning over young, carried on back.
Both: the Lord alone led him and no foreign god was with him.
Both: honey from rock, oil from stone, fruit of the fields. Latin: set him on the high land to eat; Greek: brought them up onto earth's strength and fed them.
Both list butter, milk, fat of lambs and rams, goats, wheat and grape blood. Latin names rams of Bashan; Greek adds young bulls.
Both: the beloved grew fat, kicked, forsook God his Savior. Greek opens with "Jacob ate and was filled"; Latin lacks it.
Both: they provoked God with foreign gods and abominations. Latin speaks of Him; Greek has God say "Me".
Both: they sacrificed to demons, not God, to new gods. Latin: fathers had not worshiped; Greek: fathers did not know.
Both: you abandoned the God who begot you. Latin: and forgot the Lord your Creator; Greek: forgot the God who nourishes you.
Both: the Lord saw and was angered by his sons and daughters. Latin: stirred to anger; Greek: became jealous and was provoked.
Both: God turns / hides His face from a perverse generation of faithless sons. Latin: I will consider their end; Greek: I will show what befalls them in the last days.
Both: they provoked Me with a no-god; I will provoke them with a no-people. Latin: vanities, foolish nation; Greek: idols, nation without understanding.
Both: a fire kindled in wrath burns to the depths below, devours the earth and its produce, and sets mountain foundations aflame.
Both: I will gather evils on them and spend my arrows / missiles against them.
Both: hunger, birds, and wild beasts' teeth. Greek adds incurable spasms; Latin adds serpents among the crawling creatures.
Both: the sword outside and terror within, striking young and old alike. Ravage / bereave; within / from the inner chambers.
Latin: "Where are they?" and I will end their memory; Greek: I will scatter them and end their remembrance. Both end memory among humankind.
Both: held back because of the enemies' anger, lest they boast. Greek adds "lest they persist long and adversaries join in attacking" and has it conditional rather than "I delayed".
Both: a nation without counsel or understanding.
Latin is a wish: if only they were wise and foresaw their end. Greek states they did not understand, and bids them take it to heart for the coming time.
Both: how could one chase a thousand unless God sold them. Latin: the Lord shut them in; Greek: handed them over.
Both: their gods are not like ours. Latin: our enemies are judges; Greek: our enemies lack understanding.
Both: their vine from Sodom and Gomorrah, grapes of gall, bitter clusters. Outskirts / tendril of Gomorrah.
Both: their wine is dragons' venom, asps' incurable venom. Latin first says "gall" of dragons.
Both: are these not stored with Me, sealed in My treasuries.
Both: I will repay when their foot slips; their destruction is near. Latin: vengeance is Mine, in due time; Greek: on a day of vengeance; prepared things at hand for you.
Both: the Lord judges His people and has compassion on His servants who are weakened. Latin lists the imprisoned and the remaining; Greek says failing under assault.
Both: where are their gods in whom they trusted.
Both: gods whose sacrificial fat and drink offerings they enjoyed; let them rise and help you.
Both: I alone am God; I kill and make alive, strike and heal; none rescues from My hand.
Both: I lift My hand to heaven and say I live forever. Greek adds "swear by My right hand".
Both: sharpen My sword like lightning, hold to judgment, repay enemies and haters. Latin is conditional ("if"); Greek is a statement.
Both: arrows / missiles drunk with blood, sword devours flesh, blood of the slain and captives. Latin: uncovered heads of enemies; Greek: heads of enemy rulers.
Both: Moses and Joshua speak the song to the people. Greek adds that Moses wrote the song that day and taught it, and calls it this law's words.
Both: Moses finished speaking to all Israel.
Both: set your heart on these words and command your children to keep and do all of this law.
Both: not an empty matter but your life, to live long in the land across the Jordan. Latin: commanded not in vain, each to live by them.
Both: that same day the Lord spoke to Moses.
Both: go up Abarim / Nebo opposite Jericho and see Canaan. Latin adds the gloss "the crossing" and "die on the mountain" (in Greek's next verse).
Both: you will join your people as Aaron did on Mount Hor. Greek opens with "die on the mountain you ascend", split from the Latin's previous verse.
Both: because of Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin you failed to sanctify the Lord. Transgressed / disobeyed My word; waters of contradiction / dispute.
Both: you will see the land but not enter. Latin: land opposite, which I give Israel; Greek: from a distance.
Both: the Lord from Sinai, Seir, Paran. Latin: thousands of holy ones and a fiery law in His right hand; Greek: myriads of Kadesh and angels at His right hand.
Latin: He loved the peoples; those near His feet receive His teaching. Greek: He spared His people; the consecrated are under Your hands and received His words.
Both: the law Moses commanded us, an inheritance of Jacob's assembly.
Both: a ruler when the leaders gather with the tribes of Israel. Latin: king among the most upright; Greek: ruler in the Beloved.
Both: Lord, hear Judah and help him against his foes. Latin: bring him to his people; Greek: let them enter his people.
Both: the holy man tested at the waters of dispute. Latin: You tested and judged him; Greek: they tested and reviled him, and asks to give Levi his manifestations.
Both: he disowned parents, brothers and sons and kept God's word and covenant. Latin plural "These kept"; Greek singular; I do not know / have not seen you.
Latin addresses Jacob and Israel ("Your judgments, Jacob"); Greek says they shall declare the ordinances to Jacob. Latin burnt offering; Greek incense "continually".
Both: bless his strength, accept his works, and let haters not rise. Latin strikes the enemies' backs; Greek breaks the loin of enemies who rise.
Both: Benjamin dwells securely, loved by the Lord, between His shoulders. Latin adds a bridal-chamber image; Greek has God shade him all the days.
Both bless Joseph's land with heaven's gifts, dew and the deep below. Fruits / seasons of heaven; deep / springs of the depths.
Both: produce of sun and moon. Latin: fruits brought forth by sun and moon; Greek: season of produce from the sun's turnings and months' conjunctions.
Both: ancient mountains and everlasting hills. Latin: fruits of the hills; Greek: the summit of the hills.
Both: earth's fullness and the blessing of Him who appeared in the bush upon Joseph's head. Latin: consecrated one; Greek: acceptable things, glorified one.
Both: a firstborn bull's beauty, a one-horned beast's horns, driving nations to earth's end; Ephraim's multitudes, Manasseh's thousands. Rhinoceros / one-horned animal; toss / gore.
Both: Zebulun rejoice in going out, Issachar in tents / dwellings.
Both: sacrifice righteous sacrifices and draw on the sea's wealth. Latin: call peoples to the mountain; Greek: they destroy nations. Latin has hidden sand treasures; Greek, coastal commerce.
Both: Gad blessed, rests like a lion, taking an arm. Latin: broad territory; crown of head. Greek: the One who enlarges Gad; a ruler.
Latin: a teacher is laid away in his portion and carries out the Lord's justice. Greek: the land of rulers is apportioned and the Lord Himself carried out justice. Different subject acts.
Both: Dan a lion's cub from Bashan. Latin: streams forth abundantly; Greek: leaps.
Both: Naphtali filled with the Lord's blessing, inheriting the sea and south.
Both: Asher blessed with sons, pleasing to his brothers, dipping his foot in oil.
Both: sandals of iron and bronze. Latin: as the days of your youth, so your old age; Greek: as your days, so your strength.
Both: none like God of the upright / Beloved, riding the heavens as your helper. Latin adds the clouds racing; Greek "majestic One of the firmament".
Both: everlasting arms and the enemy driven out. Latin: His dwelling is above; Greek: there is shelter from the God of old. Be crushed / may you perish.
Both: Israel dwells securely alone, with grain, wine and dew from heaven. Latin: Jacob's eye looks on the land; Greek: alone upon Jacob's land.
Both: blessed Israel, saved by the Lord; shield and sword; enemies subdued. Latin: enemies deny you; Greek: enemies lie to you.
Both: Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Nebo, Pisgah opposite Jericho, shown Gilead to Dan.
Both: all Naphtali, Ephraim, Manasseh and Judah as far as the western / farthest sea.
Both: the region of Jericho, the city of palms, as far as Zoar. Latin names the southern region and plain; Greek the wilderness and surrounding region.
Both: the land sworn to the patriarchs, seen but not entered. Greek names Moses and has the Lord say "I have shown it".
Latin: He (the Lord) buried him in the valley opposite Peor. Greek: they buried him in Gai near the house of Peor. Different burier and place name.
Both: Moses was 120 and his eyes were not dim. Latin: his teeth were not loosened; Greek: his cheeks had not deteriorated.
Both: Israel wept thirty days on the plains of Moab. Greek adds "at the Jordan opposite Jericho".
Both: Joshua filled with a spirit because Moses laid hands on him; Israel obeyed. Wisdom / understanding; obeyed / listened.
Both: no prophet has arisen like Moses, known face to face.
Both: all the signs and wonders sent to be done in Egypt against Pharaoh, his servants and land.
Both: the mighty hand and great wonders Moses did before all Israel.
